t: Characteristics and Classification of Living Organisms
x: Topic 1 · Characteristics & Classification Characteristics and Classification of Living Organisms What makes something alive, and how biologists sort the huge variety of life into groups. Expect definition marks, dichotomous key questions and "identify the group from these features" questions.

t: Characteristics and Classification of Living Organisms
h: The seven characteristics of living organisms
x: Every living organism shows all seven of these. A car moves and "respires" fuel, but it does not grow, reproduce or show sensitivity in the biological sense, so it is not alive. M ovement R espiration S ensitivity G rowth R eproduction E xcretion N utrition Characteristic Definition (mark-scheme wording) Movement An action by an organism or part of an organism causing a change of position or place Respiration The chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrient molecules and release energy for metabolism Sensitivity The ability to detect and respond to changes in the internal or external environment Growth A permanent increase in size and dry mass Reproduction The processes that make more of the same kind of organism Excretion The removal of waste products of metabolism and substances in excess of requirements Nutrition The taking in of materials for energy, growth and development Common Mistake Writing "growth is getting bigger". You must say permanent increase in size and dry mass . A plant that swells with water has not necessarily grown. Similarly, respiration is not "breathing": it is a chemical process inside cells.

t: Characteristics and Classification of Living Organisms
x: Organisms are sorted into groups using shared features . This makes the diversity of life manageable and helps scientists identify and communicate about organisms. A species is a group of organisms that can reproduce to produce fertile offspring. The hierarchy runs from large groups to small: kingdom → phylum → class → order → family → genus → species. Supplement Classification systems aim to reflect evolutionary relationships : organisms in the same group share a more recent common ancestor. Supplement Classification is traditionally based on studies of morphology and anatomy, but the sequences of bases in DNA and of amino acids in proteins are now used. The more similar the base sequences, the more closely related the two species.

t: Characteristics and Classification of Living Organisms
x: The binomial system is an internationally agreed system in which the scientific name of an organism is made up of two parts showing the genus and the species . Example Panthera leo (lion) Genus First word, capital letter Species Second word, lower case Format Italics when typed, underlined when handwritten Common names vary between languages and regions; the binomial name is the same worldwide, so there is no confusion. Panthera leo and Panthera tigris share a genus, so they are closely related.

t: Characteristics and Classification of Living Organisms
x: A dichotomous key identifies an organism through a series of paired statements, each giving two choices. You follow the choice that fits until you reach a name. 1 Pick one visible feature Choose something that splits the group into two, such as "has wings / has no wings". 2 Write it as a yes/no pair Each statement must be observable and not a matter of opinion (avoid "large" or "pretty"). 3 Keep splitting Repeat with new features for each sub-group until every organism is on its own. 4 Check For n organisms you need n − 1 pairs of statements. Test the key with each organism. Examiner Tip When constructing a key, use features you can actually see in the drawing (number of legs, presence of antennae, shape of wings). Features such as "lives in water" or "eats meat" usually cannot be checked from a picture and will not be credited.

t: Characteristics and Classification of Living Organisms
x: All cells contain cytoplasm , a cell membrane , DNA as genetic material, ribosomes for protein synthesis and enzymes involved in respiration.

t: Characteristics and Classification of Living Organisms
x: Kingdom Main features Examples Animal Multicellular; no cell walls or chloroplasts; feed on organic substances made by other organisms Humans, insects Plant Multicellular; cellulose cell walls; chloroplasts; photosynthesis Ferns, flowering plants Fungus Usually multicellular hyphae (yeast is single-celled); cell walls of chitin; no chloroplasts; feed by extracellular digestion (saprotrophic or parasitic) Mushrooms, yeast Prokaryote Single-celled; no nucleus (circular DNA free in cytoplasm); plasmids; cell wall not made of cellulose Bacteria Protoctist Mostly single-celled with a nucleus; some are animal-like, some plant-like Amoeba, Chlorella Supplement: plant groups Ferns : have roots, stems and leaves (fronds); do not produce flowers; reproduce by spores found on the underside of fronds. Flowering plants : reproduce sexually by flowers and seeds; seeds are produced inside the ovary in the flower. Feature Monocotyledons Dicotyledons Cotyledons in seed One Two Leaf veins Parallel Branching network Flower parts Usually in threes (or multiples) Usually in fours or fives (or multiples) Examples Grasses, maize, lilies Beans, roses, oak Supplement: viruses Viruses are not placed in any kingdom because they do not show all the characteristics of life; they can only reproduce inside living host cells. Structure: genetic material (DNA or RNA) surrounded by a protein coat . No cytoplasm, ribosomes or cell membrane. Model answer Explain why the binomial system is useful to scientists. [3] Each species is given a unique two-part name (genus then species) that is agreed internationally (1). Scientists in different countries therefore use the same name and avoid confusion caused by local common names (1). Organisms sharing a genus name are shown to be closely related / share a recent common ancestor (1). Quick Checklist I can define all seven characteristics of living organisms using mark-scheme wording. I can define species and write a binomial name correctly. I can use and construct a dichotomous key from observable features. I can list the features of the five vertebrate classes and four arthropod groups. I can state the features common to all cells. I can describe the five kingdoms, ferns, monocots and dicots (Supplement). I can describe the structure of a virus and explain why DNA sequences are used in classification (Supplement).

Topic 2 · Cells & Organisation Organisation of the Organism The structures inside animal, plant and bacterial cells, how cells are specialised for their jobs, and how to calculate magnification. Labelling diagrams and magnification calculations appear on almost every paper.

Structure Function Animal Plant Bacterium Cell membrane Controls which substances enter and leave the cell (partially permeable) Yes Yes Yes Cytoplasm Jelly-like fluid where most chemical reactions take place Yes Yes Yes Nucleus Contains the genetic material (DNA in chromosomes) that controls the cell's activities Yes Yes No Ribosomes Site of protein synthesis Yes Yes Yes Mitochondria Site of aerobic respiration, releasing energy Yes Yes No Cell wall Made of cellulose in plants; strengthens the cell, stops it bursting and keeps its shape No Yes Yes (not cellulose) Chloroplasts Contain chlorophyll; absorb light for photosynthesis No Yes (in green parts) No Large permanent vacuole Contains cell sap; stores substances and keeps the cell turgid No (small temporary ones only) Yes No Circular DNA Main genetic material, free in the cytoplasm No No Yes Plasmids Small extra rings of DNA (often carry genes such as antibiotic resistance) No No Yes Common Mistake Saying "plant cells have no mitochondria because they photosynthesise". Plant cells respire all the time, so they do have mitochondria. Also, root cells have no chloroplasts because they receive no light. Common Mistake Writing "the cell membrane protects the cell" or "the cell wall controls what enters". The membrane controls entry and exit; the cell wall is fully permeable and gives support. New cells are produced only by the division of existing cells .

In multicellular organisms, cells differentiate to carry out particular functions. For each, link a feature to its function . Cell Function Adaptations Ciliated cell Moves mucus (with trapped dust and pathogens) in the trachea and bronchi Cilia on the surface beat to sweep mucus upwards Root hair cell Absorbs water and mineral ions from soil Long extension increases surface area; many mitochondria for active transport Palisade mesophyll cell Photosynthesis Packed with chloroplasts; column shape; found near upper leaf surface Neurone Conducts electrical impulses Long axon to carry impulses over distance; branched endings connect to many cells Red blood cell Transports oxygen Haemoglobin; no nucleus (more room); biconcave disc gives large surface area Sperm cell Reproduction: fertilises the egg Flagellum for swimming; many mitochondria for energy; enzymes in the tip (acrosome) to digest egg jelly coat; haploid nucleus Egg cell Reproduction: fused with by sperm Large with energy stores in cytoplasm; jelly coat changes after fertilisation so only one sperm enters; haploid nucleus

1 Cell The basic unit of life, e.g. a muscle cell. 2 Tissue A group of cells with similar structures, working together to perform a shared function, e.g. muscle tissue. 3 Organ A structure made of a group of tissues, working together to perform specific functions, e.g. the heart or a leaf. 4 Organ system A group of organs with related functions, working together to perform body functions, e.g. the circulatory system. 5 Organism A complete living thing made of organ systems working together. Examiner Tip When asked to identify a level, look for clues: "a group of similar cells" = tissue; "several different tissues" = organ. The xylem is a tissue; the stem is an organ.

Formula magnification = image size ÷ actual size Rearranged actual size = image size ÷ magnification Units Magnification has no units; write it as ×400 Conversion (Supplement) 1 mm = 1000 µm Image size and actual size must be in the same units before dividing. Measure the image with a ruler in mm (to the nearest mm). Supplement Convert between millimetres and micrometres: mm → µm multiply by 1000; µm → mm divide by 1000. Worked example A drawing of a cheek cell is 36 mm long. The magnification is ×600. Calculate the actual length of the cell in µm. [2] Actual size = 36 ÷ 600 = 0.06 mm (1) 0.06 × 1000 = 60 µm (1) Common Mistake Putting units on magnification ("×600 mm") or dividing the wrong way round. Remember: the image is bigger, so magnification = image over actual gives a number greater than 1. Model answer Explain how a red blood cell is adapted to its function. [3] It contains haemoglobin, which combines with oxygen (1). It has no nucleus, so there is more space for haemoglobin and more oxygen can be carried (1). Its biconcave shape gives a large surface area to volume ratio for faster diffusion of oxygen (1). It is small and flexible so it can squeeze through capillaries (1). Quick Checklist I can label and state the function of each structure in animal, plant and bacterial cells. I can compare the three cell types and explain why some plant cells lack chloroplasts. I can relate the structure of seven specialised cells to their functions. I can define tissue, organ and organ system and give examples. I can use magnification = image size ÷ actual size and rearrange it. I can convert between mm and µm (Supplement).

t: Movement into and out of Cells
x: Topic 3 · Cells & Organisation Movement into and out of Cells How substances cross cell membranes by diffusion, osmosis and active transport. Precise definitions and water potential explanations are heavily tested, often through potato or dialysis tubing practicals.

t: Movement into and out of Cells
x: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of their higher concentration to a region of their lower concentration (i.e. down a concentration gradient), as a result of their random movement. The energy for diffusion comes from the kinetic energy of random movement of molecules and ions. No energy from respiration is needed (it is a passive process). Some substances move into and out of cells by diffusion through the cell membrane . Importance to organisms: oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange in alveoli and leaves; absorption of digested food in the small intestine; movement of urea from cells into blood. Factors that increase the rate of diffusion Surface area Larger area = faster Temperature Higher = more kinetic energy = faster Concentration gradient Steeper = faster Distance Shorter = faster Common Mistake Leaving out "net" or "random movement" from the definition. Particles move in both directions; diffusion describes the overall (net) movement. Also avoid saying particles move "along" the gradient; say "down" the gradient.

t: Movement into and out of Cells
x: Water dissolves many substances, which matters for: Digestion : enzymes and food molecules are in solution so reactions can happen. Excretion : urea and excess salts are removed dissolved in urine. Transport : glucose, ions and hormones dissolve in blood plasma; mineral ions and sucrose dissolve in xylem and phloem sap.

t: Movement into and out of Cells
x: Water diffuses through partially permeable membranes by osmosis. The cell membrane is partially permeable. Supplement Osmosis is the net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential (dilute solution) to a region of lower water potential (concentrated solution), through a partially permeable membrane. Pure water has the highest water potential. Adding solute lowers the water potential. Effects on plant and animal cells Solution outside Plant cell Animal cell (e.g. red blood cell) More dilute than cell (higher water potential) Water enters by osmosis; vacuole swells; cytoplasm pushes against the cell wall; cell becomes turgid . The wall stops it bursting. Water enters; no cell wall, so the cell swells and bursts Same water potential No net movement of water No net movement; cell keeps its shape More concentrated (lower water potential) Water leaves; cell becomes flaccid ; in extreme cases the membrane pulls away from the wall: plasmolysis Water leaves; cell shrinks and becomes crenated (wrinkled) Supplement Turgor pressure : the pressure of the cell contents pushing outwards against the inelastic cell wall. It keeps plant cells firm and supports non-woody stems and leaves. Loss of turgor causes wilting . Supplement Plants absorb water because the cell sap in root hair cells has a lower water potential than the soil water, so water moves into root hairs by osmosis. Supplement Animal tissues must be bathed in fluid of the right water potential (the blood plasma and tissue fluid), otherwise cells are damaged. Required practical: osmosis in potato (or dialysis tubing) 1 Prepare tissue Cut equal-sized potato cylinders with a cork borer; blot dry and record the starting mass of each. 2 Immerse Place one cylinder in each of a range of sucrose solutions (e.g. 0.0 to 1.0 mol/dm 3 ) at the same temperature for the same time (e.g. 30 minutes). 3 Remeasure Remove, blot gently to remove surface liquid, and reweigh. 4 Calculate Percentage change in mass = (final − initial) ÷ initial × 100. Using percentages allows fair comparison if starting masses differ. 5 Analyse Plot % change against concentration. Where the line crosses zero, the solution has the same water potential as the potato cells. With dialysis (Visking) tubing: fill with sugar solution, tie it, place in water and watch the tubing swell or a liquid level rise in an attached capillary tube as water enters by osmosis. Examiner Tip In osmosis explanations always name water (not "solution" or "sugar") as the thing that moves, state the direction in terms of water potential (Supplement) and mention the partially permeable membrane . These are three separate marking points.

t: Movement into and out of Cells
x: Active transport is the movement of particles through a cell membrane from a region of lower concentration to a region of higher concentration (i.e. against a concentration gradient), using energy from respiration. Example: root hair cells take up mineral ions (e.g. nitrate) from the soil, where they are at a lower concentration than inside the cell. Other examples: absorption of glucose in the small intestine and reabsorption of glucose in the kidney. Supplement Protein carriers in the membrane carry out active transport: the particle binds to the carrier; energy from respiration changes the carrier's shape; the particle is released on the other side. Cells that do a lot of active transport have many mitochondria . Anything that stops respiration (no oxygen, cyanide, low temperature) stops active transport.

t: Movement into and out of Cells
x: Feature Diffusion Osmosis Active transport What moves Any particles Water only Particles (ions, glucose) Direction Down concentration gradient High to low water potential Against concentration gradient Energy from respiration? No No Yes Membrane needed? No Yes, partially permeable Yes, with carrier proteins Model answer A strip of potato was placed in concentrated salt solution. After an hour it was soft and bendy. Explain why. [4] The salt solution had a lower water potential than the potato cells (1). Water left the cells by osmosis (1) through the partially permeable cell membranes (1). The vacuoles shrank and the cells lost turgor / became flaccid (or plasmolysed), so the tissue was no longer firm (1). Quick Checklist I can define diffusion and state where its energy comes from. I can describe four factors affecting the rate of diffusion. I can explain the importance of water as a solvent. I can define osmosis in terms of water potential (Supplement). I can explain turgid, flaccid, plasmolysis and turgor pressure (Supplement). I can describe and analyse the potato osmosis practical. I can define active transport and explain the role of protein carriers (Supplement).

Topic 4 · Molecules & Enzymes Biological Molecules The elements and building blocks of carbohydrates, fats and proteins, the food tests used to identify them, and (Supplement) the structure of DNA. Food tests are a favourite practical question on both theory and alternative-to-practical papers.

Molecule Elements Carbohydrates Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen (C, H, O) Fats and oils Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen (C, H, O), with much less oxygen than carbohydrates Proteins Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen (C, H, O, N); some also contain sulfur Examiner Tip "Which element is found in proteins but not in carbohydrates?" The answer is nitrogen . Use full element names or correct symbols; "N 2 " is the gas, not the element in a molecule.

Large biological molecules are built by joining many smaller units together. Digestion breaks them back down. Large molecule Built from Role Starch Glucose Energy store in plants Glycogen Glucose Energy store in animals (liver and muscles) and fungi Cellulose Glucose Forms plant cell walls Proteins Amino acids Enzymes, antibodies, haemoglobin, muscle, growth and repair Fats and oils Fatty acids and glycerol Energy store, insulation, cell membranes Common Mistake Saying fats are made of "fatty acids and glycogen". It is glycerol . Glycogen is a carbohydrate made of glucose. Also, starch, glycogen and cellulose are all made of glucose, not "sugars" in general.

Food samples are usually ground up with water first to make a solution or suspension. Substance Reagent and method Negative result Positive result Starch Add a few drops of iodine solution Stays orange-brown Blue-black Reducing sugars (e.g. glucose) Add Benedict's solution and heat in a water bath (about 80°C) for a few minutes Stays blue Green, yellow, orange or brick-red (more sugar = further along) Protein Add biuret solution (or sodium hydroxide then dilute copper sulfate) Stays blue Purple (lilac) Fats and oils Ethanol emulsion test: shake the sample with ethanol, then pour the liquid into water Stays clear Cloudy white emulsion Vitamin C Add the food solution drop by drop to blue DCPIP solution DCPIP stays blue DCPIP decolourises (turns colourless) 1 Prepare the sample Grind the food with a pestle and mortar and add distilled water. 2 Divide it Put equal volumes into separate test tubes, one for each test. 3 Add reagent Use the correct reagent; heat only for Benedict's (in a water bath, not a naked flame, for safety). 4 Record and control Record the final colour. Run a control with distilled water instead of food to show the colour change is caused by the food. Examiner Tip Always state both colours: "turns from blue to brick-red" scores; "goes red" often does not. For Benedict's, the word "heat" is an essential marking point. Wear eye protection because ethanol is flammable and Benedict's and biuret are irritants.

A DNA molecule is made of two strands coiled together to form a double helix . Each strand contains chemicals called bases . There are four bases: A, T, C and G. Bonds between pairs of bases hold the two strands together. The bases always pair in the same way: A with T and C with G . This is complementary base pairing. The sequence of bases along a strand forms the genetic code. A pairs with T C pairs with G Shape Double helix Strands Two, held by bonds between bases If one strand reads ATTGCA , the complementary strand reads TAACGT . If a DNA sample is 20% A, it is also 20% T, leaving 60% for C + G, so 30% C and 30% G. Model answer Describe how you would show that a sample of milk contains protein and reducing sugar. [4] Add biuret solution to a sample of the milk (1); a colour change from blue to purple shows protein is present (1). Add Benedict's solution to a second sample and heat in a water bath (1); a colour change from blue to green/orange/brick-red shows reducing sugar is present (1). Quick Checklist I can list the elements in carbohydrates, fats and proteins. I can state the smaller units that make up starch, glycogen, cellulose, proteins and fats. I can describe the iodine, Benedict's, biuret, ethanol emulsion and DCPIP tests with colours. I can explain why a control and a water bath are used in food tests. I can describe the double helix structure of DNA (Supplement). I can apply the base-pairing rules to work out a complementary strand or percentages (Supplement).

Topic 5 · Molecules & Enzymes Enzymes How enzymes speed up reactions, why they are specific, and how temperature and pH affect them. Graph interpretation and the "explain the shape of this curve" question are classic high-mark items.

A catalyst is a substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction and is not changed by the reaction. Enzymes are proteins that function as biological catalysts and are involved in all metabolic reactions. Enzymes are important because they keep reaction rates fast enough, at body temperature, to sustain life. Without them, reactions such as respiration and digestion would be far too slow. Made of Protein Substrate The molecule the enzyme acts on Active site Region the substrate fits into Product Molecule(s) made by the reaction

1 Collision The substrate and enzyme move randomly and collide. 2 Binding The substrate fits into the active site because their shapes are complementary. 3 Enzyme-substrate complex A temporary enzyme-substrate complex forms, and the reaction takes place. 4 Release The product(s) leave the active site. The enzyme is unchanged and can be used again. The same model works for breaking molecules down (e.g. amylase: starch → maltose) and for building them up (e.g. joining glucose to make glycogen). Supplement Specificity : each enzyme only catalyses one reaction (or one type of reaction) because the shape of its active site is complementary to the shape of only one substrate. Amylase cannot digest protein because protein molecules do not fit its active site. Common Mistake Saying the active site and substrate have "the same shape". They are complementary (they fit together like a key into a lock). Also, enzymes are not living and cannot be "killed"; they are denatured .

As temperature rises towards the optimum , the rate increases. Above the optimum, the rate falls quickly and eventually stops. Most human enzymes have an optimum of about 37°C. Supplement Rising to the optimum : molecules gain kinetic energy and move faster, so there are more frequent effective collisions between enzyme and substrate, and more enzyme-substrate complexes form. Supplement Above the optimum : the enzyme vibrates so much that bonds holding its shape break. The active site changes shape , so the substrate no longer fits and fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form. The enzyme is denatured ; this is permanent. At low temperatures enzymes are inactive but not denatured; activity returns on warming.

Each enzyme has an optimum pH at which its activity is greatest. Pepsin in the stomach works best at around pH 2; most enzymes in the small intestine, such as trypsin and lipase, work best at around pH 7 to 8. Supplement Moving away from the optimum pH (either more acidic or more alkaline) changes the shape of the active site , so the substrate fits less well and fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form. Extreme pH denatures the enzyme. Condition Effect on rate Reason (Supplement detail) Low temperature Slow Little kinetic energy; few collisions; enzyme not denatured Optimum temperature / pH Fastest Most frequent effective collisions; active site correct shape High temperature Falls to zero Active site changes shape; enzyme denatured pH far from optimum Slow or zero Active site shape altered; substrate no longer fits

h: Required practical: investigating temperature or pH
x: A typical method uses amylase and starch , testing for the disappearance of starch with iodine. 1 Set up spotting tile Put a drop of iodine solution in each well. 2 Equilibrate Place separate tubes of starch solution and amylase in a water bath at the chosen temperature for 5 minutes so they reach that temperature. For pH, add a buffer solution of known pH instead and keep temperature constant. 3 Mix and time Mix the two and start a stopwatch. 4 Sample Every 30 seconds, transfer a drop of the mixture to a fresh iodine well. 5 End point Record the time when the iodine no longer turns blue-black (stays orange-brown): all starch has been digested. Rate = 1 ÷ time. 6 Repeat Repeat at several temperatures (e.g. 20, 30, 40, 50, 60°C) and repeat each to calculate a mean. Control variables : volume and concentration of starch and amylase; pH (when varying temperature); temperature (when varying pH); sampling interval. Other suitable investigations include catalase breaking down hydrogen peroxide (measure the volume of oxygen collected) or protease acting on milk or egg white. Examiner Tip When describing a graph, quote data: "the rate increased from 20°C to a peak at 40°C and then fell to zero at 60°C." When explaining, use the key phrases kinetic energy , collisions , enzyme-substrate complexes , active site changes shape and denatured . Model answer Explain why the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction falls when the temperature rises above the optimum. [4] At high temperature the enzyme molecule vibrates and bonds holding its shape break (1). The shape of the active site changes (1), so it is no longer complementary to the substrate / the substrate cannot fit (1). Fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form (1). The enzyme is denatured, which is irreversible (1). Quick Checklist I can define catalyst and enzyme and explain why enzymes are needed. I can describe enzyme action using active site, substrate, enzyme-substrate complex and product. I can explain enzyme specificity using complementary shapes (Supplement). I can describe and explain the effect of temperature, including kinetic energy and denaturation (Supplement). I can describe and explain the effect of pH on enzyme activity. I can plan an enzyme investigation with suitable control variables. I can interpret and describe enzyme rate graphs using data.

Topic 6 · Nutrition Plant Nutrition How green plants make their own food by photosynthesis, what limits the rate, and how the leaf is built to do the job. Practical-based questions on starch testing and rate experiments appear on almost every paper.

Photosynthesis is the process by which plants synthesise carbohydrates from raw materials using energy from light. Raw materials: carbon dioxide (from the air, through stomata) and water (from the soil, through roots and xylem). Chlorophyll is a green pigment found in chloroplasts. It absorbs light energy and transfers light energy into chemical energy in molecules, for the synthesis of carbohydrates. Oxygen is released as a by-product. Equations Word equation carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (in the presence of light and chlorophyll) Supplement Balanced symbol equation 6CO 2 + 6H 2 O → C 6 H 12 O 6 + 6O 2 Common Mistake Writing that chlorophyll “makes” or “produces” energy. Energy cannot be created. Chlorophyll absorbs light energy and transfers it into chemical energy.

h: What the plant does with glucose
x: Product Use in the plant Glucose Broken down in respiration to release energy Starch Insoluble energy store (in leaves, seeds, tubers); does not affect osmosis Cellulose Builds cell walls Sucrose Soluble form transported in the phloem Nectar (sugars) Attracts insect pollinators Fats / oils Energy store in some seeds

Ion Needed for Deficiency symptom Nitrate (NO 3 − ) Making amino acids, and so proteins Stunted growth, yellowing older leaves Magnesium (Mg 2+ ) Making chlorophyll Yellowing between the leaf veins (chlorosis)

h: Practical: testing a leaf for starch
x: Starch in a leaf is evidence that photosynthesis has happened. Plants are destarched first by leaving them in the dark for 48 hours so any starch present afterwards must be new. 1 Boil in water (about 1 minute) Kills the cells, stops reactions and breaks down membranes so iodine can get in. 2 Place in hot ethanol (water bath, no flame) Removes chlorophyll so the colour change is visible. Ethanol is flammable, so heat it in a water bath. 3 Rinse in water Ethanol makes the leaf brittle; rinsing softens it. 4 Spread on a white tile, add iodine solution Blue-black = starch present. Orange-brown = no starch. Showing each factor is needed Chlorophyll: use a variegated leaf (green and white). Only green areas turn blue-black. Light: cover part of a leaf with black paper or foil. The covered area stays orange-brown. Carbon dioxide: enclose a leaf or plant in a sealed bag or flask with soda lime or sodium hydroxide (absorbs CO 2 ). Control: identical set-up without the absorber.

Use an aquatic plant such as pondweed (Elodea) in water with added sodium hydrogencarbonate (a source of CO 2 ). Count oxygen bubbles per minute, or collect gas in a measuring cylinder or gas syringe. Light intensity: move a lamp to different distances. Use a heat shield (a beaker of water) or LED lamp so temperature stays constant. CO 2 concentration: vary the concentration of sodium hydrogencarbonate. Temperature: use water baths at different temperatures. Allow the plant to acclimatise for a few minutes at each new condition before counting; repeat and calculate a mean. Hydrogencarbonate indicator (gas exchange) CO 2 level Indicator colour Typical cause Higher than air Yellow Leaf in the dark: respiration only Same as air Orange / red Dim light: photosynthesis = respiration (compensation point) Lower than air Purple Bright light: photosynthesis faster than respiration

A limiting factor is something present in the environment in such short supply that it restricts life processes. For photosynthesis the main limiting factors are light intensity , carbon dioxide concentration and temperature . On a graph, while the line is rising, the factor on the x-axis is limiting. When the line levels off (plateaus), something else is now limiting. Temperature affects the enzymes that control photosynthesis: rate rises to an optimum, then falls as enzymes denature. Growers use this in glasshouses: paraffin heaters raise temperature and CO 2 ; artificial lighting extends the day. Examiner Tip When describing a plateau, name the factor that is no longer limiting and suggest what now is. For example: “Above 40 units light intensity is no longer the limiting factor; carbon dioxide concentration or temperature is now limiting.”

Structure Description Supplement Adaptation Waxy cuticle Waterproof layer on the upper surface Reduces water loss; transparent so light passes through Upper epidermis Single layer of cells, no chloroplasts Transparent, lets light reach the palisade Palisade mesophyll Tall, tightly packed cells near the top Most chloroplasts; main site of photosynthesis; absorbs maximum light Spongy mesophyll Irregular cells with fewer chloroplasts Large air spaces allow CO 2 and O 2 to diffuse; large surface area for gas exchange Air spaces Gaps between spongy cells Connect stomata to mesophyll cells Vascular bundle (vein) Contains xylem and phloem Xylem brings water and mineral ions; phloem carries sucrose away Lower epidermis Contains most stomata Stomata on the shaded side reduces water loss Stomata and guard cells Pores controlled by a pair of guard cells Open to let CO 2 in and O 2 out; close to reduce water loss Supplement Leaves are also broad (large surface area to absorb light) and thin (short diffusion distance for gases). Model answer Explain why the rate of photosynthesis of pondweed increases as a lamp is moved closer, but stops increasing below a certain distance. [4] Moving the lamp closer increases light intensity, so more light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll (1). Light intensity is the limiting factor, so the rate increases (1). Below a certain distance the rate stays constant because light is no longer the limiting factor (1); another factor, such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature, is now limiting (1). Quick Checklist I can define photosynthesis and write the word equation (and balanced symbol equation for Supplement). I can state the role of chlorophyll in transferring light energy into chemical energy. I can list five uses of the carbohydrates made in photosynthesis. I can explain why plants need nitrate and magnesium ions. I can describe the starch test and experiments showing chlorophyll, light and CO 2 are needed. I can describe how to investigate light intensity, CO 2 and temperature on rate, and interpret hydrogencarbonate indicator colours. I can explain limiting factors using a graph. I can label a leaf cross-section and explain how each part is adapted.

Topic 7 · Nutrition Human Nutrition What a balanced diet contains, how food is broken down physically and chemically, and how the small intestine absorbs it. Expect questions matching enzymes to substrates, products and sites of action.

A balanced diet contains all the nutrients in the correct proportions, plus fibre and water, to meet the body’s needs. Energy needs depend on age, activity level and pregnancy. Nutrient Good sources Why it is needed Carbohydrates Rice, bread, pasta, potatoes Main source of energy (respiration) Fats and oils Butter, oils, nuts, oily fish Energy store, insulation, cell membranes Proteins Meat, fish, eggs, beans, lentils Growth and repair; making enzymes and antibodies Vitamin C Citrus fruit, peppers, green vegetables Making collagen for healthy skin, gums and connective tissue Vitamin D Oily fish, egg yolk; made in skin in sunlight Helps absorb calcium for bones and teeth Calcium Milk, cheese, yoghurt Strong bones and teeth; blood clotting Iron Red meat, spinach, beans Making haemoglobin in red blood cells Fibre (roughage) Wholemeal bread, fruit, vegetables Adds bulk so peristalsis moves food; prevents constipation Water Drinks, food Solvent for reactions and transport; temperature control Deficiency diseases Scurvy Lack of vitamin C: bleeding gums, poor wound healing Rickets Lack of vitamin D or calcium: soft, bent leg bones Anaemia Lack of iron: tiredness, less oxygen carried

Organ Main role Mouth and teeth Ingestion; chewing; saliva contains amylase Salivary glands Secrete saliva (amylase, mucus for lubrication) Oesophagus Moves food to the stomach by peristalsis Stomach Churning; secretes protease (pepsin) and hydrochloric acid Small intestine: duodenum Receives pancreatic juice and bile; main site of chemical digestion Small intestine: ileum Absorption of digested food and most water Pancreas Secretes amylase, protease (trypsin) and lipase into the duodenum Liver Makes bile; assimilation of nutrients Gall bladder Stores bile and releases it into the duodenum Large intestine: colon Absorbs remaining water Large intestine: rectum Stores faeces Anus Egestion of faeces Key definitions 1 Ingestion The taking of substances, e.g. food and drink, into the body. 2 Digestion The breakdown of food. 3 Absorption The movement of nutrients from the intestines into the blood. 4 Assimilation The uptake and use of nutrients by cells. 5 Egestion The passing out of food that has not been digested or absorbed, as faeces, through the anus. Common Mistake Confusing egestion with excretion . Faeces are mostly undigested food that never entered cells, so removing them is egestion, not excretion.

Physical digestion is the breakdown of food into smaller pieces without chemical change to the food molecules. It increases the surface area for enzymes to act on. Incisors: chisel-shaped, for biting and cutting. Canines: pointed, for gripping and tearing. Premolars and molars: broad, ridged surfaces for chewing and grinding. Tooth structure: enamel (hardest outer layer), dentine , pulp cavity with nerves and blood vessels, cement anchoring the root in the jaw bone, surrounded by the gum . The stomach churns food with its muscular walls, mixing it with gastric juice. Supplement Bile emulsifies fats : it breaks large fat droplets into smaller droplets, increasing the surface area for lipase to act on. This is physical, not chemical, digestion.

Chemical digestion is the breakdown of large insoluble molecules into small soluble molecules. This is needed so they can be absorbed into the blood and used by cells. Enzyme Substrate → product Secreted by Acts in Amylase Starch → simple reducing sugars (maltose) Salivary glands, pancreas Mouth, duodenum Supplement Maltase Maltose → glucose Epithelium lining of small intestine On the membranes of the epithelium of the small intestine Protease: pepsin Protein → amino acids (via polypeptides) Stomach Stomach Protease: trypsin Protein → amino acids (via polypeptides) Pancreas Duodenum Lipase Fats and oils → fatty acids and glycerol Pancreas Duodenum Acid and alkali Hydrochloric acid in gastric juice kills harmful microorganisms in food and gives the acidic pH (about 2) that is optimum for pepsin. Supplement Bile is alkaline. It neutralises the acidic mixture of food and gastric juice entering the duodenum, giving a suitable pH for enzymes in the small intestine. Examiner Tip Bile is not an enzyme . It is made in the liver, stored in the gall bladder and has two jobs: emulsifying fats and neutralising stomach acid. Say both if asked for its role.

The small intestine is the main region where nutrients are absorbed. Water is absorbed in both the small intestine (most) and the colon . The inner wall is folded and covered in villi ; each epithelial cell has microvilli . Both greatly increase the surface area for absorption.

Feature How it helps absorption Epithelium one cell thick Short diffusion distance Microvilli on epithelial cells Even larger surface area Dense network of blood capillaries Absorb glucose and amino acids; blood flow keeps a steep concentration gradient Lacteal (lymph vessel) in the centre Absorbs fatty acids and glycerol Many mitochondria in epithelial cells Release energy for active transport Model answer Explain how the structure of the small intestine is adapted for absorbing digested food. [4] The small intestine is very long, giving time for absorption (1). Villi and microvilli give a very large surface area (1). The epithelium is only one cell thick, so the diffusion distance is short (1). Each villus has a good blood supply that carries absorbed glucose and amino acids away, maintaining a concentration gradient (1), and a lacteal that absorbs fatty acids and glycerol (1). Quick Checklist I can define a balanced diet and give sources and roles of each nutrient, including vitamins C and D, calcium, iron and fibre. I can name the deficiency diseases scurvy and rickets and their causes. I can identify each organ of the digestive system and state its function. I can define ingestion, digestion, absorption, assimilation and egestion. I can describe the types of teeth, tooth structure, and the role of physical digestion. I can state the substrate, products, source and site of action of amylase, maltase, protease and lipase. I can explain the roles of hydrochloric acid and bile. I can describe how villi and microvilli are adapted for absorption.

Topic 8 · Transport Transport in Plants How water and mineral ions travel up through xylem, how water is lost by transpiration, and how sugars move in phloem. Graph interpretation and potometer practicals are common exam favourites.

Xylem Phloem Transports Water and mineral ions Sucrose and amino acids Direction Upwards only (roots to leaves) Both directions (source to sink) Other role Supports the plant — Cells Dead, hollow vessels Living cells Position in the plant Root: xylem forms a central star or X shape; phloem sits in the gaps between the arms. Stem: vascular bundles arranged in a ring near the edge; xylem on the inside, phloem on the outside. Leaf: in the veins (vascular bundles); xylem towards the upper surface, phloem towards the lower surface.

Thick walls strengthened with lignin : support the plant and stop vessels collapsing under tension. No cell contents (dead cells): nothing blocks the flow of water. Cells joined end to end with no cross walls : form a continuous hollow tube.

Root hair cells are the site of water and mineral ion uptake. Water enters by osmosis. Their long, thin extension gives a large surface area , increasing the rate of uptake of water by osmosis and mineral ions by active transport. Pathway of water 1 Root hair cells Water enters from the soil by osmosis. 2 Root cortex cells Water moves across the cortex from cell to cell. 3 Xylem Water travels up the root and stem to the leaves. 4 Mesophyll cells Water leaves the xylem in the leaf veins and enters mesophyll cells. Practical: tracing the pathway Stand a celery stalk or white flower in water containing a dye (e.g. food colouring or eosin) for a few hours. Cut thin cross-sections and view with a hand lens or microscope: only the xylem is stained.

Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from plant leaves by evaporation of water at the surfaces of the mesophyll cells followed by diffusion of water vapour through the stomata. Supplement The mesophyll cells have a large surface area and the leaf interior has air spaces, so a lot of water evaporates; the air spaces become saturated with water vapour.

h: Supplement How water moves up the plant
x: 1 Evaporation and diffusion Water evaporates from mesophyll cell surfaces and water vapour diffuses out through the stomata. 2 Transpiration pull Loss of water from the leaf draws water out of the xylem, creating tension (a pulling force) in the xylem. 3 Cohesion Water molecules are attracted to each other (cohesion), so the whole column of water in the xylem is pulled up. 4 Replacement More water enters the roots from the soil to replace what moved up.

Factor increased Effect on rate Supplement Explanation Temperature Increases Water molecules have more kinetic energy, so evaporation and diffusion are faster Wind speed Increases Water vapour is blown away from the leaf surface, keeping a steep concentration gradient Humidity Decreases More water vapour in the air reduces the concentration gradient, so diffusion is slower Light intensity Increases Stomata open wider in light Practical: investigating transpiration Use a potometer : a leafy shoot sealed into a water-filled tube with a capillary and air bubble. Cut the shoot under water and assemble under water so no air enters the xylem; seal joints with petroleum jelly. Measure the distance the air bubble moves in a set time. A potometer actually measures water uptake , which is close to the rate of water loss. Vary temperature (e.g. in rooms of different temperatures) or wind speed (a fan at different distances or settings), keeping other factors constant. Alternative: weigh a potted plant over time with the soil surface covered by a plastic bag.

If a plant loses water faster than it is taken up, cells lose water by osmosis and become flaccid . The cells no longer press against each other, so the leaves and stem lose support and droop. Common Mistake Saying “water evaporates out of the stomata”. Evaporation happens at the mesophyll cell surfaces inside the leaf; the water vapour then diffuses out through the stomata.

Translocation is the movement of sucrose and amino acids in phloem from sources to sinks. Source Part of a plant that releases sucrose or amino acids (e.g. photosynthesising leaves, a storage organ in spring) Sink Part of a plant that uses or stores sucrose or amino acids (e.g. roots, growing buds, fruits, developing seeds) Some parts act as a source at one time and a sink at another. A potato tuber is a sink in summer (storing starch) and a source in spring (supplying sugar to new shoots before leaves can photosynthesise). Examiner Tip Use precise names: sucrose (not glucose or “food”) moves in phloem, and mineral ions (not “minerals” or “nutrients”) move in xylem. Model answer Explain why a plant transpires faster on a hot, windy day. [4] At a higher temperature water molecules have more kinetic energy (1), so water evaporates faster from the surfaces of the mesophyll cells (1). Wind removes water vapour from around the leaf (1), which maintains a steep concentration gradient so water vapour diffuses out of the stomata faster (1). Quick Checklist I can state the functions of xylem and phloem and identify their positions in root, stem and leaf. I can relate the structure of xylem vessels to their function. I can describe the role of root hair cells and the pathway of water through the plant. I can define transpiration and describe an investigation using a potometer. I can explain the effects of temperature, wind speed and humidity on transpiration. I can explain water movement using transpiration pull and cohesion, and explain wilting. I can define translocation, source and sink, with examples.

Topic 9 · Transport Transport in Animals The circulatory system: how the heart pumps blood, how blood vessels are built for their jobs, and what blood is made of. Heart diagrams, vessel comparisons and coronary heart disease questions are regulars.

The circulatory system is a system of blood vessels with a pump and valves to ensure one-way flow of blood. Fish have a single circulation : blood passes through the heart once per circuit (heart → gills → body → heart). Supplement Mammals have a double circulation : blood passes through the heart twice per circuit. The pulmonary circuit goes to the lungs; the systemic circuit goes to the rest of the body. Supplement Advantages of double circulation: blood returns to the heart after the lungs so it can be pumped at high pressure to the body, delivering oxygen and glucose quickly; lower pressure in the lungs avoids damaging delicate capillaries.

Muscular wall of cardiac muscle that contracts to pump blood. Septum separates the left and right sides, so oxygenated and deoxygenated blood do not mix. Right and left atria (upper chambers) receive blood; right and left ventricles (lower chambers) pump blood out. One-way valves prevent backflow. Coronary arteries on the surface supply the heart muscle with oxygen and glucose. Supplement Ventricles have thicker walls than atria because they pump blood out of the heart, not just into the ventricles below. Supplement The left ventricle wall is thicker than the right because it pumps blood at high pressure all around the body; the right only pumps to the nearby lungs. Supplement Atrioventricular valves lie between atria and ventricles; semilunar valves lie at the bases of the aorta and pulmonary artery. Blood flow through the heart 1 Vena cava → right atrium Deoxygenated blood returns from the body. 2 Right ventricle → pulmonary artery Pumped to the lungs to pick up oxygen. 3 Pulmonary vein → left atrium Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs. 4 Left ventricle → aorta Pumped at high pressure to the body.

The atria contract , pushing blood through the open atrioventricular valves into the ventricles. The ventricles contract : pressure rises, closing the atrioventricular valves (preventing backflow into the atria) and forcing open the semilunar valves so blood enters the arteries. The ventricles relax: pressure falls, and the semilunar valves close, preventing backflow from the arteries into the ventricles.

Heart activity can be monitored by an ECG , by measuring pulse rate , and by listening to the sounds of valves closing with a stethoscope. Physical activity increases heart rate. Supplement Explanation: muscles respire faster during exercise and need more oxygen and glucose, and more carbon dioxide must be removed. A faster heart rate delivers blood to the muscles more quickly. If oxygen supply is insufficient, anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid, and heart rate stays high after exercise to remove it.

CHD is caused by blockage of the coronary arteries (fatty deposits build up in the artery walls), so heart muscle gets less oxygen and glucose. Heart muscle cells cannot respire and may die, causing a heart attack. Risk factors: diet high in saturated fat and salt, lack of exercise, stress, smoking, genetic predisposition, increasing age, and sex (males are at higher risk). Supplement Reducing risk: a diet low in saturated fat and salt reduces fatty deposits and blood pressure; regular exercise strengthens heart muscle, reduces blood pressure and helps maintain a healthy body mass.

Vessel Structure Supplement Explanation Artery Thick, muscular, elastic wall; narrow lumen Carries blood away from the heart at high pressure; elastic tissue stretches and recoils to even out the flow Vein Thin wall; wide lumen; valves Carries blood to the heart at low pressure; wide lumen reduces resistance; valves prevent backflow Capillary Wall one cell thick; very narrow Short diffusion distance for exchange of substances with tissues; huge network gives large surface area Main blood vessels Heart Vena cava, aorta, pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein Lungs Pulmonary artery (in), pulmonary vein (out) Kidney Renal artery (in), renal vein (out) Supplement Liver Hepatic artery and hepatic portal vein (in, from gut), hepatic vein (out) Common Mistake Stating that arteries always carry oxygenated blood. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood. Arteries are defined by carrying blood away from the heart .

Component Function Red blood cells Transport oxygen, using haemoglobin; biconcave shape, no nucleus White blood cells: phagocytes Phagocytosis (engulfing and digesting pathogens); lobed nucleus White blood cells: lymphocytes Antibody production; large round nucleus filling most of the cell Platelets Cell fragments involved in blood clotting Plasma Transports blood cells, ions, nutrients (e.g. glucose, amino acids), urea, hormones and carbon dioxide

Clotting prevents blood loss and stops pathogens entering through the wound. At a wound, platelets trigger a chain of reactions converting soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin . Fibrin forms a mesh of fibres that traps red blood cells, forming a clot which dries into a scab. Examiner Tip On heart diagrams, left and right are the patient’s left and right, so the left side of the heart appears on the right of the page. Look for the thicker ventricle wall to orient yourself. Model answer Explain why the wall of the left ventricle is thicker than the wall of the right ventricle. [3] The left ventricle pumps blood to the whole body, whereas the right ventricle pumps blood only to the lungs (1). The left ventricle needs more muscle to contract more strongly (1) and produce a higher pressure to push blood the longer distance around the body (1). Quick Checklist I can describe single circulation in fish and explain the advantages of double circulation in mammals. I can label the heart, including chambers, valves, septum, coronary arteries and main vessels. I can describe the sequence of contraction and valve action in the cardiac cycle. I can describe and explain the effect of exercise on heart rate. I can state the causes and risk factors of coronary heart disease and how to reduce the risk. I can compare arteries, veins and capillaries and relate structure to function. I can name the main blood vessels to and from the heart, lungs, kidneys and liver. I can state the functions of the components of blood and describe how blood clots.

Topic 10 · Health Diseases and Immunity How pathogens spread, how the body defends itself, and how vaccination and antibodies give immunity. Precise definitions and the difference between active and passive immunity earn most of the marks here.

Pathogen A disease-causing organism Transmissible disease A disease in which the pathogen can be passed from one host to another Pathogens include bacteria, viruses, fungi and protoctists. Not all diseases are transmissible. Some are caused by the immune system attacking the body’s own cells, e.g. type 1 diabetes , where the insulin-secreting cells of the pancreas are destroyed.

Route Examples Direct contact Through blood or other body fluids (e.g. HIV via shared needles or sexual contact) Indirect: contaminated surfaces Door handles, towels, shared equipment Indirect: food and water Undercooked meat, unwashed salad, water contaminated with sewage (e.g. cholera) Indirect: animals Insects such as mosquitoes (malaria), houseflies landing on food Indirect: air Droplets from coughs and sneezes (e.g. influenza)

Mechanical barriers Skin : a tough outer layer that pathogens cannot easily cross. Hairs in the nose : trap larger particles in inhaled air. Chemical barriers Mucus in the airways traps pathogens; cilia sweep it away from the lungs. Stomach acid (hydrochloric acid) kills pathogens in food and drink. Cells White blood cells : phagocytes carry out phagocytosis; lymphocytes produce antibodies. Vaccination also protects the body by giving immunity in advance.

A clean water supply . Hygienic food preparation : washing hands, cooking thoroughly, keeping raw and cooked foods apart, refrigeration. Good personal hygiene : handwashing, covering coughs and sneezes. Waste disposal : collecting rubbish so it does not attract flies and rats. Sewage treatment : prevents human waste contaminating drinking water.

Antigens are molecules (often proteins) on the surface of pathogens. Each pathogen has its own antigens with a specific shape. Antibodies are proteins made by lymphocytes that bind to antigens. Each antibody has a specific shape that is complementary to one particular antigen, so it fits only that antigen. Antibodies work by directly destroying pathogens (or clumping them together) or by marking pathogens for destruction by phagocytes .

Active immunity is defence against a pathogen by antibody production in the body. It is gained after an infection by a pathogen or by vaccination, and is long-term because memory cells are produced. How vaccination works 1 Vaccine given Contains a harmless (weakened or dead) pathogen or its antigens. 2 Antigens trigger an immune response Lymphocytes with the complementary antibody shape are activated. 3 Antibodies produced Lymphocytes divide and secrete specific antibodies. 4 Memory cells made These remain in the blood for a long time. 5 Later infection Memory cells cause a faster, larger antibody response, destroying the pathogen before symptoms develop. Vaccination is important in controlling the spread of disease: if enough people are immune, the pathogen cannot pass easily between hosts, protecting those who are not vaccinated (herd immunity).

Passive immunity is short-term defence against a pathogen by antibodies acquired from another individual, e.g. across the placenta or in breast milk. Memory cells are not produced , so the protection fades as the antibodies are broken down. Breast-feeding is important because it passes antibodies to the infant, protecting it while its own immune system is still developing. Active immunity Passive immunity Antibodies made by The person’s own lymphocytes Another individual Memory cells Yes No Duration Long-term Short-term Speed of protection Takes time to develop Immediate Examples Infection, vaccination Breast milk, placenta Common Mistake Writing that a vaccine “contains antibodies”. A vaccine contains antigens (or a harmless pathogen); the body then makes its own antibodies. Receiving ready-made antibodies is passive immunity.

1 Infection Cholera is caused by a bacterium transmitted in water contaminated with faeces. 2 Toxin released The bacterium produces a toxin in the small intestine. 3 Chloride ions secreted The toxin causes secretion of chloride ions into the lumen of the small intestine. 4 Osmosis The water potential of the gut contents falls, so water moves out of the blood and cells into the gut by osmosis. 5 Symptoms Severe diarrhoea, dehydration and loss of salts from the blood; can be fatal without oral rehydration therapy. Examiner Tip For immunity answers, always use the word specific or complementary when linking antibody to antigen, and mention memory cells when explaining why vaccination gives long-term protection. Model answer Explain how vaccination protects a person from a disease. [4] The vaccine contains a weakened or dead form of the pathogen, carrying its antigens (1). Lymphocytes produce antibodies that are specific to (complementary to) these antigens (1). Memory cells are also produced and stay in the body (1). If the real pathogen later enters, the memory cells produce antibodies much more quickly and in larger amounts, so the pathogen is destroyed before it causes illness (1). Quick Checklist I can define pathogen and transmissible disease. I can describe direct and indirect routes of transmission with examples. I can describe the body’s mechanical, chemical and cellular defences. I can explain how clean water, hygiene, waste disposal and sewage treatment control disease spread. I can explain how antibodies act on specific antigens. I can define active and passive immunity and explain how vaccination works. I can explain the importance of breast-feeding for passive immunity. I can describe how cholera causes diarrhoea and dehydration.

Topic 11 · Gas Exchange & Respiration Gas Exchange in Humans How the breathing system brings air close to the blood so that oxygen can diffuse in and carbon dioxide can diffuse out. Expect labelling questions, air-composition data and extended “explain how we breathe in” answers.

Gas exchange happens by diffusion . In humans the exchange surface is the lining of the alveoli . Any efficient exchange surface has: Large surface area Millions of alveoli give a huge total area Thin surface Alveolus and capillary walls are one cell thick, so a short diffusion distance Good blood supply Dense capillary network keeps a steep concentration gradient Good ventilation Breathing replaces air, keeping O 2 high and CO 2 low in the alveoli

Structure What it is / does Larynx Voice box at the top of the trachea Trachea Windpipe; held open by C-shaped rings of cartilage Bronchi (singular bronchus) Two branches of the trachea, one to each lung; also supported by cartilage Bronchioles Many narrow branches of the bronchi leading to the alveoli Alveoli Tiny air sacs where gas exchange takes place Lungs Organs containing the bronchioles and alveoli Ribs Bones that protect the lungs and move during breathing Intercostal muscles Muscles between the ribs (internal and external sets) Diaphragm Sheet of muscle below the lungs separating the thorax from the abdomen

Gas Inspired air Expired air Oxygen About 21% About 16% Carbon dioxide About 0.04% About 4% Water vapour Variable (lower) Saturated (higher) Nitrogen About 78% About 78% (unchanged) Test for CO 2 : bubble the gas through limewater ; it turns from colourless to milky/cloudy . Expired air turns limewater cloudy much faster than inspired air. Supplement Explaining the differences: O 2 is lower in expired air because it diffuses into the blood and is used in aerobic respiration ; CO 2 is higher because it is produced by respiration and diffuses from the blood into the alveoli; water vapour is higher because water evaporates from the moist alveolar lining.

Count breaths per minute at rest (rate) and note depth, e.g. using a spirometer or chest expansion. Exercise for a fixed time (e.g. 2 minutes of step-ups), then measure again straight away and every minute until back to resting. Control: same person, same exercise intensity and duration; repeat for reliability. Result: both rate and depth of breathing increase during and after exercise. Supplement Muscles respire faster during exercise, producing more CO 2 . The brain detects the increased CO 2 concentration in the blood and sends impulses to the intercostal muscles and diaphragm, increasing the rate and depth of breathing. This removes CO 2 faster and supplies more O 2 for aerobic respiration.

h: Supplement Ventilation: breathing in and out
x: 1 Inspiration: muscles contract External intercostal muscles contract (internal relax), pulling the ribcage up and out. The diaphragm contracts and flattens. 2 Volume up, pressure down The volume of the thorax increases, so the pressure inside falls below atmospheric pressure. 3 Air flows in Air moves into the lungs down the pressure gradient. 4 Expiration: muscles relax External intercostals relax so the ribs move down and in; the diaphragm relaxes and domes upwards. In forced expiration the internal intercostals contract to pull the ribs down. 5 Volume down, pressure up Thorax volume decreases, pressure rises above atmospheric, and air is forced out. The internal and external intercostal muscles are antagonistic : when one set contracts the other relaxes.

Goblet cells in the lining of the trachea and bronchi secrete mucus , which traps pathogens and dust particles. Ciliated cells have cilia that beat to sweep the mucus up to the throat, where it is swallowed. This stops pathogens and particles reaching the alveoli. Model answer Explain how contraction of the diaphragm and intercostal muscles causes air to enter the lungs. [4] The external intercostal muscles contract, moving the ribs upwards and outwards. The diaphragm contracts and flattens. This increases the volume of the thorax, which decreases the pressure inside the lungs below atmospheric pressure. Air therefore moves into the lungs down the pressure gradient. Examiner Tip Always link the chain in order: muscle contracts → volume increases → pressure decreases → air moves in . Marks are often lost by mentioning volume but not pressure, or pressure but not which way the air moves. Common Mistake Saying “the lungs expand, which sucks air in”. The lungs do not pull air in by themselves; the muscles change the thorax volume and pressure. Also, expired air still contains a lot of oxygen (about 16%), so never write that expired air has “no oxygen”. Quick Checklist I can list four features of an efficient gas exchange surface. I can label the larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli, ribs, intercostal muscles and diaphragm. I can compare inspired and expired air and describe the limewater test. I can describe an investigation into exercise and breathing rate and depth. I can explain the effect of exercise on breathing in terms of CO 2 detection by the brain. I can explain inspiration and expiration using volume and pressure changes. I can describe how goblet cells, mucus and cilia protect the gas exchange system.

Topic 12 · Gas Exchange & Respiration Respiration How every living cell releases energy from glucose, with or without oxygen. Equations, definitions and the oxygen debt appear in almost every paper, so learn them word for word.

Respiration: the chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrient molecules and release energy for metabolism. Aerobic respiration: the chemical reactions in cells that use oxygen to break down nutrient molecules to release energy. Anaerobic respiration: the chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrient molecules to release energy without using oxygen. Respiration is controlled by enzymes , so its rate is affected by temperature. It happens in all living cells , all the time, including plant cells.

h: Uses of energy in the body
x: Muscle contraction Protein synthesis Cell division Active transport Growth Passage of nerve impulses Maintaining a constant body temperature
Word equation glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water Supplement Balanced symbol equation C 6 H 12 O 6 + 6O 2 → 6CO 2 + 6H 2 O

Anaerobic respiration releases much less energy per glucose molecule than aerobic respiration, because the glucose is only partly broken down. Organism Word equation Uses / notes Muscles (during vigorous exercise) glucose → lactic acid No CO 2 produced; lactic acid builds up Yeast glucose → alcohol + carbon dioxide Alcohol for brewing; CO 2 makes bread dough rise Supplement Balanced symbol equation for yeast: C 6 H 12 O 6 → 2C 2 H 5 OH + 2CO 2

Feature Aerobic Anaerobic Oxygen needed? Yes No Energy released Large amount Much less Products Carbon dioxide and water Lactic acid (muscles) or alcohol and CO 2 (yeast) Glucose breakdown Complete Incomplete

h: Supplement Lactic acid and the oxygen debt
x: During vigorous exercise the heart and lungs cannot supply oxygen to muscles fast enough, so muscles also respire anaerobically. Lactic acid builds up in the muscles and blood , causing an oxygen debt : the oxygen needed afterwards to break the lactic acid down. 1 Fast heart rate continues Blood carries lactic acid from the muscles to the liver. 2 Deeper, faster breathing continues Supplies extra oxygen for the aerobic respiration of lactic acid. 3 Lactic acid broken down in the liver It is respired aerobically, which removes the oxygen debt.

Mix yeast with glucose solution and place tubes in water baths at different temperatures (e.g. 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 °C). Measure the rate by counting CO 2 bubbles per minute, measuring gas volume in a syringe, or timing how long limewater (or hydrogencarbonate indicator) takes to change colour. Control variables: mass of yeast, concentration and volume of glucose, time allowed to acclimatise. Expected result: rate rises to an optimum (around 35–40 °C) and then falls as the enzymes are denatured . Respiration in germinating seeds or small invertebrates can also be shown with a respirometer; a soda-lime absorbs CO 2 so that movement of a liquid bead shows oxygen uptake. Model answer Explain why a sprinter continues to breathe deeply and quickly for several minutes after a race. [4] During the race the muscles respired anaerobically because not enough oxygen reached them. This produced lactic acid, which built up in the muscles and blood, creating an oxygen debt. After the race, deep and fast breathing supplies extra oxygen, and a high heart rate carries lactic acid to the liver, where it is broken down by aerobic respiration. Examiner Tip Use the word release when talking about energy. Energy is released by respiration, never “made” or “produced”. Examiners regularly refuse answers that say respiration “creates energy”. Common Mistake Confusing respiration with breathing. Breathing (ventilation) is the movement of air in and out of the lungs; respiration is a chemical process inside every cell. Also remember that anaerobic respiration in human muscle does not produce carbon dioxide. Quick Checklist I can give the definitions of respiration, aerobic respiration and anaerobic respiration. I can list the uses of energy in the human body. I can write the word and balanced symbol equations for aerobic respiration. I can write the word equations for anaerobic respiration in muscles and in yeast, and the symbol equation for yeast. I can state that anaerobic respiration releases much less energy than aerobic. I can explain the oxygen debt and how lactic acid is removed. I can describe an investigation into the effect of temperature on yeast respiration.

Topic 13 · Human Systems Excretion in Humans How the body removes the waste products of metabolism, focusing on the lungs, liver and kidneys. Kidney diagrams and the nephron sequence are favourite structured questions.

Excretion: the removal of the waste products of metabolism and substances in excess of requirements. Do not confuse this with egestion , the removal of undigested food as faeces; faeces were never part of metabolism. Lungs Excrete carbon dioxide (from respiration) Kidneys Excrete urea, excess water and excess ions as urine Liver Makes urea by deamination (Supplement)

Structure Function Kidneys Filter the blood and produce urine Ureters Carry urine from each kidney to the bladder Bladder Stores urine Urethra Carries urine from the bladder out of the body In a section through a kidney you should identify the outer cortex , the inner medulla and the ureter leaving it. The renal artery brings blood in; the renal vein takes filtered blood away.

The body cannot store excess amino acids. Deamination: the removal of the nitrogen-containing part of amino acids to form urea. The rest of the amino acid can be respired for energy or converted to carbohydrate and stored. The liver also assimilates amino acids by converting them into proteins, including plasma proteins such as fibrinogen . Urea travels in the blood plasma to the kidneys. Why excretion matters: urea and other nitrogenous wastes are toxic ; if they build up they damage cells. Excess CO 2 also lowers blood pH.

Each kidney contains about a million tubules called nephrons . Parts: glomerulus, Bowman’s capsule, proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct. 1 Glomerulus: ultrafiltration Blood in the glomerulus (a knot of capillaries) is under high pressure. Small molecules are forced out into the Bowman’s capsule. 2 Bowman’s capsule: filtrate collects The filtrate contains water, glucose, urea and salts (ions). Blood cells and large proteins are too big to pass through and stay in the blood. 3 Proximal convoluted tubule: reabsorption All of the glucose, most of the water and some salts are reabsorbed back into the blood. 4 Loop of Henle Helps reabsorb water back into the blood. 5 Collecting duct More water is reabsorbed, depending on how much the body needs. 6 Urine formed The remaining liquid, urine, contains water, urea and salts and passes to the ureter. Comparing blood plasma, filtrate and urine Substance Plasma Filtrate Urine Protein Present Absent Absent Glucose Present Present Absent (in a healthy person) Urea Low Low High (concentrated as water is reabsorbed) Salts Present Present Present (excess) Model answer Explain why glucose is found in the filtrate in the Bowman’s capsule but not in the urine of a healthy person. [3] Glucose is a small molecule, so it is forced out of the glomerulus into the Bowman’s capsule during ultrafiltration. In the proximal convoluted tubule all of the glucose is reabsorbed back into the blood. Therefore none remains in the urine. Examiner Tip If a question gives you a table of concentrations, use the pattern above: proteins show filtration by size, glucose shows reabsorption, and urea rising in concentration shows water reabsorption. Quote numbers from the table where you can. Common Mistake Mixing up ureter and urethra . There are two ureters (kidney to bladder) and one urethra (bladder to outside). Another common error is saying the kidneys “make urea”: urea is made in the liver and only removed by the kidneys. Quick Checklist I can define excretion and distinguish it from egestion. I can state that the lungs excrete CO 2 and the kidneys excrete urea, excess water and excess ions. I can identify the kidneys, ureters, bladder and urethra, and the cortex, medulla and ureter in a kidney. I can define deamination and describe the role of the liver in forming urea. I can explain why urea must be removed from the body. I can name the parts of a nephron and describe ultrafiltration and selective reabsorption. I can state what urine contains and explain differences between plasma, filtrate and urine.

Topic 14 · Human Systems Coordination and Response How animals and plants detect changes and respond: nerves, the eye, hormones, homeostasis and plant tropisms. This is one of the largest topics on the syllabus and a rich source of long-answer questions.

The mammalian nervous system is made of the central nervous system (CNS) , the brain and spinal cord, and the peripheral nervous system (PNS) , the nerves outside the CNS. It coordinates and regulates body functions using electrical impulses that travel along neurones . Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the CNS; relay neurones (inside the CNS) connect sensory and motor neurones; motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors (muscles or glands). Reflex action: a means of automatically and rapidly integrating and coordinating stimuli with the responses of effectors (muscles and glands). The reflex arc 1 Stimulus e.g. hand touches a hot object. 2 Receptor Receptor cells in the skin detect the stimulus and start an impulse. 3 Sensory neurone Carries the impulse to the spinal cord. 4 Relay neurone In the spinal cord, passes the impulse to a motor neurone. 5 Motor neurone Carries the impulse to the effector. 6 Effector and response A muscle contracts and the hand is pulled away.

A synapse is a junction between two neurones, with a narrow gap called the synaptic cleft. An impulse arriving at the end of the first neurone causes vesicles to release neurotransmitter molecules into the cleft. The neurotransmitter diffuses across the gap and binds to receptor proteins on the next neurone, stimulating a new impulse. Synapses ensure impulses travel in one direction only , because only the first neurone releases neurotransmitter and only the second has receptors.

Sense organs are groups of receptor cells that respond to specific stimuli: light, sound, touch, temperature and chemicals. Part of eye Function Cornea Refracts (bends) light Iris Controls how much light enters the pupil Pupil Hole that lets light in Lens Focuses light onto the retina Retina Contains light receptors (rods and cones) Optic nerve Carries impulses to the brain Blind spot Where the optic nerve leaves; no receptors Pupil reflex: in bright light the pupil gets smaller; in dim light it gets larger. Supplement The iris contains two antagonistic muscles. In bright light the circular muscles contract and radial muscles relax , making the pupil narrower. In dim light the radial muscles contract and circular muscles relax, widening the pupil. Supplement Accommodation (focusing). Near object: ciliary muscles contract, suspensory ligaments slacken, lens becomes fatter (more convex). Distant object: ciliary muscles relax, suspensory ligaments tighten, lens is pulled thinner. Supplement Rods work in dim light and give black-and-white vision; they are spread across the retina. Cones give colour vision in bright light; there are three types, sensitive to different colours (red, green, blue). Cones are concentrated in the fovea , which gives the sharpest image.

Hormone: a chemical substance, produced by a gland and carried by the blood, which alters the activity of one or more specific target organs. Gland Hormone(s) Main effect Adrenal glands Adrenaline “Fight or flight”: increased breathing rate, heart rate and pupil diameter Pancreas Insulin (and glucagon) Controls blood glucose concentration Pituitary gland Several, e.g. FSH, LH Controls other glands Thyroid Thyroxine Controls metabolic rate Testes Testosterone Male secondary sexual characteristics Ovaries Oestrogen Female secondary sexual characteristics and menstrual cycle Supplement Adrenaline also increases blood glucose concentration , providing more glucose for respiration in muscles. Feature Nervous Hormonal Signal Electrical impulse Chemical Transmission Neurones Blood Speed Very fast Slower Duration Short-lived Longer-lasting Target Specific, localised Can affect several organs

Homeostasis: the maintenance of a constant internal environment. Supplement It works by negative feedback : when a condition moves away from the set point, changes are made to return it to the set point. Supplement Blood glucose control Blood glucose too high: the pancreas secretes insulin ; the liver and muscles convert glucose to glycogen , so blood glucose falls. Blood glucose too low: the pancreas secretes glucagon ; the liver converts glycogen to glucose, so blood glucose rises. Type 1 diabetes: the pancreas does not produce enough insulin. Symptoms include high blood glucose, glucose in urine, thirst, tiredness and weight loss. Treated by insulin injections , monitoring blood glucose and controlling carbohydrate intake. Temperature control Identify on a skin diagram: hairs, hair erector muscles, sweat glands, receptors, sensory neurones, blood vessels and fatty tissue. Fatty tissue insulates . Too hot Too cold Sweating: sweat evaporates, removing heat Shivering: muscles contract, releasing heat from respiration Supplement Vasodilation: arterioles near the skin widen, more blood flows near the surface, more heat lost Supplement Vasoconstriction: arterioles near the skin narrow, less blood near the surface, less heat lost Hair lies flat Hair erector muscles contract, hairs trap a layer of insulating air Supplement The brain monitors blood temperature and coordinates these responses.

Gravitropism: a response in which parts of a plant grow towards or away from gravity. Roots are positively gravitropic; shoots are negatively gravitropic. Phototropism: a response in which parts of a plant grow towards or away from the direction from which light is coming. Shoots are positively phototropic. Investigate using seedlings lit from one side, seedlings on their side, or a clinostat (which rotates to cancel the effect of gravity). Supplement Auxin is made in the shoot tip and diffuses down the shoot. In one-sided light it collects on the shaded side , where it stimulates cell elongation , so the shoot bends towards the light. Supplement Synthetic auxins such as 2,4-D are used as weedkillers: they cause uncontrolled growth in broad-leaved weeds. Model answer Explain how a shoot grows towards light coming from one side. [4] Auxin is produced in the shoot tip. It diffuses down the shoot and moves to the shaded side, so there is an unequal distribution of auxin. The higher auxin concentration on the shaded side stimulates cell elongation there. The shaded side grows faster, so the shoot bends towards the light. Examiner Tip For glucose control, name the organ (pancreas), the hormone (insulin or glucagon), the target (liver) and the conversion (glucose ↔ glycogen). Each is usually a separate mark. Common Mistake Mixing up glucagon (hormone) and glycogen (storage carbohydrate).
