Also, in vasodilation the blood vessels do not “move closer to the skin”: they widen, so more blood flows through the capillaries near the surface. Quick Checklist I can describe the CNS and PNS and trace a reflex arc from stimulus to response. I can describe how a synapse passes on an impulse in one direction. I can label the eye, explain the pupil reflex and describe accommodation. I can define a hormone and match glands to hormones, including the effects of adrenaline. I can compare nervous and hormonal control. I can explain blood glucose control by insulin and glucagon, and describe type 1 diabetes. I can explain temperature control by sweating, shivering, vasodilation and vasoconstriction. I can define gravitropism and phototropism and explain the role of auxin.

Topic 15 · Health Drugs What a drug is, how antibiotics treat bacterial infections, and how antibiotic resistance develops. A short topic, but the resistance explanation links to natural selection and is a common 4-mark question.

Drug: any substance taken into the body that modifies or affects chemical reactions in the body. Drugs can be medicinal (e.g. antibiotics, painkillers) or recreational. For this syllabus the focus is on antibiotics .

Used to treat Bacterial infections How they work Kill bacteria or stop them growing and reproducing Do not work on Viruses Example Penicillin (first discovered in a fungus) Antibiotics target structures and processes found in bacterial cells , such as the cell wall or bacterial enzymes and ribosomes. Because these targets are not found in human cells, the antibiotic can harm the bacteria without damaging the patient’s cells.

h: Supplement Why antibiotics do not affect viruses
x: Viruses are not cells: they have no cell wall, no ribosomes of their own and no metabolism. Viruses reproduce inside host cells , using the host’s own machinery. So there is nothing for an antibiotic to act on, and killing the virus would mean damaging the host cell. This is why antibiotics are not prescribed for colds or influenza.

Some bacteria are resistant to antibiotics. A well-known example is MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus), which is resistant to many common antibiotics and is hard to treat, especially in hospitals. 1 Variation A random mutation gives a few bacteria in a population resistance to an antibiotic. 2 Selection pressure When the antibiotic is used, non-resistant bacteria are killed. 3 Survival Resistant bacteria survive and have no competition. 4 Reproduction Survivors reproduce rapidly by binary fission, passing on the resistance allele. 5 Resistant population Over many generations the whole population becomes resistant, and the antibiotic no longer works. Reducing the development of resistant strains Use antibiotics only when essential , e.g. not for viral infections or minor infections the body can fight off. Complete the full course as prescribed, so that all the bacteria are killed and none are left to develop or spread resistance. Other helpful measures: reduce use of antibiotics in farming, good hygiene in hospitals to stop resistant strains spreading. Action Why it helps Not prescribing for viral infections Avoids exposing bacteria to antibiotics unnecessarily, so less selection for resistance Finishing the course Kills the less-susceptible bacteria that would survive a short course Hand washing and hospital hygiene Stops resistant bacteria passing between patients Model answer Explain how a population of bacteria can become resistant to an antibiotic. [4] A mutation causes some bacteria to be resistant to the antibiotic, so there is variation in the population. When the antibiotic is used, the non-resistant bacteria are killed but the resistant ones survive. The resistant bacteria reproduce and pass on the allele for resistance to their offspring. Over many generations the proportion of resistant bacteria increases until most of the population is resistant. Examiner Tip Say that the bacteria become resistant, not the person. “The patient becomes immune to the antibiotic” scores nothing. Use the natural selection words: mutation, variation, survive, reproduce, pass on allele. Common Mistake Writing that the antibiotic causes the mutation or that bacteria “learn” or “adapt” to the antibiotic. The resistance mutation arises randomly; the antibiotic only selects for it by killing the others. Quick Checklist I can define a drug in the Cambridge wording. I can state that antibiotics are used to treat bacterial infections. I can explain why antibiotics kill bacteria but do not affect viruses. I can give MRSA as an example of a resistant bacterium. I can explain how antibiotic resistance develops by natural selection. I can describe how to reduce the development of resistant strains.

Topic 16 · Reproduction Reproduction Asexual and sexual reproduction in plants and humans, from flowers and pollination to gametes, pregnancy, hormones and sexually transmitted infections. Diagrams of flowers and reproductive systems come up often, as do comparison questions.

Asexual reproduction: a process resulting in the production of genetically identical offspring from one parent. Examples: binary fission in bacteria, potato tubers, runners in strawberry plants, budding in yeast. Sexual reproduction: a process involving the fusion of the nuclei of two gametes to form a zygote and the production of offspring that are genetically different from each other. Fertilisation: the fusion of the nuclei of gametes. Gametes are haploid (one set of chromosomes); the zygote is diploid (two sets). Supplement Type Advantages Disadvantages Asexual Only one parent needed; fast; good traits kept; no energy spent finding a mate or making flowers No variation, so a whole population may be wiped out by a disease or environmental change; can lead to overcrowding Sexual Variation, so some offspring may survive changes; seeds can be dispersed widely Needs two parents (or pollination); slower; uses more energy Crop growers use asexual methods (e.g. cuttings) to keep desirable varieties, and sexual reproduction to breed new varieties.

Flower part Function Sepals Protect the flower bud Petals Often brightly coloured to attract insects Stamen (anther + filament) Male part; anther makes pollen, filament holds it up Carpel (stigma + style + ovary) Female part; stigma catches pollen, style links to the ovary Ovary / ovules Ovules contain the female gametes and become seeds; ovary becomes the fruit Pollination: the transfer of pollen grains from an anther to a stigma. Self-pollination: transfer to a stigma of the same flower or another flower on the same plant. Cross-pollination: transfer to a stigma of a flower on a different plant of the same species. Supplement Self-pollination gives less variation and depends less on pollinators; cross-pollination gives more variation, so the population is better able to adapt to change, but depends on insects or wind. Supplement After pollination a pollen tube grows down the style to an ovule, and the male nucleus fuses with the female nucleus (fertilisation). Feature Insect-pollinated Wind-pollinated Petals Large, brightly coloured, scented, often with nectar Small, dull or absent Anthers Inside the flower Hang outside on long filaments Stigma Inside, sticky Outside, feathery to catch pollen Pollen Larger, sticky or spiky, less produced Small, light, smooth, huge amounts Germination practical: seeds need water , oxygen and a suitable temperature . Test by setting up tubes of seeds with one condition missing each time (e.g. dry cotton wool, boiled water with an oil layer, a fridge) and comparing with a control that has all three.

Male part Function Female part Function Testes Make sperm and testosterone Ovaries Release eggs; make oestrogen and progesterone Scrotum Holds testes outside the body, slightly cooler Oviducts Carry the egg; site of fertilisation Sperm ducts Carry sperm to the urethra Uterus Where the fetus develops Prostate gland Adds fluid to make semen Cervix Ring of muscle at the base of the uterus Urethra Carries semen (and urine) out Vagina Receives sperm; birth canal Penis Places semen in the vagina Sperm adaptations: flagellum for swimming; many mitochondria to release energy; acrosome containing enzymes to digest through the jelly coat of the egg. Egg adaptations: energy stores in the cytoplasm; jelly coat that changes after fertilisation so only one sperm can enter. Supplement Compared with eggs, sperm are much smaller, made in far greater numbers, and are mobile (eggs are moved by cilia in the oviduct). Fertilisation and pregnancy 1 Fertilisation A sperm nucleus fuses with an egg nucleus in the oviduct, forming a zygote. 2 Embryo The zygote divides by mitosis into a ball of cells (an embryo). 3 Implantation The embryo implants into the lining of the uterus. 4 Fetus Once body systems are recognisable, the developing organism is called a fetus. Supplement The amniotic sac and amniotic fluid protect the fetus from bumps. Supplement The placenta exchanges materials between mother and fetus by diffusion: glucose, amino acids, oxygen, water and ions pass to the fetus; carbon dioxide and urea pass back to the mother. The maternal and fetal blood do not mix. Supplement The umbilical cord contains blood vessels that connect the fetus to the placenta. Supplement Some pathogens (e.g. rubella virus) and toxins (e.g. nicotine) can cross the placenta and harm the fetus.

Testosterone (testes) causes male secondary sexual characteristics at puberty: growth of facial and body hair, deeper voice, increased muscle, sperm production. Oestrogen (ovaries) causes female secondary sexual characteristics: breast development, wider hips, body hair, start of the menstrual cycle. The menstrual cycle lasts about 28 days: menstruation (days 1–5), uterus lining rebuilds, ovulation around day 14, lining maintained ready for implantation. Supplement Hormone Made in Role in the cycle FSH Pituitary gland Stimulates an egg to develop in a follicle; stimulates oestrogen production Oestrogen Ovaries Rebuilds the uterus lining LH Pituitary gland Triggers ovulation Progesterone Ovaries (corpus luteum) Maintains the uterus lining; a fall in progesterone causes menstruation

Sexually transmitted infection (STI): an infection that is transmitted through sexual contact. HIV is a virus that causes an STI; HIV infection may lead to AIDS . Transmitted by unprotected sex, sharing needles, infected blood, and from mother to baby. Control: using condoms, limiting sexual partners, testing and treatment, not sharing needles, screening blood. Model answer Describe how the structure of a sperm cell is adapted to its function. [3] A sperm has a flagellum so it can swim towards the egg. It contains many mitochondria, which release energy from respiration for swimming. It has an acrosome containing enzymes that digest the jelly coat so the sperm can enter the egg. Examiner Tip Keep pollination and fertilisation separate: pollination is pollen moving from anther to stigma; fertilisation is the fusion of nuclei inside the ovule. Many answers lose marks by using them as if they mean the same thing. Common Mistake Saying that the mother’s blood flows into the fetus. The two blood supplies stay separate; substances cross the placenta by diffusion. Also, antibodies can cross, but most cells cannot. Quick Checklist I can define asexual reproduction, sexual reproduction and fertilisation, and compare them. I can label a flower and compare insect- and wind-pollinated flowers. I can define pollination and describe self- and cross-pollination and pollen tube growth. I can describe an investigation of the conditions needed for germination. I can label the male and female reproductive systems and describe adaptations of sperm and egg. I can describe fertilisation, implantation and the roles of the placenta, umbilical cord and amniotic fluid. I can explain the roles of testosterone, oestrogen, FSH, LH and progesterone. I can define an STI and describe how HIV is spread and controlled.

Topic 17 · Genetics Inheritance How genetic information is stored, copied by mitosis and meiosis, and passed from parents to offspring. Genetic diagrams appear on almost every paper, so precise vocabulary and neat working earn easy marks.

Chromosome : a thread-like structure of DNA, carrying genetic information in the form of genes. Gene : a length of DNA that codes for a protein. Allele : an alternative form of a gene. Sex is determined by one pair of chromosomes: females are XX , males are XY . Every egg carries an X; half of sperm carry X and half carry Y, so there is a 50% chance of either sex at each fertilisation. Supplement Haploid nucleus : a nucleus containing a single set of chromosomes (e.g. gametes). Diploid nucleus : a nucleus containing two sets of chromosomes (e.g. body cells). In humans the diploid number is 46 (23 pairs); the haploid number is 23.

The sequence of bases in a gene determines the sequence of amino acids in a protein. Different sequences of amino acids give different shapes of protein, so different functions (e.g. enzyme active sites, antibodies, receptors). All body cells contain the same genes, but most cells express only some of them. A cell only makes the proteins it needs, which is why a muscle cell differs from a liver cell. 1 Transcription In the nucleus, the gene is copied into a messenger RNA (mRNA) molecule. DNA itself never leaves the nucleus. 2 mRNA leaves The mRNA moves out of the nucleus into the cytoplasm. 3 Ribosome reads mRNA The mRNA attaches to a ribosome, which reads the base sequence. 4 Amino acids assembled Amino acids are joined in the order coded by the mRNA to form the protein.

Mitosis : nuclear division giving rise to genetically identical cells. Used for growth , repair of damaged tissues, replacement of cells and asexual reproduction . Supplement Before mitosis, each chromosome is replicated (copied) so it consists of two identical strands. During mitosis the copies separate and move to opposite poles, so each daughter cell gets a full, identical set of chromosomes. Supplement Stem cells are unspecialised cells that divide by mitosis to produce daughter cells that can become specialised for specific functions. Supplement Uncontrolled cell division by mitosis can result in cancer .

Meiosis : a reduction division in which the chromosome number is halved from diploid to haploid, resulting in genetically different cells. Meiosis produces gametes (sperm, eggs, pollen nuclei, ovules). Halving the number means fertilisation restores the diploid number. The gametes are genetically different from each other, which is a source of variation . Feature Mitosis Meiosis Daughter cells Genetically identical Genetically different Chromosome number Stays the same (diploid → diploid) Halved (diploid → haploid) Where / when Growth, repair, asexual reproduction Gamete production in sex organs Number of cells made Two Four

Inheritance The transmission of genetic information from generation to generation Genotype The genetic make-up of an organism in terms of the alleles present (e.g. Tt) Phenotype The observable features of an organism (e.g. tall) Homozygous Having two identical alleles of a gene (TT or tt) Heterozygous Having two different alleles of a gene (Tt) Dominant An allele that is expressed if it is present (capital letter) Recessive An allele that is only expressed when there is no dominant allele (lower case) Pure-breeding Homozygous individuals that always produce offspring with the same phenotype Homozygous individuals only ever pass on one type of allele, so two identical homozygous parents are pure-breeding. Heterozygous individuals pass on either allele with equal probability. Laying out a genetic diagram 1 State the key e.g. T = allele for tall, t = allele for short. 2 Parental phenotypes and genotypes tall × tall; Tt × Tt. 3 Gametes Circle each: T and t from each parent. 4 Punnett square Combine gametes: TT, Tt, Tt, tt. 5 Offspring phenotypes and ratio 3 tall : 1 short (a 1 in 4, or 25%, chance of short). Heterozygous × heterozygous gives a 3 : 1 ratio of phenotypes. Heterozygous × homozygous recessive gives a 1 : 1 ratio. Pedigree diagrams show inheritance through a family. If two unaffected parents have an affected child, the condition must be recessive and both parents are heterozygous.

h: Supplement Test crosses, codominance and sex linkage
x: Test cross : cross the individual with the dominant phenotype (unknown genotype) with a homozygous recessive individual. All dominant offspring suggests homozygous dominant; any recessive offspring (roughly 1 : 1) shows it is heterozygous. Codominance : a situation in which both alleles in a heterozygous organism contribute to the phenotype. ABO blood groups : alleles I A and I B are codominant; I o is recessive to both. Group A = I A I A or I A I o ; group B = I B I B or I B I o ; group AB = I A I B ; group O = I o I o . Sex-linked characteristic : a feature in which the gene responsible is located on a sex chromosome, making it more common in one sex than the other. Red-green colour blindness is carried on the X chromosome. Write alleles as X N and X n . Males (X n Y) need only one recessive allele to be affected because the Y carries no copy; females need two, so a heterozygous female (X N X n ) is a carrier . Model answer Explain why red-green colour blindness is more common in males than in females. [3] The allele is recessive and carried on the X chromosome (sex-linked). Males have only one X chromosome and the Y chromosome does not carry the gene, so a single recessive allele causes colour blindness. Females have two X chromosomes, so they must inherit two recessive alleles; with one they are unaffected carriers. Examiner Tip Always give a key for your alleles, circle the gametes and finish with a clear statement of phenotypes with a ratio or probability. Marks are awarded for each stage, so a correct layout scores even if you slip on the final answer. Common Mistake Confusing gene and allele . Eye colour is controlled by a gene; “blue” and “brown” versions are alleles. Also, a 3 : 1 ratio is a probability, not a guarantee: a family of four children need not contain exactly one with the recessive phenotype. Quick Checklist I can define chromosome, gene, allele, genotype, phenotype, homozygous, heterozygous, dominant and recessive. I can explain how sex is inherited using X and Y chromosomes. I can compare mitosis and meiosis and state the role of each. I can draw a full genetic diagram and predict 3 : 1 and 1 : 1 ratios. I can interpret a pedigree diagram to decide if an allele is dominant or recessive. I can describe how the base sequence in DNA leads to a protein via mRNA and ribosomes (Supplement). I can use a test cross, codominance (ABO blood groups) and sex linkage in genetic diagrams (Supplement).

Topic 18 · Genetics Variation and Selection Why individuals of the same species differ, how features suit organisms to their habitats, and how natural and artificial selection change populations. Natural selection is a classic 4-6 mark sequence question, so learn the steps in order.

Variation : differences between individuals of the same species. Feature Continuous variation Discontinuous variation Pattern A range of phenotypes between two extremes A limited number of distinct phenotypes, no intermediates Examples Height, body mass, leaf length ABO blood group, seed shape in peas, tongue rolling Graph Histogram; often a smooth bell-shaped curve Bar chart with gaps between bars Supplement Cause Both genes and the environment; usually many genes Genes only; usually a single gene Genetic variation is inherited; environmental variation is caused by factors such as diet, light, temperature or accidents and is not passed on.

Mutation : genetic change. Gene mutation : a random change in the base sequence of DNA. Mutation is the way in which new alleles are formed. The rate of mutation is increased by ionising radiation (e.g. X-rays, gamma rays) and some chemicals (e.g. chemicals in tobacco smoke). Sources of genetic variation M utation M eiosis R andom mating R andom fertilisation Remember “MMRR”: new alleles come from mutation, meiosis produces genetically different gametes, and which individuals mate and which gametes fuse are both matters of chance.

Adaptive feature : an inherited feature that helps an organism to survive and reproduce in its environment. Supplement Adaptive features are the inherited functional features of an organism that increase its fitness . Supplement Fitness : the probability of an organism surviving and reproducing in the environment in which it is found. Supplement Plants in extreme water conditions Xerophytes (dry habitats, e.g. cactus, marram grass) Hydrophytes (in water, e.g. water lily) Thick waxy cuticle reduces evaporation Thin or absent cuticle; water loss is not a problem Leaves reduced to spines: small surface area for transpiration Large, flat floating leaves to capture light Sunken stomata or stomata in rolled leaves trap humid air Stomata on the upper surface of floating leaves Hairs trap a layer of moist air Air spaces (aerenchyma) keep leaves afloat and store oxygen Deep or widespread shallow roots; water storage tissue in stems Little xylem and small roots, as water surrounds the plant

1 Variation Individuals in a population show genetic variation. 2 Over-production More offspring are produced than the environment can support. 3 Competition Individuals compete for resources such as food, mates and space; there is a struggle for survival. 4 Survival of the best adapted Individuals with advantageous features are more likely to survive and reproduce. 5 Pass on alleles They pass on the alleles for these features to their offspring. 6 Change over generations The frequency of the advantageous allele increases in the population. Supplement Adaptation : the process, resulting from natural selection, by which populations become more suited to their environment over many generations.

A random mutation gives one bacterium an allele for resistance. When antibiotic is used, non-resistant bacteria are killed; the resistant bacterium survives. It reproduces rapidly by binary fission, passing the resistance allele on. The population becomes mostly resistant, e.g. MRSA. Reduce the risk: prescribe antibiotics only when needed (not for viral infections) and always finish the course. Model answer Explain how a population of bacteria can become resistant to an antibiotic. [4] A random mutation produces an allele that gives resistance to the antibiotic. When the antibiotic is used, bacteria without the allele are killed while resistant bacteria survive. The survivors reproduce and pass on the resistance allele to their offspring. Over many generations the proportion of resistant bacteria in the population increases.

Choose individuals with the desired feature (e.g. high milk yield, disease resistance, large fruit). Cross (breed) these individuals together. From the offspring, select those showing the feature most strongly. Repeat over many generations. Supplement Natural selection Selective breeding Who selects The environment Humans Features selected Those that increase survival and reproduction Those useful to humans Speed Slow; many generations Faster; stronger selection each generation Examiner Tip Use the word allele in natural-selection answers: “pass on the allele for resistance” scores; “pass on resistance” often does not. Key marking words are variation, competition, survive, reproduce, allele, generations. Common Mistake Writing that bacteria “become resistant because of the antibiotic” or “adapt to it”. The antibiotic does not cause the mutation; the mutation is random and already present. The antibiotic only selects which bacteria survive. Quick Checklist I can distinguish continuous and discontinuous variation with examples and graph types. I can define mutation and gene mutation and name factors that increase mutation rate. I can list the sources of genetic variation. I can define adaptive feature, and fitness (Supplement). I can describe adaptations of xerophytes and hydrophytes (Supplement). I can describe natural selection in sequence and apply it to antibiotic resistance. I can describe selective breeding and compare it with natural selection.

Topic 19 · Ecology Organisms and their Environment How energy flows and nutrients cycle through ecosystems, and what controls the size of populations. Expect food web interpretation, pyramid sketches, carbon and nitrogen cycle sequences and population curve analysis.

The Sun is the principal source of energy input to biological systems. Energy flows through living organisms: light energy is converted to chemical energy by photosynthesis, passed along food chains, and is eventually lost to the environment as heat. Energy is not recycled , unlike nutrients. Food chain Shows the transfer of energy from one organism to the next, beginning with a producer Food web A network of interconnected food chains Producer An organism that makes its own organic nutrients, usually using energy from sunlight, through photosynthesis Consumer An organism that gets its energy by feeding on other organisms Herbivore An animal that gets its energy by eating plants Carnivore An animal that gets its energy by eating other animals Decomposer An organism that gets its energy from dead or waste organic material Trophic level The position of an organism in a food chain or food web Consumers are classed as primary , secondary , tertiary and quaternary according to their position. Arrows point in the direction of energy flow (from the eaten to the eater). Removing or adding a species changes a food web: e.g. if a predator is removed, its prey may increase, then overgraze the producers. Ecological pyramids Pyramid What each bar shows Always pyramid-shaped? Numbers Number of organisms at each trophic level No: one oak tree supports thousands of caterpillars (inverted base) Biomass Dry mass of organisms at each level Usually; better than numbers because size is taken into account Supplement Energy Energy transferred at each level over time Always, because energy is lost at every transfer

Transfer between trophic levels is inefficient: only about 10% of energy is passed on. Energy is lost through respiration (released as heat), movement, excretion (urine, faeces) and parts that are not eaten (bones, roots, fur). This limits most food chains to fewer than five trophic levels. It is more energy-efficient for humans to eat crop plants than to eat livestock fed on crops, because a trophic level (and its energy losses) is removed, so more people can be fed per unit of land.

1 Photosynthesis Producers take CO 2 from the air and make carbohydrates. 2 Feeding Carbon compounds pass to consumers when they eat. 3 Respiration Plants, animals and decomposers release CO 2 back into the air. 4 Decomposition Decomposers break down dead organisms and waste, respiring and releasing CO 2 . 5 Fossilisation Where decay is prevented, remains form fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas) over millions of years. 6 Combustion Burning fossil fuels and wood releases CO 2 . Deforestation and combustion both raise atmospheric CO 2 : fewer trees remove CO 2 by photosynthesis, and burning or decaying wood adds CO 2 .

Nitrogen fixation : nitrogen-fixing bacteria (free-living in soil, or in root nodules of legumes such as peas and clover) convert N 2 gas into ammonium/nitrogen compounds. Lightning also fixes nitrogen. Absorption : plants take up nitrate ions by active transport through root hairs and use them to make amino acids and then proteins. Feeding : animals obtain proteins by eating, digest them to amino acids and build their own proteins. Deamination : excess amino acids are broken down in the liver to urea, which is excreted. Decomposition : decomposers break down proteins in dead organisms and urea into ammonium ions . Nitrification : nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium ions to nitrite and then to nitrate ions (needs oxygen, e.g. well-drained soil). Denitrification : denitrifying bacteria convert nitrate back to N 2 gas (in waterlogged, anaerobic soil). Model answer Explain the roles of microorganisms in recycling nitrogen from a dead animal into a form a plant can absorb. [4] Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down the proteins in the dead animal and release ammonium ions. Nitrifying bacteria oxidise the ammonium ions to nitrite ions and then to nitrate ions. The plant absorbs the nitrate ions through its root hair cells by active transport and uses them to make amino acids and proteins.

Population A group of organisms of one species, living in the same area, at the same time Community All of the populations of different species in an ecosystem Ecosystem A unit containing the community of organisms and their environment, interacting together Factors affecting the rate of population growth: food supply , competition , predation and disease . Sigmoid population growth curve (e.g. yeast in a flask) 1 Lag phase Slow growth: few individuals, adjusting to conditions and producing enzymes before reproducing. 2 Exponential (log) phase Plenty of food and space, little competition; birth rate far exceeds death rate, so numbers double repeatedly. 3 Stationary phase Limiting factors (food shortage, competition, build-up of toxic waste, disease) mean birth rate equals death rate. 4 Death phase Food runs out and toxic waste accumulates; death rate exceeds birth rate. Supplement Be ready to explain each phase in terms of birth rate versus death rate and the limiting factors acting at that time. Examiner Tip In the nitrogen cycle, name the type of bacteria and the ions precisely: “nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium ions to nitrate ions”. Vague answers such as “bacteria turn it into nitrogen” score nothing. Common Mistake Saying energy is “used up” or “recycled”. Energy is transferred and eventually lost as heat to the surroundings; it is nutrients such as carbon and nitrogen that are recycled. Quick Checklist I can define food chain, food web, producer, consumer, herbivore, carnivore, decomposer and trophic level. I can construct and interpret pyramids of numbers and biomass, and energy (Supplement). I can explain why energy transfer is inefficient and why eating plants feeds more people (Supplement). I can describe the carbon cycle including photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, fossilisation and combustion. I can describe the nitrogen cycle and the roles of the different bacteria (Supplement). I can define population, community and ecosystem. I can identify and explain the phases of a sigmoid population growth curve.

Topic 20 · Biotechnology Biotechnology and Genetic Modification How microorganisms and enzymes are used to make food, fuel and medicines, and how genes can be moved between organisms. Questions often ask you to apply enzyme and respiration knowledge to an industrial setting or to sequence the steps of genetic modification.

They reproduce rapidly , so large populations are grown quickly. They can make complex molecules (e.g. proteins such as insulin, antibiotics). Supplement There are few ethical concerns over their manipulation and growth. Supplement They contain plasmids (small circular loops of DNA), which are easily cut and used as vectors to carry genes. Supplement The genetic code is shared by all organisms, so bacteria can read a human gene and make the human protein.

Application What is used How it works Biofuels Yeast Anaerobic respiration of sugars (e.g. from maize or sugar cane) produces ethanol, used as a fuel Bread-making Yeast Respiration releases CO 2 , which makes dough rise; ethanol evaporates during baking Fruit juice Pectinase Breaks down pectin in plant cell walls, increasing juice yield and making it clearer Biological washing powders Proteases, lipases, amylases Digest protein, fat and starch stains into small soluble molecules that wash away; work at lower temperatures, saving energy Supplement Lactose-free milk Lactase Breaks lactose into glucose and galactose for people who are lactose intolerant Word equation for anaerobic respiration in yeast: glucose → alcohol (ethanol) + carbon dioxide.

Fermenters are large vessels used to grow microorganisms on a large scale to make products such as insulin (from GM bacteria), penicillin (from the fungus Penicillium) and mycoprotein (a fungal protein food). Temperature Water jacket removes heat from respiration; keeps enzymes at optimum pH Probe monitors; acid or alkali added to keep optimum for enzymes Oxygen Sterile air bubbled in for aerobic respiration Nutrient supply Glucose and amino acids supplied for growth Waste products Removed, e.g. CO 2 vented, to avoid toxic build-up Mixing and sterility Paddles stir contents; steam sterilisation prevents contamination

Genetic modification : changing the genetic material of an organism by removing, changing or inserting individual genes. Examples Insertion of the human insulin gene into bacteria to produce human insulin for people with diabetes. Insertion of genes into crop plants to give resistance to herbicides (weedkiller can be sprayed without killing the crop). Insertion of genes into crop plants to give resistance to insect pests (e.g. plants that make a toxin harmful to caterpillars). Insertion of genes to give crops additional vitamins (e.g. rice producing beta-carotene, a source of vitamin A).

h: Supplement Making human insulin with bacteria
x: 1 Isolate the gene The human insulin gene is cut from DNA using a restriction enzyme, leaving single-stranded “sticky ends”. 2 Cut the plasmid A bacterial plasmid is cut with the same restriction enzyme, producing complementary sticky ends. 3 Insert the gene The gene and plasmid are joined at their sticky ends by DNA ligase, forming a recombinant plasmid. 4 Insert into bacteria Recombinant plasmids are taken up by bacteria. 5 Replicate and express The bacteria multiply in a fermenter; each copy expresses the gene and makes human insulin, which is extracted and purified. Model answer Explain why the same restriction enzyme is used to cut both the human DNA and the plasmid. [3] A restriction enzyme cuts DNA at a specific base sequence, leaving sticky ends. Using the same enzyme gives the gene and the opened plasmid complementary sticky ends. These bases pair up so that DNA ligase can join the gene into the plasmid to form a recombinant plasmid. Supplement GM crops: evaluating the issues Advantages Disadvantages Higher yields; less crop lost to pests or weeds Seeds can be expensive; farmers may need to buy new seed each year Less insecticide sprayed, saving money and harming fewer non-target insects Pests may evolve resistance to the toxin; beneficial insects may be harmed Improved nutritional value (e.g. vitamin-enriched rice) Transferred genes could spread to wild relatives, e.g. herbicide-resistant weeds Crops can grow in poorer conditions Reduced biodiversity if monocultures expand; some public concern about safety Examiner Tip Name the enzymes: restriction enzyme cuts, DNA ligase joins. Always mention “sticky ends” and “recombinant plasmid” — these are the key words in the mark scheme. Common Mistake Saying the enzymes in biological washing powder “kill” or “eat” the stains, or that pectinase “digests the fruit”. Enzymes are not alive: they catalyse the breakdown of large insoluble molecules (protein, fat, starch, pectin) into smaller soluble ones. Also remember very hot washes denature the enzymes. Quick Checklist I can state why bacteria are useful in biotechnology and genetic modification. I can describe the use of yeast in biofuel and bread production. I can explain how pectinase, biological washing powders and lactase (Supplement) work. I can describe the conditions controlled in a fermenter and why (Supplement). I can define genetic modification and give examples in bacteria and crops. I can outline the steps in producing human insulin using restriction enzymes, plasmids and ligase (Supplement). I can discuss advantages and disadvantages of GM crops (Supplement).

Topic 21 · Ecology Human Influences on Ecosystems How food production, habitat destruction and pollution affect ecosystems, and how species and resources can be conserved. Eutrophication and deforestation are favourite extended-answer questions.

Modern technology has greatly increased food production through: Agricultural machinery to farm larger areas more efficiently. Chemical fertilisers to improve yields by supplying mineral ions (nitrate, phosphate, potassium). Insecticides to kill insect pests and herbicides to kill weeds that compete with crops. Selective breeding to improve crop and livestock yields. Negative impacts of large-scale farming Monocultures (one crop over a large area) Intensive livestock production Reduced biodiversity; habitats such as hedgerows removed Large amounts of waste can pollute water Pests and diseases spread easily, so more pesticide is used Disease spreads quickly in crowded animals; overuse of antibiotics Soil loses nutrients, so more fertiliser is needed Animal welfare concerns Pesticides may kill non-target species Cattle release methane; land cleared for grazing and feed crops Supplement Famine and food shortage have social, economic and environmental causes: increasing human population, unequal distribution of food, poverty, war, drought, flooding, climate change, pests, and poor transport or storage.

Reasons Increased area needed for food crops, livestock and housing. Extraction of natural resources (e.g. mining, logging). Freshwater and marine pollution. Humans alter food webs by removing species or introducing new ones, which can cause populations of other species to rise or fall. Undesirable effects of deforestation E xtinction L oss of soil F looding C arbon dioxide increase Extinction and loss of biodiversity as habitats are destroyed. Loss of soil : without roots to hold it, soil is eroded by rain; nutrients are leached out. Flooding : less water is absorbed and transpired, so runoff increases. Increase of CO 2 in the atmosphere: less photosynthesis, and burning or decomposing trees release CO 2 .

Plastics are non-biodegradable, so they persist. In water they entangle or are swallowed by animals (e.g. turtles, seabirds), and break into microplastics that enter food chains. On land they litter habitats and release toxic chemicals when burned. Untreated sewage and excess fertiliser entering water cause eutrophication. Supplement Female contraceptive hormones in sewage enter rivers and can cause feminisation of male fish (reduced fertility) and may contribute to reduced sperm counts in men. Supplement Eutrophication 1 Nutrients added Fertiliser or sewage runs into water, increasing nitrate and phosphate ions. 2 Algal growth Rapid growth of algae and producers (an algal bloom) on the surface. 3 Light blocked Light cannot reach plants lower down, so they cannot photosynthesise and die. 4 Decomposers increase More dead organic matter; populations of aerobic bacteria (decomposers) increase. 5 Oxygen falls Decomposers use up dissolved oxygen in aerobic respiration. 6 Animals die Fish and other aerobic organisms die from lack of oxygen. The enhanced greenhouse effect Carbon dioxide (from combustion and deforestation) and methane (from cattle, rice paddies, landfill) are greenhouse gases. They absorb and re-radiate infrared (heat) energy that would otherwise escape from the Earth, warming the atmosphere. Increasing levels cause climate change : rising sea levels, melting ice, more extreme weather, changes in species distribution. Model answer Explain why fish die in a lake after fertiliser runs off nearby fields. [4] Nitrate and phosphate ions from the fertiliser cause rapid growth of algae. The algae block light, so plants below cannot photosynthesise and die. Decomposing bacteria feed on the dead plants and their population increases. The bacteria respire aerobically and use up the dissolved oxygen, so fish die from lack of oxygen.

Sustainable resource : one which is produced as rapidly as it is removed from the environment so that it does not run out. Some resources, such as fossil fuels , cannot be replaced; others, such as forests and fish stocks, can be conserved. Resource Conservation methods Forests Replanting after felling; selective felling rather than clear-felling; education; legal protection Fish stocks Quotas; closed seasons; controls on net mesh size; protected areas; monitoring; fish farming; education Materials Recycling paper, plastic, glass and metal; treating sewage so water can be reused Endangered species Species become endangered or extinct because of climate change , habitat destruction , hunting , overharvesting , pollution and introduced species . Conservation methods: monitoring and protecting species and habitats, education, captive breeding programmes and seed banks. Supplement Deeper conservation points Sustainable development : development providing for the needs of an increasing human population without harming the environment; it requires cooperation between local, national and international groups. A population that becomes very small has reduced genetic variation , so it is less able to adapt to change (e.g. new disease) and is at greater risk of extinction. Captive breeding may use artificial insemination and in vitro fertilisation (IVF) , and may move animals between zoos to increase genetic variation. Reasons for conservation: reduce extinction, protect vulnerable environments, and maintain ecosystem functions such as nutrient cycling and resource provision (food, drugs, fuel and genes). Examiner Tip In eutrophication answers, it is the bacteria (decomposers) respiring that use up the oxygen, not the algae. Say “dissolved oxygen” and “aerobic respiration” to secure the mark. Common Mistake Confusing the greenhouse effect with ozone depletion, or saying greenhouse gases “trap the Sun’s rays”. They absorb the infrared radiation emitted by the warmed Earth; the natural greenhouse effect is essential for life, and it is the enhanced effect that causes climate change. Quick Checklist I can describe how machinery, fertilisers, pesticides and selective breeding increase food production. I can explain the negative effects of monocultures and intensive livestock farming. I can list reasons for habitat destruction and the effects of deforestation. I can describe the effects of plastics and the enhanced greenhouse effect. I can explain eutrophication step by step and the effects of contraceptive hormones in water (Supplement). I can define sustainable resource and describe how forests and fish stocks are conserved. I can explain why species become endangered, and why small populations and conservation programmes matter (Supplement).

Topic 1 · Particles & Structure States of Matter How the arrangement, movement and energy of particles explain the properties of solids, liquids and gases, and why substances change state or spread out by diffusion. These ideas underpin almost every later topic, and examiners reward precise particle language.

All matter is made of tiny particles (atoms, molecules or ions). The kinetic particle theory says these particles are always moving, and the amount of movement depends on how much kinetic energy they have. Property Solid Liquid Gas Shape Fixed shape Takes the shape of the container Fills the whole container Volume Fixed volume Fixed volume No fixed volume Compressibility Cannot be compressed Almost impossible to compress Easily compressed Arrangement Regular, closely packed (lattice) Irregular, close together Random, far apart Motion Vibrate about fixed positions Move around (slide past) each other Move quickly and randomly in all directions Forces between particles Strong Weaker than in solids Very weak / negligible Energy of particles Lowest Intermediate Highest A rrangement M otion S eparation F orces — describe all four for any state and you will pick up the marks.

Changes of state are physical changes : no new substance is made and they are reversible. Melting Solid → liquid, at the melting point Freezing Liquid → solid, at the same temperature as melting Boiling Liquid → gas throughout the liquid, at the boiling point Evaporation Liquid → gas at the surface only, below the boiling point Condensation Gas → liquid on cooling Sublimation Solid → gas directly (e.g. solid CO 2 , iodine) Explaining changes of state with particles Melting: heating gives particles more kinetic energy; they vibrate more until they overcome some of the forces holding them in fixed positions and can move past each other. Boiling: particles gain enough energy to overcome the attractive forces between them completely and escape as a gas; bubbles of gas form throughout the liquid. Evaporation: only the most energetic particles at the surface escape, so it can happen at any temperature. It is faster when the liquid is warmer, has a larger surface area, or when air moves over it. Condensing and freezing: particles lose kinetic energy, slow down and the attractive forces pull them closer together. Common Mistake Do not say particles themselves “expand”, “melt” or “get bigger” when heated. The particles stay the same size; it is the spacing and movement that change. Also avoid saying bonds break when a simple molecular substance boils — it is the forces between molecules that are overcome.

If a pure solid is heated steadily and its temperature is recorded against time, the graph shows sloping sections and flat sections. 1 Solid warming up Temperature rises; particles vibrate faster. 2 Flat section at melting point Temperature stays constant. Energy supplied is used to overcome forces of attraction between particles, not to raise kinetic energy. Solid and liquid are both present. 3 Liquid warming up Temperature rises again; particles move faster. 4 Flat section at boiling point Temperature constant while energy overcomes the remaining attractive forces. Liquid and gas both present. This plateau is longer than the melting one because more energy is needed. 5 Gas warming up Temperature rises as gas particles move faster. A cooling curve is the reverse: the flat sections occur at the boiling (condensing) point and freezing point, where energy is released as forces of attraction form, so the temperature stays constant. A pure substance melts and boils at a sharp, fixed temperature. An impure substance melts over a range and at a lower temperature, and boils at a higher temperature. Examiner Tip For the flat sections, the credited explanation is that energy is used to overcome the forces of attraction between particles (or is released as these forces form during cooling). Simply writing “the substance is changing state” describes but does not explain.

h: Supplement Effect of temperature and pressure on the volume of a gas
x: Increasing temperature (at constant pressure): particles gain kinetic energy, move faster and hit the container walls harder and more often, so the gas expands — volume increases. Increasing pressure (at constant temperature): particles are pushed closer together, so the volume decreases . Gases can be compressed because there is lots of space between particles. In a sealed container of fixed volume, raising the temperature increases the pressure , because particles collide with the walls more frequently and with more force.

Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, as a result of their random motion. It happens in gases and liquids (very slowly in liquids) but not noticeably in solids. Evidence for diffusion A purple crystal of potassium manganate(VII) placed in water: the colour slowly spreads through all the water without stirring. A smell (e.g. perfume) spreads across a room. Bromine gas in a gas jar spreads upwards into a jar of air above it until the brown colour is even throughout.

h: Supplement Effect of relative molecular mass on rate of diffusion
x: At the same temperature, gas particles with a lower relative molecular mass (M r ) move faster on average, so they diffuse faster . Higher temperature also increases the rate of diffusion because all particles move faster. The ammonia and hydrogen chloride experiment 1 Set up Place cotton wool soaked in concentrated ammonia solution at one end of a long glass tube, and cotton wool soaked in concentrated hydrochloric acid at the other. Seal both ends with bungs. 2 Observe After a few minutes a white ring (smoke) of ammonium chloride forms inside the tube: NH 3 (g) + HCl(g) → NH 4 Cl(s) 3 Conclude The ring forms closer to the HCl end. NH 3 (M r = 17) has a lower M r than HCl (M r = 36.5), so ammonia molecules move faster and travel further in the same time. Model answer In the experiment above, explain why the white solid forms nearer to the hydrochloric acid end of the tube. [3] Both gases diffuse along the tube by the random movement of their particles. Ammonia has a lower relative molecular mass (17) than hydrogen chloride (36.5), so ammonia molecules move faster at the same temperature. Ammonia therefore travels further along the tube before the two gases meet and react to form ammonium chloride, so the ring is closer to the hydrochloric acid end. Common Mistake Writing that ammonia is “lighter” or “less dense” is too vague. Use the term lower relative molecular mass and link it to the particles moving faster . Quick Checklist I can describe the arrangement, motion and forces of particles in solids, liquids and gases. I can name and explain melting, boiling, evaporating, freezing and condensing using kinetic particle theory. I can explain the difference between boiling and evaporation. I can interpret heating and cooling curves and explain the flat sections (Supplement). I can explain how temperature and pressure affect the volume of a gas (Supplement). I can define diffusion and give evidence for it. I can explain how relative molecular mass affects the rate of diffusion using the NH 3 /HCl experiment (Supplement).

Topic 2 · Particles & Structure Atoms, Elements and Compounds What atoms are made of, how electrons are arranged, and how atoms join by ionic, covalent and metallic bonding. Structure and bonding questions appear on every paper, and explaining properties from structure is a favourite source of 3–4 mark questions.

Element A substance made of only one type of atom Compound A substance made of two or more elements chemically combined Mixture Two or more substances not chemically combined A compound has different properties from the elements it contains and a fixed composition; it can only be separated by a chemical reaction. A mixture keeps the properties of its components and can be separated by physical methods (filtration, distillation, chromatography).

An atom has a tiny central nucleus containing protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons in shells. Particle Relative charge Relative mass Location Proton +1 1 Nucleus Neutron 0 1 Nucleus Electron −1 1/1840 (negligible) Shells around the nucleus Proton number (atomic number, Z): the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom. Mass number (nucleon number, A): the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom. Number of neutrons = mass number − proton number. Atoms are neutral, so number of electrons = number of protons. Notation: 23 11 Na has 11 protons, 11 electrons and 12 neutrons. Electronic configuration (first 20 elements) Shells fill in order: first shell holds up to 2, second up to 8, third up to 8 (for elements 1–20). Examples: C 2,4; O 2,6; Na 2,8,1; Cl 2,8,7; Ca 2,8,8,2. The number of occupied shells = the period number . The number of outer-shell electrons = the group number (Groups I–VII). Noble gases (Group VIII) have a full outer shell , which makes them unreactive. Helium has 2 outer electrons; the others have 8.

Isotopes are different atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Example: 35 17 Cl (18 neutrons) and 37 17 Cl (20 neutrons). Isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties. Supplement This is because they have the same number of electrons in their outer shell (the same electronic configuration), and chemical reactions involve electrons. Supplement Calculating relative atomic mass Relative atomic mass (A r ) is the weighted average mass of the isotopes of an element, using their relative abundances. Worked example Chlorine is 75% chlorine-35 and 25% chlorine-37. Calculate A r . A r = (35 × 75 + 37 × 25) ÷ 100 = (2625 + 925) ÷ 100 = 3550 ÷ 100 = 35.5

An ion is a charged particle formed when an atom gains or loses electrons. Cations are positive ions, formed when atoms (usually metals) lose electrons. Anions are negative ions, formed when atoms (usually non-metals) gain electrons. An ionic bond is a strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. Ionic bonds form between metals and non-metals. Electrons are transferred from the metal to the non-metal so both gain a full outer shell (noble gas configuration). 1 Sodium atom, Na 2,8,1 Loses its one outer electron to become Na + (2,8). 2 Chlorine atom, Cl 2,8,7 Gains that electron to become Cl − (2,8,8). 3 Dot-and-cross diagram Draw the ions in square brackets with the charge outside the top right; show the transferred electron as a cross among the dots of the chloride ion. Usually only outer shells need to be shown. Core: dot-and-cross diagrams for Group I metals with Group VII non-metals (e.g. NaCl, KBr). Supplement Dot-and-cross diagrams for other metal/non-metal combinations, e.g. MgO (Mg 2+ and O 2− , two electrons transferred) and CaCl 2 (one Ca 2+ and two Cl − ). Supplement An ionic compound has a giant lattice structure : a regular arrangement of alternating positive and negative ions, e.g. sodium chloride. Properties of ionic compounds High melting and boiling points. Good electrical conductivity when molten or in aqueous solution; poor when solid. Supplement Explanation: many strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions in the giant lattice need a lot of energy to overcome. When solid the ions are held in fixed positions; when molten or dissolved the ions are free to move and carry charge.

A covalent bond forms when a pair of electrons is shared between two atoms, giving each a noble gas electronic configuration. Covalent bonding occurs between non-metal atoms. Core dot-and-cross diagrams: H 2 , Cl 2 , H 2 O, CH 4 , NH 3 , HCl. Supplement Also: CH 3 OH, C 2 H 4 (one C=C double bond), O 2 (double bond), CO 2 (two C=O double bonds), N 2 (triple bond). Properties of simple molecular substances Low melting and boiling points (many are gases or liquids at room temperature). Poor electrical conductivity: there are no ions or free electrons to carry charge. Supplement Explanation: the covalent bonds within molecules are strong, but the intermolecular forces (attractive forces between molecules) are weak, so little energy is needed to separate the molecules. Larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces and higher boiling points. Common Mistake Saying water has a low boiling point because “covalent bonds are weak” loses the mark. Covalent bonds are strong; it is the weak forces between molecules that are overcome on boiling.

Feature Diamond Graphite Bonding per carbon Each C covalently bonded to 4 others, tetrahedral Each C covalently bonded to 3 others in flat hexagonal layers Between layers No layers; 3D network Weak forces between layers Hardness Very hard Soft and slippery; layers slide over each other Electrical conductivity Does not conduct (no free electrons) Conducts: one delocalised electron per carbon, free to move along layers Melting point Very high Very high Uses Cutting tools, drill tips Lubricant, electrodes Both have very high melting points because many strong covalent bonds must be broken. Supplement Silicon(IV) oxide, SiO 2 , has a giant covalent structure similar to diamond: each Si is bonded to 4 O atoms and each O to 2 Si atoms. It is hard, has a very high melting point and does not conduct electricity.

Metallic bonding is the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions and a “sea” of delocalised electrons. Good electrical conductivity: the delocalised electrons are free to move through the structure and carry charge. Malleable and ductile: the layers of positive ions can slide over each other without breaking the metallic bonding, because the delocalised electrons still hold them together. Examiner Tip When explaining conductivity always name the mobile charge carrier : ions for molten or dissolved ionic compounds, delocalised electrons for metals and graphite. Never say ions move in a metal or electrons move in an electrolyte. Model answer Explain why sodium chloride conducts electricity when molten but not when solid. [3] Sodium chloride is made of Na + and Cl − ions held in a giant ionic lattice. In the solid, the ions are held in fixed positions by strong electrostatic attractions and cannot move. When molten, the lattice breaks down and the ions are free to move, so they can carry charge through the liquid. Quick Checklist I can define element, compound and mixture and state the particles in an atom with their charges and masses. I can define proton number, mass number and isotopes, and work out electronic configurations for elements 1–20. I can calculate relative atomic mass from isotope abundances (Supplement). I can draw dot-and-cross diagrams for ionic compounds and simple covalent molecules. I can explain the properties of ionic and simple molecular substances from their structure. I can compare diamond and graphite and describe SiO 2 (Supplement). I can describe metallic bonding and explain conductivity and malleability (Supplement).

Topic 3 · Quantitative Chemistry Stoichiometry Writing formulae and balanced equations, and using relative masses and the mole to calculate amounts of substances. Calculation questions carry many marks on the Extended paper, and method marks are awarded for clear working even if the final answer is wrong.

The molecular formula is the number and type of different atoms in one molecule, e.g. C 2 H 6 for ethane. Supplement The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of the different atoms or ions in a compound, e.g. CH 3 for ethane. You should be able to deduce a formula from a diagram or model by counting each type of atom. Ionic formulae come from ion charges: the total positive charge must equal the total negative charge. Positive ions Negative ions Na + , K + , H + , NH 4 + , Ag + Cl − , Br − , OH − , NO 3 − Mg 2+ , Ca 2+ , Cu 2+ , Zn 2+ , Fe 2+ O 2− , S 2− , SO 4 2− , CO 3 2− Al 3+ , Fe 3+ N 3− , PO 4 3− Examples: Al 3+ + O 2− gives Al 2 O 3 ; Ca 2+ + NO 3 − gives Ca(NO 3 ) 2 . Roman numerals give the charge: iron(III) chloride is FeCl 3 .

1 Word equation magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen 2 Correct formulae Mg + HCl → MgCl 2 + H 2 (never change a formula to balance) 3 Balance with big numbers in front Mg + 2HCl → MgCl 2 + H 2 4 Add state symbols Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl 2 (aq) + H 2 (g). (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) dissolved in water. Supplement Ionic equations show only the ions that change; spectator ions are left out. Neutralisation: H + (aq) + OH − (aq) → H 2 O(l). Precipitation: Ag + (aq) + Cl − (aq) → AgCl(s). You may be asked to deduce a balanced equation from information given in words, including state symbols.

Relative atomic mass, A r : the average mass of the isotopes of an element compared to 1/12th of the mass of an atom of carbon-12. Relative molecular mass, M r : the sum of the relative atomic masses of all the atoms in a molecule. The same term (relative formula mass) is used for ionic compounds. Example: M r of CaCO 3 = 40 + 12 + (3 × 16) = 100. Relative masses have no units . Calculate reacting masses in simple proportions, e.g. if 100 g CaCO 3 gives 56 g CaO, then 25 g gives 14 g. Mass is conserved in reactions.
Concentration can be measured in g/dm 3 or mol/dm 3 . 1 dm 3 = 1000 cm 3 ; divide cm 3 by 1000 to convert to dm 3 .

h: Supplement The mole and the Avogadro constant
x: The mole (mol) is the unit of amount of substance. One mole contains 6.02 × 10 23 particles (the Avogadro constant ). The mass of one mole of a substance in grams equals its A r or M r (the molar mass, in g/mol). Moles from mass amount (mol) = mass (g) ÷ molar mass (g/mol) Gas volume at r.t.p. amount (mol) = volume (dm 3 ) ÷ 24 Solutions amount (mol) = concentration (mol/dm 3 ) × volume (dm 3 ) Particles number = amount (mol) × 6.02 × 10 23 Molar gas volume 24 dm 3 (24 000 cm 3 ) at room temperature and pressure g/dm 3 ↔ mol/dm 3 g/dm 3 = mol/dm 3 × M r Reacting masses and gas volumes Worked example What mass of calcium oxide forms when 20.0 g of calcium carbonate is heated? What volume of CO 2 is produced at r.t.p.? CaCO 3 (s) → CaO(s) + CO 2 (g) Moles CaCO 3 = 20.0 ÷ 100 = 0.200 mol Mole ratio CaCO 3 : CaO : CO 2 = 1 : 1 : 1 Mass CaO = 0.200 × 56 = 11.2 g Volume CO 2 = 0.200 × 24 = 4.80 dm 3 Limiting reactant The limiting reactant is the one that is completely used up; it controls the amount of product. The other reactant is in excess . Worked example 2.4 g of magnesium is added to 0.10 mol of hydrochloric acid. Which reactant is limiting, and what mass of MgCl 2 forms? Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl 2 (aq) + H 2 (g) Moles Mg = 2.4 ÷ 24 = 0.10 mol 0.10 mol Mg needs 0.20 mol HCl, but only 0.10 mol is present So HCl is limiting; Mg is in excess Moles MgCl 2 = 0.10 ÷ 2 = 0.050 mol Mass MgCl 2 = 0.050 × 95 = 4.75 g Titration calculations Worked example 25.0 cm 3 of sodium hydroxide solution is neutralised by 20.0 cm 3 of 0.100 mol/dm 3 sulfuric acid. Find the concentration of the NaOH. H 2 SO 4 (aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na 2 SO 4 (aq) + 2H 2 O(l) Moles H 2 SO 4 = 0.100 × (20.0 ÷ 1000) = 0.00200 mol Moles NaOH = 2 × 0.00200 = 0.00400 mol Concentration NaOH = 0.00400 ÷ (25.0 ÷ 1000) = 0.160 mol/dm 3 Empirical and molecular formulae Worked example A hydrocarbon contains 85.7% carbon and 14.3% hydrogen by mass. Its M r is 56. Find its empirical and molecular formulae. C: 85.7 ÷ 12 = 7.14; H: 14.3 ÷ 1 = 14.3 Divide by smallest: C = 7.14 ÷ 7.14 = 1; H = 14.3 ÷ 7.14 = 2 Empirical formula = CH 2 (mass 14) 56 ÷ 14 = 4 Molecular formula = C 4 H 8 Percentage yield, composition and purity Percentage yield = (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100 Percentage composition by mass of an element = (total A r of that element in the formula ÷ M r ) × 100 Percentage purity = (mass of pure substance ÷ mass of impure sample) × 100 Worked example In the calcium carbonate example above, only 9.8 g of CaO was collected. Calculate the percentage yield. Theoretical yield = 11.2 g Percentage yield = (9.8 ÷ 11.2) × 100 = 87.5% Examiner Tip Use the mole-ratio step every time: moles of known → ratio from the balanced equation → moles of unknown → convert. Write units on every line and keep 3 significant figures unless told otherwise; rounding too early is a common way to lose the final mark. Common Mistake Forgetting to convert cm 3 to dm 3 before using concentration or the 24 dm 3 molar volume. Another frequent error is ignoring the mole ratio (e.g. treating H 2 SO 4 : NaOH as 1 : 1 instead of 1 : 2). Quick Checklist I can write formulae of ionic compounds from ion charges and define molecular and empirical formula. I can write balanced symbol equations with state symbols, and ionic equations (Supplement). I can define A r and M r and calculate M r from a formula. I can convert between g/dm 3 and mol/dm 3 and between cm 3 and dm 3 . I can use the mole, the Avogadro constant and the molar gas volume in calculations (Supplement). I can identify a limiting reactant and carry out titration calculations (Supplement). I can calculate empirical formula, molecular formula, percentage yield, composition and purity (Supplement).

Topic 4 · Physical Chemistry Electrochemistry How electricity decomposes ionic compounds, how to predict the products at each electrode, and how electroplating and hydrogen–oxygen fuel cells work. Examiners regularly ask for products, observations and, on the Extended paper, ionic half-equations.

Electrolysis is the decomposition of an ionic compound, when molten or in aqueous solution, by the passage of an electric current. Electrolyte The molten or aqueous ionic compound that conducts and is decomposed Cathode Negative electrode; attracts cations Anode Positive electrode; attracts anions Inert electrodes Graphite (carbon) or platinum; do not react External circuit Wires and power supply connecting the electrodes PANIC : P ositive A node, N egative I s C athode. OIL RIG : O xidation I s L oss, R eduction I s G ain of electrons.

h: Supplement Transfer of charge during electrolysis
x: 1 External circuit Electrons move through the wires from the anode to the cathode, pushed by the power supply. 2 Electrolyte Ions move: cations towards the cathode, anions towards the anode. Ions, not electrons, carry the current in the electrolyte. 3 At the cathode Cations gain electrons (reduction). 4 At the anode Anions lose electrons (oxidation), and these electrons enter the external circuit.

Molten binary compound (two elements, inert electrodes): the metal forms at the cathode and the non-metal at the anode. In general, metals or hydrogen form at the cathode and non-metals (other than hydrogen) form at the anode. Aqueous solutions also contain H + and OH − ions from water. At the cathode: hydrogen forms if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen; the metal forms if it is less reactive (e.g. copper, silver). At the anode: with a concentrated halide solution the halogen forms; with a dilute halide solution, or a sulfate, oxygen forms.

Electrolyte (inert electrodes) Cathode product Anode product Observations Molten lead(II) bromide, PbBr 2 Lead Bromine Grey/silvery liquid metal at cathode; red-brown vapour at anode Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride Hydrogen Chlorine Bubbles at both; pale yellow-green gas at anode that bleaches damp litmus paper; solution becomes sodium hydroxide Dilute sulfuric acid Hydrogen Oxygen Bubbles at both; twice the volume of gas at the cathode Supplement Aqueous copper(II) sulfate, carbon electrodes Copper Oxygen Pink-brown coating on cathode; bubbles at anode; blue colour fades Supplement Aqueous copper(II) sulfate, copper electrodes Copper Copper dissolves (Cu 2+ ions) Cathode gains mass, anode loses mass; blue colour stays the same Gas tests Hydrogen: a lighted splint gives a “pop”. Oxygen: relights a glowing splint. Chlorine: bleaches damp litmus paper. Examiner Tip In the molten lead(II) bromide experiment, the ionic solid does not conduct until it melts because the ions cannot move in the solid. The experiment should be done in a fume cupboard because bromine vapour is toxic. Mention both points when asked about the practical.

Reduction happens at the cathode (electrons gained); oxidation happens at the anode (electrons lost). Balance atoms and charges. Electrode Half-equation Cathode (lead) Pb 2+ + 2e − → Pb Anode (bromine) 2Br − → Br 2 + 2e − Cathode (hydrogen) 2H + + 2e − → H 2 Anode (chlorine) 2Cl − → Cl 2 + 2e − Anode (oxygen) 4OH − → O 2 + 2H 2 O + 4e − Cathode (copper) Cu 2+ + 2e − → Cu Copper anode (dissolving) Cu → Cu 2+ + 2e − Common Mistake Writing the chlorine anode equation as Cl − → Cl + e − . Chlorine is diatomic, so it must be 2Cl − → Cl 2 + 2e − . Also check the charges balance on both sides, and that electrons appear on the left at the cathode and on the right at the anode.

Electroplating uses electrolysis to coat one metal with a thin layer of another metal. 1 Cathode The object to be plated (e.g. a steel spoon). 2 Anode A piece of the plating metal (e.g. silver). 3 Electrolyte An aqueous solution containing ions of the plating metal (e.g. silver nitrate). 4 Result Metal ions are reduced and deposited on the object; the anode dissolves to replace them, so the electrolyte concentration stays constant. Uses: to improve appearance (e.g. silver or gold plating on jewellery) and to resist corrosion (e.g. chromium on steel taps, tin on steel cans). Supplement Copper is purified the same way: impure copper as the anode, pure copper as the cathode, copper(II) sulfate solution as electrolyte. Impurities fall below the anode. Model answer Aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed using carbon electrodes. Explain what is seen at each electrode and why the colour of the solution changes. [4] At the cathode a pink-brown solid forms, because Cu 2+ ions gain electrons and are deposited as copper: Cu 2+ + 2e − → Cu. Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so copper is discharged instead of hydrogen. At the anode bubbles of oxygen form, from hydroxide ions losing electrons. The blue colour fades because Cu 2+ ions, which cause the blue colour, are removed from the solution and not replaced.

A fuel cell uses hydrogen and oxygen to produce electricity , with water as the only chemical product . Overall reaction: 2H 2 (g) + O 2 (g) → 2H 2 O(l) Supplement Fuel cells compared with petrol engines Advantages of fuel cells Disadvantages of fuel cells Only product is water; no CO 2 , CO, oxides of nitrogen or unburnt hydrocarbons released from the vehicle Hydrogen is difficult and expensive to store; it is a gas that must be kept under high pressure More efficient at converting chemical energy into useful energy Hydrogen is flammable and explosive Fewer moving parts, quieter Hydrogen is often produced from fossil fuels or using electricity, which may release CO 2 Do not use up crude oil (a finite resource) Few hydrogen refuelling stations; fuel cells are expensive to make Quick Checklist I can define electrolysis and identify the anode, cathode, electrolyte and external circuit. I can describe how charge is carried by electrons in the circuit and ions in the electrolyte (Supplement). I can state the products and observations for molten PbBr 2 , concentrated aqueous NaCl and dilute H 2 SO 4 . I can predict products for molten binary compounds and for dilute or concentrated halide solutions. I can describe the electrolysis of aqueous CuSO 4 with carbon and copper electrodes (Supplement). I can write ionic half-equations showing oxidation at the anode and reduction at the cathode (Supplement). I can describe electroplating and its uses, and state what a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell produces. I can give advantages and disadvantages of fuel cells compared with petrol engines (Supplement).

Topic 5 · Physical Chemistry Chemical Energetics Every reaction either releases thermal energy to the surroundings or takes it in. This topic covers exothermic and endothermic reactions, reaction pathway diagrams and (for Supplement) calculating enthalpy changes from bond energies — a reliable source of calculation marks on Paper 4.

Energy is conserved in every reaction. What changes is where it is stored: some energy is held in the chemical bonds (the system ), and some is thermal energy in everything around the reaction (the surroundings — the solvent, test tube, air and thermometer). Exothermic reaction: a reaction that transfers thermal energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases . Endothermic reaction: a reaction that takes in thermal energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases . Exothermic examples Endothermic examples Combustion of fuels, e.g. CH 4 (g) + 2O 2 (g) → CO 2 (g) + 2H 2 O(l) Thermal decomposition, e.g. CaCO 3 (s) → CaO(s) + CO 2 (g) Neutralisation, e.g. HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H 2 O(l) Photosynthesis (energy taken in as light) Reactive metals with water or acid, e.g. Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl 2 (aq) + H 2 (g) Dissolving ammonium nitrate or ammonium chloride in water Respiration Citric acid reacting with sodium hydrogencarbonate Measuring the temperature change in the lab Carry out the reaction in an insulated container (a polystyrene cup with a lid) to reduce thermal energy loss to the air. Record the starting temperature, mix, stir, and record the highest (or lowest) temperature reached. A rise in temperature shows an exothermic reaction; a fall shows an endothermic reaction. Common Mistake Saying “an endothermic reaction gets hotter because it takes in heat”. The reaction mixture and the container actually feel colder , because thermal energy is being drawn out of the surroundings into the chemical bonds of the products.

A reaction pathway diagram (energy level diagram) plots the energy of the chemicals on the vertical axis against the progress of the reaction on the horizontal axis. Exothermic Products lower than reactants; energy released to surroundings Endothermic Products higher than reactants; energy taken in from surroundings The “hump” Energy barrier the reactants must get over: the activation energy Axes y: energy; x: progress of reaction

h: Supplement Enthalpy change and activation energy
x: Enthalpy change, ΔH: the transfer of thermal energy during a reaction. Units: kJ/mol. For an exothermic reaction ΔH is negative (the system loses energy). For an endothermic reaction ΔH is positive (the system gains energy). Activation energy, E a : the minimum energy that colliding particles must have in order to react. Drawing and labelling a pathway diagram (Supplement) 1 Draw and label the axes Vertical axis “energy”, horizontal axis “progress of reaction”. 2 Reactant and product levels Draw two horizontal lines and write the formulae of the reactants and products on them. Products lower for exothermic, higher for endothermic. 3 Draw the curve Join the levels with a smooth curve that rises to a peak above both lines. 4 Label E a A vertical arrow pointing upwards from the reactant level to the top of the peak. 5 Label ΔH A vertical arrow from the reactant level to the product level: pointing down for exothermic (ΔH negative), up for endothermic (ΔH positive). Examiner Tip The activation energy arrow must start at the reactants line, not at the baseline or the products line. Arrows with a head at both ends, or arrows that do not touch the lines, commonly lose the mark.

h: Supplement Bond breaking and bond making
x: Bond breaking is endothermic — energy must be supplied to pull atoms apart. Bond making is exothermic — energy is released when new bonds form. If more energy is released making bonds than is taken in breaking bonds, the reaction is exothermic overall. If more energy is taken in breaking bonds than is released making bonds, the reaction is endothermic overall. B reaking I n (energy in), M aking O ut (energy out) — “BIMO” Calculating ΔH from bond energies ΔH = total energy needed to break bonds in reactants − total energy released making bonds in products. Worked example Calculate ΔH for H 2 (g) + Cl 2 (g) → 2HCl(g). Bond energies (kJ/mol): H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431. Bonds broken: 1 × H–H + 1 × Cl–Cl = 436 + 242 = 678 kJ Bonds made: 2 × H–Cl = 2 × 431 = 862 kJ ΔH = 678 − 862 ΔH = −184 kJ/mol (exothermic, because more energy is released than taken in) Worked example Calculate ΔH for the combustion of methane: CH 4 + 2O 2 → CO 2 + 2H 2 O. Bond energies (kJ/mol): C–H 412, O=O 496, C=O 743, O–H 463. Bonds broken: 4 × C–H = 1648; 2 × O=O = 992; total = 2640 kJ Bonds made: 2 × C=O = 1486; 4 × O–H (two in each H 2 O) = 1852; total = 3338 kJ ΔH = 2640 − 3338 ΔH = −698 kJ/mol Common Mistake Forgetting to count every bond. Draw out the displayed formula of each molecule first, then multiply by the balancing number: 2H 2 O contains four O–H bonds, and CO 2 contains two C=O double bonds. Also always include the sign in the final answer. Model answer The combustion of hydrogen is exothermic. Explain why, in terms of bond breaking and bond making. [3] Energy is taken in to break the bonds in the reactants (H–H and O=O), so bond breaking is endothermic. Energy is released when the new O–H bonds in water form, so bond making is exothermic. More energy is released in making the new bonds than is taken in breaking the old ones, so overall thermal energy is given out and ΔH is negative. Examiner Tip When asked whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic from data, always give the comparison (“more energy released making bonds than absorbed breaking bonds”), not just the name. The comparison carries the mark. Quick Checklist I can define exothermic and endothermic reactions in terms of thermal energy transfer and the temperature of the surroundings. I can give examples of each type and describe how to measure a temperature change. I can interpret a reaction pathway diagram and say whether it shows an exothermic or endothermic reaction. (Supplement) I can define enthalpy change and activation energy and state the sign of ΔH for each type. (Supplement) I can draw and fully label a reaction pathway diagram with E a and ΔH arrows. (Supplement) I can explain that bond breaking is endothermic and bond making is exothermic. (Supplement) I can calculate ΔH from bond energies, including the correct sign.

Topic 6 · Physical Chemistry Chemical Reactions This topic covers how to tell physical and chemical changes apart, what controls the rate of a reaction, reversible reactions and equilibrium (including the Haber and Contact processes), and redox. Rate graphs, collision theory explanations and equilibrium predictions appear on almost every paper.

Physical change: no new substance is made and the change is usually easy to reverse, e.g. melting ice, dissolving salt, boiling water. Chemical change: one or more new substances are formed; often accompanied by an energy change, a colour change, fizzing or a precipitate, and usually hard to reverse, e.g. burning magnesium, rusting.

Rate measures how quickly reactants are used up or products are formed. The five factors on the syllabus: Change made Effect on rate Collision theory reason Increase concentration of a solution Increases More particles per unit volume, so more frequent collisions Increase pressure of a gas Increases Particles are closer together, so more particles per unit volume and more frequent collisions Increase surface area (smaller pieces or powder) Increases More particles exposed at the surface, so more frequent collisions Increase temperature Increases Particles have more kinetic energy, move faster so collide more often, and a greater proportion of collisions have energy ≥ activation energy Add a catalyst Increases Provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy Catalyst: a substance that increases the rate of a reaction and is unchanged in mass and chemical composition at the end of the reaction. Enzymes are proteins that act as biological catalysts. They work best at an optimum temperature and pH; high temperatures denature them. Fine powders (e.g. flour, coal dust) suspended in air can burn so fast that they cause explosions — a hazard in mills and mines.

Particles react only when they collide with energy equal to or greater than the activation energy . These are successful collisions . Rate depends on the frequency of successful collisions (number per second), not just the number of collisions. Temperature has two effects: collisions become more frequent, and a larger proportion of particles have energy ≥ E a . The second effect is the more important one. A catalyst lowers the activation energy, so a larger proportion of collisions are successful at the same temperature. Common Mistake Writing “more collisions”. Examiners want more frequent collisions or more collisions per second . A reaction eventually has the same total number of collisions either way — what changes is how often they happen.
