Practical methods for following rate 1 Volume of gas produced Collect the gas in a gas syringe (or an inverted measuring cylinder over water) and record the volume at regular time intervals. Suits e.g. Mg + HCl producing H 2 . 2 Loss of mass Place the flask on a balance with a cotton wool plug (lets gas out, keeps acid spray in) and record the mass at regular intervals. Suits reactions giving off a dense gas such as CO 2 from CaCO 3 + HCl. 3 Time for a precipitate to obscure a mark Sodium thiosulfate + hydrochloric acid produces a sulfur precipitate; time how long until a cross under the flask disappears. Rate is proportional to 1/time. 4 Control variables Change one factor only; keep volumes, concentrations, mass and particle size of solid and temperature the same in every other respect. Interpreting rate graphs On a graph of volume of gas (or loss of mass) against time, the gradient shows the rate. The curve is steepest at the start (highest concentration of reactants) and levels off when one reactant is used up. A faster reaction gives a steeper initial curve. If the amounts of reactants are the same, it levels off at the same final volume , just sooner. Halving the amount of the limiting reactant halves the final volume of gas. Supplement Calculate average rate = change in volume ÷ time taken; find the rate at a point by drawing a tangent and working out its gradient. Model answer Explain why magnesium powder reacts faster with hydrochloric acid than the same mass of magnesium ribbon. [3] The powder has a larger surface area. More magnesium atoms are exposed to the acid particles, so there are more frequent collisions between acid particles and magnesium atoms. This gives more frequent successful collisions, so the rate is higher.

Some reactions can go in both directions; this is shown by the symbol ⇌. Heating blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate drives off water and leaves white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate. Adding water turns it blue again: CuSO 4 ·5H 2 O(s) ⇌ CuSO 4 (s) + 5H 2 O(l) Pink hydrated cobalt(II) chloride becomes blue when heated (anhydrous) and turns pink again when water is added: CoCl 2 ·6H 2 O(s) ⇌ CoCl 2 (s) + 6H 2 O(l) These colour changes are used as chemical tests for water (anhydrous CuSO 4 white → blue; anhydrous CoCl 2 blue → pink). To test whether water is pure , check that it boils at exactly 100 °C and freezes at 0 °C.

A reversible reaction in a closed system reaches equilibrium when the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction and the concentrations of reactants and products no longer change. Equilibrium is dynamic: both reactions keep happening. Change Position of equilibrium moves… Increase temperature In the endothermic direction Decrease temperature In the exothermic direction Increase pressure (gases) To the side with fewer moles of gas Decrease pressure (gases) To the side with more moles of gas Increase concentration of a reactant To the right (more products) Remove a product To the right Add a catalyst No change — equilibrium is reached faster Supplement The Haber process (ammonia) N 2 (g) + 3H 2 (g) ⇌ 2NH 3 (g) ΔH negative (forward reaction exothermic) Nitrogen source Air Hydrogen source Methane (natural gas) Temperature 450 °C Pressure 20 000 kPa (200 atm) Catalyst Iron Supplement The Contact process (sulfuric acid) 2SO 2 (g) + O 2 (g) ⇌ 2SO 3 (g) ΔH negative SO 2 source Burning sulfur, or roasting sulfide ores O 2 source Air Temperature 450 °C Pressure 200 kPa (2 atm) Catalyst Vanadium(V) oxide, V 2 O 5 Supplement Explaining the chosen conditions Temperature: a low temperature would give a higher equilibrium yield (forward reaction is exothermic) but the rate would be too slow. 450 °C is a compromise between rate and yield. Pressure (Haber): high pressure moves equilibrium to the right (4 moles of gas → 2) and increases rate, but very high pressures are expensive and dangerous; 20 000 kPa balances yield against cost and safety. Pressure (Contact): the equilibrium already lies well to the right, so only a low pressure is needed; higher pressure is not worth the extra cost. Catalyst: increases the rate so equilibrium is reached faster; it does not change the yield. Examiner Tip For “explain the temperature used” questions, you need both sides: why not lower ( rate too slow ) and why not higher ( yield too low because the forward reaction is exothermic). Mention the word “compromise”.

Oxidation is gain of oxygen; reduction is loss of oxygen. Redox reactions involve simultaneous oxidation and reduction, e.g. in CuO + H 2 → Cu + H 2 O, copper(II) oxide is reduced and hydrogen is oxidised. Roman numerals show the oxidation number of an element in a compound, e.g. iron(II) sulfate contains Fe 2+ , iron(III) chloride contains Fe 3+ . Supplement Electrons and oxidation numbers Oxidation is loss of electrons and an increase in oxidation number. Reduction is gain of electrons and a decrease in oxidation number. Rules: an uncombined element has oxidation number 0; a simple ion has oxidation number equal to its charge; in a compound the oxidation numbers add up to 0; in an ion they add up to the charge. Oxygen is usually −2 and hydrogen usually +1. An oxidising agent oxidises another substance and is itself reduced. A reducing agent reduces another substance and is itself oxidised. Example: Zn(s) + Cu 2+ (aq) → Zn 2+ (aq) + Cu(s) Zn → Zn 2+ + 2e − (oxidation; Zn is the reducing agent) Cu 2+ + 2e − → Cu (reduction; Cu 2+ is the oxidising agent) Tests using colour changes: acidified potassium manganate(VII) is an oxidising agent and turns from purple to colourless when it reacts with a reducing agent. Aqueous potassium iodide is a reducing agent and turns from colourless to brown (iodine forms) when it reacts with an oxidising agent. OIL — Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), RIG — Reduction Is Gain Quick Checklist I can distinguish physical and chemical changes and name the factors that affect rate. I can describe practical methods for following rate and interpret rate graphs. (Supplement) I can explain rate changes using the frequency of successful collisions and activation energy. I can describe the reversible hydration of copper(II) sulfate and cobalt(II) chloride and use them to test for water. (Supplement) I can define equilibrium and predict how temperature, pressure, concentration and a catalyst affect it. (Supplement) I can give the equations, raw materials and conditions for the Haber and Contact processes and explain the choices. I can identify redox in terms of oxygen; (Supplement) in terms of electrons and oxidation numbers, naming oxidising and reducing agents.

Topic 7 · Inorganic Chemistry Acids, Bases and Salts This topic covers the typical reactions of acids and bases, the pH scale and indicators, the classification of oxides, and how to prepare pure, dry samples of salts. Salt preparation methods are a favourite extended-writing question on both core and extended papers.

Acids contain hydrogen ions, H + (aq) , when dissolved in water. Acids have a pH below 7, turn blue litmus red, turn methyl orange red and keep thymolphthalein colourless. Reactions of acids (learn the general word equations) General equation Example acid + metal → salt + hydrogen Zn(s) + H 2 SO 4 (aq) → ZnSO 4 (aq) + H 2 (g) acid + base → salt + water CuO(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CuCl 2 (aq) + H 2 O(l) acid + alkali → salt + water HNO 3 (aq) + KOH(aq) → KNO 3 (aq) + H 2 O(l) acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide CaCO 3 (s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl 2 (aq) + H 2 O(l) + CO 2 (g) Hydrochloric acid gives chlorides , sulfuric acid gives sulfates , nitric acid gives nitrates .

Bases are metal oxides and hydroxides; they neutralise acids to form a salt and water. Alkalis are soluble bases. They contain hydroxide ions, OH − (aq) , when dissolved in water. Alkalis have a pH above 7, turn red litmus blue, turn methyl orange yellow and turn thymolphthalein blue. Bases react with ammonium salts when warmed, releasing ammonia gas: NH 4 Cl(s) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H 2 O(l) + NH 3 (g) (Test for NH 4 + : ammonia turns damp red litmus paper blue.) Indicator In acid In alkali Litmus Red Blue Methyl orange Red Yellow Thymolphthalein Colourless Blue Universal indicator Red (pH 1–3), orange/yellow (pH 4–6) Blue (pH 8–11), purple (pH 12–14); green at pH 7

pH runs from 1 to 14. Below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is alkaline. Measure it with universal indicator (compare to a colour chart) or a pH meter. Neutralisation is the reaction between an acid and an alkali: H + (aq) + OH − (aq) → H 2 O(l)

h: Supplement Proton transfer and strength of acids
x: An acid is a proton (H + ) donor; a base is a proton acceptor. A strong acid is completely dissociated in aqueous solution, e.g. hydrochloric acid: HCl(aq) → H + (aq) + Cl − (aq) A weak acid is only partially dissociated in aqueous solution, e.g. ethanoic acid: CH 3 COOH(aq) ⇌ H + (aq) + CH 3 COO − (aq) At the same concentration, a strong acid has a higher H + concentration, so a lower pH and reacts faster (e.g. with magnesium). The lower the pH, the higher the H + concentration. Each drop of 1 pH unit means a tenfold increase in H + concentration. Common Mistake Confusing strong with concentrated . Strength is about how completely the acid dissociates; concentration is about how much acid is dissolved per dm 3 . You can have a dilute strong acid or a concentrated weak acid.

Acidic oxides are usually oxides of non-metals, e.g. CO 2 , SO 2 . They react with bases to form a salt and water. Basic oxides are usually oxides of metals, e.g. CuO, CaO. They react with acids to form a salt and water. Supplement Amphoteric oxides react with both acids and bases to produce a salt and water, e.g. aluminium oxide, Al 2 O 3 , and zinc oxide, ZnO.

A salt is formed when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal (or ammonium) ion. First decide whether the salt is soluble. Soluble Insoluble (exceptions) All sodium, potassium and ammonium salts — All nitrates — Most chlorides, bromides and iodides Silver and lead(II) halides Most sulfates Barium, calcium and lead(II) sulfate Sodium, potassium and ammonium carbonates All other carbonates Sodium, potassium and ammonium hydroxides Most other hydroxides (calcium hydroxide is only partially soluble) Method A: soluble salt from an insoluble solid (excess metal, base or carbonate) 1 Warm the acid Place dilute acid in a beaker and warm it gently to speed up the reaction. 2 Add the solid in excess Add the metal, oxide or carbonate a little at a time, stirring, until no more dissolves (and fizzing stops for a carbonate). Excess ensures all the acid is used up. 3 Filter Remove the unreacted excess solid; the filtrate is the salt solution. 4 Evaporate to saturation Heat the filtrate until it is saturated (crystals form on a glass rod dipped in and cooled). 5 Crystallise Leave to cool so crystals form, filter them off, wash with a little cold distilled water and dry between filter papers. Example: making copper(II) sulfate crystals from excess copper(II) oxide and dilute sulfuric acid. Method B: soluble salt by titration (acid + alkali) Used for sodium, potassium and ammonium salts, where both reactants are solutions so an excess cannot be filtered off. Pipette a known volume of alkali into a conical flask, add a few drops of indicator (e.g. methyl orange) and add acid from a burette until the indicator just changes colour. Record the volume. Repeat with the same volumes but no indicator , then evaporate and crystallise as in Method A. Worked example 25.0 cm 3 of 0.100 mol/dm 3 sodium hydroxide is neutralised by 20.0 cm 3 of hydrochloric acid. Find the concentration of the acid. NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H 2 O(l) Moles NaOH = 0.100 × 25.0/1000 = 0.00250 mol Mole ratio 1 : 1, so moles HCl = 0.00250 mol Concentration HCl = 0.00250 ÷ (20.0/1000) = 0.125 mol/dm 3 Supplement Method C: insoluble salt by precipitation Mix two solutions that between them contain the ions of the insoluble salt, e.g. barium chloride and sodium sulfate: BaCl 2 (aq) + Na 2 SO 4 (aq) → BaSO 4 (s) + 2NaCl(aq) Ionic equation: Ba 2+ (aq) + SO 4 2− (aq) → BaSO 4 (s) Filter to collect the precipitate, wash it with distilled water to remove soluble impurities, then dry it in a warm oven. Water of crystallisation Hydrated substance: a substance that is chemically combined with water, e.g. CuSO 4 ·5H 2 O. Anhydrous substance: a substance containing no water. Water of crystallisation: the water molecules present in the crystals of a hydrated substance. Examiner Tip In a salt-preparation question, always say why the solid is added in excess (to make sure all the acid reacts) and do not say “evaporate to dryness” — heating to dryness can drive off water of crystallisation and give a powder rather than crystals. Model answer Describe how you would prepare pure, dry crystals of zinc chloride from zinc carbonate and dilute hydrochloric acid. [4] Add zinc carbonate to warm dilute hydrochloric acid, stirring, until no more fizzing is seen and some solid remains (the carbonate is in excess). Filter to remove the excess zinc carbonate. Heat the filtrate to evaporate some water until the solution is saturated, then leave it to cool so that crystals form. Filter off the crystals and dry them between filter papers. Quick Checklist I can describe the reactions of acids with metals, bases and carbonates, with equations. I can give the colours of litmus, methyl orange, thymolphthalein and universal indicator. I can describe the pH scale and write the ionic equation for neutralisation. (Supplement) I can define acids and bases as proton donors and acceptors and explain strong and weak acids. I can classify oxides as acidic or basic; (Supplement) and identify amphoteric oxides. I can use the solubility rules to choose a method and describe how to make a pure, dry soluble salt. (Supplement) I can describe preparing an insoluble salt by precipitation. I can define hydrated, anhydrous and water of crystallisation.

Topic 8 · Inorganic Chemistry The Periodic Table The Periodic Table organises the elements so that their properties can be predicted from their position. You need to explain trends in Group I, Group VII, the transition elements and the noble gases, and predict the properties of elements you have never met — a common source of “suggest” marks.

Elements are arranged in order of increasing proton number (atomic number). Periods are horizontal rows; groups are vertical columns. Across a period, elements change from metallic to non-metallic character (e.g. period 3: Na, Mg, Al are metals; Si is a metalloid; P, S, Cl, Ar are non-metals). The group number equals the number of outer-shell electrons (Group I has 1, Group VII has 7). Group VIII (Group 0) noble gases have a full outer shell. The period number equals the number of occupied electron shells, e.g. chlorine (2,8,7) is in period 3, Group VII. Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties because they have the same number of outer-shell electrons . The Periodic Table can be used to predict the charge on an ion: Group I forms 1+, Group II 2+, Group III 3+, Group VI 2−, Group VII 1−. Group I Alkali metals Group VII Halogens Group VIII Noble gases Central block Transition elements

Lithium, sodium and potassium are soft metals (can be cut with a knife) with relatively low melting points and low densities. Freshly cut surfaces are shiny but tarnish quickly in air, so they are stored under oil. They react with cold water to form a metal hydroxide (alkaline solution) and hydrogen: 2Na(s) + 2H 2 O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H 2 (g) Metal Observations with cold water Lithium Floats, fizzes steadily, slowly gets smaller Sodium Floats, melts into a ball, moves around quickly, fizzes vigorously Potassium As sodium but more violent; the hydrogen ignites with a lilac flame Trends down Group I Reactivity increases . Melting point decreases . Density generally increases (potassium is an exception, less dense than sodium). Use the trends to predict: rubidium and caesium are even softer, melt at lower temperatures and react explosively with water. Examiner Tip Observations must be things you can see : “fizzing”, “floats”, “melts into a ball”. “Hydrogen is produced” is a conclusion, not an observation, and will not score an observation mark.

Halogens exist as diatomic molecules : Cl 2 , Br 2 , I 2 . Halogen State at room temperature Colour Chlorine, Cl 2 Gas Pale yellow-green Bromine, Br 2 Liquid Red-brown Iodine, I 2 Solid Grey-black Trends down Group VII Colour becomes darker . Density and melting/boiling points increase (gas → liquid → solid). Reactivity decreases — the opposite of Group I. Predictions: fluorine is a very pale yellow gas and the most reactive halogen; astatine would be a dark solid and the least reactive. Displacement reactions A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from an aqueous solution of its halide. Halogen added Potassium chloride(aq) Potassium bromide(aq) Potassium iodide(aq) Chlorine water No reaction Turns orange (Br 2 formed) Turns brown (I 2 formed) Bromine water No reaction No reaction Turns brown (I 2 formed) Iodine solution No reaction No reaction No reaction Cl 2 (aq) + 2KBr(aq) → 2KCl(aq) + Br 2 (aq) Supplement Ionic equation: Cl 2 (aq) + 2Br − (aq) → 2Cl − (aq) + Br 2 (aq) Supplement This is a redox reaction: chlorine gains electrons (reduced, Cl 2 + 2e − → 2Cl − ) and bromide ions lose electrons (oxidised, 2Br − → Br 2 + 2e − ). Chlorine is the oxidising agent. Common Mistake Mixing up chlorine and chloride . Chlorine is the element (Cl 2 ); chloride is the ion (Cl − ) found in compounds such as potassium chloride. “Chloride displaces bromine” is wrong — chlorine displaces bromine from bromide. Model answer Aqueous bromine is added to aqueous potassium iodide. Describe what is seen and explain the result. [3] The solution changes from colourless to brown. Bromine is more reactive than iodine, so it displaces iodine from potassium iodide: Br 2 + 2KI → 2KBr + I 2 . The brown colour is due to the iodine formed.

Transition elements (e.g. iron, copper, nickel, chromium) are metals with: 1 High densities Much denser than Group I metals. 2 High melting points Iron melts at over 1500 °C, compared with sodium at about 98 °C. 3 Coloured compounds e.g. copper(II) sulfate solution is blue, iron(II) salts are pale green, iron(III) salts are yellow-brown. 4 Catalytic activity The elements and their compounds often act as catalysts, e.g. iron in the Haber process, vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process. 5 Supplement Variable oxidation numbers They form ions with different charges, e.g. iron(II) Fe 2+ and iron(III) Fe 3+ ; copper(I) and copper(II).

Helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon are unreactive, monatomic gases . Explanation: their atoms have a full outer shell of electrons (a stable electronic configuration; helium has 2, the others have 8), so they do not need to lose, gain or share electrons. Uses linked to unreactivity: argon in light bulbs and as an inert atmosphere in welding; helium in balloons (also low density). Group I gets more reactive going down ; Group VII gets more reactive going up — the most reactive elements sit at the far corners (bottom left, top right). Quick Checklist I can describe how the Periodic Table is arranged and link group and period number to electronic configuration. I can describe the change from metallic to non-metallic character across a period. I can describe the properties of Li, Na and K, their reaction with water, and predict properties of Rb and Cs. I can state the colours and states of Cl 2 , Br 2 and I 2 and describe the trends down Group VII. I can describe and explain halogen displacement reactions; (Supplement) with ionic equations and in terms of redox. I can list the properties of transition elements; (Supplement) including variable oxidation numbers. I can explain why noble gases are unreactive and monatomic.

Topic 9 · Inorganic Chemistry Metals How metals behave, why we mix them into alloys, how the reactivity series predicts their reactions, how we stop them corroding and how we get them out of their ores. Extraction of iron and aluminium and the reactivity series appear in almost every paper.

Physical properties (compared with non-metals) Property Typical metal Typical non-metal Thermal conductivity Good Poor (insulator) Electrical conductivity Good Poor (graphite is the exception) Malleability and ductility Malleable (hammered into shape) and ductile (drawn into wires) Brittle when solid Melting and boiling points Usually high Usually low Appearance Shiny when freshly cut Usually dull General chemical properties With dilute acids: metal + acid → salt + hydrogen, e.g. Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl 2 (aq) + H 2 (g) With cold water: reactive metals give a metal hydroxide + hydrogen, e.g. 2Na(s) + 2H 2 O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H 2 (g) With steam: less reactive metals give a metal oxide + hydrogen, e.g. Mg(s) + H 2 O(g) → MgO(s) + H 2 (g) With oxygen: metal + oxygen → metal oxide, e.g. 2Cu(s) + O 2 (g) → 2CuO(s). Metal oxides are basic.

Always link the use to a property. Aluminium: aircraft Low density, strong Aluminium: overhead power cables Low density, good electrical conductor Aluminium: food containers Resists corrosion (protective oxide layer) Copper: electrical wiring Very good electrical conductor, ductile

An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other elements (metals or non-metals such as carbon). Brass is a mixture of copper and zinc. Stainless steel is a mixture of iron with other elements such as chromium, nickel and carbon. Alloys can be harder and stronger than the pure metals, which is why they are more useful. Stainless steel is used in cutlery because it is hard and resistant to rusting. Supplement In a pure metal the positive ions are all the same size and arranged in regular layers that slide easily over one another. In an alloy, atoms of different sizes distort the layers, so the layers cannot slide as easily. This makes the alloy harder and stronger. You should be able to identify an alloy from a diagram: a lattice with a few differently sized circles among the regular metal ions.

P otassium S odium C alcium M agnesium A luminium C arbon Z inc I ron H ydrogen C opper S ilver G old Most reactive at the top (potassium), least reactive at the bottom (gold). Carbon and hydrogen are included as reference points. Metal Cold water Steam Dilute hydrochloric acid Potassium, sodium Vigorous; hydroxide + hydrogen (Too dangerous) Explosive Calcium Steady fizzing; hydroxide + hydrogen (Too dangerous) Very vigorous Magnesium Very slow Burns brightly; oxide + hydrogen Vigorous fizzing Zinc, iron No reaction React when heated; oxide + hydrogen Steady to slow fizzing Copper, silver, gold No reaction No reaction No reaction Displacement reactions A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt or from its oxide. Zn(s) + CuSO 4 (aq) → ZnSO 4 (aq) + Cu(s): blue solution fades, pink-brown copper forms, temperature rises. Thermite: 2Al(s) + Fe 2 O 3 (s) → Al 2 O 3 (s) + 2Fe(l) You can use displacement results (and reactions with water and acid) to put unfamiliar metals into order of reactivity. Supplement Reactivity is the tendency of a metal to form positive ions. A more reactive metal loses electrons more readily. Ionic equation: Zn(s) + Cu 2+ (aq) → Zn 2+ (aq) + Cu(s). Zinc is oxidised (loses electrons); copper ions are reduced (gain electrons). Supplement Aluminium seems unreactive (e.g. no reaction with water, slow start with acid) because it is covered by a thin, tough, unreactive layer of aluminium oxide that prevents contact with water or acid. Common Mistake Saying "copper reacts with dilute acid slowly". Copper is below hydrogen, so it does not react with dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid at all. Also do not say aluminium is unreactive: it is reactive, but protected by its oxide layer.

Rusting is the corrosion of iron and steel. It needs both water and oxygen . Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide. Classic experiment: iron nails in three tubes: (1) air and water → rusts; (2) boiled water with an oil layer (no oxygen) → no rust; (3) dry air with anhydrous calcium chloride (no water) → no rust. Salt water speeds up rusting. Preventing rusting Barrier methods keep out water and oxygen: painting, greasing or oiling, coating with plastic. Galvanising : coating iron with a layer of zinc. Supplement Barrier methods work only while the coating is unbroken. Supplement Sacrificial protection : a more reactive metal (zinc or magnesium) is attached to the iron. The more reactive metal loses electrons (is oxidised) in preference to iron, so iron does not rust. Used on ship hulls and pipelines. Zn(s) → Zn 2+ (aq) + 2e − Supplement Galvanising protects in two ways: the zinc acts as a barrier, and if scratched the zinc still corrodes sacrificially instead of the iron. Model answer Explain why blocks of zinc attached to a steel ship hull stop the hull rusting, even where the paint is scratched. [3] Zinc is more reactive than iron. Zinc loses electrons / is oxidised more readily than iron, so the zinc corrodes instead of the iron (sacrificial protection). Electrons from the zinc flow to the iron, so iron does not form ions / is not oxidised.

The ease of extracting a metal depends on its position in the reactivity series. Metals above carbon (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al) are extracted by electrolysis of the molten compound. Metals below carbon (Zn, Fe, Cu) are extracted by reduction with carbon (or carbon monoxide). Very unreactive metals (silver, gold) are found uncombined (native). Iron from hematite in the blast furnace Raw materials: hematite (iron ore, mainly Fe 2 O 3 ), coke (carbon), limestone (CaCO 3 ) and hot air. 1 Coke burns Carbon burns in hot air, releasing heat: C(s) + O 2 (g) → CO 2 (g) 2 Carbon monoxide forms Carbon dioxide reacts with more coke: CO 2 (g) + C(s) → 2CO(g) 3 Hematite is reduced Carbon monoxide reduces iron(III) oxide to molten iron: Fe 2 O 3 (s) + 3CO(g) → 2Fe(l) + 3CO 2 (g) 4 Limestone decomposes Thermal decomposition: CaCO 3 (s) → CaO(s) + CO 2 (g) 5 Slag forms Calcium oxide (basic) neutralises silicon(IV) oxide (acidic impurity, sand): CaO(s) + SiO 2 (s) → CaSiO 3 (l). Molten slag floats on the molten iron and is tapped off separately. Supplement You must be able to write all five symbol equations above. Word equations are enough for Core. Aluminium from bauxite The main ore of aluminium is bauxite , which is purified to aluminium oxide (alumina), Al 2 O 3 . Aluminium is too reactive to be reduced by carbon, so it is extracted by electrolysis . Supplement Aluminium oxide is dissolved in molten cryolite . This lowers the operating temperature (saving energy and cost) and makes a better conductor than molten alumina alone. Supplement Cathode (−): Al 3+ + 3e − → Al (molten aluminium collects at the bottom). Supplement Anode (+): 2O 2− → O 2 + 4e − . The carbon (graphite) anodes react with the oxygen to form carbon dioxide, C + O 2 → CO 2 , so they burn away and must be replaced regularly. Examiner Tip In the blast furnace, the main reducing agent is carbon monoxide , not coke. Coke's job is to provide heat and to make the CO. Limestone's job is to remove the acidic impurity silicon(IV) oxide as slag — say "removes impurities" alone and you may miss the mark. Quick Checklist I can compare the physical properties of metals and non-metals and link uses of aluminium and copper to their properties. I can describe alloys, name brass and stainless steel, and explain (Supplement) why alloys are harder using a structure diagram. I can recall the reactivity series and describe reactions of metals with water, steam and dilute acid. I can predict displacement reactions and write ionic equations for them (Supplement). I can state the conditions for rusting and describe barrier methods, galvanising and sacrificial protection. I can describe the blast furnace with equations and explain the role of each raw material. I can explain why aluminium is extracted by electrolysis, why cryolite is used and why anodes are replaced.

Topic 10 · Environment & Organic Chemistry of the Environment Water testing and treatment, fertilisers, the composition of air, the sources and effects of air pollutants, and climate change. Questions here reward precise cause-and-effect statements, so learn which pollutant comes from which source.

Chemical tests for water Test Result if water is present Add to anhydrous copper(II) sulfate Turns from white to blue Add to anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride (e.g. on paper) Turns from blue to pink These tests show that water is present ; they do not show it is pure. Physical test for purity: pure water melts at exactly 0 °C and boils at exactly 100 °C (at atmospheric pressure). Distilled water is used in practical chemistry instead of tap water because it contains fewer chemical impurities that could interfere with results. Substances found in water from natural sources and from pollution Substance Effect Dissolved oxygen Beneficial: needed by aquatic life for respiration Metal compounds Some beneficial (provide essential minerals for life); some harmful (toxic, e.g. compounds of lead or mercury) Plastics Harmful to aquatic life (swallowed, entanglement) Sewage Harmful: contains harmful microbes that cause disease Nitrates (from fertilisers) Harmful: lead to deoxygenation of water, damaging aquatic life Phosphates (from fertilisers and detergents) Harmful: lead to deoxygenation of water, damaging aquatic life Supplement You need to state which substances are beneficial and which are harmful, and why, as shown in the table. Deoxygenation happens because nitrates and phosphates cause rapid growth of algae; when the algae die, bacteria decompose them and use up the dissolved oxygen, so fish die (eutrophication). Treatment of the domestic water supply 1 Sedimentation Water stands in tanks so that large insoluble particles settle to the bottom. 2 Filtration Water passes through beds of sand and gravel to remove smaller insoluble solids. 3 Carbon Activated carbon removes substances that cause tastes and odours. 4 Chlorination Chlorine is added to kill harmful microbes. Common Mistake Writing that chlorine "cleans" the water or that filtration "removes bacteria". Chlorination kills microbes ; filtration removes insoluble solids . Neither step removes dissolved substances such as salts.

Common fertilisers are ammonium salts (e.g. ammonium nitrate, ammonium sulfate, ammonium phosphate) and nitrates (e.g. potassium nitrate). NPK fertilisers provide the three elements needed for improved plant growth: nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and potassium (K). Nitrogen is needed for making proteins, so plants grow larger and greener; phosphorus helps root growth; potassium helps flowering and fruiting. Ammonium salts are made by neutralising ammonia with an acid, e.g. NH 3 (aq) + HNO 3 (aq) → NH 4 NO 3 (aq).

Composition of clean, dry air Nitrogen Approximately 78% Oxygen Approximately 21% Remainder (about 1%) Mainly noble gases (argon), plus carbon dioxide (about 0.04%) Sources and adverse effects of air pollutants Pollutant Source Adverse effect Carbon dioxide Complete combustion of carbon-containing fuels Increased global warming, leading to climate change Carbon monoxide Incomplete combustion of carbon-containing fuels Toxic gas (reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen) Particulates (soot, carbon) Incomplete combustion of carbon-containing fuels Increased risk of respiratory problems and cancer Methane Decomposition of vegetation and waste gases from digestion in animals (e.g. cattle) Increased global warming, leading to climate change Oxides of nitrogen (NO, NO 2 ) Car engines: nitrogen and oxygen from the air react at the high temperature Acid rain, photochemical smog, respiratory problems Sulfur dioxide Combustion of fossil fuels that contain sulfur compounds Acid rain Acid rain damages buildings made of limestone and marble, corrodes metal structures, kills trees and makes lakes too acidic for fish.

The Sun's radiation passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth's surface. The Earth's surface emits thermal (infrared) energy. Greenhouse gases (carbon dioxide, methane) absorb some of this thermal energy and re-emit it in all directions, including back towards the Earth, while some is reflected back into space. Higher concentrations of greenhouse gases mean more thermal energy is kept in the atmosphere, so the average temperature rises (global warming) and climate changes.

h: Supplement Strategies to reduce environmental effects
x: Climate change Planting trees (they remove CO 2 by photosynthesis). Reducing livestock farming (less methane). Decreasing use of fossil fuels. Increasing use of hydrogen as a fuel and of renewable energy such as wind and solar. Acid rain Using catalytic converters in vehicles. Using low-sulfur fuels . Flue gas desulfurisation using calcium oxide in power stations: CaO(s) + SO 2 (g) → CaSO 3 (s) Catalytic converters Catalytic converters remove oxides of nitrogen and carbon monoxide (and unburnt hydrocarbons) from exhaust gases using a platinum or rhodium catalyst: 2CO(g) + 2NO(g) → 2CO 2 (g) + N 2 (g) 2NO 2 (g) + 4CO(g) → N 2 (g) + 4CO 2 (g) 2CO(g) + O 2 (g) → 2CO 2 (g)

Word equation: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, in the presence of light and chlorophyll. Supplement Symbol equation: 6CO 2 (g) + 6H 2 O(l) → C 6 H 12 O 6 (aq) + 6O 2 (g) Photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, which is why deforestation adds to climate change. Examiner Tip Keep your pollutant stories separate. Carbon dioxide and methane cause global warming ; sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen cause acid rain . Carbon monoxide is toxic but is not a greenhouse gas answer and does not cause acid rain. Never link CO 2 to the "hole in the ozone layer". Model answer Explain how running a car engine leads to the formation of acid rain. [3] The high temperature inside the engine makes nitrogen and oxygen from the air react. This forms oxides of nitrogen (e.g. nitrogen dioxide), which are released in the exhaust. The oxides of nitrogen dissolve in rain water (with oxygen) to form nitric acid, which falls as acid rain. Quick Checklist I can describe the tests for water using copper(II) sulfate and cobalt(II) chloride, and test purity with melting and boiling points. I can explain why distilled water is used in practical work. I can list substances found in water and say whether each is beneficial or harmful, including how nitrates and phosphates cause deoxygenation. I can describe the four stages of domestic water treatment. I can name common fertilisers and explain what NPK stands for. I can state the composition of clean air and match each pollutant to its source and effect. I can explain the greenhouse effect and strategies to reduce climate change and acid rain, including catalytic converter equations (Supplement). I can write the word (and symbol) equation for photosynthesis.

Topic 11 · Environment & Organic Organic Chemistry The chemistry of carbon compounds: naming and drawing them, fuels from petroleum, and the reactions of alkanes, alkenes, alcohols and carboxylic acids, finishing with polymers. It is a large, high-scoring topic where exact conditions and correct displayed formulae earn the marks.

Molecular formula Number and type of each atom in one molecule, e.g. C 2 H 6 O Structural formula Unambiguous arrangement of atoms without drawing every bond, e.g. CH 3 CH 2 OH Displayed formula Shows every atom and every bond General formula Formula for a whole homologous series, e.g. C n H 2n+2 Hydrocarbon Compound containing hydrogen and carbon only Functional group Atom or group of atoms that determines the chemical properties A homologous series is a family of similar compounds with similar chemical properties due to the presence of the same functional group. Supplement Members of a homologous series have the same general formula, differ from one member to the next by a CH 2 unit, show a trend in physical properties (e.g. boiling point rises with chain length) and have similar chemical properties. Saturated : only single carbon–carbon bonds. Unsaturated : contains one or more C=C double (or triple) bonds. Supplement Structural isomers are compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae, e.g. butane CH 3 CH 2 CH 2 CH 3 and methylpropane CH 3 CH(CH 3 )CH 3 ; or but-1-ene and but-2-ene.

Series Ending Functional group General formula Examples (C1–C4) Alkanes -ane C–C single bonds only C n H 2n+2 methane, ethane, propane, butane Alkenes -ene C=C C n H 2n ethene, propene, but-1-ene, but-2-ene Alcohols -ol –OH C n H 2n+1 OH methanol, ethanol, propan-1-ol, propan-2-ol, butan-1-ol Carboxylic acids -oic acid –COOH C n H 2n+1 COOH methanoic, ethanoic, propanoic, butanoic acid Esters -yl -oate –COO– — ethyl ethanoate, methyl propanoate M eth = 1 E th = 2 P rop = 3 B ut = 4 — "Monkeys Eat Peeled Bananas" Core: name and draw displayed formulae of methane, ethane, ethene, ethanol, ethanoic acid and the products of their reactions. Supplement Name and draw structural and displayed formulae of unbranched alkanes, alkenes, alcohols and carboxylic acids with up to four carbon atoms, and esters made from alcohols and acids each with up to four carbon atoms. Supplement Ester names: alcohol part first (ending -yl), acid part second (ending -oate). Methanol + propanoic acid → methyl propanoate, CH 3 CH 2 COOCH 3 .

Fossil fuels: coal, natural gas and petroleum . The main constituent of natural gas is methane . Petroleum is a mixture of hydrocarbons, separated into useful fractions by fractional distillation . The crude oil is vaporised; vapours rise up a column that is hot at the bottom and cooler at the top. Each fraction condenses where the temperature falls below its boiling point range. Fraction (top to bottom) Use Refinery gas Gas for heating and cooking Gasoline / petrol Fuel for cars Naphtha Chemical feedstock (making other chemicals) Kerosene / paraffin Jet fuel Diesel oil / gas oil Fuel for diesel engines Fuel oil Fuel for ships and home heating systems Lubricating oil Lubricants, waxes and polishes Bitumen Making roads Moving from the bottom to the top of the column: chain length decreases , volatility increases , boiling point decreases and viscosity decreases .

Saturated hydrocarbons; generally unreactive apart from combustion. Complete combustion: CH 4 (g) + 2O 2 (g) → CO 2 (g) + 2H 2 O(l) Substitution with chlorine in the presence of ultraviolet light (a photochemical reaction): a hydrogen atom is replaced by a chlorine atom. Supplement CH 4 (g) + Cl 2 (g) → CH 3 Cl(g) + HCl(g) (UV light). Further substitution can give CH 2 Cl 2 , CHCl 3 and CCl 4 .

Made by cracking larger alkane molecules, using a high temperature and a catalyst . Cracking produces alkenes and hydrogen as well as smaller alkanes, e.g. C 10 H 22 → C 8 H 18 + C 2 H 4 . Reasons for cracking: supply of long-chain fractions exceeds demand, while demand for shorter chains (petrol) and alkenes (for polymers) is greater than supply. Test for unsaturation : add aqueous bromine. Alkenes turn it from orange to colourless ; alkanes leave it orange. Supplement Alkenes undergo addition reactions in which only one product forms: Reagent Conditions Equation Bromine Room temperature C 2 H 4 + Br 2 → C 2 H 4 Br 2 (1,2-dibromoethane) Hydrogen Nickel catalyst, heat C 2 H 4 + H 2 → C 2 H 6 Steam Acid catalyst (phosphoric acid), about 300 °C, 6000 kPa C 2 H 4 + H 2 O ⇌ C 2 H 5 OH

Ethanol is made by fermentation of aqueous glucose at 25–35 °C with yeast, in the absence of oxygen: C 6 H 12 O 6 (aq) → 2C 2 H 5 OH(aq) + 2CO 2 (g) Or by catalytic addition of steam to ethene (see table above). Combustion: C 2 H 5 OH(l) + 3O 2 (g) → 2CO 2 (g) + 3H 2 O(l) Uses of ethanol: as a solvent and as a fuel . Supplement Comparison Fermentation Hydration of ethene Raw material Renewable (sugar from crops) Non-renewable (ethene from petroleum) Rate Slow Fast Process type Batch Continuous Purity of product Low; needs fractional distillation High Energy needed Low (low temperature) High (high temperature and pressure)

Ethanoic acid is a weak acid and shows typical acid reactions, forming ethanoate salts: With metals: 2CH 3 COOH + Mg → (CH 3 COO) 2 Mg + H 2 (magnesium ethanoate) With bases: CH 3 COOH + NaOH → CH 3 COONa + H 2 O (sodium ethanoate) With carbonates: 2CH 3 COOH + Na 2 CO 3 → 2CH 3 COONa + H 2 O + CO 2 Supplement Ethanoic acid forms by oxidation of ethanol: (a) by bacterial oxidation during fermentation (wine turning to vinegar), or (b) with acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII), which turns from purple to colourless. Supplement Carboxylic acids react with alcohols, with a concentrated sulfuric acid catalyst and heat, to make esters and water: CH 3 COOH + C 2 H 5 OH ⇌ CH 3 COOC 2 H 5 + H 2 O (ethyl ethanoate). Common Mistake Naming esters the wrong way round. The product of ethanol and propanoic acid is ethyl propanoate , not propyl ethanoate. Also, in formulae remember the C of –COOH is counted in the chain: ethanoic acid is CH 3 COOH (two carbons).

Polymers are large molecules built up from many small units called monomers . Plastics are made from polymers. Addition polymerisation : many alkene monomers join; the C=C opens. Ethene forms poly(ethene). Disposal problems of plastics (they are non-biodegradable): they take up space and persist in landfill ; they accumulate in oceans , harming marine life; burning them forms toxic gases. Supplement Identify the repeat unit and linkages in a polymer; deduce the polymer from a monomer and vice versa. Draw the repeat unit in brackets with continuation bonds through them and "n" outside, e.g. propene gives poly(propene) with repeat unit –[CH 2 –CH(CH 3 )]–. Supplement Addition polymerisation gives only the polymer; condensation polymerisation joins monomers with two functional groups and also releases a small molecule such as water. Supplement Nylon is a polyamide (amide linkage –CONH–) from a dicarboxylic acid and a diamine. PET is a polyester (ester linkage –COO–) from a dicarboxylic acid and a diol. PET can be converted back into monomers and re-polymerised, which aids recycling. Supplement Proteins are natural polyamides formed by condensation polymerisation of amino acid monomers, joined by amide linkages. Examiner Tip When drawing any displayed formula, check every carbon has exactly four bonds, every hydrogen one and every oxygen two. In the –COOH group draw the C=O and the O–H separately. Missing hydrogens or a five-bonded carbon lose the mark. Model answer Explain why cracking is carried out in oil refineries. [3] Fractional distillation produces more long-chain hydrocarbons than are needed (supply exceeds demand). Cracking breaks these long-chain alkanes into shorter-chain alkanes, such as petrol, for which demand is high. It also produces alkenes (and hydrogen), which are used to make polymers and other chemicals. Quick Checklist I can define homologous series, saturated, unsaturated and (Supplement) structural isomer. I can name and draw alkanes, alkenes, alcohols, carboxylic acids and esters up to four carbons. I can name the petroleum fractions, give their uses and describe trends down the column. I can describe combustion and chlorine substitution of alkanes, and cracking with its conditions. I can describe the bromine water test and (Supplement) addition reactions of alkenes with conditions. I can describe and compare fermentation and hydration of ethene to make ethanol. I can write reactions of ethanoic acid, including esterification (Supplement). I can describe addition and condensation polymers, draw repeat units and explain plastic disposal problems.

Topic 12 · Practical Skills Experimental Techniques and Chemical Analysis Choosing apparatus, carrying out titrations, separating and purifying mixtures, chromatography, and the full set of tests for ions and gases. This topic underpins the practical and alternative-to-practical papers, where exact colours and precise wording are essential.

Measuring apparatus Quantity Apparatus Notes Time Stopwatch / stopclock Seconds; start and stop at a clear, defined point Temperature Thermometer °C; read at eye level Mass Balance g; tare with the container on Volume of liquid (fixed) Volumetric pipette Very accurate for one fixed volume, e.g. 25.0 cm 3 Volume of liquid (variable) Burette Accurate to 0.05 cm 3 ; delivers any volume up to 50 cm 3 Volume of liquid (approximate) Measuring cylinder Quick but less accurate Volume of gas Gas syringe Accurate; alternatively collect over water in an inverted measuring cylinder Be ready to suggest advantages and disadvantages of methods and apparatus, e.g. a gas syringe is more accurate than collecting over water, but collecting over water cannot be used for gases that dissolve (ammonia, hydrogen chloride). Read volumes at the bottom of the meniscus, at eye level. Key terms Solvent A substance that dissolves a solute Solute A substance that is dissolved in a solvent Solution A mixture of one or more solutes dissolved in a solvent Saturated solution A solution containing the maximum concentration of a solute dissolved in the solvent at a specified temperature Residue A substance that remains after evaporation, distillation, filtration or any similar process Filtrate A liquid or solution that has passed through a filter

1 Measure the alkali Use a volumetric pipette (with filler) to transfer exactly 25.0 cm 3 of alkali into a conical flask. 2 Add indicator Add a few drops of a suitable indicator, e.g. methyl orange or thymolphthalein. 3 Fill the burette Rinse and fill the burette with acid; record the initial reading. 4 Titrate Add acid while swirling, then dropwise near the end-point, until the indicator just changes colour permanently. Record the final reading. 5 Repeat The first run is a rough titration. Repeat until you have concordant results (within 0.10 cm 3 ) and average them. End-point colours: methyl orange goes from yellow (alkali) to orange at the end-point (red in excess acid); thymolphthalein goes from blue to colourless as acid is added to alkali. Titre = final reading − initial reading. To make a pure salt, repeat without indicator using the known volumes, then crystallise.

Paper chromatography separates mixtures of soluble coloured substances using a suitable solvent. Method: draw a start line in pencil (graphite does not dissolve); spot the samples on it; stand the paper in solvent with the solvent level below the start line (so the spots do not dissolve into the bulk solvent); cover and allow the solvent to rise; remove and mark the solvent front. A pure substance gives one spot ; an impure substance (mixture) gives two or more spots. Identify unknowns by comparing their spots with those of known substances run on the same paper: spots at the same height match. Supplement Colourless substances are made visible with a locating agent , sprayed on the dried chromatogram. Supplement R f = distance travelled by substance ÷ distance travelled by solvent. R f has no units and is always less than 1. Worked example Supplement A spot moves 3.6 cm from the start line. The solvent front is 8.0 cm from the start line. Calculate the R f value. R f = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent R f = 3.6 ÷ 8.0 R f = 0.45

Technique Separates Example Filtration An insoluble solid from a liquid Sand from salt solution; excess metal oxide after making a salt Crystallisation A dissolved solid from its solution Copper(II) sulfate crystals: heat to the point of crystallisation, cool, filter, dry between filter papers Simple distillation A solvent from a solution Pure water from sea water Fractional distillation Miscible liquids with different boiling points Ethanol from water; petroleum fractions Paper chromatography Soluble substances in a mixture Dyes in ink Choose a technique from the information given, e.g. solubility and boiling point data. Assessing purity: a pure substance has a sharp melting point and boiling point. Impurities lower the melting point and raise the boiling point, and make them occur over a range of temperatures. Purity matters in food and medicines, where impurities could be harmful. Common Mistake Heating a solution to dryness to get crystals. This can decompose the salt or drive off water of crystallisation. Heat only until a drop placed on a cold tile forms crystals (the point of crystallisation), then leave to cool.
