Causes of a shift in demand P opulation I ncome R elated goods A dvertising T astes E xpectations S tate (taxes, benefits) — “PIRATES” Income : higher income raises demand for most goods; income tax cuts raise disposable income. Price of substitutes : a rise in the price of petrol cars increases demand for electric cars. Price of complements : a rise in the price of games consoles reduces demand for games. Tastes and fashion, advertising : growing environmental awareness raises demand for reusable bottles. Population : size and age structure (an ageing population raises demand for healthcare). Expectations of future prices, and interest rates (cheaper borrowing raises demand for houses and cars).

Supply is the willingness and ability of producers to sell a good or service at a given price over a given period of time. Market supply is the sum of all individual firms’ supply. As price rises, quantity supplied rises, because higher prices make production more profitable. The supply curve slopes up from left to right. A change in own price: extension or contraction along the curve. Other factors: a shift . Causes of a shift in supply Costs of production : higher wages, raw material or energy costs shift supply left. Technology : more productive methods shift supply right. Indirect taxes (shift left) and subsidies (shift right). Weather and natural events : droughts and floods linked to climate change shift the supply of crops left. Number of firms in the market, and prices of other goods the firm could produce instead. Common Mistake Never say “price rises, so demand falls, so the demand curve shifts left”. A change in the good’s own price causes a movement along the curve (a change in quantity demanded ). Only non-price factors shift the curve (a change in demand ).

Market equilibrium : the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. There is no tendency to change. Disequilibrium : if price is above equilibrium there is excess supply (a surplus), which pushes price down; if price is below equilibrium there is excess demand (a shortage), which pushes price up. Figure: An increase in demand (D → D1) raises equilibrium price (P → P1) and quantity (Q → Q1). Figure: A fall in supply (S → S1), e.g. after a drought, raises price (P → P1) and reduces quantity (Q → Q1). Change Equilibrium price Equilibrium quantity Demand increases (shift right) Rises Rises Demand decreases (shift left) Falls Falls Supply increases (shift right) Falls Rises Supply decreases (shift left) Rises Falls Chain of reasoning: an increase in demand 1 Cause A successful campaign raises demand for electric bikes; the demand curve shifts right. 2 Effect At the original price there is now excess demand (a shortage). 3 Effect Sellers raise the price; this causes a contraction in quantity demanded and an extension in quantity supplied. 4 Outcome A new equilibrium at a higher price and higher quantity; more resources move into e-bike production.

Price elasticity of demand is the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price. PED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price (% change = change ÷ original × 100) Value (ignoring the minus sign) Description Meaning Greater than 1 Price elastic Quantity demanded changes by a larger % than price Less than 1 Price inelastic Quantity demanded changes by a smaller % than price Equal to 1 Unitary Same % change; total spending unchanged 0 Perfectly inelastic Vertical demand curve; quantity does not change Infinity Perfectly elastic Horizontal demand curve; any price rise loses all sales Determinants of PED Number and closeness of substitutes : more substitutes → more elastic (one brand of bottled water is elastic; tap water in general is inelastic). Proportion of income spent on the good: a large share (cars, holidays) → more elastic. Necessity or luxury; habit-forming goods (e.g. cigarettes) → inelastic. Time period : demand is more elastic in the long run as consumers find alternatives. PED, total revenue and decisions Total revenue (consumer expenditure) = price × quantity sold. Inelastic demand: raising price increases revenue; cutting price reduces it. Elastic demand: cutting price increases revenue; raising price reduces it. Firms use PED to set prices; governments tax goods with inelastic demand (fuel, tobacco) because revenue is high and reliable, but the tax will reduce consumption only a little. Worked calculation The price of a bus pass rises from $40 to $50 and monthly sales fall from 2000 to 1800. % change in price = 10 ÷ 40 × 100 = +25%. % change in quantity = −200 ÷ 2000 × 100 = −10%. PED = −10 ÷ 25 = −0.4, so demand is price inelastic. Revenue rises from $80 000 to $90 000.

Price elasticity of supply is the responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in price. PES = % change in quantity supplied ÷ % change in price (always positive). PES > 1 is elastic, < 1 inelastic, 0 perfectly inelastic (vertical), infinity perfectly elastic (horizontal). Determinants of PES Time period : supply is more elastic in the long run (new factories, new crops planted). Spare capacity and stocks : firms with unused machinery or stored goods can raise output quickly. Mobility of factors : if resources can switch easily between uses, supply is elastic. Production time : agricultural goods (months to grow) have inelastic supply in the short run. Why it matters: when supply is inelastic, a rise in demand mainly raises price rather than output (e.g. city-centre housing). Examiner Tip For PED and PES, always interpret your number: state whether it is elastic or inelastic and what that means (“quantity demanded changes proportionately less than price”). Many candidates calculate correctly but lose the interpretation mark. Remember PED is usually negative; PES is positive.

A market economy allocates resources through the price mechanism, with private ownership of resources and minimal government involvement. Advantages Disadvantages Consumer choice and responsiveness to consumer wants Inequality of income and wealth; goods go to those who can pay Profit motive encourages efficiency and innovation Public goods may not be provided at all Resources allocated quickly through price signals, without costly planning Merit goods under-consumed, demerit goods over-consumed Competition can keep prices low and quality high External costs such as pollution ignored; risk of monopoly power

Market failure occurs when the market system leads to an inefficient allocation of resources, i.e. too much or too little of a good is produced and consumed. Public good Non-excludable and non-rival, e.g. street lighting, flood defences, national defence. Free-rider problem → not provided by market Merit good More beneficial than consumers realise; under-consumed, e.g. education, vaccinations Demerit good More harmful than consumers realise; over-consumed, e.g. cigarettes, sugary drinks Private goods Excludable and rival, e.g. a sandwich Private costs, external costs and social costs Private costs : costs paid by the consumer or producer involved (e.g. a factory’s fuel bill). External costs : costs imposed on third parties not involved in the transaction (e.g. air pollution, CO 2 emissions causing climate change, noise from an airport). Social cost = private cost + external cost . Private benefits : benefits to the consumer or producer. External benefits : benefits to third parties (e.g. vaccination protects others; a new park improves neighbours’ wellbeing). Social benefit = private benefit + external benefit . Markets ignore externalities, so goods with external costs are over-produced and goods with external benefits are under-produced . Other causes of market failure: information failure, monopoly power (higher prices, restricted output), factor immobility, and the depletion of non-renewable resources (e.g. over-fishing, deforestation) which threatens environmental sustainability. Common Mistake A public good is not simply “a good provided by the government”. Education and healthcare are provided by governments but are merit goods (people can be excluded and they are rival). A public good must be non-excludable and non-rival .

A mixed economy combines the market system with government intervention: both the private and public sectors own resources and make allocation decisions. Governments intervene to correct market failure and reduce inequality. Maximum and minimum prices Figure: A maximum price below equilibrium price P causes excess demand (Qd − Qs). Maximum price (price ceiling) Minimum price (price floor) Definition A legal limit that price cannot rise above; effective only if set below equilibrium A legal limit that price cannot fall below; effective only if set above equilibrium Aims Make essentials affordable, e.g. rent controls, staple foods Raise producers’ incomes (farm prices), minimum wage, or cut consumption of demerit goods (minimum alcohol price) Result Excess demand (shortage) Excess supply (surplus); for a minimum wage, possible unemployment Problems Queues, rationing, black markets, less incentive to supply or maintain quality Surpluses may have to be bought and stored by the government; higher prices for consumers Indirect taxes A tax on spending, e.g. VAT/GST, excise duties on fuel, tobacco, sugary drinks; carbon taxes on emissions. It raises firms’ costs, shifting supply to the left : price rises and quantity falls. Aims: reduce consumption of demerit goods, make polluters pay for external costs and promote environmental sustainability , and raise government revenue. Effectiveness depends on PED: with inelastic demand, consumers bear most of the tax and consumption falls only a little. Risks: smuggling, regressive effect on low-income households. Subsidies A payment from the government to producers (or consumers) to reduce costs, e.g. subsidies for solar panels, public transport, electric vehicles. Supply shifts to the right : price falls and quantity rises. Aims: increase consumption of merit goods and goods with external benefits, support incomes in key industries, and speed the switch to low-carbon energy. Drawbacks: opportunity cost of government spending; firms may become inefficient and dependent on support. Other forms of intervention Regulation : laws and rules, e.g. bans on smoking in public places, emissions limits for cars, compulsory schooling, banning single-use plastics. Can be effective but needs costly monitoring; fines may be too low to deter. State provision : the government directly provides public goods (defence, street lighting) and merit goods (free schools, hospitals), financed by taxation. Opportunity cost and possible inefficiency. Nationalisation : transferring a private firm or industry into public (government) ownership, e.g. to protect jobs, run natural monopolies such as water or rail in the public interest, or secure key services. Privatisation : transferring a firm or industry from the public sector to the private sector, aiming for greater efficiency through the profit motive and competition, and raising revenue for the government. Risks: private monopoly, job losses, neglect of unprofitable but socially valuable services. Model answer Explain how an indirect tax on petrol could reduce an external cost. [4] Burning petrol creates an external cost, such as air pollution and CO 2 emissions that harm third parties (1). An indirect tax raises the costs of sellers, shifting the supply curve to the left (1). This increases the price of petrol, causing a contraction in quantity demanded (1). With less petrol consumed, fewer emissions are produced, so the external cost falls and resources are allocated closer to the socially efficient level (1). However, as demand for petrol is price inelastic, the fall in consumption may be small. Examiner Tip For 8-mark “discuss whether” questions on intervention, give a developed argument for, a developed argument against, and a justified conclusion that depends on something specific: the PED of the product, the size of the tax or subsidy, the cost of enforcement, or whether the government has better information than the market. Quick Checklist I can explain how the price mechanism answers the three basic questions and distinguish micro from macroeconomics. I can draw and explain movements along and shifts of demand and supply curves, with their causes. I can show how equilibrium is reached and how it changes after a shift, using excess demand and excess supply. I can calculate and interpret PED and PES, explain their determinants and link PED to total revenue. I can assess the advantages and disadvantages of the market economic system. I can define public, merit and demerit goods and explain social cost and social benefit using externalities. I can analyse maximum and minimum prices, indirect taxes, subsidies, regulation, state provision, nationalisation and privatisation.

Topic 3 · Microeconomic Decision-Makers Microeconomic Decision-Makers This topic looks at the individual players in an economy: banks, households, workers, trade unions and firms, and how each makes choices. It is the largest topic on the syllabus and supplies many Paper 2 Section B questions, especially on wages, growth of firms and cost/revenue calculations.

Money is anything that is generally accepted as a means of payment for goods and services and settling debts. Barter (swapping goods directly) needs a double coincidence of wants , which money removes. Functions of money Medium of exchange — used to buy and sell, removing the need for barter. Unit of account (measure of value) — allows prices of different goods to be compared. Store of value — can be saved and used later (weakened by inflation). Standard of deferred payment — allows borrowing now and repaying later. Characteristics of good money Acceptable, durable, portable, divisible, homogeneous (uniform), limited in supply and difficult to forge. M edium U nit S tore D eferred — “Money Usually Stays Deferred” Central bank vs commercial banks Central bank Commercial banks Government’s bank: manages government accounts and national debt Accept deposits from households and firms (current and savings accounts) Bankers’ bank: holds commercial banks’ reserves; lender of last resort Lend to customers through loans, mortgages and overdrafts Issues notes and coins Provide payment services: cards, transfers, online banking Operates monetary policy (sets the policy interest rate, influences money supply) Offer other services such as currency exchange, financial advice, safe-keeping Manages the country’s gold and foreign currency reserves; may manage the exchange rate Aim to make a profit: interest charged on loans exceeds interest paid on deposits Regulates and supervises the banking system for stability Usually privately owned Commercial banks balance three aims: profitability , liquidity (having enough cash to meet withdrawals) and security (avoiding bad loans).

Disposable income = income after direct taxes, plus state benefits. It is split between spending (consumption) and saving . Saving = disposable income not spent. Borrowing allows spending above current income. Influence Effect on spending Effect on saving Effect on borrowing Higher income Rises (but a smaller share of income spent by the rich) Rises; rich save a larger proportion Easier to obtain credit Higher interest rates Falls Rises (greater reward) Falls (loans cost more) Higher confidence about the future Rises Falls Rises Rising wealth (e.g. house prices) Rises Falls Rises (more collateral) Easier availability of credit Rises Falls Rises Age / stage of life Young and old spend a high share of income Middle-aged save most (for retirement) Young adults borrow most (homes, education) Other influences: size of household, social attitudes to debt, availability of pensions and welfare, and expected inflation (people buy earlier if they expect prices to rise).

Factors affecting choice of occupation Wage factors : basic pay, overtime, bonuses, commission. Non-wage factors : job security, working hours and holidays, promotion prospects, training, working conditions, fringe benefits (company car, pension, health insurance), job satisfaction, location, flexibility such as remote working, and the employer’s environmental or ethical record. Wage determination In a free labour market the wage rate is set where the demand for labour (from firms) equals the supply of labour (from workers). Demand for labour is a derived demand : it depends on demand for the product the workers make. It also depends on labour productivity and the cost of capital that could replace workers. Supply of labour to an occupation depends on the wage, non-wage factors, qualifications and training needed, and the size of the working population. Wages can also be influenced by trade unions , governments (national minimum wage, public-sector pay) and employer bargaining power. Figure: A rise in demand for a product raises the derived demand for labour (D to D1), increasing the wage from W to W1 and employment from Q to Q1. Reasons for differences in earnings Skills, qualifications and training : long training restricts supply (surgeons vs cleaners). Productivity : more productive workers are worth more to firms. Demand for the product : workers in growing industries (e.g. renewable energy engineers) earn more. Unpleasant or dangerous work may earn compensating extra pay. Trade union strength and government policy (minimum wages, public-sector pay scales). Public vs private sector , skilled vs unskilled , agricultural vs manufacturing vs services . Male vs female : discrimination, career breaks, concentration in lower-paid occupations, fewer hours worked. Non-wage benefits : some jobs pay less because they offer high job satisfaction or security. Division of labour / specialisation Division of labour is when a production process is split into separate tasks, with each worker specialising in one task. Advantages Disadvantages Workers Become skilled faster; may earn more; less training time Boredom; loss of motivation; narrow skills make them vulnerable to unemployment if the task is automated Firms Higher productivity; lower average costs; easier to recruit and train Interdependence: one absence or bottleneck stops production; lower quality if workers are demotivated; higher staff turnover

A trade union is an organisation of workers that aims to protect and improve the interests of its members. Role : negotiate higher wages ( collective bargaining ), better working conditions, job security, training, and represent members in disputes; lobby government on issues such as the minimum wage. Industrial action : strikes, work-to-rule, overtime bans, go-slows. Factors that make a union strong High membership; members hard to replace (skilled); product demand is price inelastic so higher wages can be passed on in prices; strike fund; public support; favourable laws; firm is profitable. Advantages of trade unions Disadvantages of trade unions Higher wages and safer conditions for members Higher wages raise firms’ costs and may cause job losses One voice saves management time negotiating with each worker Strikes cut output, harm customers and damage the economy Can support productivity through training agreements May resist new technology and efficient working practices Balances the bargaining power of large employers Can benefit members at the expense of non-members

Classification of firms By sector : primary (extracting natural resources: farming, fishing, mining); secondary (manufacturing and construction); tertiary (services: banking, retail, tourism). As economies develop, the relative importance usually shifts from primary to secondary to tertiary. Private sector firms are owned by individuals/shareholders and usually aim for profit. Public sector organisations are owned by the government and often aim to provide a service. By size : measured by number of employees, capital employed, sales revenue or market share. Small firms Why they survive : small market size or niche markets; personal service; flexibility; local knowledge; low start-up costs; government support; they may supply larger firms; owners may not want to grow. Challenges : difficulty raising finance, higher average costs (no economies of scale), competition from large firms, reliance on few customers. Growth of firms Internal (organic) growth : expanding by reinvesting profit, opening new outlets, developing new products. External growth : a merger (two firms agree to join) or takeover (one firm buys another). Type of integration Meaning Example Main benefit Horizontal Firms at the same stage of production in the same industry Two car makers merge Economies of scale, higher market share, less competition Vertical backward Joins with a firm at an earlier stage (supplier) Chocolate maker buys a cocoa farm Secure supplies, control over quality and cost Vertical forward Joins with a firm at a later stage (customer/outlet) Brewery buys a chain of cafes Secure outlets, capture retail profit Conglomerate Firms in unrelated industries Food company buys a solar panel business Diversification spreads risk Why firms grow : to gain economies of scale, increase market share and market power, raise profits, spread risk and survive. Why some stay small : see small firms above. Economies and diseconomies of scale Economies of scale are the reductions in average (unit) cost as a firm increases its scale of production. Diseconomies of scale are rises in average cost when a firm grows too large. Internal economies (inside one firm) External economies (whole industry grows) Internal diseconomies Purchasing (bulk-buying) discounts Pool of skilled local labour Poor communication across many layers Technical : afford advanced machinery Specialist suppliers locate nearby Weak coordination and control Financial : borrow more cheaply Better infrastructure and transport links Low worker motivation, feeling unvalued Marketing : advertising spread over more output Shared research, training colleges Slow decision-making Managerial : hire specialist managers External diseconomies : congestion, rising land and labour costs as an industry crowds an area Risk-bearing : diversify products and markets Common Mistake Saying economies of scale reduce total cost. Total cost rises as output rises; it is the average cost per unit that falls.

Production is the process of converting factors of production (inputs) into goods and services (output). Demand for factors of production is derived demand. It depends on demand for the product, the price of each factor, the productivity of each factor, and the availability and cost of substitutes (e.g. machines for workers). Labour-intensive production uses a high proportion of labour relative to capital (hairdressing, handmade crafts, tea picking). Capital-intensive production uses a high proportion of capital (car assembly, oil refining). Firms choose capital-intensive methods when labour is expensive, output is large and standardised, and technology is available; labour-intensive methods suit personal services, small outputs and low-wage economies. Productivity Output per factor input per time period Labour productivity Total output ÷ number of workers Raised by Training, better capital, technology, motivation, specialisation Productivity vs production : production is total output; productivity is how efficiently inputs are turned into output. Higher productivity lowers average costs, can raise wages and profits, and improves international competitiveness.

Fixed cost (FC) Does not change with output (rent, insurance) Variable cost (VC) Changes with output (raw materials, energy) Total cost (TC) TC = FC + VC Average total cost ATC = TC ÷ output Average fixed cost AFC = FC ÷ output (always falls as output rises) Average variable cost AVC = VC ÷ output Total revenue (TR) TR = price × quantity sold Average revenue (AR) AR = TR ÷ quantity = price Profit Profit = TR − TC Worked example A bakery pays rent of $600 a week. Each loaf costs $0.80 in ingredients and energy and sells for $2.00. It sells 1,000 loaves. VC = 1,000 × $0.80 = $800; TC = $600 + $800 = $1,400 ATC = $1,400 ÷ 1,000 = $1.40 per loaf; AFC = $0.60 TR = 1,000 × $2.00 = $2,000; Profit = $2,000 − $1,400 = $600 If output doubles to 2,000, AFC falls to $0.30 and ATC to $1.10: fixed costs are spread over more units. Objectives of firms Survival — especially for new firms or in a recession. Profit maximisation — the traditional aim of private firms; rewards owners and funds investment. Growth — larger size brings economies of scale and security. Sales/revenue maximisation or market share — may be preferred by managers. Social welfare / corporate social responsibility — e.g. cutting carbon emissions, ethical sourcing; public-sector firms often aim to provide an affordable service.

Feature Competitive market Monopoly Number of firms Many One dominant firm (pure monopoly = single seller) Barriers to entry Low or none High: legal (patents, licences), economies of scale, control of resources, high start-up costs, brand loyalty Price setting Firms are price-takers; price set by market forces Price-maker (but cannot set both price and quantity) Product Similar/identical Unique, few close substitutes Profit Normal profit in the long run; high profits attract new entrants Can earn high (supernormal) profits in the long run Advantages of monopoly Disadvantages of monopoly Economies of scale can mean lower costs and possibly lower prices Higher prices and lower output than in a competitive market Supernormal profits can fund research and development and innovation Less choice for consumers Avoids wasteful duplication (natural monopoly, e.g. water pipes) Less incentive to be efficient or improve quality Stable, can invest long-term May exploit suppliers and workers Competitive markets : benefits include low prices, choice, efficiency and innovation to win customers; drawbacks include limited economies of scale and less profit available for research. 1 Chain of reasoning: horizontal merger Two supermarkets merge → larger scale of output. 2 Bulk-buying Purchasing economies of scale → lower average costs. 3 Market power Fewer competitors → greater ability to set prices. 4 Outcome Higher profits; consumers gain only if cost savings are passed on, otherwise they face higher prices and less choice. Model answer Explain why a surgeon usually earns more than a shop assistant. [4] A surgeon needs many years of training and high qualifications, so few people are able to enter the occupation and the supply of surgeons is low. The demand for surgeons is high because their skills are essential and their productivity (value of output) is great. High demand and low supply result in a high equilibrium wage. In contrast, shop assistant work requires little training, so supply is large, and each assistant can be replaced easily, so the equilibrium wage is lower. Examiner Tip In “discuss” questions about mergers, trade unions or monopoly, always give both sides and a justified conclusion that depends on conditions (e.g. “a merger benefits consumers only if the savings from economies of scale are passed on as lower prices and competition authorities prevent abuse of market power”). Common Mistake Confusing productivity with production . A firm can produce more simply by hiring more workers while productivity (output per worker) stays the same or falls. Quick Checklist I can state the four functions of money and compare the roles of central and commercial banks. I can explain how income, interest rates, confidence and age affect household spending, saving and borrowing. I can use a labour market diagram to explain wage determination and give reasons for wage differences. I can assess the role and impact of trade unions and of division of labour. I can classify firms and distinguish horizontal, vertical and conglomerate integration. I can explain named economies and diseconomies of scale in terms of average cost. I can calculate TC, ATC, AFC, AVC, TR, AR and profit from data. I can compare competitive markets with monopoly and evaluate monopoly.

Topic 4 · Government and the Macroeconomy Government and the Macroeconomy This topic covers what governments try to achieve for the whole economy, the policies they use (fiscal, monetary and supply-side), and the three big macroeconomic problems: slow growth, unemployment and inflation. Expect data-response questions using GDP, unemployment and CPI figures, and 8-mark “discuss” questions on which policy works best.

At a local level: providing services such as refuse collection, local roads and schools. At a national level: providing public goods (defence, justice), merit goods (education, healthcare), welfare benefits, regulation of markets, and managing the macroeconomy. At an international level: trade agreements, membership of international bodies, cooperation on climate change and financial stability. The government is also a producer (state-owned enterprises) and an employer .

Economic growth Sustained rise in real GDP Full employment / low unemployment Everyone willing and able to work has a job Stable prices / low inflation Often a target of around 2% a year Balance of payments stability Avoid large, persistent current account deficits or surpluses Redistribution of income Reduce inequality between rich and poor Environmental sustainability Meet present needs without damaging future generations’ ability to meet theirs Environmental sustainability as an aim includes cutting carbon emissions, protecting natural resources, reducing pollution and encouraging renewable energy, so that growth can continue in the long run. Possible conflicts between aims Growth vs stable prices : rapid growth in demand can cause demand-pull inflation. Full employment vs stable prices : as unemployment falls, workers can bid up wages, causing cost-push inflation. Growth vs balance of payments : higher incomes raise spending on imports, worsening the current account. Growth vs environmental sustainability : more output often means more pollution and resource depletion. Redistribution vs growth : very high taxes on the rich may reduce incentives to work and invest. Examiner Tip Conflicts are not inevitable. Supply-side policy can raise growth and reduce inflation together, and investment in green technology can support both growth and sustainability. Mentioning this earns evaluation marks.

Fiscal policy is the use of government spending and taxation to influence aggregate demand and the economy. The government budget Budget deficit : government spending > tax revenue (financed by borrowing, adding to national debt). Budget surplus : tax revenue > government spending. Balanced budget : the two are equal. Areas of government spending : healthcare, education, defence, infrastructure, welfare benefits and pensions, debt interest. Reasons for spending : provide public and merit goods, support the poor, improve infrastructure, influence the economy. Reasons for taxation Raise revenue to finance government spending. Redistribute income (progressive taxes). Discourage demerit goods (tobacco, sugary drinks, alcohol). Promote environmental sustainability : carbon taxes, fuel duty and landfill taxes make polluters pay for external costs. Protect domestic industries (tariffs) and manage aggregate demand. Classification of taxes Type Meaning Example Direct Tax on income or wealth, paid directly to the government by the person taxed Income tax, corporation tax, inheritance tax Indirect Tax on spending; collected by sellers from buyers VAT / sales tax, excise duty, tariffs Progressive Takes a larger percentage of income as income rises Income tax with rising bands Regressive Takes a larger percentage of income from the poor than the rich Most indirect taxes, e.g. a flat excise duty on fuel Proportional Takes the same percentage of income at all income levels A flat-rate income tax Common Mistake Defining a progressive tax as one where “the rich pay more”. Under a proportional tax the rich also pay a larger amount . A progressive tax takes a higher proportion (percentage) of income as income rises. Qualities of a good tax (canons of taxation) Equitable : based on ability to pay. Certain : taxpayers know how much, when and how to pay. Convenient : easy and timely to pay. Economical / efficient : cheap to collect relative to revenue raised. Flexible : can be changed easily when conditions change. Does not distort incentives to work, save or invest unnecessarily. Impact of taxation Taxes affect consumers (lower disposable income, higher prices), producers (higher costs, lower profits), the government (revenue) and the economy (output, employment, price level, inequality, and pollution in the case of environmental taxes). Expansionary vs contractionary fiscal policy Expansionary Contractionary Measures Raise government spending and/or cut taxes Cut government spending and/or raise taxes Aim Increase aggregate demand: boost growth, cut unemployment Reduce aggregate demand: control inflation, improve current account Drawbacks Inflation, larger budget deficit, more imports, time lags Slower growth, higher unemployment, less spending on public services

Monetary policy is the use of interest rates, the money supply and the exchange rate, usually by the central bank, to influence aggregate demand. 1 Chain of reasoning: interest rate rise Central bank raises the interest rate. 2 Borrowing costs rise Loans and mortgages become more expensive; saving is more rewarding. 3 Spending falls Households cut consumption; firms cut investment. Currency may appreciate, reducing export demand. 4 Outcome Aggregate demand falls → demand-pull inflation slows, but growth may slow and unemployment may rise. Expansionary monetary policy: cut interest rates, increase the money supply, allow the currency to depreciate. Contractionary monetary policy: raise interest rates, reduce the money supply, allow the currency to appreciate. Limitations : time lags (often 12–24 months); low confidence may stop people borrowing even when rates are cut; rates cannot fall far below zero; higher rates hurt borrowers and investment.

Supply-side policies aim to increase the productive capacity of the economy (aggregate supply) by improving the quantity and quality of factors of production and making markets work more efficiently. Education and training — raise labour productivity and occupational mobility. Improving healthcare — a healthier, more productive workforce. Infrastructure investment — transport, broadband, renewable energy grids cut firms’ costs. Lower direct taxes — stronger incentives to work, invest and start businesses. Deregulation and privatisation — increase competition and efficiency. Labour market reforms — e.g. reducing trade union power or reforming benefits to encourage work. Subsidies for research and development , including green technology. Evaluation : supply-side policies can boost growth without inflation and improve competitiveness, but they are costly, take a long time to work, and some (deregulation, benefit cuts) can increase inequality or harm the environment.

Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the total value of output produced in a country in a year. Economic growth is an increase in real GDP. Real GDP is adjusted for inflation; nominal GDP is at current prices. GDP per head = real GDP ÷ population; a better guide to average living standards. Growth rate (GDP this year − GDP last year) ÷ GDP last year × 100 Recession Two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP Causes of economic growth Actual growth (using spare capacity): increase in aggregate demand from consumption, investment, government spending or net exports. Potential growth (outward shift of the PPC): more or better resources — investment in capital, new technology, better education and training, more workers (migration, higher participation), discovery of natural resources. Causes of recession Fall in aggregate demand: falling confidence, high interest rates, a global downturn reducing exports, financial crises, or supply shocks such as sharp rises in energy prices. Benefits of economic growth Costs of economic growth Higher incomes and living standards Pollution, carbon emissions and resource depletion Lower unemployment May cause inflation if demand grows faster than capacity More tax revenue for public services, without raising tax rates Benefits may be unevenly spread, widening inequality Firms earn more profit and invest more Stress, longer working hours, congestion Policies to promote growth : expansionary fiscal and monetary policy (short run) and supply-side policy (long run). Governments increasingly aim for sustainable growth , e.g. investment in renewable energy.

Unemployment : people of working age who are willing and able to work, and actively seeking work, but cannot find a job. Changing patterns of employment : shift from primary and secondary to tertiary sector; more part-time, self-employed and gig work; more women in work; more remote working. Unemployment rate Number unemployed ÷ labour force × 100 Labour force Employed + unemployed Claimant count Number claiming unemployment benefits Labour Force Survey Sample survey using the ILO definition Types and causes of unemployment Type Cause Example Policy Frictional Short-term, workers between jobs Graduate searching for a first job Better job information, job centres Structural Long-term decline of an industry; skills mismatch; geographical immobility Coal miners after mines close Retraining, relocation grants, regional aid Cyclical (demand-deficient) Fall in aggregate demand during a recession Construction workers laid off in a downturn Expansionary fiscal and monetary policy Seasonal Demand varies with the time of year Ski instructors in summer Encourage diversification of work Technological Workers replaced by machines or automation Supermarket cashiers replaced by self-checkout Education and retraining Consequences of unemployment Individuals : loss of income, lower living standards, loss of skills, stress and poor health. Firms : lower demand for products (but a larger pool of labour and less wage pressure). Government : lower tax revenue and higher benefit spending (larger budget deficit). Economy : lost output (inside the PPC), wasted resources, possible rise in crime and inequality.

Inflation : a sustained rise in the general price level over time. Deflation : a sustained fall in the general price level. Disinflation : inflation is falling but still positive (prices rising more slowly). Measuring inflation: the Consumer Prices Index (CPI) 1 Choose a base year Index set at 100. 2 Household expenditure survey Finds what a typical household buys: the “basket” of goods and services. 3 Weight each item By its share of household spending (e.g. food more heavily than cinema tickets). 4 Record prices Collect prices regularly from many shops and regions. 5 Calculate the index Multiply price index for each item by its weight, add up and divide by total weights; compare with the base year. Inflation rate (CPI this year − CPI last year) ÷ CPI last year × 100 Example CPI 120 → 126: (6 ÷ 120) × 100 = 5% Causes of inflation Demand-pull inflation : aggregate demand grows faster than the economy’s ability to supply (“too much money chasing too few goods”). Caused by tax cuts, low interest rates, rising confidence, export booms. Cost-push inflation : rising costs of production are passed on as higher prices. Caused by higher wages, rising raw material or energy prices, a fall in the exchange rate raising import costs, or higher indirect taxes. Consequences of inflation Falls in real incomes for those on fixed incomes (pensioners, benefit recipients) whose incomes do not keep pace. Savers lose if the interest rate is below inflation; borrowers gain as the real value of debt falls. Menu costs (changing price lists) and shoe-leather costs (time spent searching for best prices or moving money). Uncertainty discourages investment; exports become less price competitive , worsening the current account. Fiscal drag : if tax bands are not raised, people drift into higher tax bands. Causes and consequences of deflation Causes : falling aggregate demand (bad deflation) or falling costs from productivity gains and new technology (good deflation). Consequences : consumers delay purchases expecting lower prices → demand falls → firms cut output and jobs → further falls in demand (a deflationary spiral ); the real burden of debt rises; however, exports may become more competitive. Policies to control inflation Demand-pull : contractionary fiscal policy (higher taxes, lower spending) and contractionary monetary policy (higher interest rates). Cost-push : supply-side policies to raise productivity; a stronger exchange rate to cut import costs; cutting indirect taxes. Deflation : expansionary fiscal and monetary policy to boost demand. Model answer Explain how a cut in income tax might reduce unemployment. [4] A cut in income tax increases households’ disposable income. With more disposable income, consumers spend more on goods and services, increasing aggregate demand. Firms respond to higher demand by increasing output, and because labour is a derived demand they need to hire more workers. This reduces cyclical unemployment. A lower tax rate may also increase the incentive to work, encouraging people to take up jobs. Examiner Tip Always match the policy to the cause. Higher interest rates suit demand-pull inflation but can make cost-push inflation worse for output and jobs. Retraining solves structural, not cyclical, unemployment. Naming the type or cause first makes your evaluation precise. Common Mistake Thinking that a fall in the inflation rate means prices are falling. If inflation falls from 6% to 3%, prices are still rising, just more slowly. Only negative inflation (deflation) means the price level is falling. Quick Checklist I can list the six macroeconomic aims, including environmental sustainability, and explain conflicts between them. I can classify taxes as direct/indirect and progressive/regressive/proportional, and state the qualities of a good tax. I can explain how expansionary and contractionary fiscal and monetary policy affect aggregate demand. I can describe supply-side policies and evaluate their effectiveness. I can define GDP and recession, calculate a growth rate, and explain the causes and consequences of growth. I can calculate the unemployment rate and match each type of unemployment to a suitable policy. I can explain how the CPI is constructed and calculate the inflation rate. I can distinguish demand-pull and cost-push inflation and explain the consequences of inflation and deflation.

Topic 5 · Economic Development Economic Development How we measure and compare living standards, why poverty exists and how it can be reduced, how populations change, and why some countries are far more developed than others. Paper 2 often asks you to use data on GDP per head, HDI or population to compare two countries, so precise definitions and clear chains of reasoning are essential.

Living standards describe the quality of life and material well-being of people in a country. Economic development is a broader idea than economic growth: it means an improvement in people’s welfare, including income, health, education and freedom of choice. Real GDP per head Real GDP per head (per capita) = real GDP ÷ population. It shows the average output (and income) per person, adjusted for inflation. “Real” removes the effect of price changes, so a rise shows more goods and services, not just higher prices. “Per head” allows for population size, so a large country is not automatically ranked above a small one. Real GDP per head Real GDP ÷ population Rise in living standards (income) Real GDP grows faster than population Fall in GDP per head Population grows faster than real GDP Limitations of real GDP per head as a measure of living standards It is an average — it hides the distribution of income. A few very rich people can raise the average while most people remain poor. Informal (hidden) economy — unrecorded activity (cash-in-hand work, illegal trade) is excluded, so GDP may understate true output, especially in low-income countries. Non-marketed output — subsistence farming, housework and voluntary work are not counted. Quality of life factors are ignored — working hours, leisure time, pollution, crime, political freedom and stress. Environmental damage — output from deforestation or heavy CO 2 emissions raises GDP but reduces sustainability and future welfare. Composition of output — high spending on defence adds to GDP but may not improve living standards as much as spending on schools or hospitals. International comparisons — figures must be converted into one currency; exchange rates may not reflect differences in the cost of living. The Human Development Index (HDI) The HDI is a composite measure of living standards published by the United Nations. It combines three dimensions into a single value between 0 and 1 (closer to 1 = more developed). Dimension Indicator used Why it matters A long and healthy life Life expectancy at birth Reflects healthcare, nutrition, sanitation and clean water Knowledge (education) Mean years of schooling (adults) and expected years of schooling (children) Education raises skills, productivity and life choices A decent standard of living Gross national income (GNI) per head, adjusted for purchasing power Reflects material income and ability to buy goods and services Advantages of HDI over GDP per head Broader: includes health and education, not just income. Income is adjusted for differences in cost of living (purchasing power). Limitations of HDI Still uses averages, so it ignores inequality between groups, regions and genders. Leaves out many aspects of well-being: environmental quality, political freedom, crime, working conditions, housing. Years of schooling measure quantity, not the quality of education. Data in low-income countries may be inaccurate or out of date. Two countries can have the same HDI with very different mixes of income, health and education. Examiner Tip When asked “Which country has higher living standards?” using data, never decide on one indicator alone. Compare GDP per head and HDI (or life expectancy, literacy), then state the limitations of each measure. A balanced conclusion (“it depends on…”) earns the top marks on 8-mark questions.

Absolute poverty : a situation where people do not have enough income to meet their basic needs — food, clean water, shelter, clothing and basic healthcare. It is often measured using an international poverty line (an income per day, in purchasing-power terms). Relative poverty : a situation where people are poor compared with others in the same society, often defined as having an income below a certain percentage (e.g. 50% or 60%) of the median income. They can meet basic needs but cannot afford the standard of living most people enjoy. Common Mistake Saying relative poverty only exists in poor countries. Relative poverty exists in every country, including the richest, because it is measured against the country’s own average. Absolute poverty can be eliminated in theory; relative poverty is much harder to remove entirely while incomes are unequal. Causes of poverty Unemployment — no earned income; may depend on low state benefits. Low wages — low-skilled, low-productivity jobs; workers in the informal sector with no protection. Illness, disability and old age — limited ability to work; high medical costs. Lack of education and training — limits access to better-paid jobs. Large family size / high dependency — income shared among more people. Poor infrastructure and lack of access to finance — hard to start businesses or reach markets. Natural disasters, climate change and conflict — destroy crops, homes and capital. Inflation — reduces the real value of low, fixed incomes. Unequal distribution of wealth and land ; corruption diverting public funds. Policies to alleviate poverty Policy How it helps Possible drawback Promoting economic growth (e.g. lower interest rates, infrastructure spending) Creates jobs and raises incomes Benefits may not “trickle down” to the poorest; may raise inflation or pollution Improving education and training Raises skills, productivity and earning power in the long run Expensive; takes many years to have an effect Improving healthcare, sanitation and clean water Healthier workers are more productive and miss fewer days High opportunity cost for government budgets Progressive taxation Takes a higher proportion from high earners, funding help for the poor May reduce incentives to work and invest; tax avoidance State benefits / transfer payments (e.g. unemployment and child benefits, pensions) Directly raises the income of the poorest Cost; may create a disincentive to seek work (poverty trap) National minimum wage Raises pay of the lowest-paid workers May cause unemployment if set above equilibrium wage Foreign aid and debt relief Funds for schools, hospitals, infrastructure Risk of corruption; dependency Microfinance / small loans Helps poor people start small businesses Small scale; risk of debt problems 1 Cause Government spends more on primary and secondary education. 2 Effect Workers gain skills and become more productive. 3 Effect They qualify for better-paid, higher-skilled jobs and are less likely to be unemployed. 4 Outcome Household incomes rise above the poverty line; the next generation is also better educated, breaking the cycle of poverty.

Factors affecting population growth Birth rate Live births per 1,000 people per year Death rate Deaths per 1,000 people per year Natural increase Birth rate − death rate Net migration Immigration − emigration Population change Natural increase + net migration Example: a birth rate of 22 per 1,000 and a death rate of 8 per 1,000 gives a natural increase of 14 per 1,000, i.e. 1.4% a year before migration. Reasons for different population growth rates between countries High birth rates in many low-income countries because: children can work and support parents in old age (no state pensions); high infant mortality encourages families to have more children; limited access to, or knowledge of, contraception; cultural and religious traditions; early marriage; fewer women in education and paid work. Low birth rates in high-income countries because children are expensive to raise and educate, more women pursue careers, people marry later, and contraception is widely available. Falling death rates everywhere due to better healthcare, vaccinations, nutrition, clean water and sanitation — but death rates remain higher where these are lacking or where there is conflict or disease. Net migration : people move to countries with more jobs, higher wages, better public services or political stability (pull factors), and leave countries with conflict, persecution, poverty or climate-related disasters (push factors). Population structure and population pyramids A population pyramid shows the age and gender structure of a population: age groups on the vertical axis, the number or percentage of males (left) and females (right) on the horizontal axis. Shape Typical country What it shows Wide base, narrow top (triangle) Low-income, developing High birth rate, high death rate, low life expectancy, young population Straighter sides, narrower base (column/beehive) High-income, developed Low birth rate, low death rate, long life expectancy, ageing population Base narrower than middle (inverted) Some high-income countries Birth rate below replacement; population likely to shrink Dependency ratio The dependent population are those not of working age: young dependants (usually under 15/16) and elderly dependants (usually over 64/65). Dependency ratio = (number of dependants ÷ number of people of working age) × 100. A high ratio means each worker supports more dependants, putting pressure on taxes and government spending. Effects of changes in the size and structure of population Change Possible benefits Possible problems Rising population size Larger labour force; bigger market for firms; economies of scale; more innovation Pressure on housing, schools, healthcare, food and water; congestion; pollution; unemployment if jobs do not grow as fast; GDP per head may fall Ageing population (more over-65s) Demand for new products (healthcare, leisure); older workers bring experience; voluntary work Higher spending on pensions and healthcare; smaller workforce; higher taxes on workers; labour shortages; less geographically and occupationally mobile labour Young population (many under-15s) Large future workforce; potentially flexible, mobile labour later High spending needed on education and child healthcare; high dependency now Net immigration Fills skill shortages; often working age, so pays taxes; widens the labour pool Pressure on public services and housing; possible downward pressure on wages in some jobs Net emigration Remittances sent home; reduces unemployment “Brain drain” — loss of skilled, young workers such as doctors and engineers Change in gender balance — Can affect future birth rates and the size of the labour force Optimum population The optimum population is the size of population that, combined with the country’s other resources and current technology, maximises output (real GDP) per head. Under-population : too few people to make full use of resources — an increase in population would raise GDP per head. Over-population : too many people for the resources available — GDP per head would rise if the population fell. The optimum is not fixed: improvements in technology, capital and education raise it over time. Model answer Explain two reasons why an ageing population may reduce a country’s economic growth. (4 marks) First, an ageing population means a smaller proportion of people are of working age. The labour force shrinks, so the country has fewer workers to produce goods and services, reducing its productive capacity and real GDP. Second, the government has to spend more on state pensions and healthcare for the elderly. This may require higher taxes on workers and firms, reducing incentives to work and invest, or it may mean less government spending on infrastructure and education, which lowers future growth.

h: 4. Differences in economic development between countries
x: Countries are often grouped as low-income (less developed), middle-income and high-income (developed). The main differences examiners expect you to explain are: Factor Low-income / less developed High-income / developed Income Low real GDP per head; more absolute poverty; often high inequality High real GDP per head; little absolute poverty Productivity Low output per worker: little capital, basic technology, low skills High output per worker: advanced capital and technology, skilled labour Population growth High birth rate, rapid growth, young population Low birth rate, slow or negative growth, ageing population Sector size Large primary sector (agriculture, mining); large informal sector Large tertiary sector (services); small primary sector; secondary sector shrinking relative to services Saving and investment Low incomes → low saving → low investment in capital Higher saving and developed banks → more investment Education Lower literacy and school enrolment, especially for girls High literacy; widespread secondary and higher education Healthcare Lower life expectancy, higher infant mortality, limited clean water and doctors High life expectancy, low infant mortality, widespread healthcare Primary sector : extraction of natural resources (farming, fishing, forestry, mining). Secondary sector : manufacturing and construction — turning raw materials into goods. Tertiary sector : providing services (banking, retail, tourism, education, healthcare). As countries develop, employment and output usually shift from primary → secondary → tertiary. The cycle of poverty (why low development persists) 1 Low incomes Most income is spent on necessities, leaving little to save. 2 Low saving Banks have few funds to lend to firms. 3 Low investment Little new capital, technology, education or infrastructure. 4 Low productivity Low output per worker keeps wages and incomes low — and the cycle repeats. Breaking the cycle may require foreign direct investment, aid, debt relief, better access to international markets (fair trade, reduced protection by rich countries), investment in education and health, and reducing corruption. Common Mistake Treating economic growth and economic development as the same thing. Growth is an increase in real GDP; development is an improvement in overall welfare. A country can grow (e.g. by exporting oil) while most people see little improvement in health, education or poverty, and while environmental damage harms future living standards. Examiner Tip For “Discuss whether a larger population always benefits an economy” (8 marks), give developed arguments on both sides (larger workforce and market vs pressure on resources and lower GDP per head), then link to optimum population : the answer depends on whether the country is currently under- or over-populated, the age structure of the extra people, and whether investment and jobs keep pace. Quick Checklist I can define real GDP per head and HDI, name the three HDI components, and give limitations of each measure. I can distinguish absolute and relative poverty, list causes of poverty and evaluate policies to reduce it. I can calculate natural increase and population change using birth rate, death rate and net migration. I can explain why birth rates, death rates and migration differ between countries. I can interpret a population pyramid and calculate and explain the dependency ratio. I can analyse the effects of population growth, an ageing population and migration. I can explain optimum population, under-population and over-population. I can compare countries by income, productivity, population growth, sector size, saving/investment, education and healthcare.

Topic 6 · International Trade International Trade and Globalisation Why countries specialise and trade, the role of multinational companies, the arguments for free trade and for protection, how exchange rates are set and why they change, and what the current account of the balance of payments shows. This topic is a favourite for data-response questions using trade and exchange rate figures.

International specialisation occurs when countries concentrate on producing the goods and services they are relatively best at producing (lowest opportunity cost), and trade to obtain others. It is based on differences in factor endowments: climate, natural resources, labour skills, capital and technology. Examples: Saudi Arabia (oil), Bangladesh (garments), Switzerland (financial services, pharmaceuticals), New Zealand (dairy). Specialisation also happens at regional level within a country (e.g. a region known for car manufacturing, wine, tourism or technology firms). Level Advantages Disadvantages National Higher total world output; economies of scale; lower costs and prices; wider choice for consumers; export earnings; more efficient use of resources Over-dependence on a few products; vulnerable to falls in world demand or price; risk of structural unemployment if demand shifts; depletion of natural resources; reliance on imports for essentials; transport emissions Regional Skilled labour pool; supporting firms and suppliers nearby (external economies of scale); reputation attracts investment Regional unemployment if the industry declines; congestion and pollution; regional inequality

Globalisation is the process by which the world’s economies become increasingly integrated and interdependent through trade in goods and services, flows of capital, movement of labour, and the spread of technology and ideas. Causes of globalisation Cheaper and faster transport (containerisation, air freight). Improvements in communication technology and the internet. Reduction in trade barriers (trade agreements, the World Trade Organization). Growth of multinational companies and freer movement of capital. Multinational companies (MNCs) A multinational company (MNC) is a firm that produces goods or services in more than one country. The home country is where its headquarters are; a host country is where it has operations. Benefits Costs Host country Creates jobs and raises incomes; investment in capital and infrastructure; transfer of technology and skills; tax revenue; exports improve the current account; more choice for consumers Profits sent back to the home country; local firms may be forced out; jobs may be low-skilled and low-paid; possible exploitation of workers; environmental damage and resource depletion; MNC may leave suddenly; political influence Home country Profits flow back, raising national income; MNC grows, gaining economies of scale; cheaper inputs lower prices for home consumers Jobs lost when production moves abroad; lower tax revenue if profits are declared elsewhere; less investment at home

Free trade is international trade without government restrictions (no tariffs, quotas or other barriers). Protectionism is the use of trade restrictions to protect domestic industries from foreign competition. Benefits of free trade Lower prices for consumers as the most efficient producers supply the market. Greater choice and variety of products. Larger markets for domestic firms, allowing economies of scale. Increased competition encourages efficiency, innovation and quality. Access to raw materials and capital goods not available at home. Higher world output and living standards through specialisation. Methods of protection Method Definition Effect Tariff A tax on imported goods Raises price of imports, reduces quantity imported, raises government revenue Import quota A physical limit on the quantity (or value) of a good that can be imported Reduces supply of imports; prices rise; no tax revenue unless licences are sold Subsidy to domestic producers Government payment to domestic firms to lower their costs Domestic goods become cheaper and more competitive against imports and in export markets Embargo A complete ban on trade (imports and/or exports) with a country or in a product Trade stops entirely; often used for political, safety or security reasons Other barriers Strict product standards and regulations, excessive paperwork, government favouring domestic firms in its purchases, exchange controls Raise the cost or difficulty of importing Reasons for protection Protect infant industries — new firms need time to grow and gain economies of scale before facing established foreign rivals. Protect declining industries / jobs — to avoid sudden structural unemployment and give time to adjust. Prevent dumping — foreign firms selling at a price below cost to drive out domestic competitors. Protect strategic industries — food, energy and defence, for national security. Improve the current account — reduce spending on imports. Raise government revenue from tariffs. Promote environmental sustainability — e.g. tariffs on goods made with high carbon emissions, bans on imports of illegally logged timber or endangered species products, standards requiring energy efficiency; this protects the environment and prevents firms in countries with strict rules being undercut by polluters. Protect consumers from unsafe or low-quality products. Consequences of protection Higher prices and less choice for consumers. Domestic firms face less competition, so may become inefficient and less innovative. Retaliation — other countries impose their own barriers, hurting exporters (a trade war). Higher costs for firms that use imported raw materials and components. World output falls as countries lose the gains from specialisation. On the positive side: jobs may be saved in the short run and infant industries given a chance to grow. Chain of reasoning: a tariff on imported steel 1 Cause Government places a tariff on imported steel. 2 Effect The price of imported steel rises, so domestic buyers switch to domestically produced steel. 3 Effect Domestic steel output and employment increase; government gains tariff revenue. 4 Outcome But car makers and builders pay more for steel, raising their costs and prices, and the exporting country may retaliate against this country’s exports. Common Mistake Confusing a tariff with a quota. A tariff is a tax (it raises price and earns government revenue); a quota is a quantity limit . Also, a subsidy protects by lowering domestic firms’ costs — it does not directly make imports more expensive.

The exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another (e.g. £1 = US$1.30). The foreign exchange market is where currencies are bought and sold. Determination in the foreign exchange market (floating rate) Demand for a currency comes from foreigners buying the country’s exports, foreign tourists visiting, foreign investors buying assets or saving in its banks, and speculators expecting it to rise. Supply of a currency comes from residents buying imports, travelling abroad, investing overseas, and speculators expecting it to fall. The equilibrium exchange rate is where demand for the currency equals supply. Figure: A rise in demand for the pound (e.g. more exports sold) shifts D to D1, so the pound appreciates from P to P1. Causes of exchange rate fluctuations Changes in demand for exports / imports — e.g. higher export sales raise demand for the currency (appreciation). Changes in interest rates — higher interest rates attract foreign savings (“hot money”), raising demand for the currency. Relative inflation rates — higher inflation makes exports less competitive, reducing demand for the currency and increasing supply (as residents buy more imports) → depreciation. Foreign direct investment flowing in or out. Speculation about future movements. Government / central bank intervention — buying or selling the currency using foreign currency reserves. Appreciation Rise in value of a floating currency Depreciation Fall in value of a floating currency Revaluation Government raises a fixed rate Devaluation Government lowers a fixed rate Consequences of exchange rate fluctuations Effect on… Appreciation Depreciation Export prices (in foreign currency) Rise → exports less competitive Fall → exports more competitive Import prices (in domestic currency) Fall → imports cheaper Rise → imports dearer Current account Tends to worsen (if demand is price elastic) Tends to improve (if demand is price elastic) Inflation Lower — cheaper imported goods and raw materials; firms under pressure to keep costs down Higher — dearer imported goods and raw materials (cost-push) Employment and growth May fall in export and import-competing industries May rise as export demand and AD increase S trong P ound I mports C heaper E xports D earer — SPICED Floating vs fixed exchange rates A floating exchange rate is determined by market forces of demand and supply without government intervention. A fixed exchange rate is set by the government (or central bank) against another currency and maintained by intervention: buying or selling the currency with reserves, or changing interest rates. Floating Fixed Advantages Adjusts automatically to help correct a current account deficit; no need to hold large reserves; interest rates can be used for domestic aims Certainty for exporters, importers and investors; encourages trade and investment; discipline on inflation Disadvantages Uncertainty makes planning of trade and investment harder; speculation can cause large swings; depreciation can be inflationary Large reserves needed to defend the rate; interest rates may have to be set to protect the currency rather than to help the economy; rate may become over- or under-valued Examiner Tip Always say whose price changes and in which currency. “A depreciation of the rupee makes Indian exports cheaper in foreign currency and imports dearer in rupees .” Then add a condition: the current account only improves if demand for exports and imports is price elastic.

h: 5. The current account of the balance of payments
x: The balance of payments is a record of all financial transactions between a country and the rest of the world over a year. The current account records trade in goods and services plus income flows and transfers. Component What it records Example of a credit (money in) Trade in goods Exports minus imports of physical goods (visible trade) Selling cars abroad Trade in services Exports minus imports of services (invisible trade) Foreign tourists visiting; insurance sold abroad Primary income Income from owning factors of production abroad: profits, interest, dividends, wages Profits from a firm’s overseas branch sent home Secondary income Transfers with nothing given in return Remittances from citizens working abroad; foreign aid received Balance of trade in goods Exports of goods − imports of goods Current account balance Goods balance + services balance + primary income + secondary income Deficit Outflows (debits) exceed inflows (credits) Surplus Inflows (credits) exceed outflows (debits) Worked calculation Goods balance −$40bn, services balance +$25bn, primary income +$5bn, secondary income −$8bn. Current account balance = −40 + 25 + 5 − 8 = −$18bn (a deficit) . Causes of a current account deficit High domestic incomes / consumer boom — more spending on imports. Lack of international competitiveness — high inflation, low productivity, high costs or poor quality. A high (appreciated) exchange rate — exports dearer, imports cheaper. Recession abroad — lower demand for the country’s exports. Lack of natural resources, so raw materials and fuel must be imported; outflows of profits to foreign MNCs. Causes of a surplus The reverse: strong competitiveness, a low exchange rate, high world demand for its exports (e.g. commodities at high prices), or low domestic demand for imports. Consequences Deficit : net outflow of money reduces aggregate demand, which may lower output and employment; downward pressure on the exchange rate; must be financed by borrowing or selling assets, building up debt; loss of reserves. It may be less of a concern if short-term, or if imports are capital goods that raise future productivity. Surplus : higher AD, output and employment; may cause demand-pull inflation; upward pressure on the exchange rate; other countries may retaliate with protection; consumers may be getting fewer goods than they produce. Policies to achieve balance of payments stability Policy How it reduces a deficit Drawback Contractionary fiscal policy (higher taxes, lower government spending) Reduces incomes and so spending on imports Lower growth, higher unemployment Contractionary monetary policy (higher interest rates) Reduces borrowing and spending on imports; lowers inflation, improving competitiveness May cause the currency to appreciate, making exports dearer Depreciation / devaluation of the currency Makes exports cheaper and imports dearer Imported inflation; only works if demand is price elastic Protectionism Reduces imports directly Retaliation; higher prices; inefficiency Supply-side policies (education, training, infrastructure, investment incentives) Raise productivity and quality, improving long-run competitiveness Expensive and slow to take effect Model answer Explain how a rise in a country’s inflation rate could cause a current account deficit. (4 marks) If the country’s inflation rate rises above that of its trading partners, its goods and services become relatively more expensive. Foreign buyers switch to cheaper products from other countries, so the value of the country’s exports falls. At the same time, domestic consumers find imports relatively cheaper than domestically produced goods, so spending on imports rises. With export revenue falling and import spending rising, debits exceed credits, causing a deficit on the trade in goods and services and so on the current account. Quick Checklist I can explain the advantages and disadvantages of specialisation at national and regional level. I can define globalisation and analyse the effects of MNCs on home and host countries. I can explain the benefits of free trade, the methods of protection and the reasons for and consequences of protection, including environmental sustainability. I can draw and explain a foreign exchange market diagram showing appreciation and depreciation. I can explain the causes and consequences of exchange rate changes and compare floating and fixed rates. I can name the four parts of the current account and calculate its balance. I can explain the causes and consequences of a current account deficit and surplus and evaluate policies to correct them.
