Topic 1 · Fundamentals The Fundamentals of Accounting This topic explains why businesses keep accounting records, who uses them, and the accounting equation that sits underneath every double entry and every statement of financial position. Equation questions appear regularly in Paper 1 and underpin the whole of Paper 2.

Accounting is the process of recording, classifying, summarising, analysing and communicating financial information about a business so that users can make decisions. Record financial transactions accurately so there is a permanent, reliable history of what happened. Calculate profit or loss for a period, so the owner knows whether the business is successful. Show the financial position — what the business owns (assets), what it owes (liabilities) and the owner’s investment (capital) at a given date. Control the business: keep track of amounts owed by customers and to suppliers, monitor cash and inventory, and detect errors or fraud. Support decision-making and planning : pricing, expansion, borrowing, cutting costs. Meet obligations to outside parties such as tax authorities and lenders.

Book-keeping Accounting Meaning The detailed recording of financial transactions in books of prime entry and ledgers Using the book-keeping records to prepare financial statements, then analysing and interpreting them Main output Up-to-date books and ledger accounts Income statement, statement of financial position, ratios, reports and advice Skill level Routine, often done by a book-keeper or by accounting software Requires judgement, often done by a qualified accountant Stage Comes first Builds on book-keeping Examiner Tip If asked to distinguish book-keeping from accounting, use the words recording (book-keeping) and summarising, analysing and communicating (accounting). One sentence for each, then a link: “accounting uses the records produced by book-keeping.”

Different people look at accounting information for different reasons. Examiners reward answers that link the user to a specific interest. User What they want to know Owner(s) Profitability, how much can be withdrawn as drawings, whether to expand, the value of their investment Managers Which products or departments are profitable, cost control, planning and budgeting Bank and other lenders Whether the business can repay a loan and interest (liquidity, profitability, security) Trade payables (suppliers) Whether the business will pay for goods bought on credit; whether to offer or increase credit Customers Whether the business is likely to continue trading to supply goods, honour guarantees and provide service Employees Job security, likelihood of pay rises or bonuses Government and tax authorities The correct tax to be charged; statistics on the economy Potential investors or partners Whether to invest money in the business and the likely return

h: The role of the accountant and ethics
x: People who prepare accounts are trusted with confidential and important information. Accountants are expected to act with: Integrity — being honest and straightforward; not manipulating figures. Objectivity — not letting bias, conflicts of interest or pressure from others affect judgement. Professional competence — keeping knowledge and skills up to date. Confidentiality — not disclosing business information without proper authority. Professional behaviour — complying with laws and regulations and avoiding actions that discredit the profession. Unethical behaviour, such as overstating profit to obtain a loan, misleads users and can lead to poor decisions, legal penalties and loss of trust.

Asset A resource owned or controlled by the business, e.g. premises, inventory, trade receivables, bank Liability An amount owed by the business to others, e.g. trade payables, bank loan, bank overdraft Capital The amount invested in the business by the owner; what the business owes the owner Drawings Money, goods or other assets taken from the business by the owner for personal use Revenue (income) Amounts earned by the business, mainly from sales of goods or services Expense Costs of running the business in a period, e.g. wages, rent, electricity Classifying assets and liabilities Non-current assets : held for use in the business for more than one year, not for resale — land and buildings, machinery, fixtures and fittings, motor vehicles. Current assets : expected to be turned into cash within one year — inventory, trade receivables, other receivables, bank, cash. Non-current liabilities : due for repayment after more than one year — long-term bank loans. Current liabilities : due within one year — trade payables, other payables, bank overdraft.

The equation Assets = Liabilities + Capital Rearranged: Capital = Assets − Liabilities and Liabilities = Assets − Capital Everything a business owns has been financed either by the owner (capital) or by outsiders (liabilities). Because every transaction has two effects, the equation always stays in balance. This is the foundation of double-entry book-keeping and is why the statement of financial position balances. Finding a missing figure A business has assets of $45 000 and liabilities of $12 500. Capital = $45 000 − $12 500 = $32 500 . Capital is $32 500 and assets are $45 000. Liabilities = $45 000 − $32 500 = $12 500 .

h: Worked example: transactions changing the equation
x: Lina starts a small gift shop. Follow how each transaction affects the equation. Notice that after every line, total assets equal liabilities plus capital. Lina pays $10 000 of her savings into a business bank account. She buys shop equipment for $3 000, paying by bank transfer. She buys inventory for $2 000 on credit from a supplier. She sells goods that cost $800 for $1 200 on credit. She pays the supplier $1 500 by bank transfer. She withdraws $300 from the business bank account for personal use. After transaction Equipment $ Inventory $ Trade receivables $ Bank $ Total assets $ Trade payables $ Capital $ 1 Capital introduced 0 0 0 10 000 10 000 0 10 000 2 Equipment bought 3 000 0 0 7 000 10 000 0 10 000 3 Inventory on credit 3 000 2 000 0 7 000 12 000 2 000 10 000 4 Credit sale (profit $400) 3 000 1 200 1 200 7 000 12 400 2 000 10 400 5 Supplier paid 3 000 1 200 1 200 5 500 10 900 500 10 400 6 Drawings 3 000 1 200 1 200 5 200 10 600 500 10 100 Transaction 1: assets up, capital up (both sides increase). Transaction 2: one asset up, another asset down — totals unchanged. Transaction 3: assets up, liabilities up. Transaction 4: inventory falls by $800, receivables rise by $1 200: assets rise by $400, and the $400 profit increases capital. Transaction 5: assets down, liabilities down. Transaction 6: assets down, capital down (drawings reduce capital; they are not an expense). The four patterns to recognise Pattern Example Effect on totals Asset up, asset down Buy a vehicle for cash; customer pays what they owe No change Asset up, liability or capital up Buy inventory on credit; owner introduces capital; take a loan Both sides increase Asset down, liability or capital down Repay a loan; pay a supplier; owner’s drawings Both sides decrease Liability up, liability down (or into capital) Loan used to pay off a supplier No change Common Mistake Saying a credit sale increases assets by the full selling price. The inventory sold leaves the business at cost, so assets only rise by the profit on the sale (selling price minus cost), and that profit is added to capital.

Profit = revenue − expenses (when revenue is greater than expenses). Loss occurs when expenses are greater than revenue. Profit increases capital; a loss reduces it. Drawings reduce capital. Extra capital introduced increases it. Formula Closing capital = Opening capital + Capital introduced + Profit for the year − Drawings (Subtract a loss instead of adding profit.) Calculation of closing capital for the year ended 31 December 2026 $ Opening capital 1 January 2026 20 000 Add Capital introduced 1 000 Add Profit for the year 6 500 27 500 Less Drawings (4 000) Closing capital 31 December 2026 23 500 The same formula can be rearranged to find a missing figure, e.g. Profit = Closing capital − Opening capital + Drawings − Capital introduced = 23 500 − 20 000 + 4 000 − 1 000 = $6 500. Model answer Explain why the accounting equation always balances. [3] Every asset a business has must have been financed either by the owner’s capital or by a liability owed to someone outside the business (1). Each transaction has a two-fold effect, so whenever one figure in the equation changes another changes by the same amount (1). For example, buying inventory on credit increases assets and increases trade payables by the same amount, so the two sides remain equal (1).

The path that every transaction follows from the moment it happens to the final statements: 1 Transaction occurs A sale, purchase, payment or receipt takes place. 2 Source document Evidence is created: invoice, credit note, receipt, bank statement, petty cash voucher. 3 Book of prime entry Transactions are first listed in a journal or cash book (sales journal, purchases journal, cash book, general journal). 4 Ledger Entries are posted using double entry to individual accounts in the sales, purchases and nominal (general) ledgers. 5 Trial balance Ledger balances are listed to check that total debits equal total credits. 6 Financial statements The income statement shows profit or loss; the statement of financial position shows assets, liabilities and capital. 7 Analysis and interpretation Ratios and comparisons help users make decisions. Examiner Tip Multiple-choice questions often ask which transaction would leave total assets unchanged, or what the effect of drawings is. Sketch three columns (Assets | Liabilities | Capital) and mark + or − for each transaction before choosing. Quick Checklist I can state the main purposes of accounting and distinguish book-keeping from accounting. I can name users of accounting information and explain what each wants to know. I can define and classify assets, liabilities and capital, including current and non-current items. I can use and rearrange the accounting equation to find a missing figure. I can show the effect of any transaction on assets, liabilities and capital. I can calculate profit or loss and closing capital, including drawings and capital introduced. I can describe the ethical principles expected of an accountant. I can describe the stages of the accounting cycle in order.

Topic 2 · Sources & Recording Sources and Recording of Data This topic covers how transactions are captured: the double-entry rules, the business documents that provide evidence, the books of prime entry, and how ledger accounts are written up and balanced. Almost every Paper 2 question expects you to make correct double entries, so this is the core skill of the whole course.

Double-entry book-keeping records every transaction twice: once on the debit side of one account and once on the credit side of another, with equal amounts. This reflects the two-fold effect of each transaction and keeps the accounting equation in balance. Debit (Dr) = left-hand side of an account. Credit (Cr) = right-hand side. The account that receives value is debited; the account that gives value is credited. Total debits must always equal total credits. D ebit: D rawings E xpenses A ssets | C redit: L iabilities I ncome C apital DEAD CLIC : drawings, expenses and assets increase on the debit side ; liabilities, income and capital increase on the credit side . A decrease goes on the opposite side. Transaction Debit Credit Reason Owner pays capital into bank Bank Capital Asset up; capital up Buy goods for resale on credit Purchases Supplier (trade payable) Expense up; liability up Sell goods on credit Customer (trade receivable) Sales Asset up; income up Pay rent by bank transfer Rent Bank Expense up; asset down Customer returns goods Sales returns Customer Reduces income; asset (receivable) down Goods returned to supplier Supplier Purchases returns Liability down; reduces purchases Buy machinery by cheque Machinery Bank One asset up, another down Owner takes goods for own use Drawings Purchases Drawings up; cost of goods for resale reduced Take out a bank loan Bank Bank loan Asset up; liability up Common Mistake Debiting an “Inventory” account when goods for resale are bought. During the year, goods bought for resale are debited to Purchases and goods sold are credited to Sales . The inventory account is used only for opening and closing inventory at the end of the year.

A ledger is the book (or file) containing all the accounts of a business. It is divided so that work can be shared and errors located more easily. Ledger Accounts it contains Sales ledger Personal accounts of credit customers (trade receivables) Purchases ledger Personal accounts of credit suppliers (trade payables) Nominal (general) ledger Nominal accounts (income and expenses, e.g. sales, purchases, wages, rent) and real accounts (non-current assets, inventory), plus capital, drawings and loans Cash book Cash and bank accounts — a book of prime entry that is also part of the double entry Personal accounts : for people and businesses (customers, suppliers, the owner’s capital). Impersonal accounts : real accounts for things owned (premises, vehicles) and nominal accounts for income, expenses, gains and losses.

Source documents provide evidence that a transaction took place and give the details needed to record it. Document Sent by → to Purpose Recorded in Purchase order Buyer → seller Requests goods; not a transaction yet, so no entry is made No entry (used for checking later) Invoice Seller → buyer Details goods sold on credit: quantity, price, trade discount, total, terms Seller: sales journal. Buyer: purchases journal Credit note Seller → buyer Reduces the amount owed, e.g. goods returned, overcharge Seller: sales returns journal. Buyer: purchases returns journal Debit note Buyer → seller Asks the seller to issue a credit note (e.g. for faulty goods) Usually no entry until the credit note arrives Statement of account Seller → buyer Summary of invoices, credit notes and payments in a period, showing the balance owed No entry; used to check records and as a reminder to pay Receipt Receiver of money → payer Proof of a payment made in cash or by other means Cash book Cheque counterfoil / paying-in slip Business’s own records Evidence of money paid out of or into the bank Cash book (bank column) Bank statement Bank → business Shows the bank’s record of the account, including bank charges, interest, direct debits and credit transfers Used to update the cash book and prepare a bank reconciliation Petty cash voucher Internal Supports each small cash payment Petty cash book Trade discount and cash discount Trade discount : a reduction in list price given to other traders, often for bulk buying. It is shown on the invoice and never recorded in the books — only the net amount is recorded. Cash discount : a reduction given for paying within a stated time. It is recorded in the cash book discount columns as discount allowed (an expense for the seller) or discount received (income for the buyer).

Transactions are first listed in a book of prime entry before being posted to the ledger. This reduces the number of entries in the ledger (totals can be posted), keeps transactions in date order and gives a reference trail back to the source document. Book of prime entry Records Source document Posting to the ledger Sales journal Credit sales of goods Copy of sales invoice Dr each customer; Cr Sales with the total Purchases journal Credit purchases of goods for resale Purchase invoice received Cr each supplier; Dr Purchases with the total Sales returns journal Goods returned by credit customers Copy of credit note sent Cr each customer; Dr Sales returns with the total Purchases returns journal Goods returned to credit suppliers Credit note received Dr each supplier; Cr Purchases returns with the total Cash book All cash and bank receipts and payments Receipts, cheque counterfoils, paying-in slips, bank statement Cash book is itself the ledger account; post the other side to each account Petty cash book Small cash expenses Petty cash vouchers Analysis column totals debited to expense accounts General journal Anything not in another book: opening entries, credit purchase/sale of non-current assets, correction of errors, year-end adjustments, irrecoverable debts written off, goods taken as drawings Internal memos, invoices for non-current assets Dr and Cr as shown in the journal Example: sales journal Sales journal – March 2026 Date Details Invoice no. $ 4 Mar R Lee S101 1 200 11 Mar J Osei S102 850 23 Mar M Chen S103 640 31 Mar Transferred to sales account 2 690 Each customer’s account in the sales ledger is debited with their invoice; the sales account in the nominal ledger is credited with the total of $2 690. Total debits ($2 690) = total credit ($2 690). Example: general journal Journal Date Details Debit $ Credit $ 9 Mar Office equipment 2 400 Tech Supplies Ltd 2 400 Purchase of a photocopier on credit from Tech Supplies Ltd Examiner Tip The general journal is a frequent Paper 2 task. Always write the debit entry first, the credit entry indented underneath, and a narrative. The purchase of a non-current asset on credit goes through the general journal , not the purchases journal, which is only for goods for resale.

h: Worked example: writing up ledger accounts
x: Tom starts trading on 1 March 2026. His transactions for March: 1 Mar — paid $8 000 capital into the business bank account 3 Mar — bought goods on credit from K Supplies, $1 500 8 Mar — sold goods on credit to R Lee, $900 12 Mar — paid rent by bank transfer, $400 18 Mar — cash sales paid directly into the bank, $650 25 Mar — paid K Supplies $1 000 by bank transfer 28 Mar — R Lee paid $600 by bank transfer Bank account Date Details $ Date Details $ 1 Mar Capital 8 000 12 Mar Rent 400 18 Mar Sales 650 25 Mar K Supplies 1 000 28 Mar R Lee 600 31 Mar Balance c/d 7 850 9 250 9 250 1 Apr Balance b/d 7 850 K Supplies account (purchases ledger) Date Details $ Date Details $ 25 Mar Bank 1 000 3 Mar Purchases 1 500 31 Mar Balance c/d 500 1 500 1 500 1 Apr Balance b/d 500 R Lee account (sales ledger) Date Details $ Date Details $ 8 Mar Sales 900 28 Mar Bank 600 31 Mar Balance c/d 300 900 900 1 Apr Balance b/d 300 Sales account Date Details $ Date Details $ 8 Mar R Lee 900 18 Mar Bank 650 The other accounts are: Capital (Cr $8 000), Purchases (Dr $1 500, details “K Supplies”) and Rent (Dr $400, details “Bank”). The balances show that Tom has $7 850 in the bank, owes K Supplies $500 (a credit balance — liability) and is owed $300 by R Lee (a debit balance — asset).

1 Add both sides Find the total of the debit side and the credit side separately (in rough). 2 Find the difference Subtract the smaller total from the larger. 3 Enter Balance c/d Write the difference on the smaller side, dated the last day of the period, as “Balance c/d”. 4 Total and rule off Both sides now have the same total; write the totals level with each other. 5 Bring the balance down Enter the same figure on the opposite side, below the totals, dated the first day of the next period, as “Balance b/d”. 6 Interpret it A debit balance b/d is usually an asset, expense or drawings; a credit balance b/d is usually a liability, income or capital. If an account has only one entry, or both sides are already equal, no balancing is needed — simply total both sides if they are equal.

A two-column cash book has a cash column and a bank column on each side. Receipts go on the debit side; payments on the credit side. A three-column cash book adds a discount column on each side: discount allowed on the debit side (given to customers who pay promptly) and discount received on the credit side (from suppliers we pay promptly). The discount columns are memorandum columns only — they are not balanced. Their totals are posted: Dr Discount allowed account; Cr Discount received account. Individual discounts are posted to each customer’s or supplier’s account. A contra entry is a transfer between cash and bank within the cash book, marked “C”. Both sides of the double entry are in the cash book itself. A credit balance on the bank column means a bank overdraft (a current liability). The cash column can never have a credit balance. Worked example: three-column cash book May 2026: opening balances cash $120, bank $2 400. 4 May A Khan paid $485 by bank in full settlement of $500 owed. 7 May paid P Ross $784 by bank in full settlement of $800. 10 May cash sales $260. 12 May paid wages in cash $150. 15 May paid $200 cash into the bank. 22 May withdrew $90 from the bank for office cash. 26 May owner’s drawings $300 by bank. Cash book Date Details Discount $ Cash $ Bank $ Date Details Discount $ Cash $ Bank $ 1 May Balances b/d 120 2 400 7 May P Ross 16 784 4 May A Khan 15 485 12 May Wages 150 10 May Sales 260 15 May Bank (C) 200 15 May Cash (C) 200 22 May Cash (C) 90 22 May Bank (C) 90 26 May Drawings 300 31 May Balances c/d 120 1 911 15 470 3 085 16 470 3 085 1 Jun Balances b/d 120 1 911 A Khan’s account is credited with both $485 (Bank) and $15 (Discount allowed), clearing the $500 debt. P Ross’s account is debited with $784 (Bank) and $16 (Discount received), clearing the $800 owed. Discount allowed account: Dr $15. Discount received account: Cr $16. Common Mistake Putting discount received on the debit side because it is “received”. In the cash book, discounts sit alongside the payment or receipt they relate to : discount allowed is next to money received from customers (debit side); discount received is next to money paid to suppliers (credit side).

h: The petty cash book and the imprest system
x: Small, frequent expenses (postage, cleaning, travel, refreshments) are paid by a petty cashier from a separate float so the main cashier is not distracted by minor items. 1 Set the imprest The main cashier gives the petty cashier a fixed float (the imprest), e.g. $200. 2 Pay with vouchers Each payment is supported by a numbered, authorised petty cash voucher and entered in the petty cash book with an analysis column. 3 Total the period At the end of the period total the payments and each analysis column. 4 Restore the imprest The main cashier reimburses exactly the amount spent, bringing the float back to $200. 5 Post to the ledger Each analysis column total is debited to the relevant expense account; the cash book (credit) records the reimbursement. Petty cash book – June 2026 Receipts $ Date Details Voucher Total $ Postage $ Cleaning $ Stationery $ Travel $ 200 1 Jun Balance b/d 4 Jun Stamps 1 18 18 8 Jun Window cleaner 2 35 35 13 Jun Printer paper 3 24 24 17 Jun Taxi fare 4 42 42 22 Jun Parcel post 5 12 12 27 Jun Cleaning materials 6 20 20 151 30 55 24 42 30 Jun Balance c/d 49 200 200 49 1 Jul Balance b/d 151 1 Jul Bank (restore imprest) Analysis totals: 30 + 55 + 24 + 42 = $151, matching the total column. After reimbursement, the float is back to $49 + $151 = $200. Advantages of the imprest system The petty cashier can never hold more than the imprest, limiting the risk of theft. Cash in hand plus vouchers must always equal the imprest, so checks are easy at any time. Analysis columns mean only totals are posted, saving time in the nominal ledger. Frees the main cashier from small, routine payments. Model answer Explain one advantage to a business of using books of prime entry. [2] Books of prime entry list similar transactions together, so only the periodic totals need to be posted to accounts such as sales or purchases in the nominal ledger (1). This reduces the number of entries in the ledger, saving time and reducing the chance of errors (1).

Most businesses now record transactions using accounting software, often cloud-based. The double-entry principles are unchanged, but the way they are carried out is different. Aspect Manual records Accounting software Entry Each entry written in a book of prime entry, then posted by hand Transaction entered once; software completes the double entry and updates ledgers automatically Documents Paper invoices and receipts Invoices generated and emailed automatically; receipts scanned; bank feeds import transactions Arithmetic Totalling and balancing by hand, risk of casting errors Automatic totals, balances, trial balance and statements Speed and information Statements prepared at period end Real-time reports, aged receivables lists, dashboards Risks Loss or damage of books, illegible entries Data input errors repeated automatically, cyber attacks, system failure, need for training and software cost Automation : recurring entries (rent, loan repayments), bank reconciliation matching and payment reminders can be automated. Data security : protect records with passwords and access levels, regular backups, encryption and up-to-date anti-virus software. Personal data about customers must be kept confidential. Limits : software cannot tell whether a transaction was entered in the wrong account with the correct amount (an error of commission or principle still balances). Human judgement and checking are still needed. Sustainability : digital invoices and records reduce paper use and storage space. Examiner Tip When evaluating accounting software, give a balanced answer: time saving and accuracy of arithmetic versus cost, training, and security risks. Avoid saying software “removes all errors” — it only removes arithmetical and posting errors, not wrong inputs. Quick Checklist I can apply DEAD CLIC to decide the debit and credit entry for any transaction. I can name the divisions of the ledger and the types of account in each. I can identify each business document, who issues it and which book of prime entry it feeds. I can distinguish trade discount from cash discount and record discounts correctly. I can write up sales, purchases and returns journals and post them to the ledger. I can prepare a three-column cash book with discounts, contra entries and balances. I can prepare a petty cash book using the imprest system and post analysis totals. I can balance an account and explain the advantages and risks of accounting software.

Topic 3 · Verification Verification of Accounting Records How a business checks that its books are accurate: the trial balance, finding and correcting errors, bank reconciliation and control accounts. These topics come up in almost every Paper 2, often as a long question with journal entries and a corrected profit.

A trial balance is a list of the balances on all the ledger accounts at a certain date. Debit balances go in one column and credit balances in the other, and the two totals should agree. Purpose of a trial balance It checks the arithmetical accuracy of the double entry: for every debit there should be an equal credit. It helps to find errors . If the totals disagree, there must be at least one mistake. It gives a summary of all ledger balances in one place, which makes it a starting point for preparing the financial statements. Limitations of a trial balance When the totals agree, that does not prove the books are free of errors. Some errors leave the totals equal. It does not show where an error is, only that one exists. It is only correct for the date on which it is drawn up. Debit balances Assets, expenses, drawings Credit balances Liabilities, income, capital Totals disagree Difference goes to a suspense account Totals agree Six types of error may still exist

h: Errors not revealed by a trial balance
x: In each of these errors the debit entry still equals the credit entry, so the trial balance totals agree. Error Meaning Example Omission A transaction is left out of the books entirely. A credit sale of $350 to T Khan is never recorded. Commission The correct amount is posted to the correct type of account, but to the wrong person’s account. A payment from R Ali is credited to R Allen’s account. Principle An entry is made in the wrong class of account (for example, capital expenditure is treated as revenue expenditure). A new computer is debited to the purchases account rather than to office equipment. Original entry The wrong amount is recorded in the book of prime entry, so both the debit and the credit are wrong by the same amount. An invoice for $760 is entered as $670 in the sales journal and posted from there. Complete reversal The correct accounts and amount are used, but the debit and credit sides are swapped. Cash sales of $200 are debited to sales and credited to cash. Compensating Two or more errors of equal value cancel each other out. The wages account is overcast by $100 and the sales account is also overcast by $100. O mission C ommission P rinciple O riginal entry R eversal C ompensating — “ O ne C areless P erson O ften R uins C alculations” Common Mistake Students often confuse commission with principle . In an error of commission the account is the right type but belongs to the wrong person, e.g. one customer instead of another. In an error of principle the account is the wrong class altogether, e.g. an expense instead of a non-current asset.

h: Errors that are revealed by a trial balance
x: Single entry: only one side of the transaction is recorded. Two debits or two credits: both entries are made on the same side. Different amounts: the debit and the credit are for different figures, for example because of a transposition such as $540 entered as $450 on one side only. Casting errors: a book of prime entry or ledger account is overcast or undercast, i.e. added up wrongly. Balance omitted from the trial balance, or entered in the wrong column.

Errors are corrected through the journal . Each entry gives the date, the account to debit, the account to credit, the amounts and a short narrative explaining the correction. The suspense account When the trial balance totals do not agree, the difference is entered in a suspense account for the time being, so that draft financial statements can still be prepared. If the debit total is larger, the suspense account gets a credit balance. If the credit total is larger, it gets a debit balance. Only errors that affect the trial balance totals pass through the suspense account. Once all of these are corrected, the suspense account balance falls to zero (the account clears ). 1 Write down what was done Note the entries that were actually made, including any that were missed. 2 Write down what should have been done Note the correct double entry. 3 Find the difference for each account Work out which accounts need an extra debit or credit, and how much. 4 Use suspense only if one side is missing or unequal If the correction involves only one account, the other half of the entry goes to the suspense account. 5 Write the journal entry with a narrative Debit first, then credit, then a brief explanation. Worked example: suspense account On 31 December 2026 the trial balance of Mira Stores showed debits of $48 650 and credits of $48 290. The difference of $360 was entered as a credit in a suspense account. Draft profit for the year was $15 000. The following errors were then found: The sales journal had been undercast by $200. Rent paid of $450 was recorded correctly in the bank account but entered in the rent account as $540. Discount allowed of $70 to customer P Dube was debited to the discount allowed account but was not entered in P Dube’s account. Office equipment bought for $1 200 was debited to the purchases account. Journal Date Details Debit $ Credit $ 31 Dec Suspense 200 Sales 200 Correction of undercast sales journal 31 Dec Suspense 90 Rent 90 Rent of $450 debited as $540 in the rent account 31 Dec Suspense 70 P Dube 70 Discount allowed omitted from customer’s account 31 Dec Office equipment 1 200 Purchases 1 200 Error of principle: equipment wrongly debited to purchases Suspense account Date Details $ Date Details $ 31 Dec Sales 200 31 Dec Difference on trial balance 360 31 Dec Rent 90 31 Dec P Dube 70 360 360 The suspense account has cleared. Error 4 did not go through suspense because both entries in it were for $1 200.

h: Effect of errors on profit and on the statement of financial position
x: If a correction changes an income or expense account (including purchases, sales and returns), it changes profit for the year . If a correction changes only assets, liabilities or capital accounts, profit stays the same and only the statement of financial position changes. When profit changes, the capital figure in the statement of financial position changes by the same amount. Statement of corrected profit for the year ended 31 December 2026 $ $ Draft profit for the year 15 000 Add Sales undercast 200 Add Rent overstated 90 Add Purchases overstated (equipment) 1 200 1 490 Corrected profit for the year 16 490 The P Dube correction makes trade receivables $70 lower and does not affect profit. The equipment correction raises non-current assets by $1 200. Examiner Tip For each error, ask two questions: “Does it touch an income statement account?” and “Which way?” An expense that was overstated means profit was understated, so you add it back. Present your answer as a statement that starts with the draft profit, never as a bare final figure.

A bank reconciliation statement explains why the bank balance in the cash book differs from the balance on the bank statement at the same date. Reasons for differences Items on the bank statement that are not yet in the cash book , so the cash book must be updated: bank charges and interest charged direct debits and standing orders credit transfers (bank transfers) received from customers dishonoured cheques, where a customer’s cheque was returned unpaid interest received Timing differences , which appear in the reconciliation statement: unpresented cheques : cheques entered in the cash book but not yet paid by the bank outstanding lodgements (amounts not yet credited): money paid in and entered in the cash book but not yet shown on the bank statement Errors , made either in the cash book or by the bank. 1 Compare Tick off every item that appears in both the cash book and the bank statement. 2 Update the cash book Enter any unticked items that are on the bank statement only. Work out the updated cash book balance. 3 Start from the bank statement balance Begin the statement with the closing balance shown by the bank. 4 Add outstanding lodgements These have been paid in but the bank has not recorded them yet. 5 Deduct unpresented cheques The bank has not yet paid them out. 6 Agree The result should equal the updated cash book balance. Worked example: bank reconciliation At 31 March 2026 the cash book of Leo Traders showed a debit bank balance of $2 340. The bank statement showed a credit balance of $3 105. When the two were compared, these items were found: Only on the bank statement: bank charges $45, a credit transfer from a customer $520, a direct debit for insurance $180, and a customer’s cheque for $150 returned dishonoured. Unpresented cheques: No. 1012 $640 and No. 1015 $310. Takings of $330 paid in on 31 March were not yet on the bank statement. Cash book (bank columns), updated Date Details $ Date Details $ 31 Mar Balance b/d 2 340 31 Mar Bank charges 45 31 Mar Credit transfer 520 31 Mar Insurance (direct debit) 180 31 Mar Dishonoured cheque 150 31 Mar Balance c/d 2 485 2 860 2 860 1 Apr Balance b/d 2 485 Bank reconciliation statement at 31 March 2026 $ $ Balance as per bank statement 3 105 Add Amount not yet credited 330 3 435 Less Unpresented cheques: No. 1012 640 No. 1015 310 (950) Balance as per updated cash book 2 485 Common Mistake Putting bank charges or credit transfers into the reconciliation statement. Those items belong in the updated cash book . Only timing differences (and bank errors) go in the statement. Also keep in mind that the bank’s “credit” balance means money in the account, which is the same as a debit balance in the cash book. Why reconcile regularly? It finds errors and omissions in the cash book and on the bank statement. It brings the cash book up to date so the bank figure in the statement of financial position is correct. It shows up stale (old unpresented) cheques and dishonoured cheques. It helps to detect fraud and theft, and it is part of good internal control.

A control account is a summary account that holds the totals of all the entries made in a ledger. Its balance should equal the total of the individual balances in that ledger. The sales ledger control account (trade receivables control) summarises all the customer accounts in the sales ledger. The purchases ledger control account (trade payables control) summarises all the supplier accounts in the purchases ledger. Sources of information Entry Source Sales ledger control Purchases ledger control Credit sales / purchases Sales journal / purchases journal Debit Credit Returns Sales returns journal / purchases returns journal Credit Debit Cash and cheques received / paid Cash book Credit Debit Discount allowed / received Cash book (discount columns) Credit Debit Dishonoured cheques Cash book Debit — Irrecoverable debts written off Journal Credit — Set-off (contra) Journal Credit Debit Opening and closing balances Totals of the ledger balances Usually debit Usually credit Set-off (contra entry): when a business both sells to and buys from the same person, it can cancel the smaller balance against the larger. This reduces both the amount receivable and the amount payable. Credit balances in the sales ledger can arise when a customer overpays or returns goods after paying. Debit balances can also appear in the purchases ledger. These are shown separately on the opposite side of the control account. Worked example: sales ledger control account July 2026 figures: balances at 1 July were $12 400 debit and $180 credit; credit sales $38 600; receipts from customers $33 250; discount allowed $850; sales returns $1 120; irrecoverable debts written off $430; dishonoured cheque $300; set-off against the purchases ledger $600; credit balances at 31 July $210. Purchases ledger control account Date Details $ Date Details $ 31 Jul Bank 24 300 1 Jul Balance b/d 9 800 31 Jul Discount received 620 31 Jul Purchases 27 450 31 Jul Purchases returns 940 31 Jul Sales ledger control (set-off) 600 31 Jul Balance c/d 10 790 37 250 37 250 1 Aug Balance b/d 10 790 Uses of control accounts They check the arithmetical accuracy of each ledger separately, which helps to locate errors faster. They give a quick total of trade receivables and trade payables for the financial statements. They help to prevent fraud , especially when the control account is kept by someone other than the ledger clerk. They allow the work to be divided between staff. Limitations of control accounts They do not reveal errors that cancel out, such as omissions, original entry errors, or a posting to the wrong customer (commission). They can themselves contain errors. They take extra time to prepare, although accounting software usually produces them automatically. Examiner Tip Some items never go into a control account: cash sales, cash purchases and provision for doubtful debts. A creation or change in the provision does not alter what individual customers owe, so it stays out of the sales ledger control account. Model answer Explain two reasons why a trader should prepare a bank reconciliation statement. [4] First, it brings the cash book up to date. Items such as bank charges and credit transfers appear only on the bank statement, so entering them makes the bank balance in the statement of financial position correct. Second, it helps to find errors and fraud. Any difference that cannot be explained by timing items, such as unpresented cheques, points to a mistake or a missing payment that the trader can investigate promptly. Quick Checklist I can state the purpose and the limitations of a trial balance. I can name, explain and give an example of each of the six errors not revealed by a trial balance. I can write journal entries, with narratives, to correct errors and clear a suspense account. I can prepare a statement of corrected profit and explain the effect of errors on the statement of financial position. I can update a cash book and prepare a bank reconciliation statement. I can prepare sales and purchases ledger control accounts from given information, including set-offs. I can explain the uses and limitations of control accounts.

Topic 4 · Accounting Procedures Accounting Procedures The year-end adjustments that turn raw ledger balances into a fair profit figure: capital and revenue items, depreciation and disposals, accruals and prepayments, irrecoverable debts and provisions, and inventory valuation. Expect at least one long Paper 2 question built around these ledger accounts and adjustments.

h: Capital and revenue expenditure and receipts
x: Capital expenditure Buying or improving non-current assets, including costs to get them ready for use Revenue expenditure Day-to-day running costs, including repairs and maintenance Capital receipts Capital or loans introduced, money from selling non-current assets Revenue receipts Income from normal trading: sales, rent received, commission, discount received Capital expenditure is money spent on buying, adding to or improving non-current assets. It includes delivery, legal fees, installation and testing. It is shown in the statement of financial position . Revenue expenditure is money spent on running the business day to day, or on keeping non-current assets in working order. It is charged to the income statement . An improvement , such as an extension to a building, is capital expenditure. A repair , such as replacing broken windows, is revenue expenditure. Effect of incorrect classification Error Effect on profit Effect on statement of financial position Capital expenditure treated as revenue (e.g. a new van debited to motor expenses) Expenses overstated, so profit is understated Non-current assets understated Revenue expenditure treated as capital (e.g. a van repair of $800 debited to motor vehicles) Expenses understated, so profit is overstated Non-current assets overstated Capital receipt treated as revenue (e.g. proceeds from selling equipment credited to sales) Income overstated, so profit is overstated Non-current asset figures misstated

Depreciation is the estimated loss in value of a non-current asset over its useful life. It is an application of the matching (accruals) principle : the cost of the asset is spread over the years that benefit from using it. Causes of depreciation Wear and tear from use Obsolescence : the asset is replaced by newer technology Passage of time : for example, a lease runs out Depletion : natural resources such as a mine are used up Depreciation is a non-cash expense . It reduces profit, but no money leaves the business. Straight-line method The same amount is charged every year. Worked calculation Depreciation per year = (cost − residual value) ÷ useful life in years A machine costs $24 000, has an estimated residual value of $4 000 and a useful life of 5 years. Depreciation = ($24 000 − $4 000) ÷ 5 = $4 000 a year . The rate may instead be given as a percentage of cost. Reducing balance method A fixed percentage is applied each year to the net book value (cost less accumulated depreciation), so the charge gets smaller each year. Year Net book value at start $ Depreciation at 25% $ Net book value at end $ 1 24 000 6 000 18 000 2 18 000 4 500 13 500 3 13 500 3 375 10 125 Straight-line suits assets that give equal benefit each year, such as fixtures or a lease. Reducing balance suits assets that lose more value early in their lives or that need more repairs as they age, such as vehicles and computers. Common Mistake Applying the reducing balance percentage to the original cost each year. That gives straight-line depreciation. Always multiply the percentage by the net book value at the start of the year. Recording depreciation The asset account stays at cost . Each year: Debit income statement (depreciation expense), Credit provision for depreciation account. The provision for depreciation account builds up the accumulated depreciation . In the statement of financial position: cost − accumulated depreciation = net book value. Disposal of a non-current asset 1 Transfer the cost Debit disposal account, credit asset account with the original cost. 2 Transfer the accumulated depreciation Debit provision for depreciation, credit disposal account with the depreciation charged on that asset to date. 3 Record the proceeds Debit bank (or a trade-in allowance against the new asset), credit disposal account. 4 Balance the disposal account A balancing figure on the credit side is a loss on disposal, debited to the income statement as an expense. A balancing figure on the debit side is a profit on disposal, credited to the income statement as income. Worked example: two years with a disposal Kofi Haulage has a year end of 31 December. On 1 January 2025 it bought van A for $20 000 and van B for $12 000. On 1 March 2026 it bought van C for $15 000. On 30 June 2026 van B was sold for $9 000 cheque. The business charges depreciation at 20% reducing balance , with a full year in the year of purchase and none in the year of disposal. 2025: van A 20% × $20 000 = $4 000; van B 20% × $12 000 = $2 400. Total $6 400 . 2026: van A 20% × ($20 000 − $4 000) = $3 200; van C 20% × $15 000 = $3 000; van B nil (year of disposal). Total $6 200 . Van B on disposal: net book value $12 000 − $2 400 = $9 600, sold for $9 000, so a loss of $600 . Under the accruals (matching) principle , income and expenses are recorded in the period they relate to, not when the cash is received or paid. Item Meaning Shown as Accrued expense An expense used up but not yet paid Other payable (current liability) Prepaid expense An expense paid in advance for the next period Other receivable (current asset) Accrued income Income earned but not yet received Other receivable (current asset) Income received in advance Income received for the next period Other payable (current liability) Expense for the year = amount paid − opening accrual + closing accrual + opening prepayment − closing prepayment. Worked example: accrued expense Electricity owing at 1 January 2026 was $240. During the year $2 860 was paid. At 31 December 2026, $310 was owing. The $310 is shown as an other payable . Worked example: prepaid expense Insurance prepaid at 1 January 2026 was $300. On 1 April 2026, $1 440 was paid for the year to 31 March 2027. At 31 December 2026, 3 months are prepaid: 3/12 × $1 440 = $360. Common Mistake Getting the sides wrong in income accounts. In an expense account a closing accrual is carried down on the debit side and brought down as a credit. In an income account everything is reversed: income received in advance is carried down on the debit side and brought down as a credit (a liability).

h: Irrecoverable debts and provision for doubtful debts
x: An irrecoverable debt is an amount owed by a credit customer that will never be received, for example because the customer has become bankrupt. Entries: Debit irrecoverable debts, Credit customer’s account (trade receivables). At the year end, irrecoverable debts are transferred to the income statement as an expense. Recovery of a debt written off: first reinstate the debt (Debit customer, Credit irrecoverable debts recovered), then record the receipt (Debit bank, Credit customer). For example, if J Lee pays $300 that was written off last year, both entries are $300 and the recovered amount is shown as income. Reinstating the debt keeps a full record of the customer’s history. A provision for doubtful debts is an estimate of the trade receivables that may not be paid. It follows the prudence concept and the matching principle: the possible loss is charged in the same year as the sales that gave rise to it. Change Entries Effect on profit Creating the provision Debit income statement, Credit provision for doubtful debts (full amount) Reduces profit Increasing the provision Debit income statement, Credit provision (increase only) Reduces profit Decreasing the provision Debit provision, Credit income statement (decrease only) Increases profit Worked example: provision for doubtful debts A business keeps a provision of 4% of trade receivables, calculated after irrecoverable debts are written off. Its year end is 31 December. 2025: trade receivables $26 000, of which $1 000 was written off as irrecoverable, leaving $25 000. Provision 4% = $1 000 (created). 2026: trade receivables $31 250. Provision 4% = $1 250, an increase of $250 . 2027: trade receivables $22 500. Provision 4% = $900, a decrease of $350 . The full closing balance is deducted from trade receivables in the statement of financial position.

Inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value . This applies the prudence concept: profit is not overstated, and losses are recognised as soon as they are expected. Cost is the purchase price plus any costs of bringing the goods to their present location and condition, such as carriage inwards. Net realisable value (NRV) is the expected selling price minus any costs still to be paid to complete and sell the goods, such as repairs or selling costs. The rule is applied to each item or group of items separately , not to the inventory as a whole. Worked example: lower of cost and NRV Line Cost $ Net realisable value $ Value used $ A: normal goods 2 400 3 100 2 400 B: selling price $1 900, selling costs $250 1 800 1 650 1 650 C: damaged, sells for $600 after $120 repairs 950 480 480 Total 5 150 5 230 4 530 Closing inventory is $4 530 . Comparing the totals ($5 150 against $5 230) would give the wrong answer of $5 150. Effect of errors in inventory valuation 1 Closing inventory overvalued For example, by $600. 2 Cost of sales understated Closing inventory is deducted in the cost of sales calculation, so cost of sales is $600 too low. 3 Profit overstated this year Gross profit and profit for the year are both $600 too high. Current assets and capital are also overstated. 4 Profit understated next year This year’s closing inventory becomes next year’s opening inventory, so next year’s cost of sales is $600 too high. Model answer Explain why inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value. [3] This applies the prudence concept. If goods can only be sold for less than they cost, for example because they are damaged or out of date, the expected loss must be recognised now rather than when they are sold. Valuing them at cost would overstate closing inventory, understate cost of sales and therefore overstate profit and current assets. Quick Checklist I can classify items as capital or revenue expenditure or receipts and explain the effect of misclassification on profit. I can calculate depreciation using the straight-line and reducing balance methods. I can prepare asset, provision for depreciation and disposal accounts and calculate a profit or loss on disposal. I can prepare expense and income accounts with accruals and prepayments and show them as other payables and receivables. I can record irrecoverable debts and debts recovered. I can create, increase and decrease a provision for doubtful debts and show it in the financial statements. I can value inventory at the lower of cost and net realisable value and explain the effect of overvaluation on profit.

Topic 5 · Financial Statements Preparation of Financial Statements How to turn a trial balance (or an incomplete set of records) into an income statement and a statement of financial position for sole traders, partnerships, limited companies, clubs and manufacturers. This is the highest-mark area of Paper 2: layout, labelling and correct treatment of adjustments earn most of the marks.

Income statement — a summary of revenue and expenses for a period (usually one year), showing gross profit and profit for the year (or loss). It is headed “for the year ended …”. Statement of financial position — a list of assets, liabilities and capital (equity) at one point in time. It is headed “at …” (a single date), never “for the year ended”. Gross profit = revenue − cost of sales. Profit for the year = gross profit + other income − expenses. Cost of sales = opening inventory + net purchases (purchases − purchases returns + carriage inwards) − closing inventory. Revenue expenditure Day-to-day running costs → income statement Capital expenditure Buying or improving non-current assets → SOFP Carriage inwards Added to purchases (cost of sales) Carriage outwards An expense below gross profit Net assets Total assets − total liabilities = capital Working capital Current assets − current liabilities

h: 1. Sole traders: from trial balance to statements
x: Year-end adjustments are applied so that the statements follow the accruals (matching) concept and prudence. Each adjustment usually affects two places : once in the income statement and once in the statement of financial position. Adjustment Income statement Statement of financial position Closing inventory Deduct in cost of sales Current asset Depreciation for the year Expense Add to accumulated depreciation; show carrying amount (cost − accumulated depreciation) Accrued expense (other payable) Add to the expense Current liability Prepaid expense (other receivable) Deduct from the expense Current asset Accrued income / income in advance Add to / deduct from the income Current asset / current liability Further irrecoverable debt Add to irrecoverable debts expense Deduct from trade receivables Increase in provision for doubtful debts Expense (a decrease is shown as other income) Deduct the full new provision from trade receivables Goods taken by owner (at cost) Deduct from purchases Add to drawings 1 Work out adjustments first Calculate depreciation, the new provision, adjusted expenses and drawings in rough workings before drawing up the statements. 2 Trading section Revenue less sales returns; cost of sales (opening inventory + net purchases − closing inventory); gross profit. 3 Profit and loss section Add other income (discount received, rent received, decrease in provision); list adjusted expenses; profit for the year. 4 Assets Non-current assets at cost, accumulated depreciation and carrying amount; then current assets in order of liquidity (inventory, trade receivables net of provision, other receivables, bank, cash). 5 Capital and liabilities Opening capital + profit for the year − drawings = closing capital; non-current liabilities (loans repayable after 12 months); current liabilities. 6 Check it balances Total assets must equal capital plus liabilities. If not, recheck the two-place rule for each adjustment. A partnership is a business owned by two or more people (usually 2 to 20) who share the profits and losses. Advantages over a sole trader: more capital, shared workload and skills, shared losses. Disadvantages: profits shared, possible disagreements, and (in an ordinary partnership) unlimited liability . The partnership agreement A written agreement normally sets out: the capital each partner contributes; the ratio in which residual profits and losses are shared; interest on capital (a reward for investing money) and its rate; partners’ salaries (a reward for extra work or responsibility); interest on drawings (a charge to discourage partners taking out too much cash); limits on drawings and rules for admitting or retiring partners. If there is no agreement, the usual legal default is that profits and losses are shared equally , with no interest on capital, no salaries and no interest on drawings. Appropriation account The appropriation account follows the income statement and shows how the profit for the year is shared. Interest on drawings is added (it is charged to partners); interest on capital and salaries are deducted ; the remainder (residual profit) is shared in the profit-sharing ratio. Capital account Fixed: changes only for capital introduced or withdrawn Current account Records appropriations (credit) and drawings (debit) Credit balance Business owes the partner Debit balance Partner has drawn more than earned; shown as a deduction Worked example: Ana and Ben Ana and Ben share profits and losses 3:2. Capitals: Ana $60 000, Ben $40 000. Interest on capital 5% per annum. Ben receives a salary of $8 000. Interest on drawings: Ana $400, Ben $250. Profit for the year ended 31 December 2026 was $42 000. Drawings: Ana $15 000, Ben $18 000. Current account balances at 1 January 2026: Ana $1 200 credit, Ben $500 debit. Ana and Ben — Appropriation account for the year ended 31 December 2026 $ $ Profit for the year 42 000 Add Interest on drawings Ana 400 Ben 250 650 42 650 Less Interest on capital Ana (5% × 60 000) 3 000 Ben (5% × 40 000) 2 000 (5 000) Less Partner’s salary: Ben (8 000) Residual profit 29 650 Share of residual profit Ana (3/5) 17 790 Ben (2/5) 11 860 29 650 Ana — Current account Date Details $ Date Details $ 2026 Dec 31 Drawings 15 000 2026 Jan 1 Balance b/d 1 200 Dec 31 Interest on drawings 400 Dec 31 Interest on capital 3 000 Dec 31 Balance c/d 6 590 Dec 31 Share of profit 17 790 21 990 21 990 2027 Jan 1 Balance b/d 6 590 Ben — Current account Date Details $ Date Details $ 2026 Jan 1 Balance b/d 500 2026 Dec 31 Interest on capital 2 000 Dec 31 Drawings 18 000 Dec 31 Salary 8 000 Dec 31 Interest on drawings 250 Dec 31 Share of profit 11 860 Dec 31 Balance c/d 3 110 21 860 21 860 2027 Jan 1 Balance b/d 3 110 In the statement of financial position the capital section becomes: Capital accounts (Ana 60 000, Ben 40 000 = 100 000) plus Current accounts (Ana 6 590, Ben 3 110 = 9 700), total $109 700 . Common Mistake Treating partners’ salaries or interest on capital as expenses in the income statement. They are appropriations of profit , not expenses, so they appear only in the appropriation account. (Wages paid to employees, and interest on a loan made by a partner, are expenses.)

Key features Separate legal entity : the company can own assets, sue and be sued in its own name. Limited liability : shareholders can lose only the amount they invested in their shares, not their personal assets. Owned by shareholders , run by directors (ownership and control may be separate). Raises capital by issuing shares; continuity of existence when shareholders change. Must follow more legal regulation and publish financial statements. Ordinary shares Preference shares Dividend Variable, decided by directors; can be nil Fixed percentage of nominal value Priority Paid after preference shareholders Paid before ordinary shareholders Voting rights Normally one vote per share Normally no vote Risk Higher (last to be repaid if the company is wound up) Lower Issued share capital : the shares actually issued, at nominal (par) value. Retained earnings : accumulated profits not yet paid out as dividends. Opening retained earnings + profit for the year − dividends paid − transfers to reserves = closing retained earnings. General reserve : profits set aside (transferred from retained earnings) for future use, reducing the amount available for dividends. It is not cash. Dividends : the share of profit paid to shareholders. Dividends paid during the year are deducted from retained earnings, not shown as an expense in the income statement. Debentures / long-term loans : borrowing at a fixed rate of interest. Debenture holders are lenders, not owners; interest is an expense (finance cost) whether or not a profit is made. Shown as a non-current liability unless repayable within 12 months. Worked example: Delta Ltd Delta Ltd has issued 200 000 ordinary shares of $1 each and 50 000 8% preference shares of $1 each. It also has $50 000 6% debentures. For the year ended 31 December 2026: revenue $480 000; cost of sales $290 000; administrative expenses $70 000; distribution costs $45 000. At 1 January 2026, retained earnings were $38 000 and the general reserve $20 000. During the year the preference dividend was paid in full and an ordinary dividend of 5 cents per share was paid. The directors transferred $15 000 to the general reserve. Non-current assets total $320 000, current assets $140 000 and current liabilities $44 000. Delta Ltd — Income statement for the year ended 31 December 2026 $ $ Revenue 480 000 Less Cost of sales (290 000) Gross profit 190 000 Less Administrative expenses 70 000 Less Distribution costs 45 000 (115 000) Profit from operations 75 000 Less Finance costs (6% × 50 000 debenture interest) (3 000) Profit for the year 72 000 Delta Ltd — Retained earnings for the year ended 31 December 2026 $ $ Retained earnings at 1 January 2026 38 000 Add Profit for the year 72 000 110 000 Less Preference dividend paid (8% × 50 000) 4 000 Less Ordinary dividend paid (200 000 × $0.05) 10 000 Less Transfer to general reserve 15 000 (29 000) Retained earnings at 31 December 2026 81 000 Delta Ltd — Statement of financial position at 31 December 2026 (summarised) $ $ Non-current assets 320 000 Current assets 140 000 Total assets 460 000 Equity Ordinary shares of $1 each 200 000 8% preference shares of $1 each 50 000 General reserve (20 000 + 15 000) 35 000 Retained earnings 81 000 366 000 Non-current liabilities 6% debentures 50 000 Current liabilities 44 000 Total equity and liabilities 460 000 Examiner Tip Read share details carefully: a dividend of “5 cents per share” is calculated on the number of shares, while “8% preference shares” is calculated on the nominal value . If shares have a nominal value of $0.50, 200 000 shares would be shown as $100 000 of share capital. Model answer Explain two differences between a debenture holder and an ordinary shareholder. (4 marks) A debenture holder is a lender (creditor) of the company, whereas an ordinary shareholder is an owner of the company. Therefore the debenture holder has no vote at general meetings, while the shareholder can vote and influence who the directors are. A debenture holder receives a fixed rate of interest that must be paid even if the company makes a loss, so it is an expense in the income statement. An ordinary shareholder receives a dividend that varies with profit and the directors’ decision and may be nil; it is an appropriation of profit deducted from retained earnings.

Clubs exist to provide facilities for members, not to make a profit. Terminology changes but the principles are the same. Business term Club equivalent Cash book summary Receipts and payments account Income statement Income and expenditure account Profit / loss Surplus (income > expenditure) / deficit Capital Accumulated fund Trading account Trading account for a club activity (e.g. café, bar) Receipts and payments account Income and expenditure account A summary of the cash/bank account Equivalent of an income statement Includes capital and revenue items Revenue items only Ignores accruals, prepayments and depreciation Applies the accruals concept; includes depreciation Balance = cash/bank at the end of the year Balance = surplus or deficit for the year Accumulated fund = club assets − club liabilities. Opening accumulated fund + surplus (or − deficit) = closing accumulated fund. Subscriptions in arrears (owed by members) = current asset. Subscriptions in advance (paid early for next year) = current liability. Profit from a club activity (e.g. café) is calculated in a separate trading account and only the profit or loss is transferred to the income and expenditure account. Worked example: Riverside Tennis Club At 1 January 2026 the club had: bank $2 400; equipment $12 000; café inventory $400; subscriptions in arrears $300; subscriptions in advance $200.
