The I&E account shows only the subscriptions earned for the year and only revenue items; equipment is capitalised and depreciated.

A manufacturer makes the goods it sells, so a manufacturing account is prepared before the income statement to find the cost of production of goods completed in the year. Direct costs Traced to each unit: direct materials, direct labour, direct expenses (e.g. royalties) Prime cost Total of all direct costs Factory overheads Indirect factory costs: supervisors’ and indirect wages, factory rent, power, machinery depreciation Work in progress Partly finished goods: add opening, deduct closing Production cost Prime cost + factory overheads ± change in WIP Office costs Stay in the income statement, not the manufacturing account Worked example: Kora Furniture Kora Furniture — Manufacturing account for the year ended 31 December 2026 $ $ Inventory of raw materials at 1 January 2026 8 000 Purchases of raw materials 64 000 Carriage inwards on raw materials 1 500 73 500 Less Inventory of raw materials at 31 December 2026 (9 500) Cost of raw materials consumed 64 000 Direct labour 48 000 Direct expenses (royalties) 3 000 Prime cost 115 000 Add Factory overheads Indirect wages 12 000 Factory rent 9 000 Factory power 6 500 Depreciation of machinery 7 500 35 000 150 000 Add Work in progress at 1 January 2026 5 000 Less Work in progress at 31 December 2026 (6 000) Cost of production 149 000 The cost of production replaces “purchases” in the income statement. With revenue $240 000, opening finished goods $14 000 and closing finished goods $16 000: Kora Furniture — Income statement (extract) for the year ended 31 December 2026 $ $ Revenue 240 000 Less Cost of sales Inventory of finished goods at 1 January 2026 14 000 Cost of production 149 000 163 000 Less Inventory of finished goods at 31 December 2026 (16 000) (147 000) Gross profit 93 000 In the statement of financial position, all three closing inventories appear as current assets: raw materials $9 500, work in progress $6 000 and finished goods $16 000. Examiner Tip When a cost is shared (e.g. rent split 3/4 factory, 1/4 office), put the factory share in factory overheads and the office share in the income statement expenses. State the split in a working so method marks can be awarded.

Many small traders do not keep a full double-entry system. The accountant must reconstruct the figures from bank statements, invoices and lists of assets and liabilities. Method A: profit from the change in capital A statement of affairs is a list of assets and liabilities on a given date; the difference is the owner’s capital (it is similar to a statement of financial position but prepared from incomplete information). Profit = closing capital − opening capital + drawings − capital introduced Statements of affairs 1 Jan 2026 $ 31 Dec 2026 $ Premises 50 000 50 000 Equipment 8 000 7 200 Inventory 6 000 7 400 Trade receivables 4 500 5 100 Bank 2 300 3 900 Cash – 300 Less Trade payables (3 800) (4 200) Less Loan – (5 000) Capital 67 000 64 700 Calculation of profit During the year the owner withdrew $14 000 and introduced additional capital of $2 000. Profit = 64 700 − 67 000 + 14 000 − 2 000 = $9 700 . Capital fell by $2 300, but the owner took out $14 000; without the drawings, capital would have risen. The $2 000 introduced is not profit, so it is removed. Method B: finding missing figures When a full income statement is required, missing sales and purchases are found with control-account style workings, and mark-up or margin is used to link cost of sales and revenue. Mark-up Gross profit ÷ cost of sales × 100 Margin Gross profit ÷ revenue × 100 25% mark-up = 20% margin (1/4 on cost = 1/5 of selling price) 50% mark-up = 33⅓% margin Worked example: Leon Diaz Leon paid suppliers $47 000 during 2026. Trade payables were $3 800 at the start and $4 200 at the end. Inventory was $6 000 at the start and $7 400 at the end. Leon sells all goods at a mark-up of 50%. Cash sales were $8 000; the rest were on credit. Trade receivables were $4 500 at the start and $5 100 at the end; discounts allowed were $400. Find purchases, revenue and the amount received from credit customers. Trade payables (purchases) working Date Details $ Date Details $ Bank (paid to suppliers) 47 000 Jan 1 Balance b/d 3 800 Dec 31 Balance c/d 4 200 Purchases (missing figure) 47 400 51 200 51 200 Workings Cost of sales = 6 000 + 47 400 − 7 400 = 46 000 . Mark-up 50%: gross profit = 50% × 46 000 = 23 000, so revenue = 46 000 + 23 000 = 69 000 . Credit sales = 69 000 − 8 000 cash sales = 61 000 . Check: margin = 23 000 ÷ 69 000 = 33⅓%, consistent with a 50% mark-up. Trade receivables (sales) working Date Details $ Date Details $ Jan 1 Balance b/d 4 500 Bank (received — missing figure) 60 000 Credit sales 61 000 Discounts allowed 400 Dec 31 Balance c/d 5 100 65 500 65 500 Leon should therefore have received $60 000 from credit customers. If the bank statement shows less, the difference may indicate an error, unrecorded drawings, or goods or cash stolen — a common follow-up question. Common Mistake Confusing mark-up with margin. A 25% mark-up is calculated on cost ; applying 25% to revenue (margin) gives the wrong gross profit. Always ask: “percentage of what?” Examiner Tip Opening capital is often the missing figure in incomplete-records questions. Prepare an opening statement of affairs first (assets − liabilities), then use it as the opening capital in the statement of financial position.

Organisation Extra statement or account Ownership section of SOFP Sole trader — Capital + profit − drawings Partnership Appropriation account; current accounts Capital accounts + current accounts Limited company Retained earnings / changes in equity Share capital + reserves (general reserve, retained earnings) Club or society Receipts and payments; subscriptions account; activity trading account Accumulated fund + surplus (or − deficit) Manufacturer Manufacturing account As for its business type Incomplete records Statement of affairs; control-account workings Capital from statement of affairs Quick Checklist I can prepare an income statement and statement of financial position for a sole trader, applying every year-end adjustment in two places. I can calculate the change in the provision for doubtful debts and show net trade receivables correctly. I can prepare a partnership appropriation account and partners’ current accounts, and explain what a partnership agreement contains. I can explain the features of a limited company, compare ordinary and preference shares, and prepare the equity section including reserves and dividends. I can distinguish a receipts and payments account from an income and expenditure account and prepare a subscriptions account. I can prepare a manufacturing account showing prime cost, factory overheads, work in progress and cost of production. I can calculate profit from a change in capital and find missing figures using statements of affairs, mark-up, margin and control-account workings.

Topic 6 · Analysis & Interpretation Analysis and Interpretation This topic is about turning the figures in the income statement and statement of financial position into ratios that measure profitability, liquidity and efficiency. Exam questions reward accurate calculation, but most of the marks go to interpreting the results, comparing them and advising the owner.

A single figure (e.g. profit for the year of $24 000) tells you little on its own. A ratio relates one figure to another so that performance can be judged and compared . Ratios fall into three groups: Profitability — how well the business turns revenue and capital into profit. Liquidity — whether the business can pay its short-term debts as they fall due. Efficiency (activity) — how well the business manages inventory, credit customers and credit suppliers. Comparisons can be made with previous years (inter-period), with other businesses (inter-firm), or with a target or industry average. Examiner Tip The 2027–2029 syllabus updated the list of ratios and some of their names. The formulae below are the standard ones, but always check your own copy of the syllabus for the exact names and the list you are required to know, and use those names in your answers.

Gross margin Gross profit ÷ Revenue × 100 Mark-up Gross profit ÷ Cost of sales × 100 Profit margin Profit for the year ÷ Revenue × 100 Return on capital employed (ROCE) Profit for the year ÷ Capital employed × 100 Capital employed Owner’s capital + Non-current liabilities Expense to revenue Named expense ÷ Revenue × 100 What each one tells you Gross margin : the gross profit earned on each $100 of sales. A fall usually means the business is paying more for goods, cutting selling prices, or suffering inventory losses (theft, damage). Mark-up : the percentage added to cost to arrive at selling price. It always gives a higher figure than gross margin for the same goods. Profit margin : the profit left from each $100 of sales after all expenses. If gross margin is steady but profit margin falls, expenses have risen relative to revenue. ROCE : the return the owner earns on the money invested. Compare it with the return available elsewhere (e.g. interest on a savings account) to judge whether staying in the business is worthwhile. Expense-to-revenue ratios (e.g. wages, rent, advertising, delivery ÷ revenue): show which expense is driving a change in profit margin. Examiner Tip Gross margin and mark-up are linked. If mark-up is 50%, gross margin is 50 ÷ 150 = 33.3%. If gross margin is 25%, mark-up is 25 ÷ 75 = 33.3%. Questions on incomplete records often expect you to convert between them.

Working capital Current assets − Current liabilities Current ratio Current assets : Current liabilities (expressed as x : 1) Liquid (acid test) ratio (Current assets − Inventory) : Current liabilities Working capital is the amount available to finance day-to-day trading. A business with too little working capital may be unable to pay suppliers, lose cash discounts, or be refused further credit. The current ratio compares all current assets with current liabilities. A figure of around 1.5 : 1 to 2 : 1 is often regarded as comfortable, but the right level depends on the type of business. The liquid ratio leaves out inventory because inventory must first be sold (and the money perhaps collected from customers) before it becomes cash. Around 1 : 1 is often treated as satisfactory. A ratio that is too high is also a problem: it suggests money tied up in idle inventory, slow-paying customers or surplus cash that could be invested to earn a return. A large gap between the current and liquid ratios shows the business relies heavily on inventory.

Average inventory (Opening inventory + Closing inventory) ÷ 2 Rate of inventory turnover (times) Cost of sales ÷ Average inventory Rate of inventory turnover (days) Average inventory ÷ Cost of sales × 365 (or 365 ÷ times) Trade receivables turnover (days) Trade receivables ÷ Credit sales × 365 Trade payables turnover (days) Trade payables ÷ Credit purchases × 365 Inventory turnover : how many times in the year the average inventory is sold and replaced, or how many days goods stay in the warehouse. A faster rate (more times, fewer days) usually means higher sales and less risk of goods becoming damaged or out of date. Perishable-goods businesses expect a very fast rate. Trade receivables turnover : the average time credit customers take to pay. Compare it with the credit terms allowed (e.g. 30 days). Longer collection means cash is tied up and the risk of irrecoverable debts grows. Trade payables turnover : the average time taken to pay credit suppliers. Taking longer keeps cash in the business, but going beyond agreed terms risks losing cash discounts, goodwill and future credit. Ideally the business collects from customers faster than it pays suppliers. Common Mistake Using total revenue or purchases when the question gives credit sales or credit purchases, or using closing inventory instead of average inventory for inventory turnover. Also, students often state a ratio has “improved” when a liquid ratio has risen to 3 : 1 — a very high ratio can signal poor use of resources.

Ratio Ways to improve it Gross margin / mark-up Raise selling prices (if demand allows); find cheaper suppliers; buy in bulk for trade discounts; reduce inventory losses through better security; change the sales mix towards higher-margin goods. Profit margin Improve gross margin (above); control expenses, e.g. renegotiate rent, cut energy use, review staffing levels, reduce waste. ROCE Increase profit for the year; use the same capital more effectively; withdraw surplus capital that is not earning a return (e.g. idle cash). Expense-to-revenue Reduce the named expense or increase revenue faster than the expense grows. Current / liquid ratio (too low) Owner introduces more capital; take a long-term loan instead of an overdraft; sell surplus non-current assets; reduce drawings; collect debts faster. Current / liquid ratio (too high) Invest surplus cash; reduce excess inventory; repay expensive current liabilities. Inventory turnover Hold less inventory (smaller, more frequent orders); clear slow-moving lines with promotions; increase sales through advertising. Trade receivables days Offer cash discounts for prompt payment; send statements and reminders promptly; credit-check new customers; reduce credit limits or credit periods; charge interest on overdue accounts. Trade payables days Negotiate longer credit terms with suppliers; pay on the last permitted day (but within terms, and weigh up any cash discount lost).

1 Cash buys inventory Goods are bought, often on credit from suppliers (creating trade payables). 2 Inventory is held Goods sit in the business until sold — measured by inventory turnover. 3 Inventory is sold on credit Trade receivables arise — measured by trade receivables turnover. 4 Customers pay Cash returns to the business and is used to pay suppliers — measured by trade payables turnover. The longer goods are held and the longer customers take to pay, the more working capital the business needs. Shortening the cycle improves liquidity without any extra capital.

Inter-period comparison : comparing the same business over two or more years to identify trends (is the business improving or getting worse?). Inter-firm comparison : comparing a business with another business, ideally in the same trade and of similar size, to judge relative performance. Limitations of comparison Inter-period limitations Inter-firm limitations Inflation means money values in different years are not directly comparable. Firms may use different accounting policies (e.g. depreciation methods, inventory valuation), so figures are not prepared on the same basis. Changes in accounting policy between years distort trends. Firms may differ in size, location, age of assets and the exact goods they sell. The business may have changed what it sells, its location or its size. Financial year-ends may differ, so seasonal effects differ. Outside conditions (economy, competitors, regulations) may have changed. Only limited published information may be available for another business. General limitations of ratio analysis Ratios are based on historic figures, so they may not predict the future. The statement of financial position shows the position on one day , which may not be typical (and can be window-dressed). Ratios ignore non-financial factors : staff quality and morale, customer loyalty, reputation, environmental impact, location. Ratios show symptoms , not causes — further investigation is needed. Historic cost means assets may be shown at values well below their current worth, distorting ROCE.

User Main interest Most useful ratios Owner Profitability, return on investment, whether to expand, how much can be drawn All, especially ROCE and profit margin Managers Controlling costs, planning, judging performance of departments Expense ratios, inventory turnover, margins Trade payables (suppliers) Whether they will be paid on time; whether to give credit Current and liquid ratios, trade payables days Banks and lenders Ability to repay loans and interest; security available Liquidity ratios, profit margin, ROCE Potential investors / partners Likely return and risk compared with alternatives ROCE, profit margin Employees Job security, prospects for pay rises Profit margin, liquidity Customers Whether the business will continue to supply goods and honour guarantees Liquidity, profitability trend Government / tax authorities Correct tax assessment, economic statistics Profit for the year

Hana runs a stationery shop. All sales and purchases are on credit. Extracts from her financial statements are shown below. Extracts for the years ended 31 March 2025 $ 2026 $ Revenue 200 000 240 000 Opening inventory 18 000 22 000 Purchases 132 000 172 000 Closing inventory (22 000) (30 000) Cost of sales 128 000 164 000 Gross profit 72 000 76 000 Less Expenses (including wages) (42 000) (52 000) Profit for the year 30 000 24 000 Wages (included in expenses) 24 000 31 200 Capital employed 150 000 160 000 Trade receivables 25 000 40 000 Bank 8 000 2 000 Trade payables 20 000 34 000 Other payables 2 000 2 000 Current assets: 2025 = 22 000 + 25 000 + 8 000 = $55 000; 2026 = 30 000 + 40 000 + 2 000 = $72 000. Current liabilities: 2025 = $22 000; 2026 = $36 000. Ratio 2025 2026 Trend Gross margin 72 000 ÷ 200 000 = 36.0% 76 000 ÷ 240 000 = 31.7% Worse Mark-up 72 000 ÷ 128 000 = 56.3% 76 000 ÷ 164 000 = 46.3% Worse Profit margin 30 000 ÷ 200 000 = 15.0% 24 000 ÷ 240 000 = 10.0% Worse Wages to revenue 24 000 ÷ 200 000 = 12.0% 31 200 ÷ 240 000 = 13.0% Worse ROCE 30 000 ÷ 150 000 = 20.0% 24 000 ÷ 160 000 = 15.0% Worse Working capital 55 000 − 22 000 = $33 000 72 000 − 36 000 = $36 000 Higher, but see ratios Current ratio 55 000 : 22 000 = 2.5 : 1 72 000 : 36 000 = 2.0 : 1 Lower, still adequate Liquid ratio 33 000 : 22 000 = 1.5 : 1 42 000 : 36 000 = 1.17 : 1 Lower, still above 1 : 1 Inventory turnover 128 000 ÷ 20 000 = 6.4 times (57 days) 164 000 ÷ 26 000 = 6.3 times (58 days) Slightly slower Trade receivables turnover 25 000 ÷ 200 000 × 365 = 46 days 40 000 ÷ 240 000 × 365 = 61 days Worse Trade payables turnover 20 000 ÷ 132 000 × 365 = 55 days 34 000 ÷ 172 000 × 365 = 72 days Paying more slowly Model answer Hana is considering whether her business performed better in 2026 than in 2025. Advise her, giving reasons for your answer. [6] Although revenue rose by $40 000, the business performed worse in 2026. Profitability fell. Gross margin dropped from 36.0% to 31.7%, so Hana is earning less gross profit on each $100 of sales — possibly because she cut prices to boost sales or her suppliers raised their prices. Profit margin fell further, from 15.0% to 10.0%, because expenses also rose faster than revenue (wages rose from 12.0% to 13.0% of revenue). Return on capital fell from 20.0% to 15.0%, so Hana’s investment is earning less, although 15% is probably still more than she could earn by depositing the money in a bank. Liquidity weakened. The current ratio fell from 2.5 : 1 to 2.0 : 1 and the liquid ratio from 1.5 : 1 to 1.17 : 1. Both are still acceptable, but the bank balance has fallen to only $2 000. Credit control is poorer. Customers now take 61 days to pay instead of 46, tying up cash and increasing the risk of irrecoverable debts. Hana is paying suppliers in 72 days instead of 55, which may damage relationships and lose cash discounts. Advice: 2026 was a weaker year. Hana should review her pricing and suppliers to restore the gross margin, control wages, and tighten credit control (e.g. offer cash discounts for prompt payment) so that cash flows in more quickly and she can pay suppliers within their terms. Examiner Tip For “Advise” or “Discuss” questions: (1) quote the figures for both years, (2) say whether each has improved or worsened, (3) give a likely reason or consequence, and (4) finish with a clear decision. Answers that only list the ratios without comment earn very few marks. Common Mistake Saying “profit increased because revenue increased”. Here revenue rose but profit for the year fell from $30 000 to $24 000. Always look at the margins, not just the size of revenue. Quick Checklist I can state and apply the formula for every profitability, liquidity and efficiency ratio on my syllabus. I can convert between gross margin and mark-up. I can calculate working capital and explain why too little or too much is a problem. I can suggest realistic ways to improve each ratio. I can explain the limitations of inter-period and inter-firm comparison and of ratio analysis generally. I can identify the users of financial statements and what each is interested in. I can write a structured “Advise” answer that quotes figures, interprets them and reaches a decision.

Topic 7 · Concepts & Modern Practice Accounting Concepts and Modern Practice Accounting concepts are the agreed rules that explain why transactions are recorded the way they are, and modern practice covers ethics, technology and sustainability. Exam questions ask you to name the concept behind a treatment, explain it in context, and judge ethical or practical situations.

Concepts (also called principles or conventions) give a common framework so that financial statements are prepared in the same way by everyone. They make statements reliable and comparable between years and between businesses. Almost every adjustment you meet in other topics — depreciation, accruals, prepayments, provisions, inventory valuation — is justified by one or more concepts.

Concept Definition Example of how it is applied Business entity The business is treated as separate from its owner. Only transactions that affect the business are recorded in its books. The owner pays her family’s holiday from the business bank account: this is recorded as drawings , not as a business expense. Her private car is not shown as a business asset. Consistency Once a method of treating an item is chosen, it should be used in every period unless there is a good reason to change. Delivery vans are depreciated by the reducing balance method every year; the business does not switch to straight line just to report a higher profit. Duality Every transaction has two aspects: one account is debited and another credited with the same amount. Assets = Capital + Liabilities always holds. Buying equipment for $3 000 on credit: debit Equipment, credit the supplier’s account; assets and liabilities both rise by $3 000. Going concern It is assumed that the business will continue to operate for the foreseeable future and has no intention of closing down. Non-current assets are shown at cost less depreciation rather than at the (lower) amount they would raise in a forced sale. Historic cost Assets are recorded at their original cost price, not at their current value. Premises bought for $120 000 ten years ago are still shown at $120 000 even though they might now sell for $200 000. Matching (accruals) Revenue earned in a period is matched with the expenses incurred in earning it in that same period, regardless of when cash is received or paid. Electricity used in December but billed in January is included as an expense for the year to 31 December and shown as an other payable (accrual). Rent paid in advance is a prepayment. Materiality Items of small value that would not affect a user’s view of the statements need not be treated strictly; they may be recorded in the simplest way. A stapler costing $8 that will last several years is written off as an expense rather than capitalised and depreciated as a non-current asset. Money measurement Only items that can be measured reliably in money terms are recorded. The skill of the workforce, good staff morale and customer loyalty are not recorded, even though they add value to the business. Prudence Profits and assets should not be overstated, and liabilities and losses should not be understated. Losses are provided for as soon as they are foreseen; profits are recognised only when reasonably certain. Creating a provision for doubtful debts; valuing inventory at the lower of cost and net realisable value. Realisation Revenue is recognised when it is earned — normally when the legal title to goods passes to the customer — not when cash is received. Goods delivered to a credit customer on 28 December are included in revenue for the year to 31 December, even though the customer pays in February. B usiness entity C onsistency D uality G oing concern H istoric cost M atching M ateriality M oney measurement P rudence R ealisation Remember the order as “ B C D G H, three Ms, P R ” — ten concepts, almost alphabetical. Concepts behind common adjustments Depreciation Matching (cost spread over useful life); consistency (same method each year) Accruals and prepayments Matching Provision for doubtful debts Prudence (also matching) Inventory at lower of cost and NRV Prudence Drawings recorded separately Business entity Small items expensed Materiality Model answer Ravi, a trader, has made the following decisions. For each, name the accounting concept applied and explain how it applies. (a) He has reduced the value of 20 damaged jackets from cost of $40 each to an expected selling price of $25 each. (b) He records the petrol for his family car, paid from the business bank account, as drawings. [4] (a) Prudence. The jackets can now only be sold for less than they cost, so the expected loss is recognised immediately. Inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value so that assets and profit are not overstated. (b) Business entity. The business is a separate entity from Ravi. The petrol is a private expense, not a cost of running the business, so it is treated as drawings and reduces his capital rather than the profit for the year. Common Mistake Naming the concept but not linking it to the situation. “Prudence means not overstating profit” earns at most one mark; you must explain what in the scenario would be overstated and how the treatment prevents it. Another frequent error is confusing realisation (when revenue is recognised) with matching (pairing expenses with that revenue).

h: Accounting policies and the qualities of useful information
x: Accounting policies are the specific methods a business chooses to apply the concepts, e.g. which depreciation method and rate to use, how inventory is valued, what percentage provision is made for doubtful debts. Policies should be chosen so that the financial statements give information with the following qualities, and should be applied consistently. Quality Meaning Example Relevance Information can influence users’ decisions; it is timely and helps them assess past or future performance. Producing the statements soon after the year-end, so the bank can decide on a loan application. Reliability (faithful representation) Information is free from material error and bias, complete, and shows what it claims to show; it can be depended upon. Inventory is counted and valued carefully; figures are supported by source documents. Comparability Users can compare the information with other periods and other businesses because it is prepared on the same basis. Using the same depreciation policy each year; disclosing any change in policy and its effect. Understandability Information is presented clearly so that users with reasonable knowledge can understand it. Using standard headings and layouts; grouping items logically; avoiding unnecessary detail. There can be a conflict between qualities: waiting to obtain fully accurate figures increases reliability but reduces relevance because the information arrives late.

Accountants are trusted by owners, lenders, tax authorities and the public. Professional bodies expect them to follow these fundamental principles: 1 Integrity Being honest and straightforward in all work; not being associated with information that is false or misleading. 2 Objectivity Not allowing bias, conflicts of interest or pressure from others to override professional judgement. 3 Professional competence and due care Keeping knowledge up to date and working carefully and thoroughly. 4 Confidentiality Not disclosing information about the business or its clients without proper authority, unless there is a legal or professional duty to do so, and not using it for personal gain. 5 Professional behaviour Complying with laws and regulations and avoiding actions that discredit the profession. Examples of unethical practice Window dressing : making the statement of financial position look better than it really is at the year-end, e.g. delaying payments to suppliers so the bank balance looks healthy, or recording next year’s sales early. Overstating profit by not providing for depreciation or doubtful debts, or by valuing inventory above cost. Understating profit to reduce tax (tax evasion). Recording fictitious sales or assets, or omitting liabilities. Changing accounting policies only to manipulate reported profit. Passing on confidential customer or employee data, or using inside information for personal benefit. Why ethical behaviour matters Users rely on the statements to make decisions; misleading figures can cause lenders, suppliers and investors to lose money. Unethical practice can lead to fines, prosecution and loss of professional membership. It damages the reputation of the business and the trust of customers and suppliers. Model answer Mei is the bookkeeper for a small business. Just before the year-end the owner asks her to leave out an invoice for $6 000 of repairs received in December, so that the business’s profit looks higher when it applies for a bank loan. Explain why Mei should refuse, referring to ethical principles and accounting concepts. [4] Leaving out the invoice would breach the principle of integrity , because Mei would knowingly be producing misleading figures. It would also breach objectivity , since she would be letting pressure from the owner override her professional judgement. The repairs relate to December, so under the matching (accruals) concept the $6 000 must be included as an expense and an other payable for this year; omitting it would also break prudence , as profit would be overstated and liabilities understated. The bank could lend money based on false information, and Mei and the business could face legal action and loss of reputation. She should explain this to the owner and record the invoice correctly. Examiner Tip In ethics scenarios, (1) name the principle, (2) say exactly what in the scenario breaches it, (3) state the consequence for users or the business, and (4) suggest the correct action. Linking ethics to a concept (such as prudence or matching) often earns an extra mark.

Accounting software : once a transaction is entered, the software posts it to the ledgers, updates balances and produces the trial balance, financial statements and reports automatically. Automation : bank feeds import transactions directly; invoices can be scanned and read automatically; recurring entries (rent, loan repayments) and reminders to customers are generated without manual input. Cloud accounting : records are stored online and can be accessed from anywhere by the owner, staff and the accountant at the same time, with automatic backups and updates. Data security : financial and personal data must be protected using passwords, multi-factor authentication, access levels for different staff, encryption, regular backups, anti-virus software and staff training against fraud such as phishing. Advantages of computerised accounting Disadvantages and risks Faster processing; large volumes of transactions handled easily Cost of software, hardware, subscriptions and staff training Fewer arithmetical and posting errors; trial balance always balances Input errors (wrong amount or account) still occur: “garbage in, garbage out” Up-to-date information and instant reports aid decision-making Risk of hacking, viruses, data theft and breaches of confidentiality Remote and shared access with cloud systems Dependence on power, internet and the software provider; system failures halt work Automatic backups and audit trails Data loss if backups fail; possible job losses and staff resistance Common Mistake Claiming that accounting software “eliminates all errors”. Software prevents arithmetical errors and one-sided entries, but errors of commission, principle, omission and original entry can still happen because a person still enters the data.

h: Sustainability and the role of accounting
x: Sustainability means meeting present needs without damaging the ability of future generations to meet theirs. Businesses are increasingly expected to consider their impact on the environment and society, not just their profit. Environmental costs include energy and fuel use, waste disposal, pollution clean-up, recycling schemes, carbon taxes or fines, and investment in cleaner equipment (e.g. solar panels, electric delivery vans). Role of accounting : Identifying and recording environmental costs separately so managers can see and control them. Measuring savings from sustainable choices (e.g. lower energy bills after installing insulation) to support investment decisions. Sustainability reporting : providing information on carbon emissions, energy use, waste and social impact alongside the financial statements, so that stakeholders can judge the business’s wider performance. Providing evidence to lenders, customers and investors who prefer to deal with responsible businesses. Limitations : many environmental effects are hard to measure in money (the money measurement concept), so they are not shown in the financial statements and must be reported in non-financial terms. Paperless accounting (digital invoices, cloud records) is itself a sustainable practice, linking technology and sustainability. Examiner Tip When asked to discuss a sustainable investment, give both sides: short-term costs reduce profit (and may reduce liquidity), but long-term savings, improved reputation and access to customers or finance may increase profit later. Finish with a justified conclusion. Quick Checklist I can define all ten accounting concepts and give an example of each. I can identify which concept justifies a given treatment and explain it in the context of the question. I can explain what accounting policies are and the four qualities of useful financial information. I can name the ethical principles and apply them to a scenario, including window dressing. I can explain how accounting software, automation and cloud systems are used, and evaluate their advantages and risks. I can describe methods of keeping accounting data secure. I can explain the role of accounting in recording environmental costs and sustainability reporting.

h: Question 7: Double entry and errors not revealed by a trial balance
x: Practice question · [7 marks] (a) Explain the principle of double entry, using an example. [3] (b) A trial balance agrees. State two types of error that may still exist and give an example of each. [4] Answer (a): every transaction has two aspects (the duality concept), so it is recorded twice: a debit entry in one account and a credit entry of the same amount in another account. For example, when a business buys office equipment for $600 by bank transfer, it debits the office equipment account $600 (an asset increases) and credits the bank account $600 (an asset decreases). Because every debit has an equal credit, total debit balances should equal total credit balances. Answer (b): any two of the following. Error of omission: a transaction is left out completely, e.g. a sales invoice for $200 is never recorded. Error of commission: the correct amount is entered on the correct side but in the wrong account of the same class, e.g. a payment from L Diaz is credited to L Dias’s account. Error of principle: an entry is made in the wrong class of account, e.g. the purchase of a delivery van is debited to the motor expenses account. Error of original entry: the wrong amount is used for both entries, e.g. a $540 invoice is recorded as $450 in both accounts. Complete reversal of entries: the debit and credit are swapped, e.g. cash sales are debited to sales and credited to cash. Compensating error: two errors of equal value cancel each other out. Why this scores In (a), marks are given for “two aspects”, “equal debit and credit” and a correct example that names both accounts. In (b), name the type of error and give a specific, accurate example. A vague example such as “wrong account” does not show which error it is.

h: Question 8: Advise on using accounting software
x: Practice question · [6 marks] Sara Lim runs a florist’s shop with two staff. She writes up her books of prime entry and ledger by hand. A friend suggests she should switch to accounting software. Advise Sara whether she should switch. Justify your answer by discussing the advantages and disadvantages. Answer: Advantages Once a transaction is entered, the software posts the double entry automatically, so balancing and arithmetic errors are far less likely and the trial balance always agrees. Reports such as aged receivables, the trial balance and the income statement can be produced instantly, helping Sara control credit and make decisions quickly. It saves time on routine work (invoicing, statements of account, bank reconciliations using bank feeds), which frees Sara and her staff for selling. Disadvantages The software and any subscription cost money, and staff need training time. Data must be protected: there is a risk of hacking, viruses or data loss, so Sara needs passwords, access controls and regular back-ups. Errors in input (wrong amount, wrong account) are still possible, and the software will process them without questioning them. Recommendation Sara should switch to accounting software. Her business is small, so a low-cost package would be affordable, and the time saved and faster information outweigh the cost. She should back up her data regularly, limit access with passwords and keep checking her input carefully. Why this scores “Advise” questions reward both sides of the argument, each point developed (what it means for Sara), and a clear decision with a reason. Relate your points to her situation (small shop, two staff). A list of generic points with no conclusion is capped well below full marks. Quick Checklist In my answer I gave every account and statement a full heading, including the business name and the correct date wording (“at” or “for the year ended”). In my answer I wrote the date and the name of the other account against every ledger entry. In my answer I balanced accounts with balance c/d, equal totals on the same line and balance b/d on the opposite side on the next day. In my answer I removed trade discount before recording and recorded cash discounts in the discount columns. In my answer I showed my workings (percentages, balancing figures) so I could earn own-figure marks. In my answer to an Advise question, I discussed both sides, applied them to the business and ended with a justified recommendation.

h: Question 1: Straight-line and reducing balance depreciation
x: Practice question · [8 marks] On 1 January 2024 Ruth Okafor bought a packaging machine for $24 000. She expects to use it for 5 years and then sell it for $4 000. Her financial year ends on 31 December. (a) Calculate the annual depreciation charge using the straight-line method. [2] (b) Calculate the depreciation charge for each of the years 2024, 2025 and 2026 using the reducing balance method at 30% per annum. [3] (c) Calculate the net book value of the machine at 31 December 2026 under each method. [2] (d) State which method gives the higher profit for 2024. [1] Answer (a): (cost − residual value) ÷ useful life = (24 000 − 4 000) ÷ 5 = $4 000 per year . Answer (b) and (c): Depreciation schedule Year ended 31 December Straight-line charge $ Straight-line NBV $ Reducing balance charge $ Reducing balance NBV $ Cost at 1 January 2024 24 000 24 000 2024 4 000 20 000 7 200 16 800 2025 4 000 16 000 5 040 11 760 2026 4 000 12 000 3 528 8 232 Reducing balance workings: 2024: 30% × 24 000 = 7 200. 2025: 30% × (24 000 − 7 200) = 30% × 16 800 = 5 040. 2026: 30% × 11 760 = 3 528. Answer (d): the straight-line method gives the higher profit for 2024, because its charge ($4 000) is lower than the reducing balance charge ($7 200). Why this scores Show the formula with figures for straight-line. For reducing balance, apply the rate to the net book value , never to cost again. Residual value is ignored when calculating reducing balance depreciation. Laying out a schedule earns own-figure marks if one line goes wrong.

h: Question 2: Provision for depreciation and disposal accounts
x: Practice question · [12 marks] Daniel Achieng owns a courier business. His financial year ends on 31 December. On 1 January 2026 he owned two vans: Vans owned at 1 January 2026 Van Date bought Cost $ Van A 1 January 2024 18 000 Van B 1 January 2025 22 000 Vans are depreciated at 20% per annum on cost using the straight-line method. A full year’s depreciation is charged in the year of purchase and none in the year of disposal. On 30 June 2026 Van A was sold for $9 500, received by bank transfer. Prepare for the year ended 31 December 2026: (a) the motor vehicles account, (b) the provision for depreciation of motor vehicles account, (c) the motor vehicles disposal account. Balance the accounts where appropriate. Workings: Annual depreciation: Van A 20% × 18 000 = $3 600; Van B 20% × 22 000 = $4 400. Provision at 1 January 2026: Van A 2 years × 3 600 = 7 200; Van B 1 year × 4 400 = 4 400; total $11 600. Charge for 2026: Van B only = $4 400 (no depreciation on Van A in the year of disposal). Van A: NBV = 18 000 − 7 200 = 10 800. Sale proceeds 9 500, so loss on disposal = 10 800 − 9 500 = $1 300 . Answer (a): Motor vehicles account Date Details $ Date Details $ 1 Jan Balance b/d 40 000 30 Jun Disposal 18 000 31 Dec Balance c/d 22 000 40 000 40 000 1 Jan Balance b/d 22 000 Answer (b): Provision for depreciation of motor vehicles account Date Details $ Date Details $ 30 Jun Disposal 7 200 1 Jan Balance b/d 11 600 31 Dec Balance c/d 8 800 31 Dec Income statement 4 400 16 000 16 000 1 Jan Balance b/d 8 800 Answer (c): Motor vehicles disposal account Date Details $ Date Details $ 30 Jun Motor vehicles 18 000 30 Jun Provision for depreciation 7 200 30 Jun Bank 9 500 31 Dec Income statement (loss on disposal) 1 300 18 000 18 000 The $1 300 loss is shown as an expense in the income statement. Check: the remaining cost of $22 000 less the provision of $8 800 gives an NBV of $13 200, which is Van B after two years of $4 400. Why this scores The disposal account follows a fixed pattern: debit the cost , credit the accumulated depreciation and the proceeds , and the balancing figure is the profit or loss. Had the van sold for $11 500, the balancing figure would be a $700 profit , debited in the disposal account and shown as other income. Read the depreciation policy carefully (year of purchase and year of disposal) before you calculate anything.

h: Question 3: Expense account with an accrual and a prepayment
x: Practice question · [8 marks] Leah Novak rents a workshop for $600 per month. Her financial year ends on 31 December. On 1 January 2026 she owed the rent for December 2025. During 2026 she made the following payments by bank transfer: Rent payments, 2026 Date Period covered $ 5 Jan December 2025 600 31 Mar January to March 2026 1 800 30 Jun April to June 2026 1 800 30 Sep July to September 2026 1 800 28 Dec October 2026 to January 2027 2 400 (a) Prepare the rent payable account for the year ended 31 December 2026, balancing it and bringing down the balance on 1 January 2027. [6] (b) State how the balance at 31 December 2026 is shown in the statement of financial position. [2] Answer (a): the charge for the year is 12 × $600 = $7 200. The opening accrual is $600. The closing prepayment (January 2027) is $600. Rent payable account Date Details $ Date Details $ 5 Jan Bank 600 1 Jan Balance b/d 600 31 Mar Bank 1 800 31 Dec Income statement 7 200 30 Jun Bank 1 800 31 Dec Balance c/d 600 30 Sep Bank 1 800 28 Dec Bank 2 400 8 400 8 400 1 Jan Balance b/d 600 Answer (b): the $600 debit balance is a prepayment. It is shown under current assets as an other receivable . Why this scores Work out the income statement figure first (time-based: 12 months × $600). Then the account balances naturally. An opening accrual is a credit b/d. A closing prepayment is carried down on the credit side and brought down as a debit .

x: Practice question · [7 marks] Omar Farouk sublets part of his premises to a tenant for $4 800 per year ($400 per month). His financial year ends on 31 December. On 1 January 2026 the tenant owed $800 for November and December 2025. In 2026 Omar received the following amounts by bank transfer: 10 January $800; 1 April $1 200; 1 July $1 200; 30 September $1 200; 20 December $2 000. (a) Prepare the rent receivable account for the year ended 31 December 2026, balancing it and bringing down the balance on 1 January 2027. [5] (b) Identify the balance at 31 December 2026 and state where it appears in the statement of financial position. [2] Answer (a): total received = $6 400. Income for the year = $4 800. The 20 December receipt of $2 000 covers October to December 2026 ($1 200) and January and February 2027 ($800 received in advance). Rent receivable account Date Details $ Date Details $ 1 Jan Balance b/d 800 10 Jan Bank 800 31 Dec Income statement 4 800 1 Apr Bank 1 200 31 Dec Balance c/d 800 1 Jul Bank 1 200 30 Sep Bank 1 200 20 Dec Bank 2 000 6 400 6 400 1 Jan Balance b/d 800 Answer (b): the $800 credit balance is rent received in advance. It is a current liability , shown as an other payable . Why this scores Income accounts are the mirror image of expense accounts: receipts are on the credit side and the transfer to the income statement is on the debit side. Income owed to the business at the start is a debit b/d (other receivable). Income received in advance at the end is brought down as a credit (other payable).

h: Question 5: Irrecoverable debts and the provision for doubtful debts
x: Practice question · [10 marks] Priya Shah’s financial year ends on 31 December. On 1 January 2026 her provision for doubtful debts was $1 000. During 2026: 12 August: J Owusu, who owed $450, was declared bankrupt and the debt was written off. 31 December: trade receivables were $25 350. Of this, $350 owed by T Kariuki was found to be irrecoverable and was written off. The provision for doubtful debts is to be maintained at 5% of the remaining trade receivables. (a) Prepare the irrecoverable debts account and the provision for doubtful debts account for the year ended 31 December 2026. [7] (b) Show the trade receivables extract from the statement of financial position at 31 December 2026. [3] Workings: remaining receivables = 25 350 − 350 = $25 000. Required provision = 5% × 25 000 = $1 250. Increase = 1 250 − 1 000 = $250 (an expense in the income statement). Answer (a): Irrecoverable debts account Date Details $ Date Details $ 12 Aug J Owusu 450 31 Dec Income statement 800 31 Dec T Kariuki 350 800 800 Provision for doubtful debts account Date Details $ Date Details $ 31 Dec Balance c/d 1 250 1 Jan Balance b/d 1 000 31 Dec Income statement 250 1 250 1 250 1 Jan Balance b/d 1 250 Answer (b): Statement of financial position at 31 December 2026 (extract) $ $ Current assets Trade receivables 25 000 Less Provision for doubtful debts (1 250) 23 750 The total charged to the income statement for bad and doubtful debts is $800 + $250 = $1 050. Why this scores Write off the irrecoverable debt before calculating the percentage. Only the change in the provision goes to the income statement: an increase is an expense and a decrease is income. Applying the prudence concept, the SFP shows receivables net of the full provision balance.

h: Question 6: Inventory valuation at the lower of cost and net realisable value
x: Practice question · [7 marks] Ana Costa sells kitchen appliances. At 31 December 2026 her inventory consisted of: Inventory at 31 December 2026 Product line Cost $ Selling information Blenders 2 400 Expected selling price $3 100 Toasters 1 800 Expected selling price $1 900; delivery and selling costs $250 Kettles 950 Expected selling price $1 400 Microwaves (water-damaged) 3 200 Can be sold for $2 100 after repairs costing $300 Coffee grinders 620 Expected selling price $620 (a) Calculate the value of inventory at 31 December 2026. [4] (b) State the effect on gross profit of valuing the inventory at cost instead. Name the accounting concept that requires this method of valuation. [3] Answer (a): NRV = expected selling price less any costs needed to complete and sell the goods. Each line is valued separately. Inventory valuation Product line Cost $ NRV $ Value used $ Blenders 2 400 3 100 2 400 Toasters 1 800 1 650 1 650 Kettles 950 1 400 950 Microwaves 3 200 1 800 1 800 Coffee grinders 620 620 620 Total 8 970 7 420 Inventory is valued at $7 420 . Answer (b): valuing at cost ($8 970) would overstate closing inventory by $1 550. Cost of sales would be $1 550 too low, so gross profit (and profit for the year) would be overstated by $1 550 . The prudence concept requires the lower of cost and net realisable value, so that assets and profits are not overstated and losses are recognised as soon as they are foreseen. Why this scores Compare cost and NRV line by line , not in total. Remember to deduct selling and repair costs to find NRV. For the effect on profit, link it through closing inventory and cost of sales, and give the amount.

x: Practice question · [6 marks] (a) State two causes of depreciation of non-current assets. [2] (b) Explain why depreciation is charged in the income statement. [2] (c) In Question 3, Leah Novak forgot to record the $600 rent prepaid at 31 December 2026. State the effect of this omission on her profit for the year and on her current assets. [2] Answer (a): any two of the following: physical wear and tear through use; the passage of time (e.g. a lease running out); obsolescence (newer technology makes the asset out of date); depletion (using up a natural resource, e.g. a quarry). Answer (b): a non-current asset helps to earn revenue over several years. Under the accruals (matching) concept , part of its cost is charged as an expense in each year it is used, matching the cost against the revenue it helps to earn. Without depreciation, profit would be overstated and the asset would be shown at more than its value to the business. Answer (c): rent expense would be overstated by $600, so profit for the year would be understated by $600 . Current assets would be understated by $600 , because the other receivable would be missing. Why this scores Short “State” items need only a precise phrase each. “Explain” needs a reason linked to a concept (accruals or matching). For effect questions, give the direction (overstated or understated) and the amount for each item asked about.

h: Question 8: Advise on choosing a depreciation method
x: Practice question · [6 marks] Lucia Moreno is starting a delivery business. She will buy three delivery vans, which she expects to replace after four years, and some office furniture, which she expects to keep for ten years. Vans lose much of their value in the first two years, and their repair costs rise as they get older. Advise Lucia which depreciation method she should use for the vans. Justify your answer by discussing the straight-line and reducing balance methods. Answer: Straight-line method Simple to calculate and understand, and the same charge each year makes profits easy to compare from year to year. However, it does not reflect the fast early loss in a van’s value, so the NBV in the early years would be higher than the van could be sold for. When combined with rising repair costs, the total cost of using the van (depreciation plus repairs) would rise each year, so later years would bear more of the cost. Reducing balance method Charges more depreciation in the early years, which matches the way vans actually lose value, so the NBV is closer to market value. High depreciation and low repairs early on, and low depreciation and high repairs later, give a more even total cost each year, which matches costs fairly against revenue. However, it is slightly more complex to calculate, and profits in the first years will be lower, which may concern a new business. Recommendation Lucia should use the reducing balance method for the vans, because it reflects their rapid early fall in value and evens out the combined cost of depreciation and repairs over their four-year life. The straight-line method would suit the office furniture, which loses value evenly over a long life. Once a method is chosen, she should apply it every year (the consistency concept). Why this scores Marks are given for points on both methods, developed and applied to vans (early loss in value, rising repairs), followed by a clear recommendation with a reason. Mentioning the consistency concept or a different method for the furniture shows extra judgement. Quick Checklist In my answer I worked out the income statement figure (charge or income for the year) first, then balanced the account. In my answer I showed depreciation workings, applying reducing balance rates to net book value and following the policy for the years of purchase and disposal. In my answer I used the disposal account pattern: cost in, accumulated depreciation and proceeds out, with the balancing figure as profit or loss. In my answer I wrote off irrecoverable debts before calculating the provision, and transferred only the change in the provision to the income statement. In my answer I valued inventory line by line at the lower of cost and net realisable value. In my answer to an Advise question, I weighed both methods against the business’s facts and ended with a justified recommendation.

Worked Examples · Set C Worked Examples: Financial Statements Six original Paper 2 style questions with full-mark answers covering sole traders, partnerships, limited companies, clubs, manufacturers and incomplete records. Preparing financial statements carries the most marks on the paper, so layout, headings and correct adjustments matter as much as the final figure.

h: Question 1: Sole trader statements from a trial balance with adjustments
x: Practice question · [16 marks] Amara Okafor runs a homeware shop. Her trial balance at 31 December 2026 is shown below. Trial balance at 31 December 2026 Debit $ Credit $ Revenue 96 000 Purchases 54 000 Sales returns 1 200 Purchases returns 800 Carriage inwards 700 Inventory at 1 January 2026 6 500 Wages 14 300 Rent 6 000 General expenses 3 100 Loan interest 400 Fixtures and fittings at cost 24 000 Provision for depreciation: fixtures and fittings 9 600 Motor vehicle at cost 18 000 Provision for depreciation: motor vehicle 7 200 Trade receivables 8 400 Provision for doubtful debts 300 Trade payables 5 900 Bank 2 600 Loan (repayable 2031) 8 000 Drawings 9 000 Capital at 1 January 2026 20 400 148 200 148 200 Additional information at 31 December 2026: Inventory was valued at $7 300. Wages of $500 were owing. Rent of $1 000 had been paid in advance for January 2027. Fixtures and fittings are depreciated at 10% per annum using the straight-line method. The motor vehicle is depreciated at 25% per annum using the reducing balance method. A debt of $400 is to be written off as irrecoverable. The provision for doubtful debts is to be maintained at 5% of the remaining trade receivables. Prepare Amara's income statement for the year ended 31 December 2026 and her statement of financial position at that date. Answer: Amara Okafor: Income statement for the year ended 31 December 2026 $ $ Revenue 96 000 Less Sales returns (1 200) 94 800 Less Cost of sales Opening inventory 6 500 Purchases 54 000 Less Purchases returns (800) Carriage inwards 700 60 400 Less Closing inventory (7 300) (53 100) Gross profit 41 700 Less Expenses Wages (14 300 + 500) 14 800 Rent (6 000 − 1 000) 5 000 General expenses 3 100 Loan interest 400 Depreciation: fixtures and fittings 2 400 Depreciation: motor vehicle 2 700 Irrecoverable debts 400 Increase in provision for doubtful debts 100 (28 900) Profit for the year 12 800 Workings: Fixtures: 10% × $24 000 = $2 400. Motor vehicle: 25% × ($18 000 − $7 200) = 25% × $10 800 = $2 700. Receivables after write-off: $8 400 − $400 = $8 000. New provision 5% × $8 000 = $400. Increase = $400 − $300 = $100. Amara Okafor: Statement of financial position at 31 December 2026 $ $ Non-current assets Fixtures and fittings (24 000 − 12 000) 12 000 Motor vehicle (18 000 − 9 900) 8 100 20 100 Current assets Inventory 7 300 Trade receivables (8 000 − 400) 7 600 Other receivables (rent prepaid) 1 000 Bank 2 600 18 500 Current liabilities Trade payables 5 900 Other payables (wages accrued) 500 (6 400) Net current assets 12 100 32 200 Non-current liabilities Loan (repayable 2031) (8 000) 24 200 Capital Opening balance 20 400 Add Profit for the year 12 800 33 200 Less Drawings (9 000) 24 200 The statement balances: net assets $24 200 = closing capital $24 200. Why this scores Marks go to full headings (name, statement, date), net revenue and net purchases shown, each adjustment applied once and appearing in both statements (for example, wages accrued in expenses and in current liabilities), and accumulated depreciation that includes this year's charge. Showing workings means a slip in one figure still earns own-figure marks further down. Common Mistake Students often deduct the whole $400 provision as an expense. Only the increase ($100) goes in the income statement. The full $400 is deducted from trade receivables in the statement of financial position.

h: Question 2: Partnership appropriation account and current accounts
x: Practice question · [12 marks] Lee and Patel are partners in a design studio. Their partnership agreement states: Interest on capital is allowed at 5% per annum. Patel receives a partner's salary of $8 000 per annum. Interest is charged on drawings: Lee $300, Patel $200 for the year. Remaining profits and losses are shared Lee 3 : Patel 2. Information for the year ended 30 June 2026 Lee $ Patel $ Capital accounts (fixed) 40 000 30 000 Current accounts at 1 July 2025 1 200 Cr 600 Dr Drawings for the year 15 000 12 000 The profit for the year was $41 000. (a) Prepare the appropriation account for the year ended 30 June 2026. [6] (b) Prepare the partners' current accounts in columnar form. [6] Answer (a): Lee and Patel: Appropriation account for the year ended 30 June 2026 $ $ Profit for the year 41 000 Add Interest on drawings Lee 300 Patel 200 500 41 500 Less Partner's salary: Patel (8 000) Less Interest on capital Lee (5% × 40 000) 2 000 Patel (5% × 30 000) 1 500 (3 500) Residual profit 30 000 Share of residual profit Lee (3/5) 18 000 Patel (2/5) 12 000 30 000 Answer (b): Current accounts Details Lee $ Patel $ Details Lee $ Patel $ Balance b/d (1 Jul 2025) 600 Balance b/d (1 Jul 2025) 1 200 Drawings 15 000 12 000 Interest on capital 2 000 1 500 Interest on drawings 300 200 Partner's salary 8 000 Balance c/d (30 Jun 2026) 5 900 8 700 Share of residual profit 18 000 12 000 21 200 21 500 21 200 21 500 Balance b/d (1 Jul 2026) 5 900 8 700 Why this scores Interest on drawings is added to profit, while salary and interest on capital are deducted before the residual profit is shared. In the current accounts, everything the partner is entitled to goes on the credit side and everything they take or are charged goes on the debit side. Bring the balances down to the next period.

h: Question 3: Limited company income statement extract and equity
x: Practice question · [12 marks] Zenith Ltd has an issued share capital of 200 000 ordinary shares of $1 each, fully paid. It also has $50 000 of 6% debentures (repayable 2034). The following information is for the year ended 31 March 2027: Gross profit was $180 000 and operating expenses were $112 000. Only $1 500 of debenture interest had been paid during the year. At 1 April 2026 the general reserve was $25 000 and retained earnings were $42 000. An ordinary dividend of $0.12 per share was paid during the year. The directors transferred $10 000 to the general reserve. (a) Prepare an extract from the income statement, starting with gross profit. [4] (b) Prepare the equity section of the statement of financial position at 31 March 2027. [5] (c) State one difference between an ordinary share and a debenture. [1] (d) State where the unpaid debenture interest appears in the statement of financial position. [2] Answer (a): Zenith Ltd: Income statement (extract) for the year ended 31 March 2027 $ Gross profit 180 000 Less Operating expenses (112 000) Profit from operations 68 000 Less Debenture interest (6% × 50 000) (3 000) Profit for the year 65 000 Answer (b): Working for retained earnings: $42 000 + $65 000 − dividend paid (200 000 × $0.12 = $24 000) − transfer to general reserve $10 000 = $73 000. Zenith Ltd: Statement of financial position (extract) at 31 March 2027 $ Equity Ordinary share capital: 200 000 shares of $1 each 200 000 General reserve (25 000 + 10 000) 35 000 Retained earnings 73 000 Total equity 308 000 Answer (c): Debenture holders are lenders who receive a fixed rate of interest whether or not the company makes a profit. Ordinary shareholders are owners who receive a dividend only if the directors decide to pay one. Answer (d): The $1 500 owing is shown under current liabilities as other payables (accrued debenture interest), because it is due within twelve months. Why this scores Debenture interest is an expense charged in full ($3 000) whatever has been paid. Dividends are not an expense and never appear in the income statement; they reduce retained earnings. Describe the share capital in full (number and nominal value) to earn the label mark. Advise question Practice question · [6 marks] The directors of Zenith Ltd need $100 000 to open a new branch. They are considering either issuing 100 000 more ordinary shares of $1 each or issuing $100 000 of 8% debentures. Advise the directors which method they should choose. Justify your answer. Answer: Issuing ordinary shares. In favour: there is no fixed annual cost, because dividends are paid only when the directors choose, and the money never has to be repaid, which protects cash flow while the branch becomes established. Against: the existing shareholders' control is diluted, and future profits are shared among 300 000 shares rather than 200 000, which may reduce the dividend per share. Issuing debentures. In favour: shareholders keep control, and the interest ($8 000 a year) is a known amount. If the branch earns more than 8%, the extra profit belongs to the shareholders. Against: interest must be paid even if the branch makes a loss, and $100 000 must be repaid in the future, which increases the company's financial risk. Recommendation: Zenith should issue ordinary shares. Profit from operations was $68 000 on equity of $308 000, so the business is profitable. However, it already has $50 000 of debentures, and a new branch's profits are uncertain at first. Adding $8 000 of compulsory interest on top of the existing $3 000 would increase risk at the time when cash flow is most uncertain. If the directors were confident that the branch would quickly earn well above 8%, debentures would be better for existing shareholders. Why this scores Discuss both options with points for and against, use figures from the question, and finish with a clear decision linked to the reasons. A recommendation with no justification earns no marks.

h: Question 4: Club subscriptions account and income and expenditure account
x: Practice question · [12 marks] The treasurer of Riverside Tennis Club provides the following information for the year ended 31 December 2026. Riverside Tennis Club: information 1 Jan 2026 $ 31 Dec 2026 $ Subscriptions in arrears 240 300 Subscriptions in advance 360 480 Refreshment bar inventory 350 410 Receipts and payments during the year included: subscriptions received $9 750, bar takings $4 200, bar purchases $2 300, bar assistant's wages $900, competition entry fees $650, competition prizes $400, court rent $5 400, groundsman's wages $3 200 and general expenses $860. Equipment costing $6 000 is depreciated at 10% per annum on cost. (a) Prepare the subscriptions account for the year. [5] (b) Prepare the income and expenditure account for the year ended 31 December 2026. [7] Answer (a): Subscriptions account Date Details $ Date Details $ 1 Jan 2026 Balance b/d (arrears) 240 1 Jan 2026 Balance b/d (advance) 360 31 Dec 2026 Income and expenditure 9 690 2026 Bank 9 750 31 Dec 2026 Balance c/d (advance) 480 31 Dec 2026 Balance c/d (arrears) 300 10 410 10 410 1 Jan 2027 Balance b/d (arrears) 300 1 Jan 2027 Balance b/d (advance) 480 Answer (b): Working for bar profit: cost of sales = $350 + $2 300 − $410 = $2 240. Profit = $4 200 − $2 240 − $900 wages = $1 060. Riverside Tennis Club: Income and expenditure account for the year ended 31 December 2026 $ $ Income Subscriptions 9 690 Profit on refreshment bar 1 060 Competition fees less prizes (650 − 400) 250 11 000 Less Expenditure Court rent 5 400 Groundsman's wages 3 200 General expenses 860 Depreciation of equipment 600 (10 060) Surplus of income over expenditure 940 Why this scores Use club wording: "surplus" (not profit) and "income and expenditure account". Arrears at the start are a debit balance and advance subscriptions a credit balance; at the end the c/d entries are reversed. Practice question · [9 marks] Kofi Mensah manufactures wooden chairs. For the year ended 30 September 2026: Kofi Mensah: manufacturing data $ Inventory of raw materials at 1 October 2025 8 200 Inventory of raw materials at 30 September 2026 9 400 Work in progress at 1 October 2025 5 600 Work in progress at 30 September 2026 6 900 Purchases of raw materials 61 500 Carriage inwards on raw materials 1 300 Direct factory wages 48 000 Royalties paid per chair made 3 500 Indirect factory wages 12 400 Rent of premises (three-quarters relates to the factory) 16 000 Factory power 7 800 Depreciation of factory machinery 6 500 (a) Prepare the manufacturing account for the year ended 30 September 2026. [8] (b) 10 000 chairs were completed in the year. Calculate the production cost per chair. [1] Answer (a): Kofi Mensah: Manufacturing account for the year ended 30 September 2026 $ $ Inventory of raw materials at 1 October 2025 8 200 Purchases of raw materials 61 500 Carriage inwards 1 300 62 800 71 000 Less Inventory of raw materials at 30 September 2026 (9 400) Cost of raw materials consumed 61 600 Direct wages 48 000 Direct expenses: royalties 3 500 Prime cost 113 100 Add Factory overheads Indirect factory wages 12 400 Factory rent (3/4 × 16 000) 12 000 Factory power 7 800 Depreciation of factory machinery 6 500 38 700 151 800 Add Work in progress at 1 October 2025 5 600 157 400 Less Work in progress at 30 September 2026 (6 900) Production cost of goods completed 150 500 Answer (b): $150 500 ÷ 10 000 = $15.05 per chair .
