h: Question 6: Incomplete records using statements of affairs and mark-up
x: Practice question · [12 marks] Sam Bello does not keep full accounting records. The following information is available. Sam Bello: assets and liabilities 1 Jan 2026 $ 31 Dec 2026 $ Equipment (net book value) 12 000 10 800 Inventory 4 500 5 200 Trade receivables 2 300 2 900 Bank 1 800 3 400 Trade payables 2 100 2 600 Other payables (expenses owing) – 300 During the year Sam withdrew $14 000 for personal use and paid in an extra $2 000 of capital from a personal savings account. Payments to trade suppliers totalled $45 800. Sam sells all goods at a mark-up of 40% on cost. (a) Calculate Sam's capital at 1 January 2026 and at 31 December 2026. [4] (b) Calculate the profit for the year. [3] (c) Calculate credit purchases, cost of sales, revenue and gross profit. [4] (d) Calculate the gross margin. [1] Answer (a): Capital = assets − liabilities. Statements of affairs 1 Jan 2026 $ 31 Dec 2026 $ Equipment 12 000 10 800 Inventory 4 500 5 200 Trade receivables 2 300 2 900 Bank 1 800 3 400 Total assets 20 600 22 300 Less Trade payables (2 100) (2 600) Less Other payables – (300) Capital 18 500 19 400 Answer (b): Calculation of profit for the year ended 31 December 2026 $ Closing capital 19 400 Less Opening capital (18 500) Increase in capital 900 Add Drawings 14 000 Less Capital introduced (2 000) Profit for the year 12 900 Answer (c): Credit purchases = payments $45 800 + closing payables $2 600 − opening payables $2 100 = $46 300 . Cost of sales = $4 500 + $46 300 − $5 200 = $45 600 . Revenue = $45 600 × 140/100 = $63 840 . Gross profit = $63 840 − $45 600 = $18 240 (check: 40% × $45 600 = $18 240). Answer (d): Gross margin = $18 240 ÷ $63 840 × 100 = 28.57% . A 40% mark-up is equal to a 2/7 margin. Why this scores Set out the profit formula with labels: closing capital − opening capital + drawings − capital introduced. Mark-up is based on cost and margin on revenue . Students who apply 40% to revenue lose all the method marks. Common Mistake Adding capital introduced instead of deducting it. Extra capital raises closing capital without being earned, so it must be taken out to leave only the profit. Quick Checklist In my answer I write a full heading with the business name, the statement title and the correct date wording ("for the year ended" or "at"). In my answer I apply every adjustment twice: once in the income statement and once in the statement of financial position. In my answer I label every subtotal (gross profit, prime cost, net current assets, residual profit, surplus). In my answer I show short workings beside or below the statement so I can earn own-figure marks. In my answer I check that net assets equal closing capital (or total equity) before I move on. In my answer I use the right wording for each organisation: surplus or deficit for clubs, appropriation for partnerships, retained earnings and dividends for companies.

Worked Examples · Set D Worked Examples: Verification & Analysis Seven original Paper 2 style questions with full-mark answers on correcting errors, suspense accounts, bank reconciliation, control accounts, ratios, an "Advise" evaluation question and accounting ethics. These questions test whether you can check that records are accurate and explain what the figures mean.

h: Question 1: Correction of errors and the suspense account
x: Practice question · [12 marks] Priya Nair's trial balance at 31 May 2026 did not agree. The debit column totalled $84 360 and the credit column totalled $83 910. The difference was entered in a suspense account. The following errors were then found: The sales journal was undercast by $300. Rent paid of $950 was correctly entered in the cash book but was posted to the rent account as $590. Cash sales of $420 were entered in the cash book but were not posted to the sales account. The purchase of office equipment for $1 500 had been debited to the purchases account. Discount received of $90 had not been posted to the discount received account. (a) Prepare journal entries to correct the errors. Narratives are required. [6] (b) Prepare the suspense account, showing the opening entry and the corrections. [4] (c) Name the type of error in item 4 and state one other type of error that is not revealed by a trial balance. [2] Answer (a): Journal Date Details Debit $ Credit $ 31 May Suspense 300 Sales 300 Correction of undercast sales journal 31 May Rent 360 Suspense 360 Rent of $950 posted as $590 (transposition), now corrected 31 May Suspense 420 Sales 420 Cash sales not posted to sales account 31 May Office equipment 1 500 Purchases 1 500 Purchase of non-current asset wrongly debited to purchases 31 May Suspense 90 Discount received 90 Discount received omitted from discount received account Answer (b): The debit total was larger, so the suspense account opens with a credit balance of $450 ($84 360 − $83 910). Suspense account Date Details $ Date Details $ 31 May Sales 300 31 May Difference on trial balance 450 31 May Sales 420 31 May Rent 360 31 May Discount received 90 810 810 Answer (c): Item 4 is an error of principle (a capital item treated as revenue expenditure). Another error not revealed is an error of omission , for example a credit sale left out of the books completely. Why this scores Each journal entry needs the correct debit, the correct credit and a narrative. Only errors that make the two sides unequal pass through suspense; item 4 does not. The suspense account must close with nothing left on it, and here both sides total $810.

h: Question 2: Effect of errors on profit
x: Practice question · [6 marks] Priya's draft profit for the year, calculated before the errors in Question 1 were found, was $21 600. Prepare a statement of corrected profit for the year ended 31 May 2026. Answer: Statement of corrected profit for the year ended 31 May 2026 Increase $ Decrease $ $ Draft profit for the year 21 600 1 Sales undercast 300 2 Rent understated 360 3 Cash sales omitted 420 4 Office equipment removed from purchases 1 500 5 Discount received omitted 90 2 310 360 1 950 Corrected profit for the year 23 550 Why this scores Ask "does this correction change an income or an expense?" Extra income or lower expenses increase profit. Extra expenses decrease it. Corrections that affect only assets, liabilities or capital (for example, a receivable posted to the wrong customer) have no effect on profit, and you should say so.

Practice question · [10 marks] At 30 September 2026 the bank column of Daniel Wu's cash book showed a debit balance of $1 840. His bank statement on the same date showed a credit balance of $2 615. Comparing the two revealed: Bank charges of $45 appeared only on the bank statement. A credit transfer of $380 from a customer, K Osei, appeared only on the bank statement. A standing order of $120 for insurance appeared only on the bank statement. A cheque for $210 from a customer, P Lin, had been dishonoured by the bank. Cheques paid to suppliers, no. 1047 for $740 and no. 1049 for $590, had not yet been presented. Takings of $560 banked on 30 September did not appear on the bank statement. (a) Update the cash book (bank column) and bring down the corrected balance. [5] (b) Prepare a bank reconciliation statement at 30 September 2026. [5] Answer (a): Cash book (bank column) Date Details $ Date Details $ 30 Sep Balance b/d 1 840 30 Sep Bank charges 45 30 Sep K Osei (credit transfer) 380 30 Sep Insurance (standing order) 120 30 Sep P Lin (dishonoured cheque) 210 30 Sep Balance c/d 1 845 2 220 2 220 1 Oct Balance b/d 1 845 Answer (b): Daniel Wu: Bank reconciliation statement at 30 September 2026 $ $ Balance as per bank statement 2 615 Add Amount not yet credited 560 3 175 Less Unpresented cheques No. 1047 740 No. 1049 590 (1 330) Balance as per updated cash book 1 845 Why this scores Update the cash book first using only the items the business did not know about (charges, transfers, standing orders, dishonoured cheques). Only timing differences (unpresented cheques and amounts not yet credited) go in the reconciliation. The statement must end exactly on the updated cash book balance. 1 Tick matching items Compare the cash book with the bank statement and tick items that appear in both. 2 Update the cash book Enter items found only on the statement, then balance and bring down the corrected figure. 3 Start from the bank statement balance Add amounts not yet credited and deduct unpresented cheques. 4 Agree the figures The result must equal the updated cash book balance. If it does not, look for a missed item or a sign error.

Practice question · [9 marks] The following information relates to Oakfield Traders' sales ledger for October 2026. Sales ledger information, October 2026 $ Debit balances at 1 October 18 450 Credit balances at 1 October 220 Credit sales 42 300 Sales returns 1 650 Cheques and transfers received from credit customers 38 900 Discount allowed 760 Irrecoverable debts written off 540 Customer's cheque dishonoured 310 Interest charged on an overdue account 90 Contra entry: set off against the purchases ledger 480 Credit balances at 31 October 180 (a) Prepare the sales ledger control account for October 2026, balancing it on 31 October. [7] (b) State two benefits of preparing control accounts. [2] Answer (a): Sales ledger control account Date Details $ Date Details $ 1 Oct Balance b/d 18 450 1 Oct Balance b/d 220 31 Oct Sales 42 300 31 Oct Sales returns 1 650 31 Oct Bank (dishonoured cheque) 310 31 Oct Bank 38 900 31 Oct Interest charged 90 31 Oct Discount allowed 760 31 Oct Balance c/d 180 31 Oct Irrecoverable debts 540 31 Oct Purchases ledger control (contra) 480 31 Oct Balance c/d 18 780 61 330 61 330 1 Nov Balance b/d 18 780 1 Nov Balance b/d 180 Answer (b): Any two of the following. It checks the arithmetical accuracy of the sales ledger and helps to locate errors in one ledger. It gives a quick total of trade receivables for preparing a trial balance or financial statements. It helps to detect fraud when the control account is prepared by someone other than the sales ledger clerk. Why this scores The control account mirrors a giant customer account. Anything that increases what customers owe (sales, dishonoured cheques, interest) is a debit, and anything that reduces it is a credit. Cash sales and the provision for doubtful debts never appear in it. With both opening and closing credit balances, there are two b/d and two c/d entries.

Practice question · [8 marks] Nadia Hassan runs a stationery business. Extracts from her financial statements for the year ended 31 December 2026: Nadia Hassan: extracts $ Revenue (of which credit sales $96 000) 120 000 Cost of sales 78 000 Gross profit 42 000 Expenses 27 600 Profit for the year 14 400 Inventory at 1 January 2026 9 000 Inventory at 31 December 2026 11 000 Trade receivables 10 000 Bank 2 000 Trade payables 6 500 Other payables 500 Capital employed 80 000 All purchases are on credit. Calculate, to two decimal places where necessary: (a) gross margin; (b) profit margin; (c) return on capital employed; (d) current ratio; (e) liquid (acid test) ratio; (f) rate of inventory turnover; (g) trade receivables turnover in days; (h) trade payables turnover in days. [8] Answer: Ratio calculations Ratio and formula Working Result (a) Gross margin = gross profit ÷ revenue × 100 42 000 ÷ 120 000 × 100 35.00% (b) Profit margin = profit for the year ÷ revenue × 100 14 400 ÷ 120 000 × 100 12.00% (c) ROCE = profit for the year ÷ capital employed × 100 14 400 ÷ 80 000 × 100 18.00% (d) Current ratio = current assets : current liabilities 23 000 : 7 000 3.29 : 1 (e) Liquid ratio = (current assets − inventory) : current liabilities 12 000 : 7 000 1.71 : 1 (f) Inventory turnover = cost of sales ÷ average inventory 78 000 ÷ ((9 000 + 11 000) ÷ 2) 7.80 times (g) Receivables days = trade receivables ÷ credit sales × 365 10 000 ÷ 96 000 × 365 38.02 days (h) Payables days = trade payables ÷ credit purchases × 365 6 500 ÷ 80 000 × 365 29.66 days Workings: current assets = 11 000 + 10 000 + 2 000 = $23 000; current liabilities = 6 500 + 500 = $7 000; credit purchases = cost of sales 78 000 + closing inventory 11 000 − opening inventory 9 000 = $80 000. Why this scores Write the formula, then the figures, then the answer with its unit (%, : 1, times, days). Use credit sales and credit purchases for the days ratios, and work out purchases if the question gives only cost of sales. Note that Nadia collects from customers (38 days) more slowly than she pays suppliers (30 days), which puts pressure on cash.

Practice question · [8 marks] Hannah has $40 000 to invest as a partner in one of two shops. She has been given the following information for the year ended 31 December 2026. Summary data Alpha Stores $ Beta Stores $ Revenue 250 000 180 000 Gross profit 75 000 63 000 Profit for the year 20 000 22 500 Capital employed 160 000 125 000 Current assets 36 000 21 000 of which inventory 20 000 15 000 Current liabilities 15 000 16 000 (a) Calculate for each shop: gross margin, profit margin, return on capital employed, current ratio and liquid ratio. [4] (b) Advise Hannah which shop she should invest in. Justify your answer. [4] Answer (a): Ratios Alpha Stores Beta Stores Gross margin 75 000 ÷ 250 000 = 30.00% 63 000 ÷ 180 000 = 35.00% Profit margin 20 000 ÷ 250 000 = 8.00% 22 500 ÷ 180 000 = 12.50% Return on capital employed 20 000 ÷ 160 000 = 12.50% 22 500 ÷ 125 000 = 18.00% Current ratio 36 000 : 15 000 = 2.40 : 1 21 000 : 16 000 = 1.31 : 1 Liquid ratio 16 000 : 15 000 = 1.07 : 1 6 000 : 16 000 = 0.38 : 1 Answer (b): For Beta Stores: Beta is more profitable on every measure. Its gross margin is 5 percentage points higher, which suggests better buying or higher selling prices. Its profit margin of 12.50% compared with 8.00% shows tighter control of expenses. Most importantly for an investor, its ROCE of 18.00% is well above Alpha's 12.50%, so each $1 Hannah invests is likely to earn more. For Alpha Stores: Alpha is much safer in the short term. Its liquid ratio of 1.07 : 1 means it can pay its current liabilities without selling inventory. Beta's liquid ratio of 0.38 : 1 means it has only $0.38 of liquid assets for every $1 owed, so it could struggle to pay suppliers on time and may rely on an overdraft. Recommendation: Hannah should invest in Beta Stores , because its return on capital employed is 5.5 percentage points higher and her aim as an investor is a good return. Her $40 000 would also solve Beta's main weakness: if it were paid into Beta's bank account, its liquid assets would rise to $46 000 and its liquid ratio to about 2.9 : 1. She should check that the cash will be kept in the business to improve liquidity, not withdrawn by the existing owners. If Hannah would rather take as little risk as possible, Alpha would be the safer but less rewarding choice. Why this scores Compare the two shops using the actual ratio figures, explain what each difference means, consider both sides, then give one clear decision with a reason. A strong answer also adds a condition or further information to check, such as trends over several years or the reason for low liquidity. Common Mistake Saying "Beta's ROCE is higher, so Beta is better" and stopping there. That earns only one mark. You must explain what the ratio means for the person making the decision and weigh it against the other evidence.

Practice question · [4 marks] Ruth keeps the accounts for a small building company. Near the year end the owner asks her to (i) leave out a $3 000 invoice for repairs received on 28 December until January, and (ii) value unsold timber at its expected selling price of $9 000 instead of its cost of $6 500, "so the profit looks better for the bank loan". Explain which accounting principles each request breaks and why Ruth should refuse. Answer: Request (i) breaks the accruals (matching) principle . The repairs were received in this year, so the $3 000 expense must be recorded in this year as an other payable, whenever it is paid. Leaving it out would overstate profit by $3 000. Request (ii) breaks the prudence principle and the rule that inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value. Using $9 000 would include a profit of $2 500 that has not yet been earned (realised). Ethics: together, the requests would overstate profit by $5 500 to mislead the bank. That would break Ruth's integrity (honesty) and objectivity (not being influenced by pressure from others). The financial statements would no longer give a true and fair view, and the bank could lend on false information. Ruth should explain the rules to the owner, record the correct figures and keep a record of the conversation. Why this scores Name the principle, apply it to the figures in the question (the effect on profit), and link the ethical point to who could be harmed. A general phrase like "it is wrong" without a named principle scores nothing. Quick Checklist In my answer I write a narrative under every journal entry and leave errors that do not affect the totals out of the suspense account. In my answer I decide whether each correction affects income or expenses before I change profit. In my answer I update the cash book before I write the bank reconciliation, and the statement ends on the updated balance. In my answer I enter control account items on the same side as they would appear in an individual customer or supplier account. In my answer I show the formula, the working and the unit for every ratio, using credit figures for the days ratios. In my answer I end every "Advise" question with a clear recommendation, justified with figures from both sides.

x: Start Here · Papers 1 & 2 Exam Technique: How Business Answers Are Marked Business Studies feels easy until the results come back. The content is common sense; the marks are not. Examiners award marks for four specific skills, and an answer that skips one of them is capped however “correct” it sounds. This section shows you what each question part wants and how to build answers that hit every mark.

x: Paper 1 Short answer & data response · 1 h 30 min · 80 marks · 50% Paper 1 layout 4 questions × 20 marks, each on a short business scenario Each Paper 1 question (a) 2 · (b) 2 · (c) 4 · (d) 6 · (e) 6 Paper 2 Case study · 1 h 30 min · 80 marks · 50% Paper 2 layout One long case in an insert, with appendices of data · 4 questions × 20 marks Each Paper 2 question (a) 8 · (b) 12 Check your syllabus year This layout is for Cambridge IGCSE Business Studies 0450. Always check the specimen paper for your exam year in case Cambridge changes the format. Sitting Edexcel International GCSE (4BS1) or OxfordAQA International GCSE (9225) instead? The content in these notes covers almost all of those syllabuses too, but the question styles differ: see “Other exam boards” at the end of this section.

t: Exam Technique: How Business Answers Are Marked
x: Every mark you earn is for one of four assessment objectives. Learn them, because the longer questions are built to test all four in a fixed order. K Knowledge & understanding A correct business point, term or idea. “Batch production lets a firm make products in groups.” A Application Using the case: the product, the numbers, the people, the problem. “Mei’s bakery could bake trays of 60 croissants before switching the ovens to muffins.” Just writing the business name does not count. An Analysis The “so what?”: the effect on costs, revenue, profit, customers, workers or reputation. “…so average cost per item falls, raising profit per item.” E Evaluation A judgement with a reason, comparing the options. “Batch is better than job because the bakery’s demand is now high and steady, so the lower unit cost matters more than customisation.”

t: Exam Technique: How Business Answers Are Marked
x: Part Typical wording Marks come from How to write it P1 (a) [2] Define / What is meant by… K only One precise sentence using the key words. No example needed, no case needed. P1 (b) [2] Identify two… / Calculate… K only Two short points, or the formula, the working and the answer with units. P1 (c) [4] Identify and explain… / Outline two… K + App Two points, each with one sentence linking it to this business. P1 (d) [6] Explain two reasons / advantages / ways… K + App + An for each point Two paragraphs: point → case link → consequence. P1 (e) [6] Do you think…? Justify your answer. K, An, E Argue both options with consequences, then decide and say why the other option is weaker. P2 (a) [8] Explain two/four… (often “using Appendix 2”) K + App + An Each point clearly labelled, applied to the case, with developed consequences. P2 (b) [12] Consider the advantages and disadvantages of… Recommend which… Justify your answer. K, App, An, E (levels) Each option: one advantage and one disadvantage, each developed. Finish with a comparative, justified recommendation.

t: Exam Technique: How Business Answers Are Marked
x: Most lost marks come from stopping too early. After every point, ask “So what does that mean for this business?” and keep going until you reach one of the business outcomes : costs, revenue, profit, cash flow, market share, reputation, motivation, productivity or survival. Point what it is → Case who, what, which number → This means… first effect → As a result… effect on the business outcome One point, three versions Weak (K only): “Training improves skills.” Better (K + App): “Training would improve the skills of the factory workers who assemble the e-scooters.” Full marks (K + App + An): “Training would improve the skills of the factory workers who assemble the e-scooters. This means they make fewer errors, so the 45 faults per 1,000 scooters should fall. As a result, fewer bikes are returned, which cuts the cost of repairs and protects the brand’s reputation and future sales.”

t: Exam Technique: How Business Answers Are Marked
x: Underline the case details as you read: product, location, size, numbers, owner’s aims, problems. Each one is a ready-made application mark. Use the numbers. “Returns of 4% are four times the industry average” is application; “returns are high” is barely so. Make the answer impossible to copy into another case. If your paragraph would work word for word for a bakery and a car factory, it has no application. Do not use the same case detail to earn two different application marks.

t: Exam Technique: How Business Answers Are Marked
x: Paper 2 (b) is marked in levels. Lists of points sit in the bottom level; balanced, applied analysis of every option sits in the middle; a recommendation that compares the options and explains why the others are worse reaches the top. 1 Option 1: advantage + disadvantage Each developed with the case and a consequence. 2 Option 2 (and 3): advantage + disadvantage Give each option equal weight; a lopsided answer looks unbalanced. 3 Recommendation “I recommend X because…” plus a new reason from the case. 4 Why not the others “Y is less suitable because…” This rejection is what most students forget. 5 It depends on… One condition that would change your mind: the size of the loan, whether demand stays high, how workers react. Common Mistake Writing two conclusions that recommend the same thing in different words, or concluding “X is better because it has more advantages”. A justified conclusion weighs the most important factor for this business, and explains why it outweighs the drawback you identified.

Say whether a change is a rise or a fall . “2.7 million” is half an answer; “profit fell by $2.7 million” is the full answer.
