Topic 1 · 1.1–1.5 Understanding Business Activity Why businesses exist, how they are classified, why some grow and others fail, the different legal forms they can take, and who they are trying to please. Questions on business types and objectives appear on almost every paper.

Needs, wants and scarcity Need: a good or service essential for survival, such as food, water and shelter. Want: a good or service people would like to have but can live without, such as a new phone. Scarcity: there are not enough resources to satisfy everyone’s unlimited wants, so choices must be made. Opportunity cost: the next best alternative given up when a choice is made. A café that spends its savings on a new coffee machine gives up the chance to use that money for a delivery scooter. Factors of production Factor Meaning Example Reward Land Natural resources Palm oil plantations, water, minerals Rent Labour Human effort, physical and mental Cashiers, engineers, designers Wages / salaries Capital Man-made goods used to make other goods Machinery, vans, computers Interest Enterprise The skill and risk-taking of bringing the other factors together The founder of a bubble-tea chain Profit Specialisation and the division of labour Specialisation is when people or businesses concentrate on what they do best. The division of labour splits production into separate tasks, each done by a different worker. Advantages Disadvantages Workers become skilled and fast at one task, so output per worker (productivity) rises. Less time is lost moving between tasks. Training is quicker and cheaper. Repetitive work becomes boring, lowering motivation and quality. If one worker is absent, the whole process can stop. Workers have narrow skills, so they are harder to move to other jobs. Why businesses exist and added value Businesses combine the factors of production to make goods and services that satisfy needs and wants. Added value is the difference between the selling price and the cost of bought-in materials and components. Example A florist buys flowers, paper and ribbon for RM25 and sells the finished bouquet for RM80. Added value = RM80 − RM25 = RM55 . Added value is not profit: wages, rent and other costs still have to be paid out of it. Ways to increase added value: raise the price through branding, better packaging, a premium location or excellent service; or cut the cost of materials by finding cheaper suppliers or reducing waste. Each has a risk: higher prices may lose customers, and cheaper materials may lower quality.

Economic sectors Primary Extracting natural resources: farming, fishing, mining, oil Secondary Manufacturing and construction: turning raw materials into products Tertiary Services: banking, retail, tourism, transport, tutoring As a country develops, the share of output and jobs moves from primary to secondary ( industrialisation ) and then towards tertiary ( de-industrialisation ). This happens because incomes rise and people spend more on services, and because manufacturing moves to countries with lower costs. Private and public sector Private sector: businesses owned by individuals or shareholders, usually aiming for profit. Public sector: organisations owned and controlled by the government, such as public hospitals, state schools and some utilities. Their aim is usually to provide a service rather than make a profit. A mixed economy has both.

Entrepreneurs An entrepreneur organises the factors of production and takes the risk of starting a business. Useful characteristics: hard-working, creative, a risk-taker, self-confident, good at communicating and able to bounce back from failure. Why people start businesses: to be their own boss, to turn a hobby or idea into income, to fill a gap in the market, or after redundancy. Business plans A business plan is a document describing the business, its objectives, its market and its financial forecasts. It helps the owner think through the idea and set targets, and it is usually needed to persuade a bank to lend money. However, it takes time to write and its forecasts may turn out to be wrong. Government support for start-ups Governments support new firms because they create jobs, add competition, can grow into large firms and pay taxes. Support includes grants and cheap loans, business advice, low-rent premises (business parks and incubators) and training. Measuring business size Method Limitation Number of employees A capital-intensive firm can be large with few workers. Value of output / revenue A firm with high prices may look larger than one selling many cheap items. Capital employed A labour-intensive service firm may have little capital but many staff. Market share Only useful within the same market. Common Mistake Using profit to measure size. Profit tells you about performance, not size: a huge firm can make a loss in a bad year. How businesses grow Internal (organic) growth: opening new branches, launching new products, selling in new markets. It is slower but lower-risk and keeps control and culture. External growth: a merger (two firms agree to join) or a takeover (one firm buys a majority of the other’s shares). It is quick but can cause culture clashes and job losses. Type of integration Joins with… Example Main benefit Horizontal A firm at the same stage in the same industry One supermarket chain buys another Bigger market share, less competition, economies of scale Vertical backward A supplier A chocolate maker buys a cocoa farm Secure, cheaper supplies; control of quality Vertical forward A customer business further along the chain A clothing factory buys a chain of shops Controls how products are sold; keeps the retailer’s profit Conglomerate A firm in an unrelated industry A property company buys a hotel chain Spreads risk across markets Problems of growth and why small firms survive Growth can bring communication problems, weaker control, cash-flow strain and diseconomies of scale. Many firms stay small because the owner wants control or a manageable workload, the market is small or local, or customers value personal service. Why businesses fail Poor management and planning, especially of cash flow. Failure to adapt to changes in tastes, technology or competition. Over-expansion: growing too fast and running out of cash. New businesses are especially at risk: little experience, no established customers, limited finance and no brand reputation.

Type Owners Liability Advantages Disadvantages Sole trader One person Unlimited Easy and cheap to set up; owner keeps all profit and makes all decisions; financial details private Unlimited liability; hard to raise finance; long hours; no one to share ideas or cover illness; no continuity Partnership 2 to about 20 partners Usually unlimited More capital and skills; workload and decisions shared Unlimited liability; disagreements; profits shared; one partner’s mistake binds the others Private limited company (Ltd / Sdn Bhd) Shareholders, often family and friends Limited Limited liability; separate legal identity and continuity; can raise capital by selling shares privately Shares cannot be sold to the public; legal paperwork; accounts must be published Public limited company (plc / Bhd) Shareholders, shares traded on the stock exchange Limited Can raise very large amounts of capital by selling shares to the public; high profile Expensive to set up; risk of takeover; owners (shareholders) separated from managers (directors); detailed accounts public Franchise Franchisee buys the right to use the franchisor’s brand Depends on franchisee’s legal form Franchisee: proven brand, training, lower risk. Franchisor: fast growth using others’ capital Franchisee: fee plus royalty on sales, little freedom. Franchisor: one poor franchisee damages the brand Joint venture Two or more firms share a new project Shared Shares costs, risks and local knowledge Disagreements; profits shared; different cultures Public corporation The government – Provides essential services that may not be profitable; can protect jobs May be inefficient without a profit motive; can rely on subsidies Unlimited liability: the owner is personally responsible for all business debts, so personal assets such as a house or car can be taken to pay them. Limited liability: shareholders can only lose the amount they invested. Their personal assets are protected. Incorporation: a company is a separate legal entity from its owners. It can sue and be sued and continues even if shareholders change. Examiner Tip When explaining unlimited liability, finish the chain: “…so if the business cannot repay its loan, the owner may have to sell their own house or car to pay the debt.” The cause of debt (e.g. falling sales, a large loan) is application; the loss of personal assets is the analysis. Common Mistake Saying shareholders “cannot lose money” with limited liability. They can lose everything they invested; what is protected is their personal wealth beyond that.

Why set objectives? They give everyone a clear target , so efforts are co-ordinated and staff can be motivated. They guide decision-making : managers can test each choice against the objective. They allow performance to be measured , showing whether a strategy is working. They help persuade banks and investors that the business is well planned. Good objectives are SMART : Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic and Time-bound. “Sell 150 units per month by December” is SMART; “grow the business” is not. Common objectives Survival Key for new firms and in recessions Profit Reward for owners; funds for reinvestment Growth Economies of scale, more security, higher status Market share Market power and brand recognition Service to society Social enterprises and the public sector Objectives change over time: survival first, then profit, then growth. A social enterprise has social and environmental objectives alongside financial ones and reinvests most of its profit in its cause (sometimes called the triple bottom line: profit, people, planet). Stakeholders A stakeholder is any individual or group with an interest in, or affected by, the activities of a business. Stakeholder Main objectives Owners / shareholders (internal) High profit, dividends, rising share price Managers and workers (internal) Good pay, job security, safe conditions, promotion Customers Good quality, low prices, safe products, good service Suppliers Regular orders, fair prices, being paid on time Lenders (banks) Repayment with interest on time Local community Jobs, low pollution, little traffic and noise Government Taxes paid, jobs created, laws followed, economic growth Conflict between stakeholders is common. Moving production to cheaper machinery may raise owners’ profit but cost workers their jobs; a new factory brings jobs to the community but also pollution. Businesses usually have to compromise, and in questions you should say which stakeholder’s view should matter most in the case and why. Objectives in the public and private sector Private sector firms usually focus on profit and growth. Public sector organisations focus on providing a service, keeping costs within budget and meeting social aims, such as keeping bus fares affordable. Quick Checklist I can define scarcity and opportunity cost and give a business example. I can calculate added value and explain two ways to increase it. I can classify a business by sector and explain why sectors change as countries develop. I can explain the four types of integration with an example and a benefit for each. I can compare sole traders, partnerships, Ltds, plcs, franchises and joint ventures. I can explain limited and unlimited liability with the full consequence. I can explain why objectives matter and identify conflicts between stakeholders.

Topic 2 · 2.1–2.4 People in Business How businesses motivate, organise, recruit, train and communicate with their workers. This is the most common topic for Paper 2 recommendation questions: “which method of motivation…”, “should the business delayer…”, “internal or external recruitment…”.

Motivation is the set of reasons that make someone want to work hard and do the job well. Motivated workers are more productive, make fewer mistakes, are absent less often and are less likely to leave (lower labour turnover ), which cuts recruitment and training costs. Motivation theories Maslow’s hierarchy: once a lower level of need is met, the next level up becomes the motivator. Maslow level How a business can meet it Physiological Enough pay to afford food and housing; breaks Security Permanent contracts, safe working conditions, pension Social Team working, staff events, friendly workplace Esteem Praise, awards, job titles, promotion Self-actualisation Challenging work, chances to develop and reach full potential Taylor: workers are motivated mainly by money, so pay them according to output (piece rate). Works for simple, measurable tasks but ignores social and esteem needs, and can lower quality as workers rush. Herzberg: hygiene factors (pay, conditions, supervision, job security) do not motivate, but if they are poor they cause dissatisfaction. Motivators (achievement, recognition, responsibility, interesting work, promotion) create real motivation. Fix hygiene factors first, then add motivators. Financial methods Method How it works Strength Weakness Wages (time rate) Paid per hour, usually weekly Easy to calculate; pay is secure No reward for working harder Salary Fixed annual amount, paid monthly Security; suits jobs where output is hard to measure No direct link to performance Piece rate Paid per unit produced Encourages speed; cost linked to output Quality may fall; no pay if machines break Commission % of value of sales made Motivates sales staff Pushy selling; unstable income Bonus Extra lump sum for meeting a target Rewards achievement Resentment if targets seem unfair Profit sharing Share of profit to all staff Workers share the business’s goals Small sums; no link to individual effort Fringe benefits Non-cash extras: car, health insurance, discounts Valued, help attract staff Costly; may be taken for granted Non-financial methods Job rotation: moving between tasks at the same level. Reduces boredom and creates flexible workers, but the tasks may be equally dull. Job enlargement: adding more tasks of a similar level to a job. Job enrichment: giving more challenging tasks and responsibility. Meets esteem and self-actualisation needs, but needs training and not everyone wants responsibility. Team working: groups take responsibility for a section of work. Meets social needs and can improve ideas and quality. Training and opportunities for promotion. Recognition and praise , such as employee of the month. Examiner Tip In a “which method” question, match the method to the workers in the case. Piece rate suits factory workers making identical items but not nurses or teachers; commission suits sales staff; job enrichment suits skilled, experienced staff who are bored rather than underpaid.

Organisational structure An organisational structure shows the levels of management and who reports to whom. It makes clear each person’s role, who they are accountable to and how communication flows, which supports delegation and accountability. Level of hierarchy: a level of management or employees with the same authority. Chain of command: the route through which instructions pass down the hierarchy. Span of control: the number of subordinates directly controlled by one manager. Tall structures have more levels and narrow spans of control; flat structures have fewer levels and wide spans. Tall structure (narrow span) Flat structure (wide span) Communication Slow; messages pass through many levels and can be distorted Faster and clearer between top and bottom Supervision Close supervision and control Less supervision; staff must be trusted and skilled Costs Many managers’ salaries Fewer managers, lower costs Motivation More promotion steps More delegation and responsibility, but fewer promotion chances and managers may be overloaded Delayering removes one or more levels of management, making the structure flatter. It saves salary costs and speeds up communication and decisions, but may cause redundancies, lower morale among remaining staff, and wider spans that managers struggle to supervise. The role of management P lanning O rganising C o-ordinating C ommanding C ontrolling Delegation is giving a subordinate the authority to carry out a task. It frees the manager’s time for important decisions and motivates staff through trust and responsibility, but the manager remains accountable and loses some control, and the task may be done less well if staff lack skills. Leadership styles Style Features Best when Drawback Autocratic Leader decides alone; one-way communication Quick decisions needed, emergencies, unskilled staff Demotivates skilled staff; no use of workers’ ideas Democratic Workers’ views sought; two-way communication; leader makes final decision Skilled, experienced staff; changes that need support Slower decisions Laissez-faire Workers make their own decisions within broad limits Creative, highly skilled, self-motivated teams Lack of direction and co-ordination Trade unions A trade union is a group of workers who join together to protect their interests, such as pay, working conditions and job security. Members gain collective bargaining power, legal advice and support if disciplined. Unions may take industrial action (overtime ban, go-slow, strike). For the business, a union gives one point of contact for negotiating with many workers, but strikes can stop production and raise costs.

The recruitment and selection process 1 Identify the vacancy A worker leaves, the business grows, or a new skill is needed. 2 Job analysis and job description The job description lists the title, duties, responsibilities and who the worker reports to. 3 Person specification The qualifications, experience, skills and qualities the ideal candidate should have, often split into essential and desirable. 4 Advertise the job Internally or externally (job websites, social media, recruitment agencies, newspapers). 5 Applications and shortlisting Application forms or CVs are compared with the person specification, and the best candidates are shortlisted. 6 Selection Interviews, tests (skills, aptitude, personality), references; the best candidate is offered the job and signs a contract. Internal recruitment External recruitment Advantages Cheaper and quicker; the candidate already knows the business; managers know their ability; motivates staff through promotion chances Wider choice of candidates; brings in new ideas and experience Disadvantages Small choice; no new ideas; creates another vacancy; may cause jealousy More expensive and slower; candidate is unknown; needs more induction Interviews let the business judge communication skills and personality and ask follow-up questions, but they take managers’ time, some candidates perform well in interviews but not in the job, and the interviewer may be biased towards people similar to themselves. Part-time and full-time workers Part-time staff give flexibility (cover busy periods such as weekends) and cost less, but may be less committed and harder to communicate with. Full-time staff are more committed and easier to manage but less flexible and more expensive. Training Type What it is Advantages Disadvantages Induction Introduces new staff to the business, its rules, layout and colleagues New staff settle quickly and become productive sooner Costs time; worker not yet productive On-the-job Learning by watching and working alongside an experienced worker Cheap; trainee produces while learning; specific to the job Bad habits passed on; trainer’s output falls Off-the-job Courses at a college or training centre, away from the workplace Expert trainers; wider skills; no disruption to production Expensive; staff may use new skills to get a better job elsewhere Reducing the size of the workforce Dismissal (being fired): because of the worker’s fault, such as misconduct or poor performance. Redundancy: the job is no longer needed (falling demand, new machinery, relocation, delayering). It is not the worker’s fault, so redundancy pay is usually given. Alternatives: natural wastage (not replacing workers who leave), early retirement, offering part-time contracts. Legal controls on employment Laws protect workers from unfair dismissal and discrimination (gender, race, religion, age, disability), set a minimum wage, limit working hours and require safe working conditions. They raise costs for businesses, but they also protect the firm’s reputation and help attract good workers.

Effective communication means the message is received and understood by the receiver, who gives feedback. Every communication has a sender, a medium, a receiver and feedback. Internal: within the business (manager to staff). External: with people outside (customers, suppliers, banks, government). One-way: no feedback expected (a notice). Two-way: the receiver responds (a meeting). Method Advantages Disadvantages Verbal (meetings, phone, video call) Quick; instant feedback; tone and body language help understanding No written record; long meetings waste time; details forgotten Written (email, letters, reports, notices) Permanent record; can be referred back to; detailed No immediate feedback; may be ignored or misunderstood; email overload Visual (charts, videos, posters) Makes data and instructions easy to understand May need explanation; not good for detailed or complex messages Barriers to communication and how to reduce them Jargon or language the receiver does not understand → use simple language and check understanding. Long chain of command distorts messages → flatter structure, direct messages. Wrong medium (complex instructions by phone) → choose written or visual methods for detail. Noise and distractions , or a receiver who does not trust the sender → quiet settings, build good relationships, ask for feedback. Quick Checklist I can explain why motivation matters using productivity and labour turnover. I can outline Maslow, Taylor and Herzberg and apply them to a workforce. I can choose and justify financial and non-financial methods for different workers. I can compare tall and flat structures and analyse the effects of delayering. I can compare autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire leadership. I can describe each stage of recruitment and selection, and compare internal and external recruitment. I can compare induction, on-the-job and off-the-job training. I can distinguish dismissal from redundancy and explain barriers to communication.

Topic 3 · 3.1–3.4 Marketing How businesses find out what customers want, segment their market, and use the four Ps (product, price, place, promotion) to sell to them, at home and abroad. Expect pricing-method and promotion questions in Paper 1 and “which marketing strategy” recommendations in Paper 2.

Marketing is identifying customers’ needs and wants and satisfying them profitably. Its roles: identify and anticipate customer needs, satisfy them, keep customer loyalty, build relationships, and gain information about the market. Why markets change Customers’ spending patterns change with income, fashion, technology and lifestyle (for example, growing demand for plant-based food). Competition grows, including from overseas firms and online sellers. Businesses respond by keeping close to customers (research), improving products and efficiency, and developing new products. Firms that do not adapt lose sales and market share. Niche and mass markets Niche market Mass market Meaning A small, specialised segment of a larger market A large market with similar products bought by most customers Example Handmade halal skincare; vintage cameras Bottled water; toothpaste Advantages Less competition; can charge higher prices; loyal customers; suits small firms Huge sales volume; economies of scale; spreads risk Disadvantages Small sales; no economies of scale; large firms may move in; vulnerable to change in one market Heavy competition; low prices; needs large-scale production and promotion Market segmentation A market segment is an identifiable sub-group of a market whose members share similar characteristics. Markets can be segmented by age, gender, income, location, lifestyle, use of the product or ethnicity/religion. Segmenting lets a firm target the right customers with the right product and promotion, so marketing spending is not wasted, and it can reveal gaps in the market.

Market research is gathering information about customers, competitors and market trends. It reduces the risk of launching a product nobody wants. Market-orientated businesses research customers first, then make what they want. Product-orientated businesses make a product they believe is good, then try to sell it (common for innovative or basic products). Primary (field) research Secondary (desk) research Meaning New data collected first-hand for a specific purpose Data that already exists, collected by someone else Methods Questionnaires (online, face-to-face), interviews, focus groups, observation, test marketing Government statistics, trade publications, newspapers, competitors’ websites and reports, internal sales records Advantages Up to date, relevant to exactly what the firm needs; competitors do not have it Cheap or free, quick to obtain, large data sets Disadvantages Expensive and time-consuming; risk of bias in sample or questions May be out of date, not exactly relevant, available to competitors Sampling: it is too costly to ask everyone, so a sample is chosen. A random sample gives everyone an equal chance of selection; a quota sample picks set numbers from each group (e.g. 30 women aged 18–25). A sample that is too small or unrepresentative gives misleading results. Accuracy of research depends on sample size and selection, question design (leading questions cause bias), honesty of respondents and how old the data is. Presenting data: tables, bar charts, pie charts and line graphs. Line graphs show trends over time; pie charts show shares of a total such as market share.

P roduct P rice P lace P romotion The four Ps must work together and fit the target market: a luxury product needs a high price, exclusive outlets and stylish promotion. Product A product can be a good or a service. Developing a new product: generate ideas → screen them → research and develop a prototype → test market → launch. New products can increase sales and market share and spread risk, but development is expensive and many new products fail. Brand image is the image or identity customers associate with a brand. A strong brand builds loyalty, makes the product recognisable and lets the firm charge a higher price. Packaging protects the product, gives information, makes it easy to use and attracts attention on the shelf. Product life cycle The product life cycle, with an extension strategy restarting growth in late maturity. Stage Sales and profit Typical marketing decisions Introduction Low sales; usually a loss as development and launch costs are high Heavy informative advertising; skimming or penetration price; limited outlets Growth Sales rise quickly; profit begins Persuasive advertising; more outlets; competitors start to appear Maturity / saturation Sales peak and level off; profit highest Competitive pricing; reminder advertising; consider extension strategies Decline Sales and profit fall Cut promotion; lower price to clear stock; withdraw product Extension strategies lengthen the life cycle: add new features or flavours, sell in new markets (export or new segments), change the packaging, or find new uses for the product. Price Method How it works Advantage Disadvantage Cost-plus Unit cost + a fixed % mark-up Simple; every sale covers its costs Ignores competitors’ prices and demand Competitive Price set at or near rivals’ prices Avoids losing customers on price May not cover costs; needs non-price competition Penetration Low price at launch to gain market share, raised later Attracts customers quickly; builds share Low profit per unit at first; customers may leave when price rises Price skimming High price for a new, unique or high-tech product, lowered later High profit early to recover development costs; prestige image Only works with few competitors; may attract rivals Promotional Short-term low price (sale, buy-one-get-one) Boosts sales; clears old stock Lower profit per item; can cheapen the brand Dynamic Price changes with demand, often online in real time Maximises revenue at peak times (e.g. ride-hailing, flights) Customers may feel unfairly treated Psychological Price chosen for its effect on perception, e.g. RM9.99 Product seems cheaper Little effect if overused Price elasticity of demand (PED) measures how much quantity demanded responds to a change in price. If demand is price elastic (many substitutes, luxuries), a price rise causes a large fall in sales and revenue falls, so the firm should keep prices low. If demand is price inelastic (necessities, strong brands, few substitutes), a price rise causes only a small fall in sales and revenue rises. Place (distribution) 1 Manufacturer → consumer Direct, including online and factory shops. Keeps all profit and control; good for customised or perishable goods. 2 Manufacturer → retailer → consumer Retailers reach many customers and handle display; manufacturer loses some profit and control. 3 Manufacturer → wholesaler → retailer → consumer The wholesaler buys in bulk and breaks it into small quantities for many small shops; useful for widely sold products but adds a mark-up at each stage. E-commerce (buying and selling online): the business reaches customers anywhere, 24 hours a day, with lower shop costs, but faces intense price competition, delivery costs, website costs and security risks. Customers gain convenience and easy price comparison but cannot see or try products and must wait for delivery. Promotion Aims: inform customers about a new product, persuade them to buy, remind them about an existing product, and build brand image. Advertising (paid communication through media): TV, radio, print, billboards, cinema and online. Informative advertising gives facts; persuasive advertising creates desire. Sales promotion : short-term incentives such as discounts, free samples, competitions, loyalty points and buy-one-get-one-free. Digital and social media marketing : targeted ads, influencers, email and search adverts. Cheaper and highly targeted; results can be measured; but negative comments spread fast. Sponsorship and public relations , personal selling and direct mail. The choice depends on the marketing budget , the target market, the stage in the product life cycle and what competitors are doing. Examiner Tip Always link the method to the target customers in the case. “Advertising on social media would suit a bubble-tea shop because its customers are mainly teenagers who spend time on TikTok and Instagram” scores; “social media reaches lots of people” barely does.

A marketing strategy is a plan combining the four Ps to achieve a marketing objective. A good strategy is based on research into the target market and fits the budget. A luxury watch brand would use high prices, exclusive retailers and glossy magazine adverts; a new budget snack would use penetration pricing, supermarkets and sales promotions. Legal controls on marketing Laws protect consumers against misleading descriptions and advertising, unsafe or faulty products, and unfair contracts. Businesses must make sure products match their description and are safe, which can raise costs but builds trust. Entering new foreign markets Opportunities: a much larger market, extra growth when the home market is saturated, spreading risk across countries. Problems: different languages, cultures and tastes; lack of local knowledge; different laws; import tariffs and transport costs; exchange-rate changes; strong local competitors. Methods of reducing the risks: a joint venture with a local firm (local knowledge), licensing a local firm to make the product, franchising, or selling through local agents and distributors. Quick Checklist I can compare niche and mass markets and explain the benefits of segmentation. I can compare primary and secondary research and explain what affects accuracy. I can draw and label the product life cycle and suggest extension strategies. I can choose a pricing method and justify it using the product and its competition. I can explain how PED affects revenue when price changes. I can compare channels of distribution and the impact of e-commerce. I can recommend promotion methods that fit the target market and budget. I can explain the problems of entering foreign markets and how to reduce them.

Topic 4 · 4.1–4.4 Operations Management How goods and services are produced efficiently, what it costs, how many units are needed to break even, how quality is kept high and where a business should locate. Break-even calculations and “job or batch or flow” questions are favourites.

Production is turning inputs (factors of production) into outputs (goods and services). Productivity measures how efficiently inputs are used: Formula Labour productivity = total output ÷ number of workers (in a given time) Ways to increase productivity: better training, more motivated staff, improved technology and automation, better organisation of the workplace. Higher productivity lowers the cost per unit, which can mean higher profit or lower prices. Inventory (stock) management Businesses hold inventory of raw materials, work-in-progress and finished goods. Holding buffer inventory means production and sales can continue if deliveries are late or demand suddenly rises. But inventory costs money: storage space, insurance, risk of theft, damage or going out of date, and cash tied up that could be used elsewhere. A business reorders when inventory falls to the reorder level , allowing for the lead time (days for delivery). Lean production Lean production aims to cut waste of all kinds (time, materials, inventory, movement, defects) to raise efficiency. Kaizen: continuous small improvements suggested by workers, often in team meetings. Cheap to introduce and motivating, but improvements are gradual. Just-in-time (JIT): materials arrive exactly when needed and finished goods are sent out immediately, so almost no inventory is held. This saves storage costs and frees cash, but needs very reliable suppliers: a late delivery stops production completely. Methods of production Method Meaning Example Advantages Disadvantages Job One product made at a time, often to a customer’s order Wedding dresses, custom furniture, bridges Unique, high-quality products; can charge high prices; motivating, skilled work High cost per unit; slow; skilled labour needed Batch A group of identical products made together, then the equipment is changed for the next batch Bread, clothing sizes, furniture ranges Some variety; lower unit cost than job; flexible to demand Equipment idle while changing batches; need storage for batches; more repetitive work Flow (mass) Continuous production of identical products on a production line Soft drinks, cars, smartphones Very low unit cost; huge output; economies of scale; often automated Very expensive set-up; boring work; little variety; a breakdown stops the whole line Examiner Tip The right method depends on the size of the market, demand for customisation and the money available. A small business with rising, steady demand often moves from job to batch, but must weigh the cost of new equipment and storage against the lower cost per unit. Technology in production Automation, robots, computer-aided design (CAD) and computer-aided manufacturing (CAM), electronic point-of-sale (EPOS) systems and contactless payments raise productivity and accuracy and lower unit costs. However, technology is expensive to buy, needs training, quickly goes out of date and may cause redundancies and lower morale.

h: 4.2 Costs, scale of production and break-even
x: Types of cost Fixed costs do not change with output in the short run: rent, salaries, insurance, loan interest. Variable costs change directly with output: raw materials, packaging, piece-rate wages. Total cost = fixed costs + total variable costs. Average cost (unit cost) = total cost ÷ output. Economies and diseconomies of scale Economies of scale are the factors that lower average cost as a business grows. Purchasing: bulk-buying discounts. Marketing: advertising costs spread over more units; can afford its own vehicles. Financial: banks lend more easily and at lower interest to large firms. Managerial: can employ specialist managers. Technical: can afford advanced, efficient machinery. Diseconomies of scale raise average cost when a business becomes too large: poor communication through many levels, low morale as workers feel unimportant, and weak co-ordination and slow decisions. Break-even The break-even point is the level of output at which total revenue equals total cost, so there is neither profit nor loss. Formulas Contribution per unit = selling price − variable cost per unit Break-even output = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit Margin of safety = actual (or planned) output − break-even output Worked example A phone-repair stall pays RM2,400 a month for rent and a worker’s wage. Each repair uses RM20 of parts and is sold for RM80. Contribution per repair = 80 − 20 = RM60 Break-even = 2,400 ÷ 60 = 40 repairs a month If it does 55 repairs: margin of safety = 55 − 40 = 15 repairs ; profit = 15 × RM60 = RM900 . Common Mistake Dividing fixed costs by the price instead of the contribution . 2,400 ÷ 80 = 30 repairs ignores the RM20 of parts each repair uses, so the business would actually make a loss at 30 repairs. Always subtract variable cost first. If the answer is not a whole number, round up (39.2 → 40 units), because 39 units would still be a loss. Break-even chart: below break-even output TC is above TR (loss); above it TR is above TC (profit). Uses of break-even: shows how many units must be sold to avoid a loss; shows the effect of changing price or costs; supports applications for loans. Limitations: assumes every unit made is sold, that price and variable cost stay the same at every output, and that fixed costs never change. It is only as accurate as the forecasts behind it. Changes to the break-even point: a higher price or lower variable cost raises contribution and lowers break-even; higher fixed costs (a new loan, bigger premises) raise break-even.

Quality means producing a good or service that meets customers’ expectations and is fit for purpose. Good quality builds reputation and loyalty, allows higher prices and cuts the cost of waste, repairs and returns. Poor quality leads to complaints, returns, lost sales and a damaged brand. Approach How it works Advantages Disadvantages Quality control Inspectors check finished products (or samples) and reject faulty ones Faulty goods are found before reaching customers; little staff training needed Waste is only found at the end, so materials and time are already lost; inspectors cost money Quality assurance Checks at every stage of production; agreed standards; workers check their own work Problems spotted earlier, so less waste; staff take responsibility Relies on workers following standards; training costs Total Quality Management (TQM) A culture where every worker aims for zero defects at every stage; each stage treats the next as its customer Very little waste; quality built in; high reputation Needs all staff to be committed and trained; costly and slow to introduce Customers also judge quality through customer service and after-sales service (repairs, warranties). Excellent service is a way to stand out from competitors, especially for small businesses that cannot compete on price.

Manufacturing business Service business (retail, cafés, banks) Near raw materials (especially bulky or perishable ones) Near the market if the product is bulky to transport Availability and cost of labour Transport links: ports, roads, rail Power and water supply Government grants and tax incentives Planning laws and environmental limits Near customers and passing trade (footfall) Near complementary businesses; away from too many competitors Cost of rent Availability of suitable staff Parking and public transport Security Technology: internet businesses can locate almost anywhere Choosing a country Firms may move production abroad ( relocation ) for lower wages and land costs, to be nearer new markets, to avoid import tariffs, or for government incentives. Risks include political instability, different laws, communication problems and damage to reputation if working conditions are poor. Legal controls on location Governments use planning permission to stop businesses locating in residential or protected areas, and may offer grants to attract firms to areas of high unemployment. Quick Checklist I can calculate labour productivity and explain ways to raise it. I can weigh up the benefits and costs of holding inventory, and explain JIT and kaizen. I can compare job, batch and flow production and recommend one for a business. I can classify fixed and variable costs and explain economies and diseconomies of scale. I can calculate contribution, break-even and margin of safety, and draw a break-even chart. I can compare quality control, quality assurance and TQM. I can explain location factors for manufacturing and service businesses.

Topic 5 · 5.1–5.5 Financial Information and Decisions Where businesses get money from, why cash is not the same as profit, and how to read an income statement, a statement of financial position and ratios. Calculations from this topic appear in nearly every paper, so practise the formulas until they are automatic.

Why businesses need finance Start-up capital: premises, equipment and first stock before any revenue arrives. Working capital: day-to-day costs such as wages, materials and bills. Expansion: new branches, machinery, research and development, buying other firms. Capital expenditure is spending on fixed assets that last more than a year (machinery, vehicles, buildings). Revenue expenditure is spending on day-to-day running costs (wages, rent, fuel). Sources of finance Source Type Advantages Disadvantages Owner’s savings Internal No interest; no loss of control Limited amount; owner risks their own money Retained profit Internal No interest or repayment; no loss of control Not available to new or loss-making firms; less for owners Sale of assets Internal Turns unused assets into cash; no interest Takes time; asset may be needed later; may sell cheaply Bank overdraft External, short-term Flexible: only pay interest on the amount used; quick to arrange High interest rates; bank can ask for repayment at any time Trade credit External, short-term Pay suppliers later (e.g. 30–60 days); no interest Lose discounts for early payment; suppliers may refuse if paid late Bank loan External, long-term Large sums; repayments planned; no loss of control Interest must be paid; may need collateral (security); fixed repayments even when sales are low Issue of shares External, long-term Large sums; never repaid; no interest Only for companies; dividends expected; owners lose some control; risk of takeover Leasing / hire purchase External Use of an asset without paying the full cost at once Costs more in total than buying outright Microfinance External Small loans for poor entrepreneurs who cannot get bank loans Small amounts; interest can be high Crowdfunding External Raises money from many people online; tests public interest Idea is public and can be copied; target may not be reached; platform fees Grants External Usually do not need to be repaid Conditions attached (e.g. location, jobs created); hard to get Choosing a source depends on: what the money is for (short-term needs → overdraft; long-term assets → loan or shares), the amount, the legal form of the business (only companies can sell shares), the owner’s wish to keep control, and existing debt (a firm that already owes a lot will struggle to borrow more and faces high interest). Examiner Tip Match the time period: never finance a new factory with an overdraft, and never fund a two-month cash gap with a ten-year loan. Saying why the timescale fits is an easy analysis mark.

h: 5.2 Cash flow forecasting and working capital
x: Cash flow is the movement of money into (inflows) and out of (outflows) a business. A business can be profitable yet still fail if it runs out of cash to pay wages and suppliers. Cash is needed to pay debts on time, keep suppliers’ trust and take opportunities. Cash flow forecast (RM) Jan Feb Mar Cash inflows (sales) 8,000 6,000 9,000 Cash outflows (wages, materials, rent) 7,000 8,500 7,500 Net cash flow (inflows − outflows) 1,000 (2,500) 1,500 Opening balance 500 1,500 (1,000) Closing balance (opening + net) 1,500 (1,000) 500 Each month’s closing balance becomes next month’s opening balance. The forecast shows a cash shortage in February, so the owner can arrange an overdraft in advance. Uses of a cash flow forecast Shows when the business will be short of cash so finance can be arranged early. Supports a loan application. Helps manage the timing of large payments. Solving a cash flow problem Method Drawback Arrange an overdraft or short-term loan Interest increases costs Ask customers to pay sooner / give less credit Customers may go to competitors who give credit Ask suppliers for longer credit Suppliers may refuse or withdraw discounts Delay or cancel capital spending Growth and efficiency may suffer Reduce inventory or sell unused assets May run short of stock; assets may sell cheaply Working capital Formula Working capital = current assets − current liabilities Working capital is the money available for day-to-day spending. Too little and the business cannot pay its bills; too much (for example, lots of unsold stock or cash sitting idle) means money is not being used productively.

Profit is total revenue minus total costs. It rewards the owners for risk, provides finance for reinvestment, and signals success to investors and lenders. Cash is not profit: a sale on credit counts as revenue now, but the cash arrives later. Income statement for the year (RM) Revenue (sales) 200,000 less Cost of sales (120,000) Gross profit 80,000 less Expenses (overheads: rent, salaries, advertising) (50,000) Profit (before tax) 30,000 less Tax (6,000) Profit after tax 24,000 Dividends to shareholders (10,000) Retained profit 14,000 Revenue = price × quantity sold. Cost of sales = opening inventory + purchases − closing inventory. Gross profit = revenue − cost of sales. Profit = gross profit − expenses. Users: managers (judge performance, set targets), shareholders (dividends, share value), banks (ability to repay), and potential investors.

Shows what a business owns (assets) and owes (liabilities) on a particular date. Non-current assets: kept for more than a year: buildings, machinery, vehicles. Current assets: held for less than a year: inventory, trade receivables (money owed by customers), cash. Current liabilities: debts due within a year: trade payables (money owed to suppliers), overdraft. Non-current liabilities: debts due after more than a year: long-term bank loans. Shareholders’ equity: share capital + retained earnings. The balance Total assets − total liabilities = shareholders’ equity

Ratio Formula What it shows Gross profit margin gross profit ÷ revenue × 100 How well the business controls the cost of making or buying its products. Higher is better. Profit margin profit ÷ revenue × 100 How well it controls all costs, including overheads. Higher is better. Return on capital employed (ROCE) profit ÷ capital employed × 100 How well the money invested in the business earns profit. Compare with interest rates and rivals. Current ratio current assets ÷ current liabilities Liquidity: can it pay short-term debts? About 1.5–2 is often seen as safe; below 1 is a warning. Acid test ratio (current assets − inventory) ÷ current liabilities Stricter liquidity test, because inventory may be hard to sell quickly. About 1 is often seen as safe. Worked example Using the income statement above: gross profit margin = 80,000 ÷ 200,000 × 100 = 40% ; profit margin = 30,000 ÷ 200,000 × 100 = 15% . If the gross margin is healthy but the profit margin falls year on year, overheads such as rent or salaries are rising faster than sales. How to improve: raise prices (if demand is inelastic), find cheaper suppliers, cut overheads, or sell more higher-margin products. To improve liquidity: sell off excess inventory, chase customers who owe money, or convert short-term debt into a long-term loan. Limitations of ratios: they are based on past data; one year alone means little, so compare with previous years and competitors; they ignore non-financial factors such as staff morale and reputation; and different firms may calculate figures differently. Common Mistake Confusing liquidity with profitability. A firm can have a high profit margin and still have a current ratio of 0.6, which means it may struggle to pay its suppliers next month. Quick Checklist I can distinguish capital and revenue expenditure, and internal and external finance. I can recommend a source of finance using purpose, amount, legal form, control and timescale. I can complete a cash flow forecast and suggest ways to solve a cash shortage. I can explain why profit and cash are different. I can calculate gross profit, profit and retained profit from an income statement. I can identify assets and liabilities on a statement of financial position. I can calculate and interpret the five ratios, and explain their limitations.

Topic 6 · 6.1–6.3 External Influences on Business Activity The things a business cannot control: the economy, government policy, the environment, ethics, globalisation and exchange rates. The key skill is explaining the chain from the outside change to the business’s revenue, costs and profit.

The business cycle Stage What happens Effect on businesses Growth (boom) GDP rising, unemployment falling, incomes rising Higher sales and profits; may struggle to recruit; costs and prices start to rise Slump / recession GDP falling (for six months or more), unemployment rising Lower sales, especially of luxuries; redundancies; some firms fail Recovery GDP starts to rise again Sales recover; firms start to invest and recruit Government economic objectives Economic growth : rising GDP means more jobs and higher incomes, so more demand for products. Low unemployment : more people with income to spend. Low and stable inflation : high inflation raises firms’ costs, makes planning hard, and makes exports less competitive. Balance of payments stability : exports and imports roughly in balance. Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the total value of goods and services produced in a country in a year. Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level. Unemployment is when people who are willing and able to work cannot find a job. Government policies and their effects Policy Change Likely effect on businesses Fiscal policy Higher income tax Consumers have less disposable income, so demand and sales fall, especially for luxuries. Higher indirect tax (sales tax) Prices rise or margins are squeezed; demand falls for price-elastic products. Higher corporation (profits) tax Less profit after tax to reinvest or pay as dividends; may discourage expansion. Higher import tariffs Imported materials cost more; but domestic firms face less foreign competition. More government spending More contracts for firms (e.g. construction) and more demand in the economy. Monetary policy Higher interest rates Loans and overdrafts cost more; consumers borrow and spend less (especially on cars and houses); expansion is postponed; the currency may rise, hurting exporters. Supply-side policy Training, privatisation, better infrastructure, deregulation Lower costs, more skilled workers and more efficient markets in the long run. Examiner Tip The effect depends on the product. When incomes fall, demand for luxury goods (jewellery, holidays, dining out) falls sharply, while demand for cheaper alternatives (own-brand groceries, budget airlines, second-hand goods) may actually rise because customers switch down from expensive brands. Always ask “what does this business sell, and who buys it?”

Externalities External costs: costs of business activity paid by third parties, not the business: air and water pollution, traffic congestion, noise, loss of habitats. External benefits: gains to third parties: new jobs, better roads built for a factory, training that workers take to other jobs. Sustainable development means meeting today’s needs without reducing the ability of future generations to meet theirs: using renewable energy, recycling, cutting waste and packaging. Pressure groups and government Pressure groups try to change business behaviour through boycotts, protests and social media campaigns. Bad publicity can cut sales quickly, so firms often respond. Governments can control harmful activity with laws (limits on emissions), taxes and fines on pollution, and permits to pollute that can be traded. Ethical decisions An ethical decision is based on moral principles, doing what is right rather than only what is profitable: not using child labour, paying suppliers fairly (fair trade), being honest in advertising, protecting the environment. Benefits of acting ethically Drawbacks Better reputation attracts customers (who may pay more) Easier to recruit and keep motivated staff Avoids fines, boycotts and pressure group campaigns Higher costs (fair wages, cleaner production, ethical suppliers) Lower profit, at least in the short run Higher prices may lose price-sensitive customers

Globalisation Globalisation is the increasing freedom of movement of goods, capital and people around the world. It is driven by free-trade agreements, cheaper transport and the internet. Opportunities: new markets abroad; cheaper materials and production; access to foreign skills and technology. Threats: more competition from foreign firms with lower costs; staff may be attracted to foreign firms. Governments may use protectionism (tariffs and import quotas) to shield domestic firms. This helps local producers but raises prices for consumers and for firms that use imported materials, and other countries may retaliate. Multinational companies (MNCs) A multinational has factories or service operations in more than one country. Benefits Drawbacks To the MNC Lower costs (wages, land); closer to markets so lower transport costs; avoids tariffs; spreads risk Communication and cultural problems; political risk; criticism over working conditions To the host country Jobs and training; tax revenue; investment and new technology; more exports Local firms may be forced out; profits sent back to the home country; can exploit workers and resources; may leave if costs rise Exchange rates An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another. When a currency appreciates it buys more foreign currency; when it depreciates it buys less. If the ringgit… Exporters (sell abroad) Importers (buy from abroad) Appreciates Their goods become more expensive abroad, so sales abroad fall Imported materials are cheaper, lowering costs Depreciates Goods become cheaper abroad, so sales abroad rise Imported materials are dearer, raising costs Memory aid SPICED : Strong Pound (currency) Imports Cheaper, Exports Dearer. Worked example A Malaysian furniture maker sells a table for RM900. At RM4.50 = US$1 it costs an American buyer 900 ÷ 4.50 = US$200 . If the ringgit appreciates to RM4.00 = US$1, the same table costs 900 ÷ 4.00 = US$225 , so American demand is likely to fall unless the firm cuts its ringgit price. Quick Checklist I can describe the stages of the business cycle and their effect on firms. I can explain the four government economic objectives. I can trace the effect of tax, interest rate and tariff changes on a business. I can explain why demand for some products rises when incomes fall. I can explain external costs and benefits, sustainability and pressure groups. I can weigh up the benefits and costs of ethical decisions. I can analyse globalisation, protectionism and MNCs from different viewpoints. I can calculate and explain the effect of exchange-rate changes on exporters and importers.

What Formula Revenue selling price × quantity sold Total cost fixed costs + (variable cost per unit × quantity) Average (unit) cost total cost ÷ output Profit total revenue − total cost Change in profit new profit − old profit (state whether it is a rise or a fall) Percentage change (new − old) ÷ old × 100 Added value selling price − cost of bought-in materials Price with mark-up (cost-plus) unit cost × (1 + mark-up %)

What Formula Contribution per unit selling price − variable cost per unit Break-even output fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit (round up to a whole unit) Margin of safety actual output − break-even output Profit (shortcut) margin of safety × contribution per unit Units needed to cover one extra cost the extra cost ÷ contribution per unit
What Formula Labour productivity output ÷ number of workers Market share firm’s sales ÷ total market sales × 100

What Formula Net cash flow cash inflows − cash outflows Closing balance opening balance + net cash flow Working capital current assets − current liabilities Cost of sales opening inventory + purchases − closing inventory Gross profit revenue − cost of sales Profit gross profit − expenses Retained profit profit after tax − dividends Shareholders’ equity total assets − total liabilities

Ratio Formula Answer as Gross profit margin gross profit ÷ revenue × 100 % Profit margin profit ÷ revenue × 100 % ROCE profit ÷ capital employed × 100 % Current ratio current assets ÷ current liabilities ratio, e.g. 1.8 or 1.8 : 1 Acid test ratio (current assets − inventory) ÷ current liabilities ratio
