Case (written for these notes) Siti is a sole trader in Penang. She designs and hand-draws batik silk scarves to customers’ orders (job production), working from a small rented studio and selling through Instagram. She borrowed RM8,000 from a bank to buy equipment and pays rent of RM600 a month. Demand has risen quickly since a celebrity wore one of her scarves, and Siti has set three objectives for next year: sell 250 scarves a month, keep at least RM5,000 in the bank for emergencies, and send every order within 5 days. Exam-style · [3 marks] Identify and explain one disadvantage to Siti of operating as a sole trader. Siti has unlimited liability . She has a RM8,000 bank loan and pays RM600 a month in rent, so if demand for her scarves falls after the celebrity effect fades, she may not be able to cover these payments. The bank could then take her personal possessions, such as her car or savings, to repay the business’s debts. Why this scores K: unlimited liability. App: the loan, rent and the celebrity-driven demand. An: personal assets taken to pay business debts. A common slip is to blame the production method (“job production is expensive”) for the debt: that may be true, but it is not why being a sole trader is a disadvantage. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Exam-style · [6 marks] Identify and explain two ways in which setting objectives could help make Siti’s business more successful. 1. Guides decisions. The objective of sending every order within 5 days tells Siti what she needs from her production method and suppliers. If hand-drawing means orders are taking 10 days, she knows she must change how she works, for example by hiring help or moving to batch production, before slow delivery leads to bad reviews on Instagram and lost customers. 2. Allows her to measure progress and spot problems early. Each month she can compare sales with the target of 250 scarves and check her bank balance against the RM5,000 safety level. If her cash falls towards RM5,000, she can cut spending or arrange an overdraft before she is unable to pay the RM600 rent, which reduces the risk of the business failing. Why this scores Each way has K (what objectives do), App (one of Siti’s specific objectives) and An (the consequence for her success). Do not write that objectives “motivate staff” here: Siti works alone, so it is not applied to the case. Written your own answer? Get it marked →

Case (written for these notes) Arjun left his job at a phone shop because he disliked being told what to do. He started FixIt, visiting customers’ homes and offices to repair phones and laptops, and promised “same-day fixes and friendly service”. He now wants to open a small shop in Johor Bahru and recruit one technician through interviews. Exam-style · [3 marks] Explain one reason Arjun had for starting his own business. Arjun wanted independence : he left his job because he disliked being told what to do. As the owner of FixIt, he makes all the decisions himself, such as which customers to visit and how to run the new shop, which gives him the control and job satisfaction he did not have as an employee. Why this scores A clear reason, evidence from the case, and an explanation of how owning a business meets that need. Only one reason is asked for, so do not spend time adding a second. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Exam-style · [3 marks] Explain one disadvantage to Arjun of using interviews to select his technician. Interviews only test how well candidates talk , not how well they repair devices. A candidate could interview confidently but lack the practical skill to fix phones on the same day, as FixIt promises. If Arjun chooses the wrong person, repairs may be slow or faulty, damaging FixIt’s reputation, and he would have to pay to recruit and train someone again. A practical repair test would be more reliable. Why this scores The disadvantage is applied to this specific job (a technician) and this business’s promise (same-day fixes). Interviewer bias and time taken are also valid, but must be linked to Arjun’s situation to earn the application mark. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Exam-style · [6 marks] Analyse one reason why Arjun chose to focus on excellent customer service. Excellent customer service gives FixIt a unique selling point over larger repair shops. Arjun travels to customers’ homes and offices, so they do not have to queue at a mall, and he offers same-day fixes with friendly service. This means customers who are busy at work are likely to choose FixIt even if its price is slightly higher than a shop’s. Satisfied customers are also likely to become loyal and come back the next time a device breaks. They will recommend FixIt to colleagues and leave positive online reviews, which is free promotion for a small business with little money for advertising. As a result, FixIt can build a steady base of repeat customers and revenue, which is what Arjun needs before opening the new shop in Johor Bahru, as the shop adds rent and a wage to his costs. Why this scores “Analyse” wants a developed chain: service → USP / loyalty → repeat sales and word of mouth → steady revenue to cover new costs. One reason is analysed in depth rather than listing several. Written your own answer? Get it marked →

Case (written for these notes) KL Scoot assembles electric scooters. Its factory has five levels of hierarchy: managing director → factory manager → 4 section managers → 16 team leaders → 240 production workers. Last year it switched to the cheapest parts supplier and cut staff training by half. Faults found at the factory rose from 12 to 45 per 1,000 scooters (industry average 10), and customer returns rose to 3.5% (industry average 1%). A new managing director proposes to delayer : remove all the section managers and half of the team leaders, so that 8 team leaders, each responsible for 30 workers, report directly to the factory manager. Exam-style · [12 marks] Analyse the benefits and drawbacks of delayering for KL Scoot. Recommend whether KL Scoot should delayer the factory’s structure. Justify your answer. Benefit: lower costs. Removing the section managers and 8 team leaders means KL Scoot no longer pays 12 management salaries. As returns of 3.5% are already adding repair costs, these savings could help restore profit, or be spent on better parts or the training that was cut. Benefit: faster communication. Information from the production line would pass through three levels instead of four before reaching the managing director. Workers who see faults first-hand could report problems such as poor-quality supplier parts quickly and with less distortion, so the managing director could act on the rise in faults from 12 to 45 per 1,000 sooner. Drawback: weaker supervision. Each team leader’s span of control would double from 15 to 30 workers. With training already halved, workers need more guidance, not less. Fewer checks could push faults even higher above the industry average of 10 per 1,000, increasing returns and damaging KL Scoot’s reputation further. Drawback: lower morale. Section managers and team leaders may be made redundant, and the remaining staff may fear for their own jobs. Demotivated workers take less care, so quality could fall further, and skilled workers may leave, raising recruitment and training costs. Recommendation. I recommend that KL Scoot does not delayer yet . Its most urgent problem is quality, and doubling team leaders’ spans of control reduces exactly the supervision that untrained workers need, so the cost savings could easily be wiped out by more faulty scooters and returns. The cost savings are real, but they are smaller than the cost of losing customers in a market where rivals have a return rate of just 1%. KL Scoot should first fix the causes of poor quality by restoring training and choosing a more reliable supplier, then remove the section-manager layer once fault rates are back near the industry average, keeping all 16 team leaders on the production line. This decision depends on how skilled the remaining team leaders and workers are: if they were experienced and well trained, delayering would carry much less risk. Why this scores Two benefits and two drawbacks, each applied with figures from the case and developed to a business outcome. The recommendation makes a clear decision, explains why the main drawback outweighs the main benefit for this firm now , offers a realistic alternative and states what the answer depends on. That is top-level evaluation. A conclusion such as “delayer because it is easier to communicate with fewer people” just repeats one advantage and would stay in a lower level. Written your own answer? Get it marked →

Model Answers · Topics 3–4 Model Answers: Marketing & Operations Exam-style questions on inventory, quality, suppliers and production methods, including a full 12-mark job-versus-batch recommendation. The cases continue from the People answers.

Exam-style · [4 marks] Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to a business of holding buffer inventory. Advantage: the business can keep producing and selling if a supplier’s delivery is late or demand suddenly rises. Customers’ orders are met straight from inventory, so sales are not lost to competitors. Disadvantage: inventory ties up cash that cannot be used elsewhere, for example to pay suppliers or invest. It also adds storage costs such as warehouse rent and insurance, and goods may become damaged or out of date before they are sold. Why this scores One mark for each point and one for each explanation. The disadvantage mentions cash tied up as well as storage cost: the opportunity cost of the cash is the point many students miss. Written your own answer? Get it marked →

Case reminder KL Scoot switched to the cheapest parts supplier and cut staff training by half. Faults found at the factory rose from 12 to 45 per 1,000 scooters (industry average 10); returns rose to 3.5% (industry average 1%); the average time to repair a returned scooter rose from 1 hour to 2.5 hours. Exam-style · [6 marks] Using the data, analyse the implications of poor quality for KL Scoot’s profits. Poor quality raises KL Scoot’s costs . Faults found at the factory have almost quadrupled, from 12 to 45 per 1,000 scooters, which is four and a half times the industry average. Every faulty scooter has to be repaired or scrapped before it can be sold, which uses extra labour and parts. Returned scooters now take 2.5 hours each to repair instead of 1 hour, so labour costs per return have more than doubled. Higher costs per scooter reduce profit on every sale. Poor quality also reduces revenue . A return rate of 3.5% is more than three times the 1% industry average, so customers are far more likely to have a bad experience with KL Scoot than with rivals. Unhappy customers post negative reviews and tell friends, damaging the brand’s reputation. Future sales are likely to fall, or KL Scoot may have to cut prices to keep customers. With costs rising and revenue falling, profit is squeezed from both sides, so the savings from the cheaper supplier are probably smaller than the losses caused by poor quality. Why this scores The data is interpreted (compared with the past and the industry average), not just copied out. Each point is followed to its effect on costs or revenue and then on profit. Listing the figures without saying what they mean would earn little more than application. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Exam-style · [6 marks] KL Scoot chose its new supplier because it was the cheapest. Identify and explain two other factors KL Scoot should consider when choosing a supplier. Factor 1: Quality of the parts. Faulty batteries or brakes from a supplier go straight into finished scooters. Since KL Scoot’s faults are now 45 per 1,000 against an industry average of 10, choosing a supplier with a record of high-quality parts would cut repairs and returns, protecting its reputation and profit even if each part costs more. Factor 2: Reliability of delivery. KL Scoot needs parts to arrive on time and in the right quantity, otherwise the production line stops and workers are paid while waiting. A reliable supplier means scooters are finished on schedule, so orders from shops are met and KL Scoot does not lose sales to competitors. Why this scores Two factors (K), each linked to KL Scoot’s situation (App) and developed to a consequence (An). Other valid factors: payment terms and credit offered, location and delivery cost, flexibility to change order size. Don’t write the same point twice in a second paragraph. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Exam-style · [6 marks] Identify and explain two problems for KL Scoot caused by reducing staff training by half. Problem 1: More errors in production. With less training, workers may not learn the correct way to fit new components or the quality standards each scooter must meet. They make more mistakes, which helps explain why faults have risen to 45 per 1,000 scooters, increasing repair costs and customer returns. Problem 2: Lower motivation and higher labour turnover. Workers may feel the business no longer values them or their development, and they lose chances to gain skills for promotion. Demotivated staff take less care, and some may leave for competitors that offer training. KL Scoot would then face higher recruitment costs and a less experienced workforce, making the quality problem worse. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Exam-style · [6 marks] Analyse how Total Quality Management (TQM) might improve the quality of KL Scoot’s output. TQM makes every worker responsible for quality at every stage , with the aim of zero defects. Instead of relying on checks at the end of the line, each worker treats the next stage as their customer and checks their own work before passing it on. A loose wire or badly fitted brake would be caught as soon as it happened, rather than after the scooter is finished. This should cut the 45 faults per 1,000 scooters, reducing wasted parts and repair time. TQM also uses quality circles : small groups of production workers who meet regularly to find the causes of problems and suggest improvements. Because they work on the line every day, they are best placed to spot, for example, that a batch of parts from the cheap supplier does not fit properly. Solving causes rather than symptoms means fewer faulty scooters reach customers, so the 3.5% return rate should fall towards the industry average, protecting KL Scoot’s reputation. However, TQM will only work if staff are trained and committed, which means KL Scoot would need to reverse its training cuts. Why this scores The answer explains how TQM works (K) and follows each feature through to the case data (App, An). Writing about unrelated changes in the case, such as delayering or the new managing director, would not answer the question. Written your own answer? Get it marked →

h: Siti’s Batik Studio: job or batch? [12]
x: Case (written for these notes) Siti hand-draws each batik scarf to order and currently sells about 75 a month, close to the most she can make by hand. She is considering switching to batch production : printing batches of 20 scarves of one design using silk screens, then changing the screens for the next design. She would need a RM12,000 loan for equipment (repayments RM400 a month) and a storeroom (RM300 a month). Her objectives are to sell 250 scarves a month and send every order within 5 days. Per month Job (now) Batch (planned) Maximum output 80 scarves 400 scarves Selling price RM45 RM35 Variable cost per scarf RM15 RM9 Fixed costs RM900 RM1,600 Exam-style · [12 marks] Analyse the advantages and disadvantages to Siti of switching from job to batch production. Recommend whether she should switch. Justify your answer. Advantage: much higher capacity and profit. Siti can make at most 80 scarves a month by hand, so she cannot meet her target of 250. With batch production she could make 400. Using the data, her best possible profit now is 80 × (45 − 15) − 900 = RM1,500 a month. If she sold 250 batch-printed scarves, profit would be 250 × (35 − 9) − 1,600 = RM4,900 a month, more than three times as much. Advantage: faster delivery. Printing 20 scarves at once is far quicker than drawing each one, so popular designs can be kept ready and sent the same day. This helps her meet the objective of sending every order within 5 days, which keeps online reviews positive while demand is high. Disadvantage: higher fixed costs and risk. Fixed costs rise from RM900 to RM1,600 because of the loan and storeroom. Her break-even rises from 900 ÷ 30 = 30 scarves to 1,600 ÷ 26 = 61.5, so 62 scarves a month. Demand rose because of one celebrity; if it fades, she still has to pay RM700 a month more, and as a sole trader with unlimited liability, her personal assets are at risk. Disadvantage: loss of uniqueness. Her scarves are currently hand-drawn and made to order, which is why customers pay RM45. Printed scarves in batches of 20 are less exclusive, which is why the price has to fall to RM35. Some loyal customers may feel the brand is no longer special, and she will compete with cheaper factory-made scarves. Unsold batches also take up storage and tie up cash. Recommendation. I recommend that Siti switches to batch production , because job production makes her main objective impossible: she can never sell 250 scarves a month if she can only make 80. Even allowing for the higher fixed costs, she only needs to sell 62 scarves to break even, fewer than she already sells by hand, so the risk of a loss is low and the potential profit is much higher. The loss of exclusivity matters less than the lost sales from customers waiting too long. To protect her brand, she could keep a small, premium hand-drawn range at RM45 alongside the printed range. This depends on demand staying above about 62 scarves a month after the celebrity effect fades, so she should start with a few designs and check sales before printing large batches. Why this scores The calculations are used as evidence inside the argument, not as an add-on. Every point is applied to Siti (her objectives, prices, unlimited liability, the celebrity effect). The recommendation compares the options directly, explains why the main disadvantage is outweighed, and states the condition it depends on. Note that batch production is not usually “more expensive”: fixed costs rise, but cost per unit falls. Written your own answer? Get it marked →

Case (written for these notes) BrewHaus is a coffee chain with 12 cafés in Kuala Lumpur, mostly near universities and offices. Sales have flattened as new competitors open nearby. The marketing manager has three ideas: (1) a loyalty app giving every 10th drink free, (2) a 20% price cut on all drinks for three months, (3) paying popular local food influencers to promote a new menu. Exam-style · [12 marks] Consider the advantages and disadvantages of each option. Recommend which BrewHaus should choose. Justify your answer. Loyalty app. Students and office workers buy coffee almost daily, so a free 10th drink gives them a reason to return to BrewHaus rather than trying a new competitor, building long-term loyalty. The app also collects data on what and when customers buy, helping target future promotions. However, it costs money to develop, and the free drinks reduce revenue; it mainly rewards existing customers rather than attracting new ones. 20% price cut. Students are price-sensitive, so a lower price could quickly win customers back from rivals and raise sales volume. But it cuts the profit on every drink, and if competitors cut prices too, BrewHaus gains no customers and simply earns less. When the price goes back up after three months, price-sensitive customers may leave again, and the cut may make the brand look cheap. Influencers. Influencers reach large numbers of young people in KL who match BrewHaus’s target market, and a recommendation from someone they follow can feel more trustworthy than an advert. It could attract new customers to try the new menu. However, results are uncertain and hard to measure, popular influencers are expensive, and the effect may last only as long as the posts are being seen. Recommendation. I recommend the loyalty app . BrewHaus’s problem is customers drifting to new competitors nearby, and its customers buy frequently, so rewarding repeat visits tackles the cause directly and keeps working long after launch. It reduces revenue far less than the price cut, which gives a 20% discount on every drink, including to customers who would have paid full price, and which can easily be copied. The influencer campaign might bring in new customers, but without a reason to return they may not stay. This depends on the app being easy to use; if few customers download it, a short influencer campaign promoting the app could be used alongside it. Why this scores Each option gets a balanced advantage and disadvantage, applied to BrewHaus’s customers and problem. The recommendation explains why the chosen option beats both alternatives, which is what lifts an answer into the top level. Written your own answer? Get it marked →

Model Answers · Topics 5–6 Model Answers: Finance & External Influences Calculation questions with full working, plus explain and analyse questions on the economy. The calculations show exactly the layout examiners want to see.

Exam-style · [2 marks] In her first month Siti sold 60 scarves at RM45 each. Materials cost RM15 per scarf and her fixed costs were RM900. Calculate her profit for the month. Show your working. Revenue = 60 × RM45 = RM2,700 Total cost = RM900 + (60 × RM15) = RM900 + RM900 = RM1,800 Profit = RM2,700 − RM1,800 = RM900 Why this scores Formula, working and answer with units. If one figure is mis-multiplied, the correct method still earns a mark. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Exam-style · [2 marks] KL Scoot’s revenue was RM52.0 million in 2024 and RM54.5 million in 2025. Total costs were RM48.4 million in 2024 and RM53.9 million in 2025. Calculate the change in profit between 2024 and 2025. Show your working. Profit 2024 = 52.0 − 48.4 = RM3.6 million Profit 2025 = 54.5 − 53.9 = RM0.6 million Change = 0.6 − 3.6 = −RM3.0 million (profit fell by RM3.0 million) Common Mistake Subtracting the wrong way round and writing “3.0 million” as if profit had risen. Change = new − old ; a negative answer means a fall, so show the minus sign or say “fell by”. Keep the units: “million” and the currency. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Exam-style · [2 marks] Arjun will pay his new technician RM700 a week. Each repair uses RM15 of parts and customers pay RM50 per repair. Calculate how many repairs a week are needed to cover the cost of employing the technician. Show your working. Contribution per repair = RM50 − RM15 = RM35 Repairs needed = RM700 ÷ RM35 = 20 repairs a week Common Mistake Dividing by the price: 700 ÷ 50 = 14 repairs. That ignores the RM15 of parts used in every repair, so 14 repairs would only bring in 14 × RM35 = RM490 towards the wage, leaving RM210 uncovered. Use contribution , and round up if the answer is not a whole number. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Exam-style · [4 marks] A business has current assets of RM45,000, of which RM25,000 is inventory, and current liabilities of RM30,000. Calculate the current ratio and the acid test ratio, and comment on its liquidity. Current ratio = 45,000 ÷ 30,000 = 1.5 Acid test ratio = (45,000 − 25,000) ÷ 30,000 = 20,000 ÷ 30,000 = 0.67 The current ratio looks acceptable, but the acid test ratio is well below 1. More than half of the current assets are inventory, so if the business cannot sell its inventory quickly it may struggle to pay its short-term debts on time. Written your own answer? Get it marked →

Exam-style · [2 marks] Explain why demand for some products might rise if consumers’ incomes fall. When incomes fall, consumers can no longer afford their usual, more expensive choices, so they switch to cheaper substitutes . For example, they buy supermarket own-brand rice instead of a premium brand, or take the bus instead of driving, so demand for these cheaper products rises even though people are poorer. Why this scores The key idea is switching from expensive products to cheaper alternatives, with an example. Saying that people “still need” cheap products only explains why demand doesn’t fall; it does not explain why it rises . Written your own answer?
